23174-a-good-for-nothing-1876:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published A Good for Nothing in 1876, a work of fiction centred on a boy named Ralph. The opening follows Ralph from babyhood into early childhood. His mother reads deep meaning into small habits, taking his thumb-sucking and quiet corner-sitting as signs of a poet's brooding mind.

By age five, Ralph has become the ruling force in his own home. Boyesen tells this with gentle irony, letting the mother's proud reading sit beside the plain facts of a spoiled small child. Readers get a wry portrait of family pride, early character, and how adults can build large hopes on very small evidence.
abridgement-of-elements-of-phrenology-18: Abridgement of Elements of Phrenology, 1876. The abridged elements. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
account-of-an-alchemical-roll-on-parchme: Account of an Alchemical Roll on Parchment, 1876. The Cromarty roll. This book preserves that account. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Volume V of the Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica appeared in 1876, the halfway point of Allen's ten. The symptoms of each remedy stand in strict anatomical order, a habit that lets a busy reader land on the right page fast. Sources are cited, so claims can be traced.

Some entries run for pages, proof of how often a drug was tested in that busy age of provings. Others stay brief. All of it feeds the same craft: choosing one remedy whose proved picture matches the sick person's signs. The volume keeps the archive's standard of full record over fine writing.
arxiv-2510-00076:
Xin Lyu wrote this 2025 theory paper on learning under a strict privacy rule. The setting is Littlestone classes, a standard family of tasks for online learning theory. The learner must keep each person's data private while still making few mistakes. Earlier private learners for this task paid a very high cost in extra errors.

Lyu gives a private online learner whose mistake bound improves on the old one doubly exponentially. The gain comes from a cleaner reading of a trick called irreducibility, plus careful use of a sparse selection method. The same ideas also improve the batch version of the learner, with the best possible dependence on target accuracy. The result comes close to the known lower bound for private learning here. It narrows a long-standing gap between private and ordinary online learning.
arxiv-2510-00176:
Alicia Middleton and fourteen colleagues published this 2025 instrumentation paper for the Simons Observatory in Chile. The observatory maps the cosmic microwave background with tens of thousands of superconducting detectors. Each detector module needs a routing wafer that carries bias lines and tiny shunt resistors. The team tested every wafer, more than seventy in all, before assembly.

Wafers were screened warm in the lab and again at a tenth of a degree above absolute zero. The average shunt resistance landed close to the design value of four hundred micro-ohms. Spread across all wafers was only about four percent of that value. Resistance dipped slightly toward each wafer's edge, a trend smaller than wafer-to-wafer differences. Warm factory data predicted the cold results well, which closed out screening for the observatory and its upgrade.
arxiv-2510-00476:
Arushi Sharma and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on opening the black box of language models trained on code. Such models power tools that demand trust, yet their internal concepts stay hidden. The team proposes Code Concept Analysis, which clusters token embeddings into human-readable concept groups. Static analysis tools and prompted language models jointly label the clusters at scale.

The framework tracks how concepts distribute across layers and shift under fine-tuning. Discovered concepts stayed stable when code was rewritten in meaning-preserving ways. Fine-tuning reshaped them predictably, sharpening syntax or spreading semantics across languages. A user study on programming-language classification showed concept-based explanations beat token-level attribution scores. Human judges found the token roles far clearer, with explainability up by thirty-seven percentage points. The authors release a labeled concept resource to ground future interpretability work.
arxiv-2510-00676:
Martinez and Zelazo present a formation control method for groups of moving agents in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such groups, from drone swarms to satellite fleets, must settle into a planned shape while each agent only talks to a few neighbors. Most methods fix distances or bearings between agents. Their approach instead uses only rotation symmetry constraints between neighbors.

A potential function built from those symmetries defines the control law that steers the agents. The authors prove that a spanning tree with just n minus one links, the fewest that keep a group connected, is enough to run the scheme. They then extend the design so the whole formation can travel, rotate, and scale along a planned path. Simulations, including a cube formation in three dimensions, confirm the method works as claimed.
arxiv-2510-01176:
Lee and seven co-authors at Meta present a real-time, audio-driven facial animation system at SIGGRAPH Asia 2025. Photorealistic 3D avatars could make virtual reality meetings feel face to face, but driving them from speech alone usually means slow offline processing. Their system encodes audio into latent facial expression sequences as the sound arrives, then decodes them into a photorealistic avatar. Generative diffusion modelling supplies the rich range of expressions that natural conversation needs.

Two design choices keep latency under fifteen milliseconds of GPU time per frame. An online transformer never waits for future audio, and a distillation pipeline compresses iterative denoising into a single step. The framework also accepts emotion conditions and gaze data from headset eye cameras. In experiments it beat offline state-of-the-art baselines on animation accuracy while running one hundred to one thousand times faster, and live VR demos confirmed the pipeline.
arxiv-2510-01376:
Pathrikar listens to how a quantum-corrected black hole rings and radiates, compared with its classical counterpart. The Frolov black hole replaces the crushing singularity with a regular core, courtesy of quantum gravity ideas. Perturbing it with light and matter waves produces characteristic quasinormal tones.

Standard approximation methods extract the dominant tone and its first overtone, plus the filtering factors for escaping radiation. Deviations from the classical charged black hole quantify the quantum corrections' fingerprints. An associated temperature estimate completes the emission picture. Ringing, in short, can audition candidate quantum black holes. Grey-body factors describe how the hole's gravity filters escaping waves. Sixth-order approximations, cross-checked higher, secure the numbers. Padé averaging steadies the approximation where plain series wobble. Electromagnetic and Dirac probes ring at different tones. Regular black holes are testable in principle, not just prettier.
arxiv-2510-01676:
Nasr and colleagues at Google and Google DeepMind wrote this 2025 security study of a live production system. The system is Gmail's malware detection pipeline, which scans files attached to mail. One model in the pipeline, Magika, identifies each file type and routes the file to a specialist checker. The authors ask whether fooling that one model can break the whole pipeline.

By changing just 13 bytes in a malware sample, the team fooled Magika in most test cases. Misrouted files then reached the wrong detector, which raised the chance of slipping through. The attack worked in nine out of ten cases they tried. The authors also built a defense and deployed it with Google engineers. Against the defended model, even a well-funded attacker needed 50 changed bytes for a far lower success rate.
arxiv-2510-01776:
Zayyani and three co-authors raise the data rate of noise-based communication in this 2025 letter. Noise modulation sends information inside random thermal noise, using almost no transmit power. A generalized quadratic modulator encodes bits in the mean and variance of that noise. The authors simply add the outputs of two such modulators together.

The combined signal forms a 16-ary modulator, much like quadrature amplitude modulation in classical radio. Bits now ride on four different means and four different variances at once. The authors give conditions that keep the sixteen states distinguishable at the receiver. With parameters chosen to meet those conditions, simulations beat both the single quadratic modulator and a Kirchhoff-law Johnson noise scheme. The gain is a smaller bit error probability, paid for with more complex hardware. Adding still more modulators could push the scheme to even higher orders.
arxiv-2510-01976:
Dobrinoiu and four co-authors ask whether annotation habits reveal how a person reads values in this 2025 paper. Value concepts mean different things to different people, shaped by culture and experience. AI systems that miss that subjectivity tilt toward majority viewpoints. The authors test whether a language model can predict one person's value interpretation from examples of their other judgments.

The examples cover four subjective dimensions: sentiment, emotion, argument, and topic annotations, shortened to SEAT. Across zero-shot and few-shot settings, giving the model all four dimensions at once worked best. Single dimensions helped less, and a no-information baseline trailed them all. Annotators also varied widely in how predictable they were. The study is small and controlled, but the authors say it is the first to use annotation behavior, rather than demographics, as the lens. It lays groundwork for larger validation of personalized value prediction.
arxiv-2510-02076:
He, Shuryak, Wu, and Zahed build light pentaquark states on the light front in this 2025 particle physics paper. Pentaquarks hide five quarks inside one hadron, and their spectra test how confinement really works. Light-front dynamics suits partonic questions, but constructing clean states there is tricky. The authors place the states on a regular four-simplex geometry.

Their explicit basis diagonalizes the Hamiltonian for light pentaquarks with confinement built in. The resulting eigenstates are free of center-of-mass motion and satisfy exact boundary conditions. Hyperfine interactions, in color-spin or flavor-spin form, lift the degeneracy among the sixteen states. The split spectrum compares fairly with some empirical excited nucleon states. The authors also discuss the quark probability distributions inside these states. A tidy basis like this turns pentaquark spectroscopy into systematic computation. It connects the constituent quark picture with the partonic language experiments actually probe.
arxiv-2510-02176:
Williams, Cleeves, Gross, and Baker chase the missing sulfur in planet-forming disks in this 2025 astrochemistry paper. Sulfur is essential to life, yet gas in protoplanetary disks shows strikingly little of it. The element must hide in forms that telescopes barely register. The team updated a two-dimensional, time-dependent disk chemistry model with new sulfur species and hundreds of new reactions.

They varied the volatile sulfur supply, the carbon-to-oxygen ratio, the starting molecular form, and the cosmic-ray rate. The most abundant sulfur carriers included CS, SO, and the ices of sulfur dioxide and carbonyl sulfide. Gas-phase sulfur abundances swung strongly with the carbon-to-oxygen ratio. Model columns were checked against values derived from disk observations. Much of the sulfur evidently locks into ices and less visible reservoirs. Knowing its hiding places matters for tracing sulfur from clouds into planets, and eventually into biology.
arxiv-2510-02276:
Li and co-authors present BioX-Bridge, a cheaper way to move knowledge between body signal types. Their 2025 health machine learning paper starts from a simple fact. Signals like heart and brain traces reflect one connected body. A model trained on one signal type often cannot help with another. Labeled data for the new type is scarce. Classic transfer runs a big teacher model beside the student. That pairing costs heavy compute and memory. BioX-Bridge instead learns a small bridge between two frozen models.

The bridge uses prototypes to link the two representation spaces. A two-stage search picks the best layers to connect. Tests spanned several biosignal datasets and tasks. Performance matched or beat leading transfer methods. The bridge needed far fewer trainable parameters to do it. Clinics with modest hardware could adapt models this way. Scarce labels stop being a hard wall.
arxiv-2510-02476:
Li and co-authors pick ensemble members by trusting a model own uncertainty estimates. Their 2025 paper studies biomolecule efficacy prediction with tabular foundation models. The test task predicts how well siRNA molecules silence their targets. TabPFN, an in-context learner, beat specialized predictors on the task. It used only straightforward sequence based features. Performance, though, swings with the context examples provided. Ensembling models trained on different subsets can stabilize results. The question is which members deserve a seat. Their method, OligoICP, reads each model predicted spread. Models with the lowest mean uncertainty join the ensemble.

Uncertainty and true error correlated negatively in their tests. Confident models really did err less on this task. The chosen ensemble beat naive averaging clearly. It also beat one model trained on all data. Labels are unavailable when tuning real deployments. A label free selection rule is therefore valuable.
arxiv-2510-02876:
Hassan and co-authors grade eggs without cracking them open. Egg grade and freshness shape food safety and price. Checking them the usual way means breaking eggs for lab tests. That wastes product and slows packing lines. The team's framework, ELMF4EggQ, judges eggs from the outside only. It uses a photo plus the egg's shape and weight. The study also built a small public data set for the task.

The set holds 186 brown-shelled eggs. Experts labeled each egg by lab measures like yolk index and Haugh unit. Deep networks pulled features from the photos. Classic classifiers then voted as an ensemble on the fused features. The combined approach beat photo-only and table-only models by clear margins. Grade calls reached a strong accuracy level, while freshness proved harder. The authors still see real promise for packing plants. The method is cheap, fast, and gentle on the product.
arxiv-2510-02976:
Paz and co-authors control a heavy skid-steered platform in real time. Such machines turn by skidding their wheels against the ground. Precise path tracking, though, is hard under shifting loads and terrain. The team built a nonlinear predictive controller for the job. It looks ahead along the path and plans each move. A multiple-shooting method shapes that planning step.

Careful buffer handling keeps the solver from wasting cycles. Warm starts and a capped step count bound the run time. Each control update thus lands within a fixed, known window. The controller matched the pace of its fastest sensor. Tests on three path shapes showed sharp gains. Position and speed errors fell far below prior published results. Those gains came on a full-size, heavy-duty machine, not a toy. Safe, exact motion matters most where such platforms work near people.
arxiv-2510-03376:
Ghosh, writing from Siemens in Germany, presents a 2025 arXiv paper on checking object detection inside industrial plant diagrams. Piping and instrumentation diagrams guide how plants are built, run, and repaired. Turning them into digital twins starts with spotting every symbol and tag correctly. Detection software has grown strong, yet few tools grade its output without slow human review. The paper uses a visual language model as an automated judge instead.

The judge scans detector output for missing symbols and clashing labels. It also checks tag text tied to symbols and judges how well boxes hug their targets. Local close up passes then hunt for objects the first pass missed. Automating these checks cuts the review load on engineers sharply. It also enables workflows that adapt when diagrams arrive in varied styles. Plants gain a faster path from paper drawings to living digital models.
arxiv-2510-03476:
Bakić, Horawa, Li-Huerta, and Sweeting present a 2025 arXiv paper that proves a twenty five year old number theory conjecture in its first cases. Gross proposed in 2000 that certain coefficients of quaternionic modular forms hide special values of L-functions for cubic twists. The forms live on the exceptional group G2 and echo a classic pattern found by Waldspurger for quadratic twists. That older pattern even fed into progress on the congruent number problem. Until now, no cases of the cubic version were known.

The team proves the conjecture when the underlying modular forms are dihedral. Their proof gives the first examples where the predicted link between coefficients and L-values holds in full. The result opens a door: methods that settle the dihedral case may extend to wider families. Arithmetic geometers gain a new bridge between automorphic forms and the values that govern deep questions about numbers and curves.
arxiv-2510-03776:
Almeida and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how robots predict where nearby people and machines will move. The team studies agents with different roles and motion patterns, such as pedestrians, cyclists, and workers. Their question is whether using class labels for each agent makes forecasts more accurate. They focus on small and uneven datasets, a common problem for a robot in a new place.

The authors compare pattern-based methods with deep learning methods on two datasets, one from robotics and one filmed outdoors by drone. Class labels improved accuracy in most settings for every method they tested. Deep learning worked best when training data was balanced and plentiful. Pattern-based methods did better when data was scarce or some classes were rare. The results help builders choose a prediction method that fits the data they actually have.
arxiv-2510-03976:
Onah and Gutiérrez-Vega wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on equilateral triangular waveguides. A waveguide channels electromagnetic waves along a hollow tube, and the triangle is a rare shape with exactly buildable wave patterns. Instead of solving Maxwell's equations head-on, solutions come from superposing plane waves that obey the boundary conditions. Earlier masters, including Lamé and Schwinger, used that trick for this shape.

The authors push further into two practical properties: attenuation, meaning how fast signals weaken, and the quality factor of each mode. They derive fully analytic, closed-form expressions for both, which the literature previously lacked for this waveguide. Number theory, through the Eisenstein integers, gives them a rigorous ordering of the allowed eigenvalues. Their attenuation curves match known results and show sharp turning points unlike those of elliptic waveguides. The work completes a classical problem with exact formulas engineers can use.
arxiv-2510-04076:
Vahidi-Moghaddam and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv survey on making data-driven control policies fast enough for real machines. Model predictive control is safe and but needs an accurate model, which complex systems rarely provide. Data-driven alternatives learn from interaction or raw input-output data, and language model agents now draft control formulations from instructions. These methods share a weakness: heavy computation and memory that strain onboard hardware.

The paper organizes the landscape across model predictive control, its learning-based variants, reinforcement learning, and data-enabled predictive control. It then details eight efficiency strategies, including reduced-order modeling, function approximators, and convex approximations. For data-enabled control, combining singular value reductions with a neural approach looked especially promising. The authors sketch hybrid designs that balance data-driven adaptability against model-based reliability. The survey gives practitioners a roadmap for deploying optimal control under real-time limits.
arxiv-2510-04376:
Abdulrahman Tamim wrote this 2025 paper on a new way to think about how neural networks learn. Most accounts treat training as a walk downhill on a loss surface, guided by gradients. Tamim instead treats learning as a map between network settings and learned features. He uses category theory, a branch of math on structure and maps. The key question is whether two training paths can be bent into each other smoothly.

Tests on image tasks gave a clear pattern. Networks trained along paths that bend into each other scored within half a percent of each other. Networks on paths that do not bend together differed by more than three percent. A shape tool also picked out stable spots that predicted good test scores. The paper argues that these shared structures explain why very different training runs can end up working the same way. It also offers tools for transfer learning.
arxiv-2510-04476:
Tomas Figliolia and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making attention in large models cheaper. Attention lets each token in a sequence look at every other token, which is powerful but costly. Its memory cache also grows with sequence length, so long contexts get expensive fast. Earlier fixes shrank the cache but left the main compute cost mostly untouched. The team moved the whole attention step into a smaller shared space.

Their method, called compressed convolutional attention, projects queries, keys, and values down before the attention math runs. A grouped variant adds head sharing on top for even tighter savings. In tests, the grouped version beat rival methods at equal cache size on dense and mixture models. It reached eightfold cache compression with no quality drop against standard attention. Training and first pass generation also ran much faster on modern graphics hardware.
arxiv-2510-04676:
Qiyu Wei, Haowei Wang, Richard Allmendinger, and Mauricio Álvarez wrote this 2025 paper on finding optima faster when tests are expensive. Bayesian optimization steers costly experiments with a statistical stand in model. Versions treat every past trial as equally useful for the search. The authors argue that some trials matter far more than others. Their method scores each past sample by counterfactual credit. The score asks how the search would have gone without that sample.

That credit feeds into the rule that picks the next trial point. Budget then flows toward regions where good trials proved the optimum likely hides. The team proved the method keeps a sublinear regret guarantee over time. On synthetic and real benchmarks, it reached the global optimum sooner than rivals. Simple regret, the gap to the best value, also fell faster. The idea suits tuning and design tasks where each run costs real time or money.
arxiv-2510-04776:
Ebenezer Awotoro and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a platform that unifies data on membrane proteins. Membrane proteins stud cell surfaces and are targets of over half of modern drugs. Their structures fill several databases that disagree, drop fields, and block computing. The team built MetaMP, a web framework that merges those sources into one place. Machine learning inside the platform enriches and checks the metadata.

Eight interactive views let users explore structures without wrestling files. Built in tools classify structures and flag outliers for review. The authors demonstrate three uses of AI on the platform. It predicts which segments cross the membrane. It reconciles legacy databases against each other. And it classifies structures with explanations a human can inspect. In validation, MetaMP settled seventy seven percent of data conflicts. It named the class of new proteins correctly ninety eight percent of the time, beating expert curation.
arxiv-2510-04976:
A. Koujok and six co-authors demonstrate a new kind of signal filter in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their device mixes two technologies that process waves instead of electric charge. One part, a nano-oscillator, produces a broad and messy microwave signal. The other part is a magnonic circuit that carries spin waves.

The team feeds the messy signal into the magnonic circuit. By adjusting only a magnetic field on that circuit, they pick out one narrow frequency band. The output is a clean spin-wave signal with a far narrower linewidth. Turning the field retunes the chosen frequency at will. The result points toward compact, low-energy filters for future wave-based computing.
arxiv-2510-05076:
Praise Adeyemo, Dominic Bunnett, and Fabián Levicán study how to embed weighted projective spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper. A projective variety can be placed inside ordinary projective space using powers of an ample line bundle. Small powers may fail to give a clean embedding. Geometers ask for the smallest power that works and also yields projective normality.

Weighted projective spaces correspond to simple polytopes called rectangular simplices. The authors give several criteria, based on arithmetic properties of the weights, for bounding the needed power. Their bounds are sharp in many cases. They also build combinatorial tools that construct families showing extreme behavior. The results extend earlier work by Payne, Hering, and Bruns and Gubeladze.
arxiv-2510-05476:
Wang and colleagues rethink how supercomputer programs talk across machines. The standard tool, MPI, lets programs on separate nodes exchange data through network links. Those links rely on complex software stacks built for Ethernet and similar hardware. Their 2025 paper, cMPI, routes the same exchanges through shared memory instead.

The shared memory uses CXL, a newer link that lets processors treat pooled memory like their own. Both one-sided and two-sided MPI exchanges run through the shared memory pool. The team built cMPI on a real CXL platform and solved problems with data layout and cache consistency. The study was presented at the SC25 supercomputing conference. For small messages, the new route cut latency sharply compared with network paths. Gains reached dozens of times on some latency and bandwidth tests. The work opens a path for CXL inside high-performance computing systems.
arxiv-2510-05576:
Daryanoosh adapts a quantum optimization algorithm to systems with many states per site. Qubit hardware speaks binary, but bosons and other systems live in larger local spaces. Mapping those spaces onto qubits leaves an infeasible region that pollutes calculations. His 2025 paper removes the pollution by design rather than by penalty.

The trick is choosing mixing Hamiltonians that never leave the feasible subspace. He compares binary, symmetric, and unary encodings under this lens. For symmetric mapping, the standard bit-flip mixer proves optimal by gate count. The other encodings pay a cost that grows with the number of QAOA layers. Penalty terms remain the common alternative, but they waste search effort as dimensions grow. He then finds ground states of the repulsive Bose-Hubbard model. The method works in both strong and weak interaction regimes. The framework also covers quantum approximate thermalization tasks.
arxiv-2510-05676:
Vandervorst and colleagues bring gradient boosting to graph data for fraud detection. Boosted trees dominate tabular learning, while neural networks own graph learning. Fraud, though, lives in relationships between people, claims, and accounts. Their 2025 G-GBM method grows trees that read graph neighborhoods directly.

The method concatenates feature vectors along simple paths inside each node's egonet. A case-weight adaptation lets the boosting machinery use those graph features soundly. On simulated random graphs, G-GBM competes with popular graph neural networks. It also Pareto-dominates plain gradient boosting in their experiments. Real insurance datasets, open and proprietary, confirm the fraud-detection power. The estimator stays consistent with intrinsic-feature-only learning by construction. Organized fraud rings are exactly what relationship-aware models should catch. Inductive learning lets it score new nodes without retraining everything. Standard tree explainability tools then reveal what drives each prediction.
arxiv-2510-05776:
Selstø and Dalen reformulate a photoelectron spectroscopy method for autonomous systems. Their PESCADO method reads photoelectron spectra from absorption on a small numerical domain. Earlier versions required simulating long after the laser pulse ended. Their 2025 semi-analytical version extrapolates to infinite time instead.

The team demonstrates energy- and angle-resolved spectra for hydrogen. Well-converged distributions emerge even under hard truncation of the domain. Two features explain the robustness of the approach. The method accommodates the Coulomb potential's long range unusually well. Waves absorbed at different times also interfere coherently in momentum space. Placing the absorber extremely close to the atom distorts angular patterns, like a real nearby detector. That detector analogy links the method to quantum arrival-time studies. In position space the aggregation stays incoherent for a local absorber.
arxiv-2510-05876:
Choudhury and Mahajan formalize proof systems for quantified Boolean formula solvers. QCDCL is a leading approach to deciding quantified Boolean formulas. Cube learning lets solvers verify true formulas, not just refute false ones. Their 2025 paper adds dependency schemes at every stage of the process.

Dependency schemes detect spurious dependencies implied by quantifier order alone. The authors state sufficient conditions for soundness and completeness. Two standard schemes provably shorten refutations when decision order relaxes. Their relative strengths receive detailed analysis in the level-ordered setting. Surprisingly, schemes do not always help under level-ordered decisions, even with cube learning. The hardness traces mainly to the level-ordered nature of decisions. Equality formulas showcase the exponential gaps in resolution-based systems. Known exponential separations from resolution systems fail to transfer automatically. Solver design gains a clearer map of when schemes pay off.
arxiv-2510-05976:
Adhikarla and colleagues survey diffusion models for low-light image brightening. Poor light hurts surveillance, driving, and medical imaging exactly where trust matters. Diffusion models restore such images by step-wise denoising of learned patterns. Their 2025 survey weighs them against GAN and transformer methods.

A six-part taxonomy sorts over thirty recent methods. The parts span decomposition, spectral-latent, accelerated, guided, multimodal, and autonomous approaches. Benchmark gaps and failure modes get direct study. A speed-quality trade-off governs the whole results landscape. The field is shifting toward steerable, task-aware brightening. Deployment limits like memory and energy are treated as first-class concerns. Foundation models are flagged as the rising path for the field. Brightening errors can mislead safety-related downstream choices, raising ethical stakes. Clarity and transfer trade against run-time speed throughout. Real-time tuning remains an open research question.
arxiv-2510-06276:
Rabiee and three co-authors improve epilepsy lesion segmentation in brain MRI with a new loss in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Focal cortical dysplasia causes drug-resistant epilepsy, yet its lesions are tiny and subtle. Accurate 3D segmentation guides the surgery that can cure such patients.

The framework uses a transformer-enhanced encoder–decoder for multimodal 3D scans. Its novelty is a loss combining Dice with an anisotropic total variation term. That term encourages smoothness and anatomical consistency, cutting false positive clusters without post-processing. On a public dataset of eighty-five patients, the model beat standard losses clearly. Dice improved about twelve percent and precision about thirteen percent over baseline. False positive clusters fell by more than sixty percent. Cleaner lesion maps let surgeons plan resections from trustworthy boundaries.
arxiv-2510-06476:
Gadde and three co-authors build an optimized support vector regression framework for electric load forecasting in a 2025 power systems paper. Load forecasting challenges grid operators as systems grow more complex. Extreme weather and shifting demand increasingly cause conventional forecasts to fail. Errors propagate into planning and resource allocation.

Their model was benchmarked against the industry standard forecaster. The model proved more accurate across every operationally important metric. It cut mean squared error by over half. Mean absolute error improved by roughly a third. Gains held across the remaining reported metrics. The framework serves as an additional accuracy-checking tool for operators. Integrated with existing tools, it validates plans before operators commit resources. The improvements matter most during stressed periods, when operators must allocate resources under time pressure. For utilities facing extreme-weather demand swings, a stronger forecaster insures against costly misallocation.
arxiv-2510-06576:
Meng-Sen Ma, Yun He, Xiao-Ming Wang, and Huai-Fan Li study the thermodynamics of an unusual black hole. Their 2025 paper examines the regular Bardeen black hole placed in anti-de Sitter space. It is built from a singular parent black hole by adding one extra constraint. That constraint removes the central singularity.

Removing the singularity comes at a price. The standard first law of black hole thermodynamics breaks down. The parent black hole shows a reentrant phase transition, similar to rotating black holes. The regular one shows pressure-volume behavior like a charged black hole, yet its free energy looks different. The familiar swallow-tail shape vanishes, replaced by an eight-shaped or c-shaped curve. Those shapes signal first-order or zeroth-order transitions between small and large black holes. The study warns that small changes to a black hole model can alter its phase behavior.
arxiv-2510-06776:
Phillip Rothenbeck, Sai Vemuri, Niklas Penzel, and Joachim Denzler reconstruct how COVID-19 spread across Germany. Their 2025 paper applies physics-informed neural networks to the SIR epidemic model. The model splits people into susceptible, infectious, and recovered groups. Fitting it to noisy real case data is the hard part.

They use infection records from the Robert Koch Institute covering twelve hundred days. The networks infer transmission and recovery rates for each federal state. From those rates, they estimate how the reproduction number changed over time. Transmission behavior varied strongly from state to state. Higher vaccination uptake in a state tracked with lower estimated transmission rates. Peak reproduction numbers showed the same regional link to vaccination. Balancing the data loss against the physics loss proved crucial for training. State-level weights needed different settings than national fits. The study shows how machine learning can audit epidemic policy after the fact.
arxiv-2510-06876:
Samir Haidar and four co-authors build a fast network for labeling LiDAR scans. Their 2025 paper serves self-driving cars and mobile robots, which must parse laser scans in real time. Older accurate methods are slow, while fast projection methods throw away 3D shape detail. Test-time tricks slow things further, which embedded hardware cannot afford.

Their network, HARP-NeXt, fuses two views of the same scan at several scales. It merges the range image with the 3D points, keeping fine detail and context together. A redesigned preprocessing step cuts overhead before the network starts. A feature block squeezes out the patterns with cheap convolutions. On the nuScenes and SemanticKITTI benchmarks, the model matched the PTv3 system. It ran twenty-four times faster than that rival. It needed no ensembles or test-time augmentation to get. The design shows speed and accuracy can stop being a trade-off.
arxiv-2510-06976:
Ustin Yanikov, Vasily Kulikov, and Andrey Shirokov speed up calculations of how charged particles scatter off nuclei. Their 2025 paper applies the Efros method, expanded in oscillator functions, to Coulomb scattering. Nuclear reaction theory needs phase shifts and cross sections for such collisions. The full HORSE formalism computes them accurately but at heavy cost.

Their version trims that cost sharply while keeping the accuracy. Wave functions are expanded in a series of harmonic oscillator functions. Only a small number of short-range functions proved necessary in their tests. Model problems with known exact answers confirmed the agreement. A narrower resonance case, proton scattering on nitrogen-15, also behaved well. The method slots into the no-core shell model workflows that nuclear theorists already use. Cheaper scattering calculations open the door to more ab initio reaction studies. Those studies matter for astrophysics, where charged-particle reactions drive stellar burning.
arxiv-2510-07076:
Paul Zivich leads a team urging epidemiologists to widen their error bars when they estimate several effects at once. Their 2025 paper concerns confidence regions for multiple parameters. A standard confidence interval covers one parameter reliably. Used for several parameters at once, the set understates the true uncertainty from random error.

The fix is confidence bands, which extend intervals to whole vectors of parameters. Bands promise simultaneous coverage of every parameter in the set. The authors illustrate the method with three case studies on public data. One estimates several causal effects together. The others handle effect modification by a binary trait and by a continuous one. Worked code in SAS, R, and Python accompanies each example. The authors stress a judgment call at the start. Analysts should decide whether interest lies in one parameter or a set. That choice, not habit, should dictate the reported region.
arxiv-2510-07276:
Rustagi, Wray, and Saisubramanian rework multi-agent path finding for teams that care about several goals at once. Their 2025 paper addresses robots or vehicles sharing one space without collisions. Older methods compute the whole frontier of trade-offs between objectives. That frontier explodes as objectives multiply, and it ignores which goal the user ranks first. The authors instead build the user's priority order directly into the problem. Their algorithm, LCBS, returns one plan that respects that order.

LCBS pairs a priority-aware shortest-path search with conflict-based search between agents. It never builds the costly trade-off frontier. The team proves optimality and studies how the method scales. On standard and randomized benchmarks, LCBS beat leading baselines in success rate. It handled up to ten objectives, far beyond prior methods. Warehouse and traffic planners with clear priority rankings could adopt the approach directly.
arxiv-2510-07376:
Jones and co-authors measure how black hole mass relates to galaxy mass in the early universe. Their 2025 paper uses seventy broad-line active galaxies seen when the universe was a fraction of its present age. The James Webb telescope found many such objects with seemingly oversized black holes. About forty-three percent of the sample are the mysterious compact sources nicknamed little red dots. Black hole masses come from emission line widths, while galaxy masses combine image profile fits with full spectrum modeling.

Fifty of the seventy systems show black-hole-to-galaxy ratios ten to a hundred times the local norm. A careful Bayesian model accounting for selection effects still places the early relation well above the local one. The scatter around the relation is large and stays constant across the sampled era. Little red dots dominate the sample at the highest redshifts.
arxiv-2510-07476:
Capistrano, Gutierrez-Pineres, and Coimbra-Araujo study the shadow of a rotating black hole embedded in a five-dimensional world. Their 2025 paper extends the Kerr solution, general relativity's spinning black hole, through a classic line element that adds an embedding in flat higher-dimensional space. In this view the hole behaves like a charged object in five dimensions. An extrinsic curvature term from the embedding bends the effective gravitational field.

In the limit where the embedding fades, the shadow and its brightness pattern match telescope observations of the M87 galaxy's core. Away from that limit, the model predicts measurable deviations in shadow shape and visibility amplitude. Future higher-resolution imaging could therefore test whether our black holes are secretly higher-dimensional embeddings.
arxiv-2510-07676:
Li, Wang, and Wang wrote this 2025 paper on the accuracy of a sampling method used in statistics and physics. Langevin Monte Carlo draws samples from complex probability distributions. A random splitting variant reduces the method's first-order bias with little extra work. Until now, its sampling error lacked a theoretical account. The authors build that account under the Wasserstein distance, a way to compare distributions.

They first pin down a sharp local error using entropy methods and explicit semigroup formulas. They then prove the method settles geometrically fast toward its steady distribution. Combining both pieces gives an error bound that holds uniformly over time. The method's steady measure approximates the true target with second-order accuracy in the step size. Numerical experiments back up the theory. The results tell users how small a step they need for trustworthy sampling in Bayesian work and molecular simulation.
arxiv-2510-08076:
Hong, Liu, and six coauthors wrote this 2025 photonics paper proposing a beam splitter built on topological surface waves that travel one way only. Conventional splitters suffer backscattering, narrow bandwidth, and ratios that drift with frequency. Their device routes unidirectional surface magnetoplasmons through gyromagnetic waveguides. Mode coupling at the ports sets the split. Because the waves cannot turn back, obstacles barely disturb them.

The splitter held its ratio steady within one percent across nearly the whole operating band, at any chosen ratio. Transmission stayed near total, without backscattering. Changing the external magnetic field slides the operating band while the robustness survives. That tunability fixes a long-standing weakness of topological designs. The authors target integrated photonic circuits and reconfigurable microwave systems. A splitter ignoring fabrication flaws and frequency drift could simplify both.
arxiv-2510-08176:
Mancini, Serrà, Torroni, and Mitsufuji wrote this 2025 paper introducing WEALY, a reproducible pipeline that matches songs by their lyrics using only the audio. Lyrics matching serves copyright protection, music discovery, and songwriting tools. Text is often unavailable or restricted, so matching from sound is attractive. Prior audio methods suffered from poor reproducibility. WEALY takes embeddings from the Whisper speech model's decoder, straight from raw audio, with no transcription step. A contrastively trained transformer shapes them for retrieval.

Experiments put WEALY on par with state-of-the-art methods that cannot be reproduced. It consistently beat transcription-based pipelines and scaled to large collections. Whisper's latent multilingual properties preserved cross-language cues useful for matching. Fusing WEALY's distances with audio-content models improved version identification further, showing the cues complement each other. The authors stress the benchmark role: a transparent, repeatable baseline lets the field measure progress honestly.
arxiv-2510-08576:
Justus Flerlage, Alexander Acker, and Odej Kao compare language models that turn user intentions into machine actions in a 2025 arXiv paper. Interfaces are shifting from clicking through graphical menus to stating goals in natural language. A model then orchestrates steps across applications on the user's behalf. Most current systems depend on cloud-based proprietary models, raising privacy and autonomy concerns.

The study examines open-source and open-access models that can run locally as intent resolvers. Their workflow generation for varied user intentions is benchmarked against GPT-4-based systems sold by OpenAI. Local deployment is framed not as convenience but as an imperative for trusted language-first interfaces. Results give empirical insight into how practical open models already are for this role. The authors position the work toward future intent-based operating systems. Privacy, autonomy, and scalability all hinge on that local capability.
arxiv-2510-08776:
Basu, Kolari, and Yu test how language models answer moral questions across languages, in this 2025 arXiv study. People now use these models in many countries, yet most safety checks run in English. The team posed questions to leading commercial and open models in both widely spoken and less served languages. Each answer was graded on a five-point scale across five dimensions, with another model acting as judge.

One model, GPT-5, earned the best average score in every category the team used. Other models swung much more between languages and topics. The widest gaps appeared in consent and autonomy and in harm prevention and safety. There, the lowest-scoring model averaged under two points where the leader scored well above three and close to five. The authors say such swings show why safety testing must cover language shifts directly.
arxiv-2510-08976:
Li and co-authors speed up image search that matches parts of a picture rather than the whole, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Retrieval systems increasingly split each image into segments and each query into sub-queries, then match the pieces. That multi-vector approach is accurate but wasteful: objects appear at wildly different sizes, and many fine segments repeat each other. Their framework, HiMIR, schedules the matching work in a hierarchy.

Images are represented at several middle levels of detail, so each query piece meets objects at a scale that fits it. A consistency check across levels, plus the natural sparseness of the hierarchy, prunes matching steps that cannot change the answer.  In experiments, accuracy rose substantially over the existing multi-vector system. Computation fell at the same time, by as much as three and a half times in the best case.
arxiv-2510-09176:
Kato and Mitsuka automate the delicate tuning that keeps Japan's record-breaking particle collider fed with beam, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The SuperKEKB collider smashes electrons and positrons to mass-produce exotic particles, and holds the world record for collision rate. That rate depends on injection efficiency, the share of each fresh beam pulse that settles into the storage rings. Operators used to tune injection by hand, leaning on experience as settings grew tangled.

Their tool hands the search to Bayesian optimization, a machine learning method that learns from each trial where to try next. Injection behaves like a black box no simulation reproduces, which suits the method's trial-and-learn style. In test operations during late 2024, it raised injection efficiency by up to about a third. The authors present it as a step toward record performance without exhausting operators.
arxiv-2510-09276:
Montalcini and Rousseeuw redesign Tukey's classic boxplot so it can reveal data that clusters around two values instead of one, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A boxplot compresses a batch of numbers into a box and whiskers, a fine summary when values bunch together. When the data are bimodal, with two humps, the box hides the split and the subgroups behind it. Their bixplot first clusters the values along the number line, then draws a display for each cluster.

The clustering behaves: clusters stay contiguous, never interleaving, and each holds at least a set minimum of distinct values. On top of the boxes, the display plots the individual data points, which draws the eye to isolated stragglers. Implementations in Python and R come with many options, demonstrated on real datasets. One option shades the display by an external variable, using color gradations to hint at what distinguishes the subgroups.
arxiv-2510-09376:
Adnan Ghribi describes an open-source pipeline for keeping a review article alive in a 2025 arXiv paper. The topic is artificial intelligence and machine learning in accelerator physics, the science of particle accelerators. Printed reviews freeze a fast-moving field at one moment, so Ghribi built a system that keeps gathering and sorting new papers on its own.

The pipeline harvests publications from six bibliographic sources, removes duplicates, and filters them for both accelerator and machine learning relevance using sentence embeddings. It then sorts the survivors into thematic categories shaped by expert input. About twelve thousand raw papers a month shrink to a focused corpus of roughly two percent. The curated set is exported in several formats, including web and bibliography files, forming the basis for a community-driven review that can keep evolving.
arxiv-2510-09676:
Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Ben Liang, and En-Hui Yang propose a new sampling method for inverse problems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Inverse problems ask us to rebuild a signal, unknown at the start, from noisy or incomplete measurements, as in medical imaging and remote sensing. Diffusion models serve as powerful priors for such recovery, but existing posterior sampling either forces measurement consistency with heuristic updates or approximates the likelihood, causing artefacts and instability in heavy noise.

Their framework, C-DPS, runs a forward stochastic process through the measurement space, in parallel with the usual data-space diffusion. The coupling yields a closed-form posterior that conditions each step on both spaces at once. Sampling then proceeds recursively from a well-defined distribution, with no constraint tuning and no likelihood approximation. Across several benchmarks, C-DPS consistently beat existing baselines in visual quality and quantitative scores.
arxiv-2510-09776:
Yufa Zhou, Yixiao Wang, Surbhi Goel, and Anru Zhang prove limits on transformers as forecasters in a 2025 arXiv paper. Time series forecasting resists machine learning's usual tricks, and even powerful transformers often fail to beat simple linear models at it. A rigorous explanation of that failure has been missing, and this paper supplies one through the theory of in-context learning.

Under autoregressive data of a standard form, they establish three results about linear self-attention. First, it cannot beat classical linear models in expected squared error for in-context forecasting. Second, as context length grows without bound, it recovers the optimal linear predictor exactly. Third, under chain-of-thought style inference, its predictions collapse exponentially fast toward the plain mean. Carefully designed experiments validate the theory. The authors offer practical guidance for building forecasting architectures and urge scrutiny before applying ever fancier models.
arxiv-2510-10076:
Nilomber Roy, M. M. B. Sheraj, and M. K. Hassan study percolation on growing networks in this 2025 arXiv paper in statistical physics. Percolation asks when scattered connections suddenly link a network into one giant cluster. The authors use mediation-driven attachment networks, which grow by mediation-driven rules between nodes, and a choice-based bond process.

In the generalized Achlioptas process, several candidate bonds are drawn, and the one that least grows the largest cluster is chosen, the best-of-M rule. The paper examines how that choice and the network's topology jointly shape the transition. Delaying the giant cluster changes how abrupt the takeover is. The results speak to controlling connectivity in networks that grow by attachment.
arxiv-2510-10276:
Salvatore, Hao Wang, and Qiong Zhang explain the lost-in-the-middle effect in this 2025 arXiv paper on language models. Models often use facts placed at the start or end of a long context well, but miss the same facts buried in the middle. The pattern mirrors primacy and recency effects in human memory.

The authors argue the effect is an emergent property of information retrieval demands placed on the models. When a model must find one fact among many similar ones, position biases arise from how retrieval itself works. Framing the quirk as emergent, rather than a simple defect, changes what fixes are plausible. Their account links a famous failure mode to the retrieval task models are implicitly asked to perform.
arxiv-2510-10376:
Florian and co-authors report a lensed galaxy nucleus caught changing type in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. The James Webb Space Telescope has built samples of obscured, type II active galactic nuclei at cosmic noon, the peak era of galaxy growth. Comparisons with unobscured type I nuclei support an evolutionary link between the classes.

Strong gravitational lensing magnifies this one system, letting the team watch an active nucleus passing from type II to type I. Mergers are thought to disturb galaxies and trigger such changes by clearing obscuring material. A transition caught in the act tests that story directly. Lensing makes the rare, brief phase bright enough to study in detail.
arxiv-2510-10676:
Mukul Lokhande and seven co-authors co-design a translation system and the hardware it runs on, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, Bhasha-Rupantarika, translates between Indian and international languages and targets resource limited settings. The team tests deployment at very low numerical precision, down to four bit formats. At that level the model shrank by a factor of 4.1 and inference ran 4.2 times faster, reaching 66 tokens per second.

They deployed the system on FPGA accelerators, the reconfigurable chips common in embedded devices. The design cut lookup table use by a factor of 1.96 and flip flop use by 1.65 compared with a reference design, and it raised throughput several fold over two prior accelerators. The evaluation covers both translation directions in low resource language pairs. Code and data are public. The authors present the work as a viable recipe for deployable multilingual AI on small devices.
arxiv-2510-10876:
Shutong Lin and three co-authors attack the long tail problem in LiDAR perception with synthetic data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Real world point cloud datasets drive progress in tasks like segmenting objects for autonomous driving. But some object classes appear rarely, so models learn them poorly. The team's dataset, RareBoost3D, is a synthetic point cloud collection that supplies many more instances of the classes that real datasets lack.

Synthetic data only helps if models can transfer what they learn to real scans. The authors therefore propose a cross domain semantic alignment method, the CSC loss. It aligns the feature representations of the same class across the synthetic and real domains. In experiments, this alignment significantly improved LiDAR segmentation performance on real world data. The work treats synthetic data as a complement to real datasets, not a replacement.
arxiv-2510-10976:
Wentao Wang and ten co-authors teach video models to reason about space and time precisely, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multimodal language models understand video semantics well but stumble on exact spatial and temporal questions: where objects are, how they move, how scenes are laid out. Existing methods focus on the video alone and ignore physical structure. The team's Video-STR method attacks this with graph based reinforcement learning.

The model is trained to infer a scene's spatio temporal structure as a relation graph while it thinks. Training uses a graph based variant of group relative policy optimization with verifiable rewards. Data was the other bottleneck, so the team built STV-205k, with 205,000 question answer pairs covering dynamic multi object scenes indoors and outdoors. Video-STR reached state of the art results on several benchmarks, beating its base model by 13 percent on STI-Bench in the reported experiments.
arxiv-2510-11076:
Lingyue Fu and seven co-authors build an AI teaching assistant that debugs student code the way a good tutor does, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In programming classes, students bring broken code, an error message, and a problem statement, while the teacher also holds a reference solution. Models facing all these inputs at once often reason poorly. DebugTA instead acts as an agent with specialized tools: one retrieves the standard code, another aligns it with the student's code by substituting variables, and an external compiler analyzes the code live.

Guided by explicit teaching and debugging principles, the agent splits the job into sequential steps, each with its own tool. Aligning the reference code closely lets the model focus on genuine logic errors. To judge suggestion quality, the team built a student simulator that interacts with the teacher agent. On three real world datasets, DebugTA improved teaching effectiveness while cutting costs.
arxiv-2510-11676:
Chuan He and Zhaosong Lu study optimization when the data guiding the search is noisy in a nasty way. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats convex problems, where the goal function has no deceptive local dips. The noise is heavy-tailed, meaning rare huge errors occur often enough to wreck naive methods. Common fixes clip or rescale the noisy gradient estimates. The authors ask whether such fixes are really needed.

Their answer is no. A plain accelerated stochastic method, with no clipping or normalization added, reaches optimal speed for this problem class. They prove that its cost, measured in calls to the noisy oracle, is universally optimal. The proof covers smooth, weakly smooth, and nonsmooth objectives in one framework. Computer experiments back the theory. The result simplifies practice: careful acceleration, not noise surgery, is what restores the best possible rate.
arxiv-2510-12176:
Matthew T. Darby, Muhammad Saleh, Marialore Sulpizi, and Clotilde S. Cucinotta model a platinum electrode's skin atom by atom. Platinum step edges rule fuel-cell chemistry, yet their behavior at voltage was murky. Their 2025 arXiv paper runs ab initio molecular dynamics at set voltages on a stepped platinum-water surface with realistic edges.

The split of labor surprises. Capacitance near the potential of zero charge comes almost entirely from voltage-driven water chemisorption on the flat terraces, not the famed edges. Step edges arrive pre-soaked with chemisorbed water even below that point, so they add nothing to capacitance changes. Instead, edges hoard excess positive charge and a locally raised electrostatic potential, discouraging electron build-up. Their higher d-band centers and sharper density of states fit the picture of edges as active, positively charged centers. The results explain why the zero-charge potential shifts with step density.
arxiv-2510-12476:
Gao and a large team show that text detectors trained to spot machine writing can fail badly when the writing imitates a personal style, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Language models can now mimic an individual's voice, raising impersonation risks. No earlier work had tested detectors on personalized machine generated text. The authors built StyloBench, a benchmark pairing literary and blog texts with model generated imitations.

Across detectors they found large performance gaps in personalized settings, with some leading models dropping a lot. They attribute this to a feature inversion trap. Cues that reliably signal machine text in general domains flip meaning in personalized text and mislead the detector. Their StyloCheck method predicts these failures by finding the latent directions tied to inverted features and building probe datasets that vary mainly along them. StyloCheck predicted both the direction and size of performance changes, correlating strongly with the actual gaps observed.
arxiv-2511-00376:
Nitin Kumar, Nicholas Jerla, John Ponis, Sarbajit Banerjee, and G Sambandamurthy study a layered crystal with a mouthful of a name, beta sodium vanadium oxide, prized for switching its electrical resistance. They track how charge order, a patterned arrangement of electrons, shows up in transport and in low-frequency resistance noise as the crystal cools through two transitions.

Above the transitions, noise behavior points to electrons hopping between near neighbors. Below the sodium-ordering transition, sodium ions settle into a zig-zag pattern that reshapes the electronic state. Below the charge-ordering transition, noise drops sharply, a sign of correlated electron motion. A strong electric field can break the ordered state and flip the crystal into a conducting state, with switching across a wide cold range driven by electronics, not heating. Stable, quiet states hint at uses in cryogenic memory.
arxiv-2511-00476:
Ghazal Kalhor and Afra Mashhadi test whether large language models remember scholarship fairly. As these models move into search and discovery tools, they increasingly answer questions about who worked with whom. The authors ask three prominent models to reconstruct coauthor lists for researchers, then compare the output against bibliographic reference data across disciplines and world regions.

A systematic pattern emerged: highly cited researchers were recalled far better, so memorization favors scholars who are already visible. The tilt was not uniform, though. Clinical medicine and parts of Africa showed more balanced reconstruction than the global trend. The findings warn that discovery tools built on model memory can quietly amplify existing inequalities, and they argue for careful auditing of memorization-driven bias before such systems are trusted.
arxiv-2511-00676:
Easton Huch, Fred Feinberg, and Walter Dempsey build a Bayesian approach for causal effects that leans on randomization itself for strength. Instead of modeling how outcomes arise in a whole population, they fix the observed potential outcomes. The likelihood is built from the randomization distribution of a statistic, the distribution created by the experiment's own assignment lottery. A treatment effect model is still needed, but marginal outcome distributions often are not.

The weaker assumptions buy provable strength: a Bernstein-von Mises theorem and large-sample behavior for posterior means are proved. The posterior mean matches classical Hodges-Lehmann estimators in the large-sample limit, bridging to weighted estimators of the inverse-probability and Hájek kinds. Posterior randomization tests allow model checking in the same language. A nutrition case finds strong effect variation that moderation checks had missed.
arxiv-2511-01176:
Wenqing Zhu and colleagues test how well large language models detect code clones, duplicated code fragments that maintenance tools need to find. Earlier studies reported strong results, but left open whether performance holds across data sets and whether the models answer the same question the same way twice.

They built seven clone data sets from the CodeNet and BigCloneBench collections, sampling code pairs by their text similarity, and evaluated five language models under four published prompts. Models did well on CodeNet derived sets, with one reaching a high F1 score, but performance fell greatly on BigCloneBench derived sets. Consistency was a bright spot: over ninety percent of judgments stayed the same across repeated submissions, and score fluctuations from inconsistency were tiny.
arxiv-2511-01276:
Yiyao Ma, Kai Chen, Kexin Zheng, and Qi Dou generate dexterous robot grasps by transfer. A multi fingered hand must grasp stably and adapt to the task, yet analytical methods are slow and generative methods, trained on limited data, generalize poorly to new objects and tasks.

Their idea is to transfer a high quality grasp from a shape template to a new object in the same category. That is reformulated as generating the object's contact map. A conditional diffusion model does the work, seeing shape similarity and task requirements. A dual mapping mechanism handles complex shape differences, and two extra maps encode contact parts and directions for stability. A cascaded diffusion framework transfers all three maps consistently, and a recovery step picks reliable contact points and optimizes the final grasp.
arxiv-2511-20376:
Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller recover hidden cliques from messy random graphs. Their 2025 paper studies random intersection graphs, a network model. Many cliques of roughly size k are planted at random. Each vertex joins each clique independently with some probability. Vertices can belong to polynomially many cliques at once. That overlap defeats simple and even spectral methods.

The authors give the first efficient recovery algorithms here. Both exact and approximate recovery are achieved. The methods tolerate noise and monotone adversaries. They even survive an optimal number of corrupted edges. Recovery works once cliques exceed roughly the square root threshold. The proofs-to-algorithms route runs through sum-of-squares optimization. Certificates must prove no large clique hides outside the truth. Modified biclique certificates supply that ingredient. A sharp concentration property keeps false positives away. The same ideas certify that the recovered clustering is optimal.
arxiv-2511-20576:
Lin, Anand, and Brown cut the measurement rounds quantum error correction needs. Their 2025 paper introduces local single-shot checks for toric codes. Syndrome measurements detect errors but are themselves noisy. Standard schemes repeat them many times per decoding round. That repetition costs heavy time overhead in fault-tolerant machines.

Single-shot correction uses one round, but usually needs heavy checks. Heavy checks wreck circuit-level performance in practice. The new checks cap their weight by acting on small lattice patches. A dynamic measurement scheme rotates which checks run when. Required rounds shrink by a factor tied to patch size. Simulations used sliding-window decoding under circuit-level noise. Local checks beat conventional ones at reduced window sizes. Fixed-width checks preserve the effective circuit distance with bare qubits. Variable-width checks won under phenomenological noise instead, with higher thresholds.
arxiv-2511-20776:
Hiroyuki Yamase and colleagues build in 2025 a strong-coupling theory of plasmons, collective charge oscillations, in bilayer materials like the cuprate superconductors. A bilayer supports two plasmon modes where a single layer has one, and earlier work described them only in the weak-coupling regime, ignoring the fierce electron correlations that define cuprates. The team's t-J-V model, with no double occupancy and a long-range Coulomb term, treats them head-on.

The two modes survive, resembling their weak-coupling counterparts. One twist: particle-hole excitations are noticeably suppressed, so the plasmon modes stay sharp across a wider range of momenta. Superconductivity in these materials emerges near 5 percent hole doping and peaks around 16 percent. The authors propose that plasmon signals in yttrium-based cuprates correspond to the lower of the two modes, and call for experiments to test the claim.
arxiv-2511-21076:
Aaditya L. Kachhadiya introduces in 2025 the Deceptron, a learned module that helps solve physics inverse problems, where the unknown input must be recovered from measured output. Such problems are ill-conditioned: plain gradient steps crawl and depend touchily on step size. The Deceptron learns a local inverse of a forward model. Training adds a supervised fit, forward-reverse consistency, and a Jacobian composition penalty. That penalty pushes the product of the two Jacobians toward the identity.

At solve time, its D-IPG algorithm steps downhill in output space, pulls the step back through the learned inverse, and projects, under the same safeguards as baselines. On recovering the initial condition of a one-dimensional heat problem, it hit the target tolerance in about 20 times fewer iterations than projected gradient. A damped oscillator problem needed 2 to 3 times fewer, rivalling Gauss-Newton in cost. A 2D variant, DeceptronNet, previews image-space corrections.
arxiv-2511-21176:
Retractions were once rare embarrassments; lately they arrive by the ten thousand as paper mills and sloppy work flood journals. Zhengyi Zhou, Ying Lou, Zhesi Shen, and Menghui Li study global retractions in 2025 through a topic lens, asking which subjects, not just which fields, carry the problem. They assign topics to roughly 46,000 of some 55,000 retracted papers and pair them with Web of Science publication counts from 2000 to 2024. A relative retraction rate then compares each topic against the global background.

Retracted papers grew from 140 in 2000 to over 11,000 by 2022, far outpacing overall publication growth from 785,000 to about 2.8 million papers a year. The year 2023 set a record with over 14,000 retraction notices. Electrical engineering and computer science alone account for more than 9,700 retractions, about 31 per 10,000 papers. Some low-rate fields hide badly hit topics, and some topics show suspicious publication surges alongside high retraction rates, flags the authors offer for targeted integrity checks.
arxiv-2511-21276:
Sutirtha Biswas and Kshitij Kumar Yadav blend physical law with deep learning to predict how buildings shake in earthquakes, in 2025. The standard finite element method is accurate but too slow for large-scale or real-time seismic analysis. Purely data-driven networks are fast, yet they often fail on new shaking patterns because nothing forces them to respect mechanics.

Biswas and Yadav propose PhyULSTM, a physics-informed network marrying a U-Net, which reads patterns across scales, with LSTM layers that track sequences over time. Governing physical laws are written into the training loss, curbing overfitting and improving generalization when data are scarce. The model beats earlier seismic predictors such as PhyCNN on the authors' tests. It can even run without explicit physical constraints, extending it to structures whose material behavior is only partly known.
arxiv-2511-21376:
Lukas Pin, Stef Baas, Gianmarco Caruso, David Robertson, and Sofía Villar bring system to a guesswork corner of clinical trial design in 2025. Response-adaptive randomization shifts enrollment toward treatments that look better as results accumulate, benefiting patients. Trials first need a burn-in, an opening phase of plain equal randomization that stabilizes estimates; 88 percent of such trials use one. Picking its length, though, has been improvised, with no guideline.

Pin and his coauthors build the first systematic framework for that choice. Their formula blends total sample size, problem difficulty, and two new metrics, reactivity plus the expected error in final allocation, into one principled rule. Simulations grounded in real trial designs show the formula finds a sweet spot. Type-I error inflation and estimation error stay controlled, while the power and patient-benefit advantages of adaptation survive, replacing rule-of-thumb choices with a defensible calculation.
arxiv-2511-21476:
Filippo Stocco, Michele Garibbo, and Noelia Ferruz survey how to steer protein-generating AI toward rare but valuable designs, in a 2025 review. Generative models have produced working binders, receptors, and new enzymes, but they imitate their training data, so they mostly sample the most probable proteins. The unusual regions of protein space, where novel functions hide, stay underexplored.

Stocco and his coauthors organize the steering toolbox into two camps. One camp changes the model itself, through reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning toward target properties. The other leaves the model frozen and guides sampling instead: conditional generation, retrieval-augmented prompting, Bayesian guidance, and tailored sampling schemes. Their taxonomy maps which knobs suit which constraints. The review closes on an open tension: natural protein fitness is fluid and context-dependent, so no single score defines the design goal.
arxiv-2511-21576:
Ridha Horchani imagines a force of nature that only quantum objects can feel, in a 2025 theoretical proposal. His Quantum Latent Gauge framework adds a hidden gauge interaction, a cousin of electromagnetism, that couples exclusively to quantum coherence. The trick is a coherence current built by coarse-graining the ordinary mass current: it vanishes for classical matter but switches on for superpositions and entangled states.

The theory keeps gauge invariance, causality, and healthy time evolution while staying invisible to every classical fifth-force search. It predicts three distinctive signatures. Interferometers should see phase shifts growing in step with fringe visibility. Decoherence rates should grow with the square of mass in a pattern unlike collapse models. Distant entangled masses should feel selective forces. Horchani works out a benchmark version in detail. Current atom interferometers and levitated nanoparticles can already place the first constraints, opening a new window on the quantum-classical border.
arxiv-2511-21976:
Thomas and colleagues compute how shear Alfvén waves, ripples along magnetic field lines, behave when the field becomes chaotic. Perturbation coils in tokamaks, added to tame edge instabilities, break field symmetry and create chaotic trajectories that may change Alfvén instabilities; analyses had assumed the waves stay unchanged.

The team built special pseudo straight field-line coordinates for chaotic regions using quadratic flux-minimized surfaces, which survive where ordinary flux surfaces do not. With those coordinates they turned the reduced magnetohydrodynamic equations into an eigenvalue problem and solved it numerically at several perturbation strengths, watching flux surfaces break as the perturbation grew stronger. Wave solutions on a flux surface stay relatively unchanged while it survives, and retain some original features even when it is destroyed. This gives a firmer basis for judging whether coils suppress or amplify Alfvén activity.
arxiv-2511-22376:
Andrews and San Mauro analyse argumentation frameworks, diagrams of arguments linked by attacks that mark conflicts between them. The grounded extension collects the conclusions even a maximally sceptical reasoner must accept, built by repeatedly applying a defence rule until nothing changes. For finite frameworks this settles quickly. The authors ask what happens when the framework is infinite, so the process may need infinitely many rounds.

Using computability theory and set theory, they pin down exactly how long the process can run: the number of rounds reaches the first non-computable ordinal, the standard ceiling for such constructions. They also show that deciding whether an argument is grounded-accepted is complete for a very high complexity class, making it maximally hard in a precise sense. That contrasts sharply with finite frameworks, where the same question is answerable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2511-22476:
Lin and colleagues improve the starting point for a family of quantum chemistry circuits. The unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz and its local variant are promising trial wavefunctions for variational quantum algorithms, normally initialised from a classical coupled-cluster calculation. Cutting the circuit down to fit real hardware, with fewer repetitions and dropped interactions the processor cannot connect, degrades that starting point and the final energy accuracy.

The team offers two fixes. Compressed double factorisation rebuilds a better approximation of the classical amplitudes within the truncated circuit, helping both expectation-value and sampling-based algorithms. For sampling-based methods, tensor network simulation further tunes parameters so the circuit produces better samples. Tests on exact simulators with up to 52 qubits and on superconducting processors with up to 65 qubits showed improvements. In one sampling method, the compressed start even beat the untruncated ansatz because its samples were more diverse.
arxiv-2511-22576:
Kapuriya, Hatami, and Buitelaar test whether text-to-image story generators respect the cultures they depict. Story visualisation turns story lines into matching pictures, and models have grown consistent, but cultural fidelity is rarely checked. The authors propose a Progressive Multicultural Evaluation Framework with five new metrics: cultural appropriateness, visual aesthetics, cohesion, semantic consistency, and object presence. The authors automate scoring with a jury of multimodal language models, checked against human evaluations.

The results expose a Western tilt. Models produced more coherent, appealing, culturally appropriate stories for real-world datasets than animated ones, aligning most strongly with English-speaking cultures on nearly every metric. Chinese scored in the middle, even beating English on cohesion, while Hindi ranked lowest on all metrics except visual aesthetics. Supplying cultural focus points helped judging in English but barely in Chinese or Hindi. The framework is offered as a foundation for more faithful story generators.
arxiv-2511-22876:
Nakayashiki takes a classical identity of integrable systems to a degenerate limit, harvesting new formulas. Tau functions of the KP hierarchy, a universal system encoding many soliton equations, satisfy addition formulas; the determinant form expresses shifted tau functions through other tau functions. Taking a careful limit of that formula, Nakayashiki obtains a degenerate addition formula expressing tau function shifts through Wronskian determinants of wave functions.

The formula settles a visible puzzle: vertex operators and Darboux transformations both manufacture new KP solutions from old. On quasi-periodic backgrounds their outputs looked alike, in genus one nearly identical, without proof. The degenerate formula clarifies the exact relation between the two constructions. Applied to theta function solutions, the machinery also yields a new addition formula for Riemann theta functions, differing from every formula in Fay's standard reference. Soliton techniques and theta function theory end up bound into one identity.
arxiv-2511-22976:
Ruibal Ortigueira and colleagues connect two ways of measuring how different two probability descriptions are, one classical and one quantum. In quantum physics, an open system's evolution is often unraveled into random paths of pure states, described by the stochastic Schrödinger equation. So a quantum state becomes a classical distribution over pure states. The team asks how to define relative entropy, a measure of dissimilarity, directly on those distributions.
