They show the smallest classical divergence between two such distributions is reached exactly when both are written on a shared, possibly non-orthogonal basis of the two quantum states. They give a constructive algorithm for finding that basis. The resulting entropy turns out to equal the known Belavkin-Staszewski quantum relative entropy. And the shared basis yields a new proof that relative entropy shrinks under Lindblad evolution, the standard equation for open quantum systems.
arxiv-2511-23076:
García-Consuegra and Rajantie compare two definitions of the effective potential, the quantum-corrected energy landscape that decides a scalar field's vacuum state, in de Sitter spacetime. De Sitter spacetime is the expanding geometry that approximates the universe during inflation. The two definitions agree in flat spacetime but diverge in de Sitter, and the authors compute both explicitly at one-loop order, the first level of quantum correction.

For light fields, the standard textbook potential is wrecked by infrared contributions, very long wavelength fluctuations. Its perturbative calculation fails to converge. The constraint potential proposed in 1986 stays free of that problem and can be computed reliably. The authors also give evidence for an earlier conjecture that the constraint potential is the one that belongs in the Starobinsky-Yokoyama stochastic theory of inflation. At one loop it reproduces the field's probability distribution, its long-distance correlations, and the vacuum lifetime.
arxiv-2511-23376:
Li Siyan and colleagues ask whether an AI assistant should adapt its answers to the skill of each user. Novices tend to want clear steps in plain words, while experts want short answers in terms they know. The team built this quiet tailoring into an assistant on a customer data platform. The assistant answered questions drawn from product documents. Skill was judged by topic as well as by role.

The team ran a study in which people took timed exams with help from the assistant. Some used the tailored version, and others used the standard one. The tailored version cut the load people said they felt and won better ratings. When time ran short, users wanted short answers, even when they liked fuller ones with no clock. The authors say quiet tailoring alone is not enough. It should sit beside controls that let users set their own style.
arxiv-2511-23476:
Shu and colleagues teach language model agents to reason about how their environments work by doing, not by following a rigid scripted reasoning template. Their method WMAct trains agents through multi-turn interaction with real feedback. Using a reward rescaling mechanism that pays for effective actions to discourage redundant moves. Plus an annealing strategy that progressively cuts the maximum allowed interaction turns during training in reinforcement learning.

Forcing the agent to manage with fewer and fewer turns makes it internalize the environment's dynamics instead of leaning on constant feedback. And on Sokoban, Maze, and Taxi tasks the trained models solve in a single turn problems that previously needed multiple interactions in experiments. The learned world-model reasoning also transfers strongly to more new complex environments and improves overall performance across a suite of separate reasoning benchmarks, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-00376:
Protein language models learn from amino acid sequences, and their layers may store different kinds of knowledge. Ajit Kumar and Indra Prakash Jha probe those layers for kinase functional prediction in 2025. Most applications use only the final layer's embeddings, possibly missing useful signals.

The authors systematically evaluate embeddings from the ESM-2 model with unsupervised clustering and supervised learning. Kinases are enzymes central to cell signaling and drug design, so predicting their function matters. If intermediate layers carry extra functional information, practitioners can improve predictions simply by reading more of a model they already use. Kinases are heavily studied drug targets, so even small prediction gains have wide impact.
arxiv-2512-00476:
Heavy sterile neutrinos are hypothetical particles that could explain why known neutrinos have mass. Tim Kretz and Ulrich Nierste compute QCD corrections to charged-current decays involving such neutrinos in 2025. Searches profit from precise predictions of inclusive decay rates, which set branching fractions and lifetimes.

Once semi-hadronic decay channels open, reliable rates require the neutrino to be heavy enough for perturbative calculation. The situation mirrors the well-known case of semi-hadronic tau decays. Precise rates sharpen experimental searches, including those using tau decays, by removing theory uncertainty from the list of excuses for a null result. Branching fractions decide which decay channels experimentalists should watch most closely. Inclusive rates sum over many final states, which is what makes them computable.
arxiv-2512-00676:
Kiri Wagstaff, a computer scientist, wrote a 2025 paper on reading handwritten numbers. Most past work asked machines to name one digit at a time. Real life is messier, since numbers usually come as strings of digits written by one person.

Wagstaff looks at cases like ZIP codes, check amounts, and appointment times. In such strings, digits can touch, slant, or change style from one to the next. A system that shines on single digits may fail on these groups. The paper sets out the challenges that a fair, realistic test of number reading must face.
arxiv-2512-01176:
Cole Treyturik and four coauthors revisit two puzzling supernova remnants in a 2025 astronomy paper. The remnants 3C 397 and W49B have long been debated. Did each come from a thermonuclear explosion, a white dwarf blowing up, or a core-collapse explosion of a massive star? Earlier studies gave conflicting answers.

The team presents a systematic, spatially resolved spectroscopic analysis of both remnants using the XMM-Newton telescope. Spectroscopy across each region maps the elements left behind, which differ between explosion types. Settling the engines behind these remnants sharpens our picture of how stars die and seed space with heavy elements.
arxiv-2512-01276:
Guy Blanc and co-authors ask if learning gets easier when data can be sampled. Classic learning theory asks a learner to work for all data spreads. Some of those spreads are too hard to even draw samples from. That demand may be stronger than real tasks need.

A weaker rule asks for success only on spreads that can be sampled. The team shows that this weaker rule can make some tasks much easier. They give cases where the gap is large. The result helps sort which hard tasks are hard due to learning, and which are hard due to odd data spreads.
arxiv-2512-01476:
Peter Lott and co-authors build a frame to rebuild fly-by events of black hole pairs. In such events, two black holes sweep past each other once. They do not merge. The pass sends out a short, single-cycle wave burst. These bursts should occur in dense star clusters and galaxy cores.

Their frame makes few prior claims about the burst shape. That freedom helps it fit odd real events. It can work on both loud and faint bursts. A model-free tool raises the odds of spotting these rare passes in wave data from current detectors.
arxiv-2512-01576:
Nihaal Bhojwani and co-authors model how black holes and galaxies grow together with neural operators. The physics spans a huge range of scales. Gas near the hole acts at tiny scales. Galaxy-wide feedback acts at vast scales. Full simulations of both ends are too costly.

Their neural operator frame learns the coupled dynamics fast. It bridges accretion at the center with feedback across the galaxy. Fast surrogates let teams scan many what-if cases. Those scans test how black hole growth steers star birth over cosmic time. Surrogate speed also lets observers fit live merger data faster, since galaxy feedback priors can be scanned while wave data is still fresh.
arxiv-2512-01676:
Jiangdong Ai and co-authors study feedback vertex sets in directed graphs with bounded degree. A feedback set hits every directed cycle. Removing it leaves the graph acyclic. In oriented graphs, with no opposite arc pairs, the task has set traits.

Degree here sums in-arcs and out-arcs at each vertex. Bounded degree caps how linked each node can be. The team proves bounds for feedback sets under that cap. Such sets help break deadlocks in networks and find orderings in dependency graphs. Bounded degree mirrors real networks, where each router or person links to few peers, so the bounds stay tight for practical cases.
arxiv-2512-01876:
Engineers often must learn how an unknown machine behaves by feeding it test signals and watching the response. A 2025 paper by Amir Shakouri, Henk J. van Waarde, and M. Kanat Camlibel asks how to design those test signals for a linear system whose inner workings are not known in advance.

The data gathered must be good enough either to identify the system or to design a controller that keeps it stable. The authors build in prior knowledge about two key properties, controllability and stabilizability, so the experiment respects what is already known. Their approach aims to collect the right data the first time, instead of relying on trial and error.
arxiv-2512-01976:
Designing proteins from scratch with AI depends on training data, and synthetic datasets often pair sequences with structures they could never actually fold into. Danny Reidenbach and a large team tackle that quality problem in 2025, aiming for fully atomistic designs with far greater structural variety.

Their approach leans on ProteinMPNN, whose proposed sequences are known to be experimentally friendly and able to fold. Combined with structure prediction models, it aligns synthetic structures with sequences that can genuinely realize them. Cleaner training pairs should make generative design models more reliable, widening the range of new proteins they can credibly propose.
arxiv-2512-02076:
Learning from data spread across many owners, each holding several kinds of data, runs into privacy, imbalance, and forgetting problems at once. Haozhe Wu's 2025 paper proposes FDRMFL, a federated feature extraction method for multi-modal regression that is driven by the task itself.

The method combines information maximization, squeezing the most signal from each modality, with contrastive learning to fuse them. It is built for three real-world headaches: limited data that are not identically distributed, the need to merge different data types well, and catastrophic forgetting as learning proceeds. Federated designs like this aim to learn jointly without pooling private raw data.
arxiv-2512-02176:
Kagome metals, whose atoms sit in a woven triangular pattern, can frustrate magnetism into strange quantum states. R. Guehne and nine co-authors study one such compound in 2025, a scandium-manganese kagome metal, hunting for signs that its electrons pair up in a spin-singlet pattern.

The material drew attention as a place where geometric frustration and mobile electrons might cooperate to keep magnetism disordered at the quantum level. The team combines bulk thermodynamic probes, low-noise transport on tiny cut devices, and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements. Converging evidence from several probes is what a claim of emergent pairing in such an exotic metal requires.
arxiv-2512-02576:
Yafei Song, Peng Zhang, and Bang Zhang generate videos of speakers whose hands move naturally with their words. Co-speech gestures make a talking avatar feel alive, but syncing them with speech is hard. Recent methods borrow motion from graphs built out of existing video clips.

Choosing the right path through that graph is the weak point. Older methods match audio features to motion features, or embed both in one shared space. The team's motion based graph retrieval picks clips by motion fit. More natural gesture video could improve virtual presenters, sign aware tools, and remote communication. Hands do much of the talk in a speech, so stiff hands make the whole clip feel false at once.
arxiv-2512-02776:
Fivos Perakis, Takeshi Kawasaki, and Shinji Saito study a particle wandering through an environment that flips between two states. In their Langevin model, friction switches at random between low, liquid like values and high, glassy ones. Two clocks govern the motion: the switching time and the velocity relaxation time.

The ratio of those clocks decides how diffusion behaves. The team finds conditions where switching enhances diffusion beyond either state alone. Flickering environments occur in cells and soft materials, so these results help explain transport where surroundings never sit still. A flicker can speed a trip, a quirk that shows up in gels and in the goo that lines our lungs as well.
arxiv-2512-02876:
Yinke Cheng and a large team build light sources that emit many evenly spaced colors at once, at useful power. Soliton microcombs, made in tiny optical resonators, promise compact sources for next generation communication. Power per comb line, though, has fallen short of what real systems need.

Their integrated Fabry-Pérot microresonator sidesteps the usual dispersion engineering limits. The platform yields bright soliton microcombs with record power per line, the authors report. Stronger comb lines could carry more data channels from a chip sized source, cutting cost and energy in optical networks. More power per line means more lanes per chip, and more lanes per chip is the whole game for cheap fast links in towns.
arxiv-2512-03176:
Reasoning models think for a long time before they answer. Anthony Liang and co-authors propose a change to that pattern in this 2025 work. While a model thinks, users get no hint if it is on track, and no chance to correct it.

Their method, called Plantain, weaves planning and answering together. The model shares parts of its plan as it goes, so users can step in early. Early feedback could save time and stop flawed reasoning sooner. The work speaks to anyone who uses AI tools for complex tasks. Users gain a window into the plan early, rather than a long silence before the reply.
arxiv-2512-03676:
Daria Kryvosheieva and colleagues locate grammar inside large language models and ask whether agreement rules of each kind share hardware. Subject-verb, pronoun, and determiner agreement all police the same sentence marks. Their 2025 study borrows functional localization from brain science to find the units behind sixty-seven syntactic phenomena.

Across seven open-weight models, the units tuned to syntax were reused again and again and truly backed performance. Different rule types drew on shared unit sets, a sign that agreement is a real working category for the models, not a made-up label. The pattern held in Russian and Chinese too. Among fifty-seven languages, languages closer in structure shared more subject-verb units.
arxiv-2512-03876:
Entropy counts how disordered a system is, and for dense matter full of strongly interacting particles the bookkeeping is subtle. David Blaschke, Gerd Röpke, and Gordon Baym revisit a classic tool for that bookkeeping in a 2025 nuclear theory preprint: the Beth-Uhlenbeck formula. They generalise it for dense fermion systems where two-particle correlations, including bound states, cannot be ignored.

Working inside the Phi-derivable framework for thermodynamic potentials, the authors write entropy as an integral over a distribution function times a special spectral density. Near the mass shell, that density takes a squared Lorentzian shape rather than the expected Lorentzian one. The connection between the classic formula and their framework is exact at the two-loop level. Their version also handles bound states dissolving at high density, as Levinson's theorem requires. Applications to nuclear matter and quark matter are discussed.
arxiv-2512-03976:
Large language models speak major languages fluently and low-resource ones poorly, because training data for the latter barely exists. Lifeng Chen, Ryan Lai, and Tianming Liu tackle that gap for Tibetan in a 2025 language technology preprint. Tibetan is morphologically rich and underrepresented online, so a general model starts with weak grounding in how the language works.

Their two-stage recipe first continues pretraining a three-billion-parameter Qwen model on Tibetan text, then fine-tunes it under supervision for tasks and translation. Perplexity on Tibetan fell sharply, and Chinese-to-Tibetan translation quality rose several-fold on standard scores. A layer-by-layer look inside a related model showed adaptation concentrated in embeddings, output heads, and later projection layers. The authors read this as the first stage building a Tibetan semantic space while the second sharpens task behaviour gently. They release the framework openly for other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2512-04976:
João Brito, Atsushi Higuchi, and Luís Crispino study what happens to gravity's energy when a small mass falls straight into a black hole. Simple theory says the share of energy swallowed by the hole grows without limit, which cannot be right. The trouble traces back to treating the falling body as a perfect point, with an infinitely strong field packed tightly around it.

The authors break the falling mass's field into layered wave patterns near the point where it crosses the black hole's edge. Piece by piece, they show the endless energy comes from that trapped field around the particle itself, which pours into the hole along with it. Each layer contributes a steady, matching amount, which clears up the puzzle without new physics. The result sharpens how physicists model small bodies spiraling into black holes.
arxiv-2512-05176:
Brittany Johnson, Erin Reddick, and Angela Smith argue that judging whether language models respect a community's values needs a benchmark built for communities, not nations. General-purpose models tend to reflect majority Western narratives, and recent culturally informed models try to correct that — but the tools to evaluate them lag behind. A national-level benchmark, the authors contend, cannot capture the range of cultural identities inside the United States.

Their proposal, CIVIQ, adapts the process behind KorNAT, a Korean national alignment benchmark, to the community level. It would test how well a model infers and honours the social values and common knowledge of specific communities, giving developers a way to measure cultural alignment where people actually live it. The work lays groundwork for building and evaluating culturally informed models in practice, rather than assuming one national yardstick fits a diverse country.
arxiv-2512-05276:
Yvelin Gansou, Karim Oualkacha, Marzia Cremona, and Lajmi Lakhal-Chaieb introduce a statistical test for whether genes and chemical marks on DNA interact in shaping a trait. The question is whether DNA methylation — marks that regulate genes — modifies the effect of a set of genetic variants on a measurable outcome. Methylation is naturally a curve over genomic position, so the authors treat it functionally, extending functional regression models into a test of the overall interaction.

In extensive simulations, the test holds its false-positive rate at the promised level while beating existing methods on power, especially when several interactions act at once — the realistic case. The authors then apply it to data from obesity patients and controls, showing the procedure at work on a real question. The contribution is a sharper instrument for a subtle effect: not whether genes or marks matter alone, but whether they matter together.
arxiv-2512-05576:
Ting-Ting Xie and Yixin Zhang diagnose why small clinical language-model agents fail at diagnosis despite finding the right evidence. Agents like TxAgent retrieve information competently thanks to supervised fine-tuning, then fail to ground their conclusions in it — a failure the authors name Context Utilization Failure. Their CureAgent framework separates the two skills. Small agents execute tool calls with syntactic precision, while long-context foundation models do the clinical reasoning over what was retrieved.

An ensemble strategy, preserving the diversity of evidence instead of pooling it, beats global pooling. Stress tests add two warnings: stretching the context too long injects noise and degrades accuracy, and enlarging the toolset creates a dimensionality curse that demands hierarchical retrieval. Without end-to-end fine-tuning, the training-free architecture reaches state-of-the-art results on a benchmark — an argument that in medical AI, architecture can substitute for training.
arxiv-2512-05776:
Muhib Omar leads an eleven author team that detects nuclear magnetic resonance signals with a sensor carved from diamond, at almost no magnetic field. Ordinary NMR needs strong magnets. At near zero field, signals shrink to a few cycles per second, but carry sharp chemical fingerprints from nuclear couplings. The diamond sits in a tiny truncated pyramid, with samples approaching within a millimeter.

Samples were boosted with parahydrogen through a reversible exchange trick. The sensor then read the expected coupling pattern of acetonitrile, with signal lines at just a few hertz. Its sensitivity reaches tens of picotesla per root hertz. Because no magnet is needed, the platform could become portable. The authors point to uses in medical diagnostics on tiny samples, sensing through metal walls in industry, and field ready analytical devices. It is a step toward NMR that travels to the sample, not the other way round.
arxiv-2512-05976:
Antonio Varagnolo, Giuseppe Romano, and Raphaël Pestourie teach a neural network just enough physics to design materials that steer heat at the nanoscale. Heat at this scale obeys the Boltzmann transport equation, exact but too slow for design loops. Cheaper solvers err wildly; data driven learners demand thousands of simulations. Their surrogate couples a differentiable Fourier solver with a neural generator that learns corrections.

A learned mixing coefficient slides between the macroscopic picture and the nanoscale one. Uncertainty driven active learning picks the simulations worth running. The payoff: training data needs fall by up to seventy percent against data driven baselines. Errors sit near five percent with only three hundred full simulations, and porous geometries were designed with average errors near four percent. The mixing parameter also tells engineers which regime a design lives in. The pattern travels well beyond heat.
arxiv-2512-06376:
Xinhao Xiang, Abhijeet Rastogi, and Jiawei Zhang ask whether videos of driving made by AI are good enough to train self driving cars. Text to video tools can spin up street scenes from a sentence, cheaply and in any mix. That promise only holds if clip cars move like real ones and obey road rules, which often they do not.

The team maps the common faults: warped images, motion no real car could make, and breaches of traffic sense. They build a bench of driving clips with human quality grades and dense labels for tasks like spotting and tracking cars. Their scorer blends scene meaning, motion cues, lane keeping, and vision model checks into one grade per clip. Raw clips hurt car training; clips filtered by their scorer helped. The study shows made up video can aid real driving work, if it is screened first.
arxiv-2512-06576:
Maxim Grigoriev and Mikhail Markov study what happens at the edge of anti de Sitter space, the curved spacetime that anchors much of modern gravity theory. Fields such as gravity itself live in the bulk of that space, but their observable fingerprints sit on its boundary at infinity. Making that edge precise is tricky, because infinity is not a place until the theory treats it as one.

Their approach folds the function that defines the boundary into the fields of the theory itself, so the boundary becomes an ordinary surface inside spacetime. A new notion, the Q boundary, systematizes that move. The payoff is a boundary calculus: a step by step recipe that writes down the equations the boundary fields obey and how their gauge freedoms act, for higher dimensions. Famous obstruction equations fall out, plus a higher Yang Mills equation in eight dimensions.
arxiv-2512-06976:
Ondřej Ježek and co-authors solve a finishing problem in topology optimization, the engineering method that lets an algorithm carve a part into its lightest strong shape. The raw output is a fuzzy density map, and turning it into clean geometry for manufacturing usually trades off smoothness, exact volume, and fine features. Their method describes the boundary with a signed distance function, which stores at each point its distance to the surface.

A two-stage process first builds that distance description from the density contours, then polishes the shape with radial basis functions. The result looks as though it came from a far finer calculation than the coarse one actually run, saving computing effort. In tests, peak stress dropped compared with standard methods, thanks to smooth transitions. The implicit surface exports directly to common manufacturing formats, skipping the usual rebuilding step that can introduce errors.
arxiv-2512-07076:
Chen-Yang Wang and co-authors argue that the scores used to grade camouflage-finding systems ignore the very thing camouflage is about: context. A hidden animal fools the eye by blending with its surroundings, yet standard metrics compare a predicted map against a binary ground truth as if each pixel stood alone. The authors name two flaws. Predictions carry both labels and probabilities while truth carries labels only, a dimension mismatch. And pixel-by-pixel scores miss dependencies spanning the whole image.

Their replacement, Context-measure, enriches the ground truth with pixel-level contextual affinity, scoring how each point relates to its surroundings. A perception cycle then judges predictions in a way designed to track human judgment more closely. Across experiments scored by four meta-measures, the new metric beat every widely used rival for camouflaged object segmentation.
arxiv-2512-07276:
Mai Tsujimoto and co-authors build a benchmark that asks vision-language models to reason about the three-dimensional world from ordinary aerial photographs. Planning cities, adapting to climate change, and assessing environments all need height-aware spatial reasoning. Yet the professional tools depend on pricey sensors like LiDAR that much of the world cannot deploy. Geo3DVQA instead gives models plain color imagery and asks questions involving elevation, how much sky a point can see, and land cover patterns.

The set holds a large bank of curated question-answer pairs across sixteen task categories, from single-feature reading to multi-feature reasoning and applied analysis. Ten leading models were put through it, and the results expose basic limits in how they infer three-dimensional structure from flat color. Focused instruction tuning on the domain lifted performance in every category, including open-ended questions.
arxiv-2512-07476:
Klaus Jansen, Dirk Nowotka, Lis Pirotton, Corinna Wambsganz, and Max Wiedenhöft wrote this 2025 paper in theoretical computer science. It studies patterns, which are strings mixing fixed letters with variables. Filling each variable with real letters yields the pattern's language.

In the classic setup, two uses of one variable must receive the same filler. Relational patterns loosen that rule in an organized way. Variables can be tied by many other relations, set independently of the pattern's shape. The authors carry three classic questions over to this richer world. The questions ask whether two patterns agree, whether one sits inside another, and whether a word fits. They test the questions across a wide range of chosen relations. Their results give a broad foundation for all three lines of work. Pattern languages matter wherever exact string structure must be reasoned about.
arxiv-2512-07976:
Lazar Milikic, Manthan Patel, and Jonas Frey wrote this 2025 robotics paper on teaching machines to navigate. End-to-end policies that steer robots straight from camera images are hard to train. Simulation skills transfer poorly, and real action labels are scarce.

Their framework, VLD, splits the problem into perception and control. A distance-to-goal predictor is trained first, on internet-scale video alone. Self-supervision lets it judge how far any image sits from a goal. Goals may arrive as pictures or as plain text descriptions. A reinforcement learning policy then learns to minimize that predicted distance. Training happens entirely in simulation with true geometric distances. Noise is injected to mimic the predictor's real-world uncertainty. At deployment, the policy consumes the learned distance signal instead. Semantic knowledge of where to go comes from the video training. Sturdy low-level steering comes from the simulated practice.
arxiv-2512-08076:
Min Seung Ko, Jae Woong Shim, and Hao Zhu, power systems engineers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is the strain that hyperscale artificial intelligence datacenters place on the electric grid. Huge training loads ramp and fluctuate sharply, stressing grid frequency and voltage stability for everyone else on the network.

The authors propose a hybrid energy storage system that pairs a battery with a supercapacitor under coordinated control. A filter splits demand into slow and fast parts, sending slow swings to the battery and fast ones to the supercapacitor. Extra mechanisms handle repeating patterns and keep both devices at healthy charge levels over long, random training cycles. Case studies show the scheme smooths both ramping and fluctuation, steadies system frequency, and keeps storage use sustainable. The work offers grid operators a practical buffer against datacenter load shocks.
arxiv-2512-08276:
Kristoffer Simula, Johannes Hauskrecht, Evelin Martine Corvid Christlmaier, and colleagues, quantum chemists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is computing the wave functions of solids accurately, a task plagued by three errors at once: finite size, incomplete basis sets, and electron correlation. They bring a method called transcorrelation, long used for molecules, into the world of crystals.

The team extends transcorrelated theory to periodic systems and unifies it with embedding, where a fragment of the solid gets a high level solver. Silicon serves as the test case, checked against coupled cluster and quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks for the bulk crystal. They then compute formation energies for two silicon self interstitial defects, a classic hard problem. The transcorrelated approach converged fast with basis size and gave reliable defect energies at modest cost. That eases the basis set bottleneck that has limited wave function methods for real, defected materials.
arxiv-2512-08576:
Hannah Bakker, Gianfranco Guastaroba, Stefan Nickel, and M Grazia Speranza, operations researchers in Germany and Italy, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their problem is a logistics classic: choose which warehouses to open, and assign every customer to exactly one, without overloading any facility. Their method, PaKS, is a two phase heuristic that first reads the geography hidden inside the problem.

Phase one applies pattern recognition to split candidate sites and customers into regions where siting and assignment choices are tightly linked. Phase two runs an enhanced kernel search, a method that solves small chosen sub problems exactly, now guided by those regional links. On over a hundred benchmarks, PaKS beat standard kernel search and the best known heuristic, landing essentially on the best known solutions. On fresh, larger instances it again found the most best solutions.
arxiv-2512-08676:
Dung The Tran extends a classic result in combinatorics on partitions of the natural numbers to curved surfaces with circle symmetry. Raimi theorem says a partition of the numbers has a strong unavoidability property under any finite coloring. Recent work carried a similar idea to the circle group, using measurable partitions and rotations.

Tran shows the phenomenon also holds on spheres, on rotational power surfaces such as cones and paraboloids, and on circular cylinders. Each surface carries a rotation action by the circle and splits as a product, so a partition from the base circle can be lifted to the surface. A general circle bundle theorem unifies the three cases. The proof checks the needed symmetry and measure properties for each family of surfaces.
arxiv-2512-08776:
Ferhat Tas introduces surfaces built from brachistochrone curves, the paths that minimize travel time under gravity. The classic brachistochrone is a cycloid in a constant gravitational field. Tas first builds a Newtonian worldsheet whose rulings are such time minimizing paths between pairs of endpoints.

The construction is then extended to stationary relativistic spacetimes. Arrival time problems there reduce to length problems of Finsler or Jacobi type on a spatial manifold, so relativistic brachistochrones become geodesics of that structure. Worked examples cover flat spacetime, where the curves are straight timelike lines and a simple ruled family is fully geodesic. The curved Schwarzschild case is also treated, with time minimization at fixed energy reduced to a Jacobi metric and a numerical scheme outlined. Basic geometric properties and natural Jacobi fields along the rulings are discussed.
arxiv-2512-08976:
Isha Chaturvedi and coauthors introduce Contrastive Region Masking, a training free diagnostic for how multimodal language models use visual regions during reasoning. Prior tools look only at final answers or at attention maps, which cannot show causal dependence on specific image regions. Their method fills that gap at the level of individual reasoning steps.

The diagnostic masks annotated regions one by one and contrasts the resulting reasoning traces with an unmasked baseline. Applied to a visual argument data set, it reveals distinct failure modes across models. Some models keep their reasoning structure but invent details when key evidence is masked. Others ground tightly to visual cues yet collapse when the input is perturbed. By shifting evaluation from answer correctness to reasoning faithfulness, the method reframes visual benchmarks as diagnostic tools. The authors argue that future evaluation should measure robustness and fidelity of reasoning, not just final performance scores.
arxiv-2512-09676:
Shahroze Shahab, Aditi Chakrabarty, and Sanjoy Datta study how two ingredients reshape the topological phases of one-dimensional p-wave superconductors. The ingredients are Rashba spin-orbit coupling and non-Hermiticity, the gain and loss that appears when a system is open. Kitaev chains are the model of such superconductors and host boundary modes. The two ingredients had been studied separately.

The authors consider two kinds of complex on-site potential: a uniform gain-loss term, and a complex quasiperiodic potential. Rashba coupling's impact proves model-dependent. In the uniform model it leaves the Hermitian topological boundary untouched but alters the landscape once non-Hermiticity is on. In the quasiperiodic model it moves boundaries in both regimes. Combining non-Hermiticity with Rashba coupling drives topological transitions at much lower potential strengths than the Hermitian limit. Expressions for the transitions are checked against numerical spectra and real-space winding numbers.
arxiv-2512-09876:
Frédéric Déglise, Niels Feld, and Fangzhou Jin build a general theory of Milnor-Witt cycle modules over arbitrary base schemes. The new theory works over an excellent base scheme equipped with a dimension function. From any such module the authors build a Rost-Schmid type complex. Its homology gives a Borel-Moore style intersection theory with quadratic coefficients, enjoying the standard package of properties.

The theory enjoys homotopy invariance, localization, pushforwards, pullbacks, and Gysin maps. Using duality data from pinning structures, the authors define a matching cohomological theory and prove the two versions are equivalent. As applications, Chow-Witt groups now extend to schemes over possibly singular or arithmetic bases. They prove Bloch formulas, representability results, and finiteness in low dimension.
arxiv-2512-10076:
Luca Moreno-Louzada, Guilherme Figueira, and Pedro Picchetti scrutinize a popular research design in economics: using commodity prices to study how regions absorb economy wide shocks. Regions differ in their exposure to a commodity, so one global price swing hits them unevenly, mimicking an experiment. Unlike shift share designs that blend many shocks, this design leans on a single one, which strains identification and statistical inference. The authors ground the design in a multi sector labor model.

Those estimands turn out to be weighted averages of region and sector effects, plus contamination terms driven by how prices covary and by general equilibrium responses. The authors give conditions for a clean causal reading, plus simple sensitivity checks when conditions fail. They also show standard errors in this design overreject: results look significant too often. Their corrected estimator, tested in simulations, behaves better. In their Amazon case, the headline effect loses significance.
arxiv-2512-10176:
Phuc V. Trinh leads a team reviewing how classical and quantum communication might share one set of radios. Next generation wireless networks want quantum communication integrated for security against quantum computing attacks. Running it as separate infrastructure is expensive, creates compatibility problems, and demands extra hardware everywhere. The alternative explored here is simultaneous classical and quantum communication: a single transceiver jointly encodes and decodes both kinds of information on the same signal. The authors survey recent progress on such protocols and what they make possible.

A second theme is range beyond optics. Most quantum communication lives in optical bands; the authors argue for pushing into terahertz and even millimeter wave and microwave frequencies, where future wireless systems will operate. That would widen where quantum security can be applied. The paper closes by naming three open challenges that block practical deployment.
arxiv-2512-10476:
Ricardo Peña Román and a large team report the first detailed magnetic imaging of a synthetic antiferromagnet, a layered material built to hold complex three-dimensional spin textures. Reading those textures without disturbing them is essential for learning how they work and how to tailor them. But measuring their stray fields at the nanoscale, in numbers, has stayed hard.

The team used a scanning probe built around nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond, working at room conditions, and ran it in several imaging modes with probes of different orientations. They mapped antiferromagnetic domains whose borders hold narrow ferromagnetic stripes, and separated steady stray fields from the hiss of thermal spin waves at gigahertz rates. The result is a non-invasive way to measure modern magnetic materials with nanometre detail and high sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-10676:
Ali Ghalavand and co-authors probe the anti-Ramsey number, a quantity from a 1975 problem of Erdős and others. Colour the edges of a complete graph with as many colours as possible while avoiding a rainbow copy of a target graph, one using every colour distinctly. The most colours possible without one is the anti-Ramsey number. The authors study which edges of the target are neutral, removable without changing that number.

Their target is a disjoint union of paths, some of length four and some single edges, and they focus on the inner edges of the longer paths. Neutrality was known when the single edges outnumber the paths. This paper finds the values where neutrality survives in the opposite regime, for graph sizes in a set range. And since matching numbers are understood, that completes the anti-Ramsey number in those cases. A conjecture extends the pattern further.
arxiv-2512-10776:
Bruce Elmegreen, Deidre Hunter, and Edvige Corbelli test whether pressure governs star formation in the smallest galaxies. In spiral galaxies, the rate of star formation tracks the midplane pressure, the weight of gas, stars, and dark matter pressing on the gas layer. The authors take twenty-four dwarf irregular galaxies from the LITTLE THINGS survey and ask whether the link survives where pressures are feeble and dark matter rules the gravity.

The correlations held at every resolution. They compare with the outer disc of M33, a similar, slightly richer galaxy in metals, where carbon monoxide can be detected. From that comparison they estimate the molecular share. The star formation rate per molecule comes out constant across the dwarfs. At low pressure and metal content, carbon monoxide traces dense gas, like HCN does in spirals. So the CO-bright regions in dwarfs should be self-gravitating.
arxiv-2512-10876:
Pierre-Alexis Roy and a large team report a surprise from the James Webb Space Telescope: three similar sub-Neptune planets with three different skies. Transits of K2-18b and TOI-270d had shown molecular absorption and little haze, suggesting temperate sub-Neptunes have clear atmospheres and water-rich compositions. Whether that held for the whole class was an open question. And LP 791-18c was the third test, sitting between the other two in size, mass, and temperature.

Its transmission spectrum looks drastically different. Methane is present, as in the others, but haze scattering dominates the spectrum and no carbon dioxide absorption shows. The team infers a deep, metal-enriched atmosphere with little carbon dioxide relative to methane, implying less water in the envelope and a dry birth inside the water ice line. Near-twins in density and temperature, it turns out, can differ wildly in haze and chemistry.
arxiv-2512-10976:
Xin Li proposes a new framework for understanding how the brain turns messy sensory input into fast, coherent thought. Brains run on slow, noisy, costly tissue, yet perception feels quick and unified. Older theories based on vectors and instant error correction struggle to explain that gap between slow learning and fast understanding.

The Homological Brain view uses algebraic topology, the math of shapes and holes, to describe neural computation. A parity principle splits stable content from changing context, and a three step process of search, closure, and condensation turns hard searches into easy navigation over learned structure. Li links this process to sleep, memory consolidation, and fast versus slow thinking, treating the brain as an engine that reduces topological complexity.
arxiv-2512-11076:
Jack Brady, Andrew Dailey, Kristen Schang, and Zo Vic Shong survey how event based cameras could help cities track human movement while protecting privacy. These cameras do not record full colour frames. Instead, they register changes in light, which lets them work in low light and capture fast motion with little redundant data.

The survey traces how urban monitoring grew from manual observation to cameras and sensors, then reviews event camera uses, strengths, and limits. Because the devices record motion patterns rather than detailed images, they can supply useful crowd and traffic information with less intrusion. The authors also propose pairing them with infrared, lidar, or vibration sensors. Such fusion, they argue, could overcome the cameras' weaknesses and improve studies of city dynamics.
arxiv-2512-11976:
Anastasiia Zbandut and Carolina Goldstein map a quiet power shift in decentralized credit. In DeFi lending, ERC 4626 vaults and outside curators, not the base protocols, increasingly pick loans and set leverage. The authors measure how these modular vaults differ in capital use, concentration, and liquidity risk.

A small curator set handles an outsized share of total value, moves in clustered tail patterns, and earns very unlike fee margins on similar collateral. Risk, they argue, has moved up from protocol rule books to a curator layer where managers compete with little shared reporting. They propose simple on chain disclosures so users and DAOs can compare curator strategies like money market funds.
arxiv-2512-12076:
Yu-Chia Huang and co-authors present SigTime, a system that learns and shows the signature patterns inside time series data. Finding the shapes that separate one class from another drives diagnosis and forecasting, yet classic tools are slow or opaque. In medicine, such patterns in body signals can change care.

The learning frame trains two transformers together. One reads shapelets, short local patterns that act as readable signatures. The other reads classic statistical features. A visual analytics front end then lets experts inspect the signatures from several views at once. Tests cover eight public data sets and one private clinical set, plus case work on ECG data and preterm labor with domain experts.
arxiv-2512-12176:
Xiao Wang and Kai-Kai Duan test a dark matter claim in a 2025 paper. A recent report found extra gamma rays near 20 GeV in the halo of the Milky Way and suggested dark matter as the cause. The claim points to particles of 0.5 to 0.8 TeV that destroy each other into bottom quarks.

Such particles should also make many antiprotons, which the AMS-02 detector on the space station can measure. The authors compute that signal and find the flux near 100 GeV already sits above what AMS-02 sees. The rate needed is a few tens of times too high. They conclude the excess is not a viable dark matter signal.
arxiv-2512-12276:
Jeffrey van der Voort, Martin Verlaan, and Hanne Kekkonen mix machine learning with a classic filter to track complex systems in a 2025 paper. Weather and ocean forecasts use ensemble Kalman filters, which run many model copies to estimate a system's state. Full models are costly, so cheap stand-in models can help if they stay accurate enough.

Their multi-fidelity filter pairs a few full runs with many runs of a machine learning surrogate. Tests used the Lorenz-2005 model and a quasi-geostrophic model. Keeping the full model beat swapping it out fully, and accuracy rose within the same computing budget. The surrogate also sped things up more than a low resolution model did.
arxiv-2512-12576:
Xueru Wen and eight co-authors present CoVRL, a reinforcement learning method for language model reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning improves reasoning when rewards can be checked, but many tasks lack a verifier. Verifier free methods use the model's chance of producing a reference answer as a reward. Yet they sample reasoning traces from the question alone. That wastes exploration and loosens the tie between trace and answer.

CoVRL couples prior and posterior distributions through hybrid sampling, joining variational inference with reinforcement learning. That keeps exploration efficient while thought and answer stay coherent. On math and general reasoning benchmarks, it improved 12.4 percent over the base model and added 2.3 percent over top verifier free baselines.
arxiv-2512-12676:
Jiawei Yan, Ju Liu, Weidong Liu, and Jiyuan Tu make variational Bayes robust to dirty data in a 2025 paper. Variational Bayes approximates a posterior distribution with a simpler one, scaling Bayesian inference to large data. Outliers and contamination can pull that approximation off course, a risk that grows as data sets get messier.

Their method splits data into m disjoint subsets and aggregates local posteriors with a min-max median rule instead of a mean, blunting the effect of bad subsets. A two stage aggregate and rescale step handles local latent variables. Theory gives near optimal rates for the posterior mean and smaller approximation error than direct aggregation. Extensive simulations support the method.
arxiv-2512-12876:
Helmut Prodinger studies skew 2-Dyck paths, walks made of steps that go up, down, or take a new kind of down step. A rule bans two short patterns: an up step right before or right after the new step can never occur. Counting such walks is the core task.

Prodinger builds a small machine, an automaton, that checks the ban as a walk is read. He then uses the kernel method on three equations to obtain counting formulas, called generating functions. The paper also sketches how the setup extends to a broader family of paths. Prefixes of those paths are counted as a side benefit.
arxiv-2512-13176:
Siyuan Shen and co-authors present EDAN, a tool that measures how sensitive a program is to memory latency. Modern supercomputing increasingly pulls data from remote memory over a network, which adds delay. Knowing which programs suffer most guides where that design is safe.

EDAN builds an execution graph, a DAG, from a program's recorded instruction trace. From that graph it estimates latency sensitivity and the memory-level parallelism built into the code, without special hardware or slow simulators. The team applied it to benchmarks such as PolyBench, HPCG, and LULESH. It also gives theoretical bounds for performance measures under varied hardware setups.
arxiv-2512-13276:
Yan Li and co-authors present CogniEdit, a framework for instruction based image editing that follows fine details: exact colors, positions, and counts. Diffusion editors often miss such specifics. Methods that tune them with policy optimization give feedback only step by step, a sparse signal.

CogniEdit joins three parts. A multimodal language model splits complex instructions into clear directives. A token focus mechanism highlights the fine attributes during generation. A dense version of policy optimization sends gradients across consecutive steps for trajectory level supervision. Benchmark tests showed state-of-the-art results, balancing faithful fine-grained edits with image quality and preservation of untouched areas.
arxiv-2512-13376:
Carla Monteiro and co-authors tackle polyp segmentation, the automatic outlining of polyps in colon images, a step toward earlier colorectal cancer detection. Deep models often fail to generalize to new hospitals and scarce data settings. Many also rely on heavy, task specific designs.

Their framework uses the key features inside the self-attention of DINO, a self-supervised vision model, fed into a simple convolutional decoder. They test it on a multi-center data set under two strict protocols, including training on a single domain only. It reached state-of-the-art results and beat established models such as nnU-Net. A note in the paper flags a code bug, so the team says the claims await corrected results.
arxiv-2512-13476:
Miguel Jimenez-Redondo and co-authors record high resolution overtone spectra of the molecular ions HNC+ and HCN+, species of interest in space chemistry. The spectra were measured between 6200 and 6800 inverse centimeters in a cryogenic ion trap. Two action spectroscopy schemes were used to probe the fragile ions.

Several vibrational bands were measured with high resolution for the first time, including an overtone band of HNC+ and combination and vibronic bands of HCN+. The team derived spectroscopic constants, band origins, and radiative lifetimes. Fits to HCN+ revealed strong vibrational couplings that perturb its excited levels. The paper also compares the two probing schemes for future ion studies.
arxiv-2512-13576:
Dorian Koch and co-authors carry out the first large, independent study of denoising language models for speech recognition. Such models use context from both sides and can adapt to the error patterns of a speech system. Their complex training path had limited wider study until now.

The team built and released a full, repeatable pipeline and tested dozens of settings. They varied data boosts, text-to-speech systems, and decoding plans. Denoising models beat classic language models only past a clear compute tipping point, but then scaled better with more training. Gains were smaller than in past character-based work. Feeding the model many speech hypotheses helped most, and their new DLM-sum decoding beat the prior method.
arxiv-2512-14576:
Ekaterina Artemova and five co-authors present a tutorial for people who build language tools for languages with little data. It is aimed at NLP practitioners, researchers, and developers who want fairer tools for languages that big tech tends to skip.

Participants work through a full pipeline, from data collection and web crawling to mining parallel sentences and training machine translation. Later steps reach text classification and work that mixes text with other media. The stress throughout is on social impact: better corpora are the first step toward tools that serve small language communities well.
arxiv-2512-14876:
Daniel Perkins, Davis Hunter, Dhrumil Patel, and Galen Flanagan work on teaching computers to read single signs from American Sign Language. Sign language uses complex visual cues, so the speech and text tools boosted by recent AI gains do not transfer directly. Reading one sign at a time from video is a first step toward fuller translation.

Their model cuts computing costs while staying robust when signers vary. It first estimates pose, pulling out the joint points of the hands and face from each frame. A segmentation step then isolates the parts of the image that matter. A ResNet Transformer backbone reads space and time patterns together to name the sign. The design aims at scarce training data per sign, a core limit in this field.
arxiv-2512-15076:
Shlok Tomar and five coauthors search for better prompts for code writing AI, using tests as the judge. A language model's code is only as correct as the prompt that asked for it, and prompt choice is a combinatorial hunt. Their method, BODE-GEN, treats the hunt as Bayesian optimization.

An auxiliary model maps text prompts into a continuous embedding space, where a Gaussian process surrogate can guide the search. Random projections and scaled priors keep that high dimensional search effective. Each tried prompt is scored by how well the code it produces passes a set of test cases. On the HumanEval+ benchmark, across several base models, the method beat fixed prompts and hand tuning. It was also sample efficient, needing few rounds to improve code accuracy, a practical route to test driven generation.
arxiv-2512-15776:
Shaun Baek, Sam Liu, and Joseph Ukpong study privileged information bias in pairs of embodied agents in a 2025 paper, dated December 13. A knowledgeable leader agent often fails to guide a sensor limited follower, because it assumes the follower shares its view. The authors call this the curse of knowledge and set out to measure it.

Inside the AI2-THOR simulator, the leader perceives the target in 35.0 percent of episodes, yet the team succeeds only 17.0 percent of the time. Nearly half of feasible plans fail on communication grounding alone. A pull based protocol, where the follower actively asks questions, proves far more robust than pushed instructions. Successful episodes show twice as many clarification requests.
arxiv-2512-15876:
Paul Aigner and Wolfgang Dur show that a single moving quantum sensor can outperform a fixed sensor network in a 2025 paper. Quantum sensors measure fields with precision beyond classical limits, and networks of them are usually assumed stronger. Motion, though, gives one sensor access to many positions over time.

With control of its path or its internal state, one moving sensor can pick out any linear functional of a spatially correlated scalar field. Examples include a gradient or a Fourier coefficient. At the same time it can cancel all noise signals with orthogonal spatial correlation. Fixed entangled networks can suppress only as many noise signals as they have positions. Moving sensors also beat the static scaling limit for quantum Fisher information.
arxiv-2512-15976:
Kaustub Anand, Matija Cuk, and David Minton propose the sesquinary catastrophe as a brake on the orbital excitation of Deimos in a 2025 paper. Mars's outer moon Deimos has a calm orbit, low eccentricity of 0.00027 and modest inclination, yet impact based origin stories would have stirred it strongly. Tidal damping inside Deimos is too weak to calm it afterward.

A sesquinary catastrophe is a runaway collisional cascade triggered by debris from the moon itself. N-body simulations with fragmentation show that a more excited Deimos would break apart once an excitation measure passes about 8, within thousands of years. Reaccumulated from the damped debris disk, Deimos would be a porous sand pile, matching its smooth surface.
arxiv-2512-16176:
Saikat Chakraborty, Sergio E Joras, and Alberto Saa compare analysis toolkits in this 2025 arXiv paper, accepted by Classical and Quantum Gravity. Modified gravity theories in the f(R, phi, X) family change Einstein's rules by mixing curvature, a scalar field, and its motion. Dynamical systems methods turn their equations into maps of possible cosmic histories.

The authors present two such formulations that cover a large class of these theories. The first, applied to a nonminimal derivative coupling toy model, finds invariant sub-spaces but all its fixed points are non-hyperbolic, limiting the analysis. One surprise: the qualitative behavior does not depend on the coupling strength. The second formulation handles a mixed R squared plus Higgs inflation model cleanly, recovering each single model's behavior in the right limits, with phase portraits to show the dynamics.
arxiv-2512-16376:
Tatsuo Kobayashi and Hajime Otsuka extend symmetry physics in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Particle theories use selection rules to say which interactions may occur. Non-invertible rules, built from fusion algebras where combining charges need not be reversible, are a modern generalization now drawing intense study.

The authors label fields by conjugacy classes of a finite group rather than by its standard representations. When the fusion rules carry a twofold symmetry matching charge conjugation, a consistent CP symmetry, the mirror symmetry between matter and antimatter, can be defined alongside parity. Mixing group flavor symmetries with CP then forces a generalized CP transformation. The framework even allows spontaneous CP violation, where the symmetry breaks by itself, with consequences for Yukawa textures, the pattern of fermion masses and mixings.
arxiv-2512-16676:
Hao Liang and a large team present DataFlow, a system that unifies how training data for large language models is prepared. Good data is in high demand, yet most pipelines are ad hoc scripts that are hard to reuse, check, or extend.

DataFlow offers about 200 reusable operators and six broad pipelines covering text, math, code, text-to-SQL, agent search, and knowledge extraction, all built with a PyTorch-style interface. A companion agent turns plain requests into working pipelines. Across six tasks, DataFlow data beat curated human sets and purpose-built baselines. A mixed set of just 10,000 samples let base models beat rivals trained on one million samples of Infinity-Instruct data.
arxiv-2512-16876:
Astrid Brull and a large international team use federated learning to diagnose collagen VI related dystrophies, a group of rare inherited muscle diseases. Patient data for these diseases are scarce and split across hospitals in many countries, and privacy law blocks pooling the scans in one place.

Federated learning trains one shared model while the data stay at each home site. Two worldwide groups trained on microscopy images of collagen VI taken from patient cell cultures. The joint model sorted the images into three disease mechanism groups and scored well above the models that each site trained alone. The team expects the shared approach to help read gene variants of unclear meaning as well.
arxiv-2512-16976:
Edward W. Kolb and coauthors study raritrons, spin-3/2 particles that could fill the role of dark matter if made by gravity during inflation. The spin-3/2 field was first framed by Rarita and Schwinger and later housed in supergravity as the graviton partner.

Using Bogoliubov methods, the team maps which masses and inflation scales yield the observed dark matter share for stable raritrons. The yield hinges on the mass versus the Hubble rate at inflation end. Light raritrons see their sound speed shrink or vanish, which hugely boosts high-momentum output. A time-varying mass can dodge the vanishing speed yet still lift output past the heavy case.
arxiv-2512-17476:
Eleanor K R Mackay and four co-authors read the hidden choreography of crowded particles from the flicker in their counts. In a dense suspension, particles jostle as hard spheres that cannot overlap. Counting how their number in a fixed window rises and falls over time gives a spectrum, and that spectrum, the team shows, encodes motion at many scales at once.

Fast flicker in the spectrum mirrors single particles diffusing on their own. Slow flicker betrays long-lived group patterns: pairs swapping places at small scales and whole patches rearranging at large ones. The method needs no tracking of single particles, a hard task in thick samples. It gives labs a fresh probe for gels, coatings, and other crowded soft matter.
arxiv-2512-18076:
Owen S. Matthews Acuña leads a ten author team mining a giant galaxy survey for more than redshifts. The eBOSS survey gathered over 2.2 million galaxy spectra mainly to map cosmic structure. Most of the light's detail sat unused. Their pipeline, adapted from a sister survey's tools, reads the full spectra in one even way.

From 1,899,553 clean spectra they measured gas line flows, star and gas motions, and the ages and makeup of star groups. Repeat views of the same galaxies let them check how steady those measures are. The public catalogs open the set to fresh work on how galaxies grow and change across cosmic time.
arxiv-2512-18376:
Anestis Fotiadis and Giannis Polychrou find exact solutions for maps into curved surfaces whose bend changes from place to place. Harmonic and wave maps stretch one space into another as evenly as they can, and exact forms are known mostly for flat or evenly curved targets. Lumpy targets usually defy pen and paper.

Their frame reshapes the task for a broad family of such surfaces. A travelling wave guess, fit to the shape, turns the governing system into a set of first order equations that can be solved outright. One frame covers both the still and the waving case. Worked examples reach into egg shaped surfaces, saddle forms, and the space outside a black hole.
arxiv-2512-18476:
V. I. Yudin and a large team of physicists identify a measurement shift in atomic interferometers that earlier work had not discussed. These devices split and recombine atoms to measure gravity and other quantities with extreme precision. The shift comes from the laser field being chirped not only while atoms evolve freely but also during the Ramsey pulses that probe them, which skews the spectral lineshape.

The authors show the shift falls as one over T cubed, where T is the gap between pulses, unlike the one over T squared pattern typical in this field. That steeper scaling makes the effect matter most in compact devices with short baselines. For rubidium gravimeters at T near one millisecond, they estimate shifts of 0.1 to 1 milligal. At a tenth of that gap the shift can reach 0.1 to 1 Gal.
arxiv-2512-18676:
Tamim Aziz and Sanjoy Ghosal develop a rough form of convergence for sequences in normed spaces in this 2025 functional analysis paper. Their setup weights each term of a sequence and filters convergence through an ideal, a chosen family of negligible index sets. They define the rough weighted ideal limit set and the cluster point set, then prove results on maximal ideals and on how closed sets can be represented in this language.

They also find the smallest roughness degree that keeps the limit set nonempty, and show that for an analytic P-ideal the limit set has a specific descriptive form. The pair then defines weighted equi-ideal convergence for sequences of functions. As an application, they prove a Korovkin-type approximation theorem that both generalizes a 2008 result and corrects one from 2017.
arxiv-2512-18876:
Lauren McClure and four co-authors clean up the hunt for tiny whirlpools on the Sun. Small vortices in the photosphere ferry mass and energy upward, but shear in the flow fools detection algorithms into reporting vortices that are not there. Their fix, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and submitted to The Astrophysical Journal, is a preprocessing step: normalize the velocity field by its magnitude before detecting anything.

Tested on high-resolution Bifrost simulations with the d-criterion as approximate truth, three standard methods produce many false positives on raw data; normalization removes most of them. The Gamma method, which underpins most observational studies, stays accurate but misses many real flows. After normalization the other methods find four to five times more vortices, suggesting the Sun's true vortex coverage is badly underestimated today.
arxiv-2512-18976:
Jie Fan and Xiangdi Huang settle a basic question for a heated, compressible fluid in two dimensions: do strong solutions exist for all time, no matter how violent the start? Their model couples density to a transported entropy, so pressure depends nonlinearly on both, differing from the standard heat-conducting Navier-Stokes-Fourier system. Since 1995, large-data results existed only for the cooler isentropic case. Their 44-page paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, extends them.

Global strong solutions are proven on periodic domains and on bounded domains with Navier-slip boundaries, even with vacuum in the initial density and with no smallness assumed. The conditions are mild: constant shear viscosity and a bulk viscosity growing like density to a power above four thirds. Density stays uniformly bounded, so solutions settle to equilibrium over time. Gas dynamics simulations, from engines to atmospheres, rest on exactly this kind of well-posedness.
arxiv-2512-19076:
Yiming Gao, Yansong Feng, Honggang Hu, and Yanbin Pan give a faster deterministic method for factoring certain hard numbers. Their tool is Coppersmith's method, run on a small lattice of rank three. Unusually, they use the second vector in the reduced lattice basis, not the shortest, to dodge trivial collisions in a step of the method.

For a balanced semiprime, the product of two similar primes, their runtime beats the best known result of Harvey and Hittmeir. Gains also follow for numbers built as sums or differences of powers, and for finding power divisors. The work is pure algorithm theory, aimed at the math behind factoring.
arxiv-2512-19276:
Gianmarco La Rosa and Manuel Mancini study the Lie-holomorph of a Leibniz algebra, a construction Souris recently adapted from Lie theory. Leibniz algebras loosen Lie algebras by dropping skew-symmetry, so old constructions need fresh checks. The holomorph packages an algebra with its derivations into one larger algebra.

The authors connect the construction to Loday's algebra of biderivations. They prove a map is a Lie-derivation exactly when it is both a derivation and an anti-derivation. As a payoff, they classify the Lie-holomorphs of all low-dimensional non-Lie Leibniz algebras, over fields where two is not zero. The result tidies a corner of non-associative algebra.
arxiv-2512-19376:
Eneko Lazpita, Andrés Bell-Navas, Jesús Garicano-Mena, and Petros Koumoutsakos compare two ways of compressing blood flow inside the heart's left ventricle. Flow patterns there track heart health and can warn of decline early. Proper orthogonal decomposition is the classic linear tool; autoencoders are its neural, flexible cousins.

Both were fed flow fields from fluid simulations of the ventricle. At a well-chosen latent size, autoencoder modes came out nearly independent and looked much like the classic modes, capturing the same share of kinetic energy. Adding more latent modes, though, made the neural modes overlap and repeat each other. The study maps where each method earns its keep.
arxiv-2512-19476:
Tadashi Kuramoto, Yasutaka Imai, Takahiko Masuda, and Yutaka Shikano give optical-cavity axion hunters a careful account of mirror birefringence. Cavity searches for axion-like dark matter read tiny polarization signals. Real mirrors split polarizations, and that flaw, plus small misalignment, can quietly eat the sensitivity.

Their framework is exact, not perturbative, and folds in reflectance variation and polarization misalignment together. Both flaws hurt most at low axion mass. Picking a postselection angle above the misalignment angle recovers much of the loss. Birefringence also plants an extra resonance peak at high mass, largely immune to the other flaws.
arxiv-2512-19576:
Kirill Djebko, Tom Baumann, Erik Dilger, and Frank Puppe report the first in-orbit run of an AI satellite attitude controller. Pointing a satellite the classical way takes long design work and suffers when the real craft differs from its model. A reinforcement learning agent instead learns pointing maneuvers by trial in simulation, but the jump to real hardware is the known hard part.

The agent flew on InnoCube, a three-unit nanosatellite built by Würzburg and Berlin partners and launched in January 2025. The paper covers the agent's design, its training, and the gaps between simulated and observed behavior. A head-to-head comparison with the classical controller is included.
arxiv-2512-19676:
Mojtaba Safari leads a thirteen-author team tackling a familiar clinical trade-off: sharp MRI scans take a long time to acquire. Their super-resolution framework upgrades lower-resolution scans after the fact, using multi-head selective state-space models paired with a light channel network. Hybrid scanning over two-dimensional patches lets the model gather long-range context while each block mixes in convolutions and gated channels.

Tested on 7-tesla brain maps from 142 subjects and prostate scans from 334 patients, the model beat interpolation, GAN, transformer, Mamba, and diffusion rivals on standard quality measures. It did so with only about nine hundred thousand parameters, using a small fraction of the compute of the strongest diffusion baseline. The authors argue that combination of accuracy and thrift suits real clinical deployment.
arxiv-2512-19876:
Christian Malacaria leads a twenty-three-author team examining an X-ray pulsar caught at unusually low brightness. Accreting X-ray pulsars change character with feeding rate, and MAXI J0655-013 was observed by XMM-Newton and NuSTAR in a low-luminosity regime around five times ten to the thirty-third ergs per second. The team dissected its spectrum and its thousand-second pulse rhythm in detail.

The spectrum fits a double Comptonization model, two humps attributed to different polarization modes, matching recent theory for the low-accretion transition. Timing gives a spin period near 1081.86 seconds, still spinning up, which caps the magnetic field below nine times ten to the thirteenth gauss. Pulse profiles show one broad peak cut by a sharp dip where the hardness ratio rises, and the pulsed fraction climbs toward one hundred percent in the ten to thirty kiloelectronvolt band.
arxiv-2512-20176:
Aaron Chan and five co-authors propose running AI inference on blockchains with no need to trust hardware claims. Decentralized inference faces a trilemma of integrity, latency, and cost. Zero-knowledge proofs are too slow for billion-parameter models. Optimistic schemes impose dispute windows that kill real-time use. Quality-based proofs drop integrity for subjective scores. Their Optimistic TEE-Rollups mix the parts in a new way.

Confidential-computing enclaves give sub-second provisional finality. Optimistic fraud proofs back them up. Stochastic zero-knowledge spot-checks guard against hardware side channels. A new consensus notion binds execution traces to hardware attestations in cryptographic form. That guarantees the claimed model truly ran. Simulations report throughput near ninety-nine percent of centralized baselines. The marginal cost is seven cents per query.
arxiv-2512-20376: Marta Moscati and co-authors summarize the FAME 2026 Challenge, a competition on matching faces to voices when the spoken language changes between training and testing. Most people worldwide are bilingual, so systems that link a face to a voice must survive exactly that switch. The challenge was held at ICASSP 2026.
arxiv-2512-20676:
Rishabh Mishra rescues turbulence measurements from blurry sensors. Industrial and aeroacoustic instruments often cannot resolve the smallest eddies, so spectra get truncated and turbulent kinetic energy is underestimated. Mishra derives an analytical spectral model from a variational principle about cascade resistance, yielding a Ginzburg-Landau domain-wall shape.

Unlike the classic Pao and Pope models, this spectrum has bounded support with a hard cutoff at the Kolmogorov wavenumber and no adjustable parameters beyond the Kolmogorov constant. Against high-Reynolds-number experimental data, the model captures the spectral rolloff faithfully. It restores nearly all the variance even when spectra are truncated very early in the dissipation range. For engineers stuck with bandwidth-limited sensors, the correction offers a principled way to recover what the hardware missed.
arxiv-2512-21076:
Suraj Kumar, Chandranath Adak, and three co-authors organize digital libraries the way librarians actually think. Genre is not flat, and a book's official blurb and its crowd-sourced reviews describe it in different voices. Their framework, HiGeMine, first uses the blurb to filter reviews, keeping the ones semantically consistent with it and damping noisy, genre-irrelevant readings. Separate graph-convolution branches then reason over blurb and review evidence, so narrative description and reader interpretation never blur together.

Classification runs coarse to fine: fiction versus non-fiction first, then specialized multi-label classifiers for fine-grained genres, informed by a graph of which labels co-occur. A new hierarchical Goodreads benchmark with paired blurbs and reviews anchors the evaluation, where the method outperforms hierarchical classifiers, graph approaches, pretrained language models, and large language models. Learning platforms gain a scalable shelving system.
arxiv-2512-21176:
Fabrizia Mealli and Javier Viviens examine the assumption empirical economists most often leave unstated. Difference-in-differences, the workhorse design comparing treated and control groups before and after an intervention, rests on SUTVA, the assumption that units neither affect each other nor receive hidden variants of treatment. Spillovers are plausible in most real settings, yet the no-interference half of the assumption is rarely even declared. Their technical note asks what the standard estimate actually measures when interference of unknown form is present.

The answer is sobering: the estimand recovers a contrast between causal effects, a difference that cannot be decomposed into either effect on its own without extra assumptions. The authors then catalog assumption sets under which specific effects do become identifiable, and revisit Card and Krueger's classic minimum-wage study to show what changes. Practitioners get a precise warning label for one of their favorite tools.
arxiv-2512-21876:
Ryunosuke Takahashi, Tsuyoshi Kimura, Hiroki Wadati, and their co-authors use Raman spectroscopy to find the fingerprint of ferroaxial order in a phosphate crystal. Ferroaxial order appears when a crystal's lattice twists, breaking mirror symmetry along its main axis. The twist should couple to certain lattice vibrations, but those phonons had never been assigned.

The team measured polarization-resolved Raman spectra of sodium barium nickel phosphate crystals in their ferroaxial phase. They combined the data with first-principles calculations, so each observed mode could be matched against symmetry predictions. The result is a full assignment of the Raman-active modes of the ferroaxial phase. Several low-frequency modes show extra linewidth broadening, suggesting the twist weakly disturbs them. The authors frame the work as a symmetry-based method for ferroaxial materials generally.
arxiv-2512-22276:
H. Susanto and N. Karjanto study kinks, localized wave profiles, in the phi-six model when space is replaced by a lattice. In the continuous model, kinks can sit anywhere. On a lattice they are usually pinned, so finding discretizations whose static kinks can center at any position relative to the lattice sites is a special prize. The authors derive two broad classes with exactly that property.

Their construction runs through a 1D map that generates the discretizations systematically. Numerics on two representative cases show the discrete kinks have no internal modes, matching the continuum theory, though an extra high-frequency mode can appear above the phonon band. Generic discretizations fail to hold static kinks at all, producing self-accelerating kinks that radiate as they travel.
arxiv-2512-22676:
Sergey Salishev's thesis develops signal processing algorithms that use as little parallelism and memory as possible, aiming at energy-efficient low-power hardware. Chips that compute with fewer active parts and smaller memories burn less power, but squeezing an algorithm down without wrecking its accuracy or speed takes care. The thesis attacks that trade-off from several directions at once.

One part builds a power model for clocked CMOS logic that helps choose the best level of parallelism for a design. Another gives integer-friendly approximations of elementary functions with guaranteed accuracy, shrinking lookup tables through piecewise-polynomial constructions. A third part arranges data and execution order for streaming fast Fourier transforms so that multi-bank and single-port memories never conflict, including a self-sorting variant. The final part analyzes the fast Schur algorithm for solving Toeplitz systems, a workload motivated by echo cancellation.
arxiv-2512-22776:
S. A. Bogatyi, E. A. Reznichenko, and A. A. Tuzhilin prove a stability result about maps between metric spaces that almost preserve distances and almost cover their targets. The setting uses cardinality homogeneous spaces, where every nonempty open piece has as many points as the whole space, and both spaces have the same total cardinality. A map that is nearly an isometry and nearly surjective is shown to be close to a perfect one.

Precisely, a near-isometry with a small surjectivity defect between such spaces guarantees a genuine bijective map whose distance error is only slightly larger. That bridge lets the authors reduce the Dilworth-Tabor theorem to the earlier Gevirtz-Omladič-Šemrl approximation theorem. In particular, hard questions about when Banach spaces must be isometric can be rerouted through approximation results, connecting two lines of work in the geometry of metric and normed spaces.
arxiv-2512-23276:
Soonki Hong and Sanghoon Kwon introduce a chamber zeta function for complexes of groups, lifting a graph invariant into higher-rank geometry. For graphs, the Ihara zeta function counts closed walks through an Euler product, and its Ihara-Bass formula uses a determinant.
