The authors replace walks with chamber galleries, sequences of adjacent chambers, inside the Bruhat-Tits building of the group PGL3 over a non-archimedean local field.

Working on the arithmetic quotient of that building, they prove a determinant formula of Ihara-Bass type. The chamber zeta function equals the reciprocal of a characteristic polynomial of a defined chamber transfer operator. A consequence is that the zeta function is rational in its parameter, a finiteness statement. The formula yields counting identities for classes of closed galleries built from tailless galleries. It gives spectral asymptotics governed by the chamber operator's eigenvalues, extending graph-theoretic ideas into building theory.
arxiv-2512-23476:
Laura Weidensager develops sensitivity analysis for functions defined on a sphere rather than in ordinary flat space. Sensitivity analysis splits a function's output into contributions from separate input variables and their interactions, a splitting known as an ANOVA decomposition. On a sphere the variables are naturally dependent through the geometry, so the classical flat-space version does not apply directly.

Her formulas decompose a function on the sphere into terms that each depend only on a chosen subset of the coordinates. The decomposition also separates parts of different parity, which adds a second index beyond the classical one. Working with suitable orthogonal basis functions, the method can approximate functions of many variables whose behavior is driven by low-dimensional interactions among them. The aim is to learn which inputs drive a model and which ones can be left out.
arxiv-2512-23576:
Ethan Chern and six co-authors built LiveTalk, a system for real-time interactive video avatars driven by text, image, and audio. Standard diffusion video models denoise all frames at once through many passes, which blocks live interaction. Distillation can make them fast and step-by-step, but the leading on-policy method produced flicker, black frames, and quality loss under multimodal conditioning.

The team improved the distillation recipe by focusing on the quality of the condition inputs and on how the on-policy training is initialized and scheduled. Their distilled model matched full-step baselines at about twenty times lower cost and latency on avatar benchmarks. Combined with audio language models and a long-video technique, LiveTalk answered in real time where systems such as Sora2 and Veo3 needed one to two minutes.
arxiv-2512-23776:
Dennis Wayo, Rodrigo Dias, Leonardo Goliatt, and Sven Groppe introduce DifGa. A way to undo noise in photonic quantum circuits while keeping the whole pipeline differentiable, so a computer can optimize the fix by gradient descent. Continuous-variable photonic systems suffer Gaussian loss, which leaks light into the environment, plus weaker non-Gaussian phase noise. Their testbed is a three-mode Gaussian circuit, signal, ancilla, and environment, built in the PennyLane simulator.

Error mitigation comes from a small trainable Gaussian recovery layer appended to the circuit, tuned to restore the signal mode's measured quadratures. Under pure loss the optimized recovery drove reconstruction error essentially to zero at moderate loss levels. With phase noise present, training that included Monte Carlo samples of the noise cut errors by more than tenfold compared with recovery trained on Gaussian loss alone. Runtime scaled linearly with the number of noise samples.
arxiv-2512-24076:
João Augusto Sobral, Pietro Bonetti, Subrata Mandal, and Mathias Scheurer build exactly solvable models of a recently named phase of matter: the altermagnetic quantum spin liquid. Spin liquids are magnetic states where spins never settle into order, yet this variety breaks time-reversal symmetry like an altermagnet while its net magnetic moment cancels out by symmetry.

Working with Majorana-based methods on two lattice designs, a square-octagon lattice and a checkerboard, the team studies spin three-halves and spin seven-halves versions. The smaller-spin model has a single ground state, a g-wave altermagnetic spin liquid. The larger-spin model is richer, with several chiral spin liquids competing against a d-wave variant. The authors also catalog the excitations of these phases, sorting which carry topological character and which do not, and showing how symmetry and topology combine in this new state of matter.
arxiv-2512-24176:
Xingyu Zhou and four colleagues improve diffusion transformers, the models behind much image generation. A diffusion model learns the full spread of its training data. Rare, low-probability regions get little training signal, though. Samples from those regions come out poorly. Guidance methods push sampling toward high-probability areas. The standard method often overshoots. Samples turn simplified or distorted.

Their strategy, Internal Guidance, uses the model itself. An auxiliary signal trains an intermediate layer. At sampling time, outputs of intermediate and deep layers are extrapolated. The recipe needs no extra degradation scheme. It also needs no extra training passes or sampling steps. Image quality and training efficiency both improved across baselines. One pairing reached the best reported score of its kind on ImageNet. The authors present the method as simple and broadly portable.
arxiv-2512-24376:
Shufang Su and four colleagues look for compressed Higgsinos at a forward detector. In the minimal supersymmetric model, these particles can be nearly equal in mass. A tiny mass gap makes the next-to-lightest neutralino long-lived. Such particles are produced in large numbers at the Large Hadron Collider. They escape the main detectors unseen, though.

The FASER experiment sits far downstream of a collision point. It is built to catch long-lived particles like these. The authors examine its discovery reach for this case. The upgraded FASER 2 could cover neutral masses up to about a hundred thirty giga-electronvolts. The relevant splittings are only a few to a few tens of mega-electronvolts. The coverage complements other searches. Main-detector hunts and displaced-track searches cover neighboring mass gaps. Together they leave these particles fewer places to hide.
arxiv-2512-24776:
Akos Prucs, Nara Csutora, Matyas Antal, and Mark Marosi map how open-source reasoning language models trade computing cost against accuracy. Long reasoning chains improve scores on hard math and reasoning tests, but they are expensive, and papers often ignore that burden. Their evaluation counts test-time compute alongside accuracy for newer and older models.

Mixture of Experts designs emerged as a strong balance of performance and efficiency in their setting. Tracing the frontier over time shows accuracy gains per unit of compute, plus a saturation point where extra reasoning stops helping. Industry readers get a practical guide for choosing models under real resource limits.
arxiv-2601-06676:
Yingchaojie Feng and co-authors present IDRBench in 2026, an interactive deep research benchmark. Deep research agents use language models for multi-step reasoning. They explore the web and generate long-form reports from findings.

Most existing systems operate autonomously, assuming fully specified user intent. They are evaluated only on their final outputs, the authors note. In practice, research goals are often underspecified at the start. Goals also evolve during exploration as users learn more. Sustained interaction is thus essential for robust alignment with users. IDRBench evaluates agents across that interaction, not just final reports. Benchmark designers get a model for testing dialogue-driven research. Agent builders can see where clarification helps or hurts quality.
arxiv-2601-07076:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ewa Bednarczuk and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Primal-Dual algorithms for abstract convex functions with respect to quadratic functions. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The authors consider the saddle point problem where the objective functions are abstract convex with respect to the class of quadratic functions.

The authors propose primal-dual algorithms using the corresponding abstract proximal operator and investigate the convergence under certain restrictions. We test our algorithms by several numerical examples. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07176:
Guanglin Rang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with local linearization for the nonlinear damped stochastic Klein-Gordon equation. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Abstract: For the 1+1 dimensional nonlinear damped stochastic Klein-Gordon equation driven by space-time white noise. We prove that the second-order increments of the solution can be approximated.

After scaling with the diffusion coefficient, by those of the corresponding linearized stochastic Klein-Gordon equation. This extends the result of Huang et al. [ 18 ] for the stochastic wave equation. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07776:
Roger Casals writes a short note linking two counts from different parts of mathematics. Bruhat numbers come from real Morse theory, which studies smooth functions through their critical points. Cluster variables come from braid varieties, spaces tied to algebraic combinatorics. Casals relates the first to the second. The note appears as a 2026 preprint on wall-crossing coordinates in Cerf theory.

Wall-crossing coordinates track how quantities change as a path crosses a boundary between regimes. Cerf diagrams organize families of functions and their changes. Finding cluster variables inside this story connects Morse theory to a fast-growing algebraic framework. Short bridges like this often open new computation tools on both sides. The note is aimed at geometers and topologists. Its subject classifications span contact geometry, topology, and cluster algebras.
arxiv-2601-07976:
Hongwei Lin and Howard C. Gifford advance task-based assessment of medical images with a model observer that searches like a person. Their 2026 preprint develops an anthropomorphic thresholded visual-search model observer. The model is an ideal observer adapted to thresholded data and inspired by the human visual system. It selectively processes high-salience features. That filtering improves discrimination performance in the search task.

Model observers predict how well imaging systems support real diagnostic tasks. Thresholding mimics how humans ignore low-value detail to focus effort. Filtering out irrelevant variability raises accuracy and computational efficiency together. Such models let designers compare scanners without costly human reader studies. The paper serves medical imaging scientists. It refines a tool used to judge image quality by task value rather than looks.
arxiv-2601-08076:
Mikolaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki reply to a recent proposal in quantum theory. Their 2026 arXiv comment examines a paper by Vigoureux on superposition of states. Vigoureux had suggested swapping the usual linear superposition rule for a Mobius-type composition law.

The proposal drew on three sources for support. They were bounded composition laws in special relativity, transfer-matrix formulas in layered optics, and the inclusion-exclusion rule for classical chance. A comment paper tests whether such analogies can carry a change to a core quantum rule. Readers get a close check on a bold claim, written for physicists who follow debates over quantum foundations.
arxiv-2601-08176: Lavanya Prahallad and co-authors study how prompt design shapes automatic clarity scoring for political answers. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that judging language model responses needs clarity, not just factual correctness. Political question answering makes clarity and evasion especially important to track. Recent datasets supply human labels for clarity and evasion in this setting. The team uses the CLARITY dataset from the SemEval-2026 shared task. Their focus is the underexplored effect of prompt wording on whether automatic judges match human clarity judgments.
arxiv-2601-08376: Masahiro Kawamata and co-authors determine the magnetic structure of EuTi2Al20. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a compound where magnetic europium ions form a diamond network. The team used neutron and resonant X-ray diffraction on powder and single-crystal samples. From these measurements they fixed the propagation vector at (1, 0, 0) in reciprocal lattice units. The structure is collinear, with moments aligned along one axis. Diamond lattice magnets host rich physics, so a firm structure anchors later work on their excitations.
arxiv-2601-08676:
Yilei Zhao and five co-authors work on green and fair scores for firms. Such scores judge how a firm treats the earth, its staff, and its own rules. The facts for these scores lie in many loose text sources. That spread makes expert checks slow and hard to do well.

The team builds an expert level agent for this task. An agent here is a program that can plan steps and use tools. They also build a broad test set for green finance work. The test set lets others check how well such agents do. A reader gets both a new tool and a fair way to grade tools of this kind.
arxiv-2601-08776:
Yanhua Zhao works on a way to make lab images look like the stained slides doctors know best. In most labs, tissue is dyed pink and blue so staff can read it with ease. Light sheet scans give rich views, but they look quite unlike those dyed slides. Staff may find them hard to read at first.

Zhao uses a pair of rival nets called a CycleGAN. One net turns light sheet views into fake dyed views. The next net turns them back, which keeps the first net true to the source. No paired slides are needed to train the pair. A reader in lab work gets a bridge from new scan types to a form the eye knows well.
arxiv-2601-09676:
Rob Behary and eight co-authors study how a steady electric field tilts a quantum transparency effect. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines electromagnetically induced transparency involving highly excited Rydberg states. The team varies the angle between the laser polarization and the external field.

That orientation changes the transparency resonances in ways the paper maps out. Rydberg atoms are prized sensors because their outer electrons reach far and react strongly. Knowing how a stray field's direction shifts the signal matters for precision devices. The results help calibrate sensors that use transparency as their readout.
arxiv-2601-09776:
Khalid Oublal and four co-authors explain black-box forecasts of time series with sparse decoding. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents TimeSAE, built for faithful explanations. As pretrained models spread in time series work, users need to know why a forecast came out as it did.

The stakes are highest where trust matters, such as medicine and finance. Most explanation methods work only inside the training distribution. They falter on new regimes, exactly where explanations are needed most. TimeSAE aims for explanations that stay faithful well beyond the range of the training support.
arxiv-2601-10076:
Matthew Zhang proves sharp rates for how a crowd of grains acts as one. Each grain is pushed by the rest. Over time, the crowd can settle to a fixed spread. That shift is named propagation of chaos. It says the grains act more free as the crowd grows.

Zhang works at the rest state of such a crowd. He uses a ranked chain of facts from past work. He bounds the gap in Rényi terms, a broad gap gauge. The bounds hold when the base spread is well curved and the push is weak. The rates are sharp, which means no slack is left.
arxiv-2601-10176:
Mingyu Zhao, Haoran Bai, Yu Tian, Bing Zhu, and Hengliang Luo guess the long term worth of a user. This worth is named lifetime value. It is a core call in ad work. Most users are worth a small sum. A few whales are worth a vast sum.

That shape makes the guess hard. The mass of small users can swamp the whales in the math. Small users also vary a lot among them. The team built CC-OR-Net to split the task in two. It parts users by kind first. It then makes a worth call for each kind on its own terms.
arxiv-2601-10376:
Mohammad Rowshan and Vlad-Florin Drăgoi build polar codes with both reach and weight in mind. Polar codes rank their bit paths by trust. That rank plan gives codes that can hit the cap of a line. But it can yield poor low weight forms at short lengths.

Low weight words set how oft a code fails at high trust. Past algebra gives each path's part in those words in closed form. The team blend the two guides. Trust ranks one part. Weight counts rule the rest. The aim is a code that is sound on both counts.
arxiv-2601-10576:
Shaohua Yue, Siyu Miao, Shuhao Zeng, Fenghan Lin, and Boya Di study massive MIMO, a core tool planned for 6G wireless networks. Massive MIMO uses many antennas at once. It offers many degrees of freedom, which raise how much data can flow at once. The team asks how many of those degrees a real system can truly reach.

They bring in characteristic mode analysis, a tool from antenna theory, to derive the reachable degrees of freedom. The method looks at the natural modes of the antenna structure itself. That view can guide how antennas are shaped and placed. The paper speaks to engineers who design the next wave of wireless hardware.
arxiv-2601-11276:
R. Ricci studies a new class of special functions in this 2026 preprint. The functions arose in work on hot, magnetized plasma. There they enter the linear susceptibility tensor, a core plasma tool. The class sits close to Bessel, Anger, and Weber functions.

Ricci checks the basic traits of these new functions. They solve a Bessel-type equation with an added term. Set starting values pin down which solution is meant. The added term meets a known condition due to Nielsen. Such checks turn a handy formula into a sound tool. Plasma physics can then use the class with more trust.
arxiv-2601-11376:
Karsten Muller and Michael Taktikos make a deep number theory bound effective. Their 2026 preprint links the ABC conjecture to Roth's theorem. Roth's theorem bounds how well irrationals can be approximated. Bombieri showed in 1994 that ABC would imply Roth's result.

Van Frankenhuysen gave a full proof of that link in 1999. The new work builds on an explicit formula by Bombieri. Van der Poorten shares credit for that formula on coefficients. The formula covers continued-fraction coefficients of algebraic numbers. The team narrows it to cubic roots as the test case. From it they derive a hard bound for a Roth-type constant. The bound holds if an effective form of ABC is true.
arxiv-2601-11476:
Allen Shafter and Kamil Hornoch read basic traits of novae in M31. Their 2026 preprint uses a large sample from Clark and others. Novae are stellar blasts on white dwarfs in the Andromeda galaxy. Peak brightness and fade rate are logged for each nova.

The team fits those logs with Yaron's nova models. From the fits they estimate traits of the whole population. The white dwarf mass spread comes out near Gaussian in form. Its mean sits near 1.16 solar masses in their count. That is heavy, close to the known Chandrasekhar limit. Such census work tests how novae enrich and shape galaxies. It also checks the models used to read stellar blasts.
arxiv-2601-11776:
Kaituo Zhang, Zhimeng Jiang, and Na Zou present a way to clean toxic output from large language models. Large models can fix and grade their own text to some degree. Most clean-up tools so far do not use that skill. They add outer parts, hand marked data, or human help, which is slow and hard to scale.

Their frame leans on the model's own self-checks in place of outer help. A self-led clean-up could stay more smooth as models grow. It could also cut the cost of marked data. The work tests if a model can spot and fix its own toxic text in a sound loop.
arxiv-2601-12076:
Haochen Jiang, Yuzhe Sun, Zhe Dong, Tianzhu Liu, and Yanfeng Gu track objects named in text in remote sensing video. The task joins video segmentation with a text brief for the target. Far views make targets faint, and dynamic scenes often cut off key views.

Their tool, named in the work, controls memory quality as it tracks. Good memory keeps the target's traits clear across frames. Weak memory lets drift and clutter spoil the cut. The work aims for steadier cuts in hard aerial video.  Good tracks help watch coasts, fields, and roads from air.
arxiv-2601-12376:
Ofek Raban, Ethan Fetaya, and Gal Chechik write on watermarking text from language models. A watermark marks text so that readers can tell it came from a model. It also helps link the text back to its source. Most past methods were built for models that write one token at a time, in strict order.

That order based design fits a world that is now changing. A newer class of models, called diffusion language models, does not write in the same strict sequence. Old marks lean on the text sampled so far, so they may not carry over well. The team puts forward LR-DWM, a mark built for this newer class. The goal is a mark that stays fast and still holds up.
arxiv-2601-12476:
Omkar Dhamane and a large team study energy conversion in the solar wind during a solar storm. The storm is an interplanetary coronal mass ejection, a cloud of plasma thrown off by the Sun. Inside the magnetic cloud of such an event, bursts of turbulence are less common than outside. The team found two such bursts in data from the Wind spacecraft.

The data come from June 8 and 9 in the year 2000. The plasma there is weakly collisional, so particles rarely bump into each other. The team characterize the wave types present in the two bursts. Waves are a main route for energy to move in such plasmas. Knowing which waves appear helps explain how energy converts during these storms.
arxiv-2601-12776:
Yonghui Bo and Yushun Wang construct numerical schemes for Hamiltonian partial differential equations. Hamiltonian systems conserve energy, and good schemes should preserve that trait. Their approach uses Lagrange multipliers to build linearly implicit schemes of arbitrary order. Linearly implicit methods are cheap per step, while high order keeps errors small.

A widely used rival approach relies on auxiliary variables. That approach needs the nonlinear part of the energy to be bounded below. The new method drops that requirement, offering broader applicability. Energy preserving schemes run longer without drifting off course. They matter for waves, plasmas, and molecular dynamics alike. The work was supported by Chinese science foundations.
arxiv-2601-12976:
Wenhao Gao and ten co authors jointly analyze galaxy clustering and galaxy galaxy lensing from BOSS galaxies. Clustering maps how galaxies group in space, while lensing measures the mass around them. A joint analysis squeezes more cosmology from the same sky survey. Their method uses simulation based emulation with a halo occupation model.

The emulators are built from a suite of N body simulations with massive neutrinos. Those simulations treat neutrinos as an independent particle species. Emulation replaces slow full simulations with fast learned surrogates inside the fit. Small scale data carry rich signal but are hard to model directly. This approach aims to unlock that signal for cosmology.
arxiv-2601-13076:
Gabriele Parisi wrote a thesis on heavy quarks in the first instants of proton ion crashes. Heavy quarks are the heaviest bits of matter, made fresh in high energy hits. The thesis rests in large part on joint papers with Vincenzo Greco and Marco Ruggieri.

One named paper treats uneven swings of momentum and of spin like motion for heavy quarks. That work sits in the pre balance stage of proton nucleus crashes at the Large Hadron Collider. It appeared in Physical Review D in 2025. Readers get a guide to how heavy quarks move before the hot matter from the crash settles.
arxiv-2601-13176:
Joseph G. Schulze, Natalie R. Hinkel, Wendy R. Panero, and Cayman T. Unterborn warn care in how small far worlds are read. The bulk make up of a small world ties straight to how it was born. Yet no probe can see inside such a world. Its make up must be read from mass and size alone, through a model.

Those models lean on star make up and on laws for how stuff acts at high crush. The team sets models side by side and asks where the laws part ways. They urge care in how much trust a single model read gets. For world birth staff, the piece is a check list for sound claims about rocky worlds.
arxiv-2601-13476:
Jinhao Li and Hao Wang fill gaps in electric vehicle charge data with a retrieval led language model in one joint frame. Charge data feeds demand guesses for the charge grid. Real sets are full of gaps. Old fill tools bend poorly to the rich mix of charge data. Many train one model per station, a form that wastes shared facts.

Their frame imputes gaps in a variational way, a chance based fill with a firm score. A language model fed by pulled kin cases leads the fill. One frame serves all stations at once. For grid teams, a sound fill of charge gaps lifts all down stream guesses.
arxiv-2601-13676:
Fabian Greifeneder and co-authors build a fast brain tissue simulator for virtual neurosurgery in 2026. True-to-life training tools must show how brain tissue bends and shifts. Tool-tissue contact makes complex, nonlinear shapes as the work goes on. Classic solvers can capture that, but they run too slowly for live use.

The team uses autoregressive deep learning, which predicts each next state from the last. That style can run fast once trained, step by step in real time. Trainees could then feel how tissue reacts as they work. Fast, true tissue models could make surgical training safer and richer.
arxiv-2601-14376:
Xiyuan Gao and Amir N. Khan study neutrino masses in this 2026 paper. Neutrinos are the lightest known particles with mass. The authors assume all three known neutrinos are Dirac fermions, particles distinct from their antiparticles. Under that take, the U(1) B-L symmetry can be exact. B-L is baryon number minus lepton number.

The team then relaxes one rule: charge quantization. With that change, the B-L charges of two of the three right-handed neutrinos can be enhanced by arbitrarily large factors. All other fermions keep their canonical charges. Their title calls this enhanced B-L symmetry. The paper maps what such an enhanced symmetry does to neutrino mass models.
arxiv-2601-14776:
Xiaofan Yang and seven co-authors improve multi-modal object detection in this 2026 paper. Recent advances in multi-modal detection have significantly improved detection accuracy in challenging environments, such as low light and overexposure. Integrating RGB images with modalities such as thermal and depth increases data redundancy and system robustness. Significant challenges remain, though.

The hard parts are extracting task-relevant information within and across modalities, and achieving precise cross-modal alignment. Their model, M2I2HA, is based on intra- and inter-modal hypergraph attention. Hypergraphs let one link join many items at once, a natural fit for cross-sensor groups. Rain, glare, and dusk are where weak tools fail, and this one is built for them. When one sense fails, the rest must pick up the slack. Readers get a fusion design for detectors that must work when one sense goes dark.
arxiv-2601-14876:
Antonin Grateau, Alexander Boeschoten, Tanguy Favin-Lévêque, Isael Herrera, and Nicolas Treps test a way to see two light sources that sit very close together. Their 2026 arXiv paper is about beating the blur limit of normal optics. The two sources shine on their own, with no shared phase.

The team sorts the light by its spatial modes, a method called SPADE. They use two such sorters, with one shifted on purpose. In the lab they gauge the gap, the center point, and the brightness split at once. The gaps they find sit well below the classic blur limit.
arxiv-2601-15176:
Alain Lecavelier des Etangs, Paul Strøm, and Darryl Z. Seligman propose names for single comets beyond our solar system. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with exocomets, comets that orbit other stars. The field has entered a new phase in recent years.

At first, scientists just had to prove that a signal truly came from an exocomet. Now single detections are studied in detail to characterize each body. That shift calls for a nomenclature, a shared naming scheme. The authors set one out so that teams can refer to the same object clearly.
arxiv-2601-15576:
Chenyang Xu and Ziquan Zhuang survey open problems in K-stability in a 2026 arXiv paper. K-stability theory concerns Fano varieties, a class of geometric spaces. A central aim in geometry is to find an optimal structure on a manifold. In differential geometry, one such structure is a metric solving the vacuum Einstein equations. The Kähler-Einstein problem asks when such metrics exist. K-stability gives an algebraic test linked to that question.

Rather than solve one problem, the note gathers many open ones. It maps where the theory stands and where it is stuck. Survey notes like this guide a field's next steps. Young researchers can see which questions are ripe. Senior readers get a compact status report on a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2601-15876:
Taofeng Xue and a large team train computer-use agents from synthetic practice in a 2026 arXiv paper. Computer-use agents operate software through its interface. They mark a real leap in multimodal AI. Their growth is bottlenecked by static data scaling, though. Learning by imitating fixed datasets misses causal dynamics. Long computer tasks hinge on causes: one click changes what the next should be. Their system is EvoCUA.

EvoCUA evolves agents through scalable synthetic experience, per the title. Synthetic tasks can be generated in bulk and varied at will. Agents learn by doing, not just by watching. That shift mirrors how people gain computer skill. For software automation, agents that recover and adapt across long tasks are the goal this work pursues.
arxiv-2601-15976:
Gloria Odak and Salvatore Ribisi extend a variant of general relativity in a 2026 arXiv paper. The variant is Weyl-transverse gravity. It is classically equivalent to general relativity, the authors note. Its gauge symmetry is smaller, though. It allows Weyl transformations and transverse diffeomorphisms only. A fixed background volume form is part of the setup. The authors develop its covariant phase space formulation in the presence of boundaries.

Boundaries can be timelike or spacelike in their treatment. Edges matter in phase space methods because charges live there. A formulation that handles general boundaries makes the theory usable for finite regions. Such regions are where physics is actually computed. The work serves relativists comparing alternative formulations of gravity.
arxiv-2601-16376:
Vani Nigam, Achuth Chandrasekhar and Amir Barati Farimani set an agent to design polymers. Their 2026 preprint, named PolyAgent, deals with on call polymer finds. New polymers serve health, build and strength fields. Lab trials for them are slow and eat much time and stock. Past machine tools sped finds but still need much hand work.

An agent built on a large language model can plan find steps. It can call tools, read results and pick next tries on its own. That loop cuts the hand work in each find round. The team tests the agent on real design tasks. The work seeks fast, low cost polymer finds.
arxiv-2601-16476:
The BESIII group hunts a rare glow decay of a strange charmed meson. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Ds meson and a K star end state. The hunt uses clash data from the BESIII probe. Data span a set range of clash heat at its heart. A joint fit hunts the faint sign of the rare decay.

Rare decays test the known model of grains in fine ways. A seen sign would pin a rate the model must match. No sign sets a cap that the model must not cross. Both ends thus sharpen grain maths in the charm field. The work is a probe note from a big group.
arxiv-2601-16576:
W. Geremew, V. S. T. Long, N. M. Nam, and A. Solano-Herrera work on a hard math task. A firm must place sites, like depots or shops, to serve many users. The best count of sites is not known in advance. Their 2026 preprint builds a new model for this task.

The model adds a cost term that curbs needless sites. The team then finds a way to solve it step by step. They prove that best-fit answers do exist. They also study traits of those best answers. Tests on a screen back the math. The work may aid plans for stores, clinics, and charge points.
arxiv-2601-16676:
Andrii Dmytryshyn, Froilán Dopico, and Rakel Hellberg work on a niche task in matrix math. Some tasks use rules that link numbers in a grid over time-like steps. A few of those grids must stay skewed, with a mirror twist. Real data grids are rough and may break that trait. Their 2026 preprint finds the near skewed grid of a set rank.

Their method builds on fresh work on grid forms and splits. It takes a rough grid and trims it to the near fit. The rank cap keeps the fit from mere copy. Such near fits help in tests of speech, signals, and forms. Clean math here feeds tools far past pure math.
arxiv-2601-16776:
Jiaqi Hu, Shu Tian, Xiaopeng Cui, Rebing Wu, Man-Hong Yung, and Yu Shi extend a famed math link in gauge theory. Gauge rules on a grid can map to spin grids in a twin form. That twin form is called Wegner duality. On odd shapes, like rings with holes, the link stayed unclear. Their 2026 preprint clears that fog for all shapes and depths.

Their twin spin grids code shape in far-off wall paths. The work also sets up how quantum sims can use the link. Odd shapes show up in codes that guard quantum data. A clear twin map helps build and test those codes.
arxiv-2601-16876:
Moisés Davi tests guards for the power lines of sea wind farms. Sea farms send power to land through deep cables. New grid gear turns that power for long hauls. Faults in farm cables act in odd ways there. Both cable ends feed fault flow from smart gear. That trait can fool old-style guards.

His 2026 preprint checks how split guards fare on such cables. Split guards compare flow at both ends of a line. The work maps where those guards hold or fail. Sound guards stop faults fast and save costly gear. Sea wind growth makes such checks more key each year.
arxiv-2601-16976:
Estela Sánchez-Carballo, Francisco Melgarejo-Meseguer, and José Luis Rojo-Álvarez grow fake attack data to guard smart gear. Guards that watch net traffic learn from past flows. Attack flows are rare next to plain flows. That skew makes guards blind to rare attacks. Past fixes copy rare flows or grow crude fakes.

Their 2026 preprint grows fakes with a spread-based AI. Such AI can make fakes that look rich and true. It can also run at fair cost on small gear. Rich fakes may teach guards to catch rare IoT attacks. Smart homes and wards need that guard skill.
arxiv-2601-17076:
Jiajun Chen and a team of eight co-authors teach web tools that learn in hard, mixed streams. Web apps join text, shots, and sound from many sources. Class sets grow as new themes show up. Views oft miss from the stream, with gaps in spots. Their 2026 preprint builds a prompt-learn tool for that mix. The tool is named E2PL.

Prompt learning tunes small prompt marks, not whole nets. That keeps cost low as classes grow. The tool must still hold old class skill. It must also cope with views that drop out. Web shops and feeds need such steady growth.
arxiv-2601-17176:
Michael Adams and Andreas Michels build a lean model for swirls in round magnet grains. Grains past a set size form swirl-like spin forms. Those forms come from a fight of two energies. Exchange pulls spins to align as one. Stray field pulls them to loop and close. Their 2026 preprint gives a semi-analytic path for those swirls. Past work leaned on heavy screen sims for them.

Their path shows how swirls are born and flip. Hysteresis loops for round grains fall out too. Lean paths let teams scan grain traits fast. Such grains serve memory and sensor work.
arxiv-2601-17576:
Gauge-mediated supersymmetry models motivate this search for a long-lived stau. The stau is the supersymmetric partner of the tau lepton. In these models it can live long on particle scales. Its decay then yields tau leptons far from the collision point. That displaced signature is rare and striking. The search uses proton-proton collision data.

A displaced tau is hard to fake with standard processes. That makes the hunt clean, if the tools can catch it. No author is named in the record for this entry. The work tests a key supersymmetry breaking scheme. A find would reshape particle physics. A null result still trims the space of viable models.
arxiv-2601-17676:
Jiexin Ding and six co-authors present GazeSummary, a study of gaze as a prompt for assistants. Smart glasses now pair language models with rich inputs. Most inputs still need explicit prompts, which can be obtrusive. Gaze tracking offers an implicit signal of intent. The team asks if models can read gaze for text tasks. Personalization is the goal of that read.

If gaze works as a prompt, help can arrive with less friction. A glance could tell the model what text matters. Privacy and accuracy are clear concerns to test. The study is an early probe of that channel. It may shape how glasses assist in daily reading. Hands-free help is the draw.
arxiv-2601-17976:
Alexey A. Kryukov builds a new frame for the quantum measurement problem. His 2026 preprint asks how a quantum system comes to show one definite outcome. His dynamics stay unitary, which means no step breaks the rules of quantum evolution. The twist is randomness: Hamiltonians are drawn at random from a classic ensemble, and they drive the state in a stochastic yet unitary way. Detector limits then group states into classes that act as classical readings.

With that setup, Kryukov revisits famous quantum paradoxes. He traces how the classical world emerges from quantum motion. The frame tries to keep both worlds in one set of rules. Work of this kind tests the deep story physics tells about observation itself.
arxiv-2601-18176:
Malihe Heydari-Fard and Mohaddese Heydari-Fard construct rotating black holes that sit inside a dark matter halo. Their 2026 preprint starts from known static, round black holes in a Hernquist-type halo. That profile describes how dark matter thins out with distance from a galaxy's center. Using the Newman-Janis algorithm, the authors spin those static solutions up into rotating ones. The result is a stationary, axially symmetric metric for a black hole in this galactic setting.

They also study the light given off by the hole's accretion disk. Real black holes live in galaxies, not in empty space. Halo-aware models give truer predictions for what telescopes see. The work joins galaxy structure with black hole physics.
arxiv-2601-18276:
Claudio Macci and co-authors prove a large deviation principle for wide neural networks. Their 2026 preprint deals with fully connected multi-layer perceptrons. The weights are random Gaussian values under LeCun initialization. The activation functions may be any Lipschitz ones, which includes the popular ReLU. A large deviation principle describes how unlikely, extreme outputs behave as the network grows wide. The authors establish the principle for the whole output process on any compact input set.

Extreme behavior matters for safety bounds and for rare-event estimates. A functional result covers curves of inputs, not just single points. The work extends the theory of wide networks past average behavior. It gives probabilists and learning theorists a shared tool.
arxiv-2601-18376:
Jens Kosiol and Steffen Zschaler write a short note for work on graphs and the rules that sort them. Their tools, called nested conditions, state what a small graph must or must not hold for a rule to pass. The rules can stack, with one rule set inside the next. That stack makes them hard to read and to use.

The pair show that the stack can be flattened. For the kind of graph sets at hand, each rule can be put in a form with no nest at all. The flat form says the same thing as the stacked form. A flat rule is far less hard to check by hand or by machine. The note thus cleans up a tool that shows up in graph based design and in checks on code and data.
arxiv-2601-18676:
Miles Martinez and Alex Williams build deep learn tools that find a very low, clear code for rich data sets. Most such tools learn a code by a guess-and-check path that needs a trained guide net. That path can blur the code and make it hard to read. Their plan skips the guide net. It works out the true score of each code by a near-dice sum with a smart twist.

The twist uses points spread with more care than pure chance, so the sum is firm with fewer points. With a firm score in hand, the tool can hunt for codes that are both small and true. A small, clear code for a rich set could show its deep form at a glance. That would help in fields from gene maps to shot sets.
arxiv-2601-18776:
Laura Buchanan and fourteen colleagues report a sky hunt that read the hues of far small worlds past Neptune. Those worlds are scraps left from the birth of our sun's brood. Their hues hold clues to where each was born and what coats its face. The hunt caught a full set down to a set glow, so no hue was missed by chance. Like past hunts, it found two hue crowds: red, and still more red.

The team put forth a new way to sort the coats, by how they drink light in the near red band past sight. That sort may map the crowds to birth zones with more truth than hue alone. A firm sort could help tell how the young brood was stirred and spread. The hunt's full set makes its counts a firm base for that work.
arxiv-2601-18876:
Danny Horta and six colleagues find a new way to read how fast stars run in rings around our galaxy's core. That speed, at each span from the core, is a key chart. It sets the mass of the galaxy and the pull of its dark halo. Past reads lean on the paths and speeds of stars read head on. Those reads are dear and can be bent by gas and dust.

Their path leans on the stuff in stars. The mix of stuff in a star tracks the ring path it was born to, in a known way. By how that mix shifts with a star's in-out speed, the team can read the ring speed curve. A new path to the curve gives a check on the old reads. It could also work where head-on reads fail.
arxiv-2601-18976:
Wolf-Rüdiger Hannes and Guido Burkard design a way to build up shared quantum links between long lived units. Their units are qudits, held by the spins of atomic nuclei inside defect centers in a crystal. Each node also has an electron spin, which serves as the talkative partner that can link to other nodes.

Links between electrons, perhaps made through light, can then be handed over and stored in the quiet nuclei. Stacking such handovers could grow a web of stored entanglement. Stored links of this kind are a raw good for quantum networks and repeaters that pass quantum data over distance.
arxiv-2601-19076:
Can Polat and four co-authors test whether models that dream up materials can jump across scales. Models for making new materials do well on bulk crystals that repeat without end. Real use often needs finite grains, where surfaces rule and size warps the shape, and skill across that jump is mostly untested.

Their bench, C2NP, scores models as they move from unit cells to nanoparticles. It checks whether the deep patterns a model learned at one scale still hold at the other. A clear scale test matters because drugs, catalysts, and devices all live at the small end of the scale.
arxiv-2601-19176:
Yi Lyu, Pei-Chieh Lo, and Natan Lidukhover build a benchmark for data lakes. Data lakes store vast mixed data for later use, and their use keeps growing. Yet few standard benchmarks exist to grade them, so claims about speed and cost rest on uneven tests.

A shared benchmark would give a fair, comparative view of rival systems. Buyers could see which lake design fits their loads, and builders could prove gains on common ground. The team sets out the problem and their plan for filling that gap in how these systems are judged.
arxiv-2601-19276:
Shengjia Zhang and seven co-authors aim recommender training squarely at the top of the list. A recommender's job is to surface a small set of items that best match a user's taste. Users see only the top few, so quality there matters far more than quality deep in the ranking.

Their method, Talos, optimizes top K accuracy directly rather than a loose proxy. Training for the metric that users feel should sharpen the head of the list where clicks happen. The work was shared at the ACM Web Conference, a main venue for web scale ranking research.
arxiv-2601-19376:
Viacheslav Sydora, Guner Dilsad Er, and Michael Muehlebach teach machine learning to teens with LEGO robots. Their platform, Machine Learning with Bricks, pairs a web tool with a two day course for students aged twelve to seventeen. No programming is needed: the robots and the screens carry the ideas.

Students meet three core methods through hands on play: nearest neighbors, linear regression, and Q-learning. Interactive visuals show what each method does as the robot acts. Early, tactile contact with these ideas can demystify AI for students long before they meet its math.
arxiv-2601-19676:
Jannik Zenner, Karl Ulrich Schreiber, and Simon Stellmer work on giant ring lasers. A longer laser cavity gives a narrower, purer beam. In large gas lasers, though, the gap between the cavity's natural tones shrinks. It can become far smaller than the width of the gain profile that feeds the laser.

That crowding means many tones can grow at once, spoiling the single clean tone users want. The authors study how to steer the light in such a large ring. Optical steering offers a way to favour the desired mode. Large ring lasers serve in precision measurement, including rotation sensing for geodesy. Controlling their modes keeps those measurements sharp.
arxiv-2601-20076:
Abhishek Chakraborty and Angelia Nedić study how to minimize a function while staying inside a feasible set defined by many convex constraints. Projecting onto that set can be too costly, so exact projection methods fail here. The authors use a randomized feasibility method that samples a few constraints at each step and moves using Polyak steps.

They pair those feasibility steps with gradient steps on the objective. Two cases are covered: a smooth, strongly convex objective, and a convex objective that may be nonsmooth. Step sizes adapt as the method runs. The work gives theory for optimization problems where the constraint set is known only through many separate pieces.
arxiv-2601-20376:
Alessandro Cerioni tackles zero-order diffraction, a bright unwanted spot that plagues computer-generated holography. In phase-only holograms shown across the full field of view, this stray light sits in the middle of the image. Cerioni introduces an interferometric method that cancels it with a suppression beam.

The beam is arranged to interfere destructively with the zero-order light, in a plane matched to the spatial light modulator that shows the hologram. A camera in the loop guides the setup. Cleaner holograms matter for holographic displays and imaging, where the central artifact now limits quality.
arxiv-2601-20476:
Evanfiya Logacheva and five colleagues test whether giving examples in context improves AI-generated diagrams for teaching. Generative AI is now widespread in computing education, yet the quality of its materials worries teachers and students. The authors build a method for diagram code generation that uses in-context examples shaped by rhetorical structure theory.

The method aims to align model output with user expectations. Their title flags the catch: one hallucinated example can spoil the whole set. The study speaks to any teacher using AI to draft figures, code, or exercises. One bad example, as the title warns, can spoil the whole bunch.
arxiv-2601-20576:
B.-H. Yue and six colleagues probe the link between halo mass and radio jet activity in quasars. Quasars that look very similar can show a wide range of radio jet powers, and the reason is not understood. The large-scale environment is thought to play an important role.

A quasar's halo, the dark matter structure hosting it, sets much of that environment. If halo mass tracks jet power, environment would explain part of the spread. The answer would connect the small-scale physics of black hole feeding to the cosmic structures galaxies live in.
arxiv-2601-20676:
Zhuo Chen and six co-authors build a smarter agent for answering questions about images. Their 2026 paper tackles visual question answering, or VQA. A VQA system must join what it sees with what it reads. Only then can it answer well. The team adds a planning step to guide that work.

One known boost for VQA is retrieval-augmented generation. The system fetches extra image and text evidence before it answers. But the standard recipe chains many stages, and each stage waits on the last. The authors propose a planning agent to run this process with less waste. The paper speaks to the push for AI that answers hard, knowledge-heavy questions about pictures.
arxiv-2601-21076:
Abhijith Shaji and five co-authors fill in missing brain scans with a generative model. Their 2026 paper concerns Alzheimer's disease classification from magnetic resonance imaging. Deep learning predicts such disorders well from MRI. Combining multiple scan types can raise diagnostic performance. T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted scans each carry distinct information. Complete multimodal datasets, however, are not always available. Missing scans can block a patient from the best model.

The authors use a conditional diffusion model to impute the missing scans. It generates diffusion-weighted images from T1 scans. The filled-in data then feed the classifier. This multi-modal imputation keeps patients in the pipeline despite gaps. The approach serves clinics where scan time and cost vary. It is a practical step toward robust medical AI.
arxiv-2601-21276:
Haoming Huang and five co-authors study what happens to code quality when AI agents write pull requests. These agents now help with coding tasks and can produce changes fast. Speed, though, may come with costs that only show up later in review and upkeep.

The authors compare AI-written changes with human ones and track how reviewers react. Their title sums up the worry: more code, but less of it reused. Large fresh blocks can be harder to review and maintain than small edits that build on what exists. The study gives teams data on how agent output lands in real projects.
arxiv-2601-21676:
Dongsu Bak and Jae-Weon Lee ask how the seeds of supermassive black holes formed inside halos of ultralight dark matter. The early universe shows giant black holes surprisingly soon after the Big Bang. Their seeds must have grown from something, and light dark matter halos offer a setting.

The authors focus on the halo's Jeans scale and its dense central core, called a soliton. Gas trapped by that core can collapse directly into a heavy seed. The team identifies the conditions for that monolithic collapse. The picture connects the odd bright objects dubbed little red dots to a concrete seed story.
arxiv-2601-21776:
Chiara Ribaldone and Jacques Kontak Desmarais work on a basic task in the study of solids: computing the electrostatic potential inside a crystal. Because a crystal repeats forever, the sums behind that potential converge slowly, and Ewald-type techniques exist to speed them up.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a model charge density designed to cancel the multipole moments of the crystal's charge distribution, up to any chosen order. With those moments removed, the Ewald sums converge faster. Faster and more accurate potentials matter for simulating materials. Since electric forces shape almost everything a solid does, from its structure to how it carries charge and heat.
arxiv-2601-22176:
Isabel Tardón and Pablo Martín-Santamaría turn a French composer's craft into math. Jean Barraqué wrote stark, fierce music in the last age. He built his works from rows of notes that grow and spread, called proliferating series. In the old serial craft, the gaps from note to note stay fixed as a row is worked.

Barraqué kept a new thing fixed. What stays the same is the swap of notes that takes place from one step of the growth to the next. The pair sort and rank these rows with math. Their work lets us test scores and notes with care. It shows how this dense music was planned from the inside, note by note.
arxiv-2601-22276:
Mingyu Lu, Soham Gadgil, Chris Lin, Chanwoo Kim, and Su-In Lee value the people whose work trains image models. Their 2026 preprint, SurrogateSHAP, needs no fresh training runs to do the job. Text-to-image models now sit inside daily creative work, so fair pay for data is a live issue.

The method scores a whole set of a person's data at once, not one item at a time. Fair scores can back fair pay and a sound market for data. The team frame their tool as a base for that market. It gives a clear path from use to credit.
arxiv-2601-22376:
Run Wang and a large team build road maps for self-driving cars from whatever cameras a car happens to have. High-grade maps mark lanes and road parts in fine detail. Their 2026 preprint, FlexMap, notes that most builders demand a fixed, tuned camera rig. A dead camera or a new fleet layout can break them.

FlexMap aims to work from loose, varied camera setups. It turns flat views into a top-down road map in a way that bends with the rig. Safer maps from any rig would help fleets grow. The work targets a real weak point in road AI.
arxiv-2601-22476:
Ruizhe Zhong, Xingbo Du, and Junchi Yan built one learner that plans chip layouts under many design rules at once. Floorplanning sets the place and shape of each block on a chip. Their 2026 preprint, RulePlanner, notes that 3D stacks of layers make the rules far harder to obey.

Their reinforcement learner aims to meet the full rule set in one pass, not rule by rule. A unified planner could cut design time for dense chips. It could also find layouts human teams miss. The work targets a key step in chip design. It treats rules as the core problem.
arxiv-2601-22676:
Jinrui Sun, Tong Jia, Minghua He, and Ying Li built VarParser, a log parser that leans on the variables inside log lines. Logs are the first place engineers look when a big service fails. Their 2026 preprint notes that parsing — turning raw lines into clean events — is the first step for fault hunts.

Past parsers lean on the fixed text and slight the variable parts. VarParser flips that focus, and finds the variables carry rich signal. Better parses mean faster, truer fault diagnosis. The work serves the teams that keep online services alive. It is a small shift with wide reach.
arxiv-2601-23076:
Jayadev Joy and Sundeep Rangan recover signals in crowded, noisy radio bands planned for 6G. Receivers in the upper mid-band must work over wide bandwidths near strong neighboring signals. Under ideal hardware, linear receivers could suppress those neighbors.

Real hardware saturates and quantizes coarsely, so interference leaks across the spectrum in nonlinear ways. Their learning-based recovery is built for that messy reality. Cleaner reception in shared bands is key to faster, more reliable future wireless networks. Front-end nonlinearities are the practical villain: saturation and coarse quantization leak strong interference into the wanted band. The setting is upper mid-band spectrum planned for sixth-generation networks, where wide bandwidths meet dense neighboring signals.
arxiv-2601-23176:
Christian Robles and Suvrath Mahadevan test a new chip of tiny mirrors for solar spectroscopy. The device, a high-efficiency digital micromirror unit, works as a reconfigurable light modulator. It can reshape the field of view in real time during observations.

That flexibility allows targeted spectra of magnetically active solar regions, plus full-disk scans. The authors report the motivation and early tests for the instrument. Agile targeting could help solar physicists catch fast-changing regions as they flare and evolve. Early tests are the paper's scope, checking that the micromirror device performs as the spectroscopy design requires.
arxiv-2601-23276:
Shuhong Liu and eight co-authors model CCD noise from physics to clean deep-sky images. Sky imaging stays noise-limited under real observing conditions. Standard pipelines remove structured flaws, but random noise in the sensor is mostly left unresolved.

Learning-based cleaning is promising, yet paired training data are scarce and science needs interpretable models. Their physics-based making framework generates realistic CCD noise for training. Faithful noise models let cleaners learn the sensor's true behavior instead of generic blur. Physically interpretable, reproducible noise models are a stated requirement, since scientific imaging cannot rest on black-box flaws.
arxiv-2603-01576:
Earth models that map the planet from space have had little fair testing on ice and snow regions. Saurabh Kaushik, Lalit Maurya, and Beth Tellman fill that gap with a new test set in this 2026 work. Their Cryo-Bench covers glaciers with debris, glacial lakes, sea ice, and glacier fronts across many regions and sensors.

The team scores fourteen large Earth models against two standard image baselines. With frozen cores, a classic baseline still leads on mean overlap score, while top Earth models sit close behind. With just a tenth of the training data, Earth models pull ahead, which suits sparse polar labels. Full tuning gives mixed gains unless learning rates are tuned too, a practical tip the authors stress for users.
arxiv-2603-01976:
Luu Le, Hoang-Loc Cao, Ha-Hieu Pham, and colleagues classify white blood cells under messy real-world conditions. Their 2026 work serves hematology tasks like infection checks, leukemia screening, and treatment monitoring. Stain and scanner differences shift cell appearance a lot between labs and data sets.

Rare but vital cell types also drown in a sea of common ones, a severe imbalance problem. Their framework first normalizes stain, then splits training into two decoupled stages. Stage one learns transferable features with instance-balanced sampling across all cells. Stage two rebalances the classifier with class-aware sampling and a hybrid loss that weights rare classes. At test time, ensembles of backbones plus augmentation steady the final calls, and the system topped a named 2026 challenge leaderboard.
arxiv-2603-02076:
David Almog, Lucas Lippman, and Daniel Martin test how workers react when AI, not a human, will judge their work. Their 2026 online experiment assigns a real work task under known evaluator types. Firms and schools increasingly weigh AI assessment for reviews, hiring, and grading.

Workers told an AI would judge them produce a higher quantity of output. Controlling for quantity, their output quality runs lower by both human and AI grades. They also reach for external tools, including language models, more often under AI judgment. That extra tool use does not explain the quantity or quality gaps between groups. The hidden cost is a shift in effort allocation, not merely cheating, which evaluators should weigh before adopting AI judges.
arxiv-2603-02176:
Hao Li, Chunjiang Mu, Jianhao Chen, and colleagues tackle skill overload for AI agents in this 2026 paper. Agent skills are small add-on tools that agents can call to do tasks. Thousands now exist, so picking and chaining the right ones is hard. Their framework, AgentSkillOS, sorts skills and then runs them as linked plans.

First, skills are filed into a tree of skills by what each one can do. Next, a task is split into a chart of steps, each matched to skills. The team built thirty rich tasks to test how well agents pick skills. Tree search came close to perfect picking, even as skill counts grew huge. Planned chaining also beat plain calling with the same skill set.
arxiv-2603-02276:
Ahmad Al-Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, and colleagues build a black hole model with extra matter in this 2026 paper. The model is a charged Hayward black hole in anti-de Sitter space. A Hayward core replaces the central singularity with a smooth de Sitter center. Two added ingredients are a cloud of strings and a perfect fluid form of dark matter.

Treating the cosmic constant as pressure, the team derives the hole's heat traits. They confirm a classic relation and find a small-large phase switch like a gas-liquid one. Free energy shows the swallowtail shape expected below the critical pressure. Expansion cooling reaches far lower relative values than a standard charged hole. A holographic engine cycle runs at fair efficiency, helped by strings and hurt by the dark fluid.
arxiv-2603-02376:
Bodun Hu, Yoga Sri Varshan V, Saurabh Agarwal, and Aditya Akella automate GPU kernel writing in this 2026 paper. Kernels are the small programs that run the math on graphics chips. In large model training, kernels must move data between chips as well as compute. Hand-writing kernels that do both well is slow and error-prone.

Their framework, CUCo, uses AI agents and needs no training of its own. Agents generate kernels that orchestrate compute and communication together. That joint view opens gains that compute-only tuning cannot reach. Prior tools focused almost only on computation, leaving communication largely untouched. CUCo beat leading baselines and cut end-to-end latency by up to about one and a half times. The work targets large-scale training and inference alike.
arxiv-2603-02476:
Favreau Jean-Marie, Gerard Yan, Lafourcade Pascal, and Robert Léo solve a tiling puzzle in polynomial time in this 2026 paper. The Calisson puzzle fills a hexagon of triangles with lozenge tiles. Some edges are prescribed as tile boundaries, and neighbors across them must tilt differently. No fast algorithm was known for this recent game.

Their advancing surface algorithm runs in cubic time in the hexagon's side length. It can even be run by hand with pencil and eraser. The method reframes classic height function ideas from Conway and Thurston. Tilings lift to stepped surfaces, and heights solve a system of difference constraints. A graph layer makes the hidden algorithmic structure explicit. A region is tilable exactly when its weighted graph has no negative cycle.
arxiv-2603-02576:
Zhaoyu Zhu, Shuhan Zhang, Rui Gao, and Shuang Li rework a core learning method for agents that choose smooth, continuous actions. Their 2026 paper starts from the geometry of Wasserstein distance, a way to measure how far one spread of choices is from another. From a stepwise update in that geometry, they derive a new policy gradient method.

The method, called WPPG, swaps between a transport step and a smoothing step done by blurring with a bell curve. It never needs the policy's log density, so it suits flexible policies defined as push-forward maps. The authors prove steady linear convergence, even with rough value estimates. Wicaksono Leksono Muhamad, Joanito Agili Lopo, Tack Hwa Wong, and colleagues entered a shared logic task with a parsing-first method. Their 2026 system paper addresses content effects, where the topic of a logic problem sways a model's judgment. The effect grows worse across languages.

Their method rewrites each syllogism, a short two-premise argument, into a standard logical form. A strict parser then decides validity by rule, not by feel. On the SemEval-2026 Task 11 multilingual benchmark, the system placed in the top five on every subtask. It also cut content effects sharply. Eliseo Bao, Anxo Pérez, Xi Wang, and Javier Parapar build a scorecard for AI personas that imitate people in conversation. Simulated personas now stand in for users in modeling, social reasoning, and behavior studies. Most current grading leans on another model acting as judge, giving one opaque number with little grounding in real human talk.

Their framework, Eval4Sim, grades along three axes. Adherence checks whether the persona's background quietly shows in its lines, consistency checks whether the identity stays distinct across chats, and naturalness checks whether the flow feels human. Scores compare against a real human corpus and penalize drifting too far in either direction. The method works with any dialogue dataset that labels its speakers.

Jakob Hofstad pins down the largest tree that hides inside a random graph. Each edge of the graph shows up with a set chance, picked on its own. The biggest tree that fits, using only edges that show up, tends to land on one of two next-door values.

Past work proved this tight result for fixed chances, and for chances that fade slowly. Hofstad extends it to all fading chances above a stated floor. Below that range, the picture flips. For chances in a lower band, the biggest tree provably does not settle at the value plain averages predict. The two results draw a sharp line where simple averages stop describing random graphs.

Shengbang Tong, David Fan, John Nguyen, and a large team train multimodal models from scratch to learn what actually makes them work. Native models that mix language and vision are usually adapted from language-first systems, muddying every design lesson. Their 2026 study runs controlled pretraining experiments with no language pretraining in the way.

Four findings stand out. One visual representation excelled at both understanding and generation. Vision and language data proved complementary, each boosting the other. bentham-theory-legislation-hildreth-1876:
Bentham's Theory of Legislation reached English readers through R. Hildreth's translation. Bentham himself never wrote the book in this form. His French editor Dumont built it from Bentham's manuscripts into a French redaction. Hildreth then carried that version into English for this edition.

Inside stands the utilitarian science of law: how to frame codes that raise happiness and cut pain. Civil and penal law both receive rules drawn from the one great principle. Legislators across Europe and Latin America studied the work for generations. It spread Bentham's name wider than his own tangled English prose could. The system here is clear, bold, and practical.
bonatti-astrologers-guide-1676:
Guido Bonatti was the most famed star man of the 1200s in Italy. His aphorisms, short sharp rules of the craft, came to England late. William Lilly turned them into English in 1676 as The Astrologer's Guide. The Latin name of the work is Anima Astrologiae.

One hundred and forty-six rules guide the star man in his work. They tell when a chart speaks true and when it lies. The rules draw on Arab craft passed down through Spain. The book forms a bridge from the old Arab art to the English school of Lilly.
bradley-ethical-studies-1876:
F. H. Bradley published Ethical Studies in 1876, a set of essays on moral philosophy. Bradley attacks hedonism, the view that pleasure is the good, and Kantian duty done for duty's sake alone. Against both he sets self-realization: the self grows whole by taking its place in a moral community. My station and its duties is his famous phrase for that view.

Morality, he argues, lives in the customs and roles of a real society. Yet the self must also go beyond mere social rules toward an ideal. The book is the great statement of idealist ethics in English. It shaped welfare liberalism through readers like T. H. Green.
britten-art-magic-1876:
Emma Hardinge Britten said a sage's ghost taught her the lore in Art Magic, her dense tract of 1876. The ghost bears the name Cheval Louis de B. Through her hand he maps the schools, rites, and laws of the occult from old Egypt to her own day.

Ranks of spirits, charms, and the risks of rite fill the book. Britten casts it as fact, not tale. Groups in the United States took it as a core text of rite. It is a ground stone of magic in that land. Britten had a flair for the grand claim, and she backs it here with dense lore. Fans must sift her zeal from her facts with care.
britten-ghost-land-1876:
Tales of hunts for truth in far lands fill Ghost Land, Emma Hardinge Britten's book of 1876. It is the mate to her Art Magic of the same year. Britten tracks adepts, bands, and marvels through Europe and past it. She writes as one who claims to have seen much at first hand.

Ghost lore here mixes trek tale with creed. Dark rooms, odd cures, and bands with hid names crowd the pages. Britten kept the teller's name hid at first print. The pair of books maps the hid world she claimed to know. Her claims drew both faith and scorn in her own day. That split still marks the book, which fans read as trek tale and creed at once.
burton-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-1876:
Richard Burton, the boldest traveler of his age, went after the gorilla in 1876. Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo tells his search in Gabon. Burton had crossed Africa and Arabia; the great ape still drew him on.

He tells of rivers, trade, fevers, and the falls of the Congo, with the gorilla as his grail. His pen is dry, learned, and full of the lore of the coast. The book adds his great name to the gorilla shelf of his century. Few explorers wrote with his mix of grit and wit.
cia-0000009376:
Japan's strategic importance is spelled out in a CIA paper dated April 1948. Japan then sat under American occupation, three years after its defeat in the Second World War. Planners were deciding whether Japan would stay a ward or become an ally.

The paper weighs Japan's ports, industry, and position off the Asian mainland in Cold War terms. An anchored Japan guarded sea lanes and faced the Soviet Union across narrow waters. Judgments like this one fed the policy turn toward rebuilding Japan as a partner. The file shows that turn being reasoned out on paper.
cia-0000009676:
Six American prisoners were held at the Krong R'buk detention camp, a March 1971 item reports, in a Cambodian district the title cuts short. Detention camps in Cambodia's east held men captured as the war spread across the border in 1970. Conditions in such camps were rough and poorly documented.

Naming the camp and its count of Americans gave officials a concrete target for follow-up. Six men at one site could be checked against recent border losses. The report also shows captivity becoming a Cambodian story, not only a Vietnamese one. Its details preserve a camp that few outsiders ever saw.
cia-0000009876:
Four American prisoners were seen on May 15, 1968, walking north near a Laotian village. The title cuts the village name off at Ban Nath, and the report was filed that June. A precise date stands out in files where many sightings float undated. Walking north suggested movement toward central camps or toward Vietnam.

Dated sightings let analysts build timelines no memory could blur. Four men on a road on a known day could be matched against camp movements. The northward direction fit the prison system's known flow. This file preserves the day, the direction, and the number, a small hard point in a soft record.
cia-0000010476:
Britain's position in Egypt is examined in a September 1951 CIA paper. British troops still held the Suez Canal Zone, and Egyptian nationalists demanded they leave. Egypt's government was weeks from scrapping the old treaty that kept them there.

The paper weighs the canal's strategic worth against the rising cost of holding it. Suez guarded the sea road to Asia and Middle East oil routes alike. Within five years, the Suez crisis would humiliate Britain before the world. This file catches the position early, as analysts measured an empire's slowly loosening grip in the autumn of 1951.
cia-0000012276:
Joseph Bulik, a CIA officer on the Soviet side of the house, wrote a memo for the record in July 1960 about a briefing of Mr. Helms. Richard Helms then ran the agency's clandestine side, and briefings to him carried weight. The memo sits in the Penkovsky file, among the earliest papers of the case that would define Helms's watch.

A memo for the record fixes what was said while memory is fresh. This one preserves an officer's account of decisions taken near the top. For readers, it shows the great case being weighed at the level where careers and policy met.
cia-0000012376:
Soviet intelligence had to be told, formally, that the United States cared about Oleg Penkovsky, and an April 1963 plan works out how. Informing the KGB and GRU of American concern was a signal, not a courtesy. Washington hoped open concern might soften the colonel's treatment, or at least mark that his fate was watched from the highest level.

Signaling games like this were planned as carefully as operations themselves. Draft messages to Moscow were weighed word by word for tone and leverage. For readers, the plan preserves the endgame's strange diplomacy, where even grief was expressed by design.
cia-0000014776: A printed protest from Haditu fills a CIA file dated June 5, 1953. The group spoke out against the death sentence passed on the Rosenbergs. Haditu sought freedom for its own land, per the title's plain words. The Rosenbergs died later that same month. Small groups far away still took up their cause in print.
cia-0000015276: Flying saucers are the clipped subject of a CIA file dated August 2, 1952. The name at the head of the title is cut out as deleted. The summer of 1952 was the peak of the first great saucer wave. A file from those weeks belongs to the season when Washington itself reported lights overhead.
cia-0000015376: A flying object was observed near a deleted place, in a CIA file dated September 6, 1955. The source date is marked unknown in the title. With the place cut out, little can be checked or weighed. The file still marks that a sighting claim reached the agency and was kept. The sighting claim is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015476: Non-orbit sightings of unidentified flying objects, from December 10, 1953, into March 1954, fill a CIA record filed in 1954. The odd label non-orbit sets these reports apart from satellite tracking. Winter sightings across three months were bundled for review. Such dated bundles were the bookkeeping of the saucer watch, letting staff count and sort claims season by season.
cia-0000037176:
An American man was sighted hiding in the southern part of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated March 2, 1980 reports. A man in hiding was a stranger claim than a man in a camp. The report raised questions the file itself could not answer at once.

Inside, the sighting is recorded with the odd detail that made it memorable. Was the man a prisoner, a deserter, or someone else entirely? The record leaves the question open. Files like this show the wide range of stories the postwar search had to sort, from solid leads to tales that never found an explanation.
cia-0000042676:
Further reportage on the murder of Jesuit priests fills a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. The title links the coverage to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The killings in San Salvador shocked readers far beyond El Salvador.

Inside, more reporting on the murders is gathered as it appeared. Each new account added names, places, and claims to a fast-growing file. The record shows an atrocity becoming a world story in print. Priests killed at a university drew the eyes of churches, parliaments, and editors onto one small country's war.
cia-0000042876:
El Salvador: Update on Jesuit Killings, 4, is a CIA record dated February 4, 1990. The fourth update came a month after the third in the series. That slower pace marked the case's move into legal channels.

Inside, the investigation's February position is set down in brief. Court steps, rather than fresh accusations, fill updates of this stage. The file shows the probe becoming a court case in form. Its dry entries are the sound of a scandal turning into procedure. Hard cases are usually won or lost in that dry country, far from the headlines that opened them.
cia-0000045276: President Jose Napoleon Duarte spoke in 1985 about his armed forces backing peace talks with El Salvador's rebels. A CIA item dated September 6, 1985, preserves the president's remarks. Army support mattered because the military held real power beside the elected government. cia-0000049076: Actions taken by El Salvador's minister of defense against officials accused of wrongdoing are recorded in a CIA item from 1983. cia-0000124276: A January 1958 CIA item lists Soviet stations for watching artificial earth satellites by eye, with their map coordinates, drawn up for the International Geophysical Year. cia-0000126876: An August 1968 CIA report surveys how the world's communist parties reacted to the invasion of Czechoslovakia. cia-0000139476: Father Lawrence Jenco's second debriefing leads this task force report. It covers 9-15 August 1986. Jenco was a released hostage.
