coley-clavis-astrologiae-1676:
Henry Coley was a London astrologer and mathematician who succeeded William Lilly as the art's leading English teacher. His Clavis Astrologiae Elimata, published in 1676, is his complete textbook of astrology. The Latin title promises a key, filed smooth for the student's hand.

Coley teaches the casting of charts, the judgment of questions, and the reading of nativities in plain, ordered lessons. He trims Lilly's vast practice into rules a beginner can actually carry into a consultation. The Clavis served English astrologers as their standard manual into the next century. His almanacs kept his name before the public year after year.
europmc-pmc10344776:
Prjibelski and colleagues built IsoQuant in 2023, a tool for long-read RNA data. RNA carries gene messages out of DNA, and one gene can make many message forms. Long reads can span a full message, but errors make the forms hard to rebuild. IsoQuant maps the reads to a genome and traces the joins between gene parts.

The tool works with or without a known gene list. Prjibelski found that it cut false finds fivefold when a gene list was used. In free mode, with no list, false finds fell by a factor of 2.5. It links splice joins, the cut points in a message, into a graph. Paths through that graph give the full message forms and their counts.
europmc-pmc10435576:
Agu and co-authors reviewed in 2023 a computer method that helps find what food compounds do in the body. The method is molecular docking. It predicts how well a small compound grips a target protein. Food-derived compounds with health effects are called nutraceuticals.

Docking can reveal which proteins a nutraceutical may act on. Agu covers the main software tools and the basic steps of a docking run. Scores from the method can mislead, so lab proof must follow, the authors warn. Case work spans sickle cell disease, cancer, heart disease, gut and womb health, and brain decline. New paths found this way may seed fresh drugs.
europmc-pmc1088276:
Okada and colleagues filmed immune cells meeting inside living lymph nodes in this 2005 study. B cells make antibodies, the proteins that tag germs, and they need help from T cells to do it well. How the two cell types find each other was unclear. The team used a laser microscope that can image deep in intact tissue.

After B cells met their target germ part, they moved toward the T cell zone, the authors found. A signal receptor called CCR7 guided that drift. Paired B and T cells stayed joined for ten minutes to over an hour and kept moving as a pair. Pairs with the wrong target broke up in under ten minutes. The work gives early proof of directed immune cell movement inside the body.
europmc-pmc1189076:
Hannah, Heyer, and Hincha charted cold response genes in a small plant in 2005. The plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, can gain freezing tolerance after chilly days. That gain is called cold acclimation. Hundreds of genes shift activity while it happens.

Earlier work tracked only a few genes at a time. Here, genome-wide chips followed 14 days of cold exposure. Data from two chip types and past studies were merged. The result is a database covering more than 22,000 genes. Hannah gives plant science a shared map of cold response over time. The team also tracked which pathways matter most at each stage of the cold response.
europmc-pmc12230676:
Blin and many co-authors released version 8 of antiSMASH in 2025. Microbes make small active compounds that shape soil and microbe life. Many such compounds become drugs or farm chemicals. Their recipes hide in gene clusters inside microbe genomes.

Since 2011, antiSMASH has been the lead tool for finding those clusters. Version 8 detects 101 cluster types, up from 81. Support grew for terpene compounds and for tailoring enzymes. Big builder enzymes also get sharper analysis. Blin keeps the tool current as genome data floods in. It appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2025. The tool scans genomes from both bacteria and fungi for these clusters.
europmc-pmc1420676:
Some cancer cells switch off genes that would curb growth, without changing the DNA code. Pruitt and co-authors probed one such switch in 2006, a protein called SIRT1 that trims chemical tags from gene packaging. They found SIRT1 sitting on the start sites of silenced tumor suppressor genes in breast and colon cancer cells.

Blocking SIRT1 woke those genes back up. The genes spoke again even though a dense methyl tag layer, long blamed for the silence, stayed in place. Pruitt also saw shifts in cancer cell traits after the block. The work points to a fresh drug target for turning curbed genes back on.
europmc-pmc1525176:
Older women in Spain use health care more than older men. Redondo-Sendino and co-authors asked why, in a 2006 survey of 3,030 people aged 60 and over. Women saw doctors more often, got more home visits, and took three or more drugs more often. Hospital stays and flu shots showed no gap.

Much of the gap shrank once illness was taken into account. Women carried more chronic diseases and worse quality of life, classed as need factors. Schooling, marital status, and social ties also explained part of the gap. Redondo-Sendino concludes the higher use largely reflects greater health need, not waste.
europmc-pmc1877876:
Mosher, Ostrander and colleagues found in 2007 a gene fault that makes whippets both bulkier and faster. Double muscling, seen in cattle and sheep, comes from faults in the myostatin gene, which normally limits muscle growth. In whippets the extreme form is nicknamed the bully whippet.

Bully dogs carry two copies of a two-letter deletion in the gene's third section, which stops the protein early at amino acid 313. Dogs with one copy were on average more muscular than normal dogs. They were also significantly faster in competitive racing events, a measured link between this fault and athletic performance. It is the first time a myostatin mutation has been tied quantitatively to racing success. Two copies overshoot into the bully form, while one copy hits a racing sweet spot.
europmc-pmc1899176:
Lee, Jayaraman and Wood demonstrated in 2007 that indole, a chemical E. coli bacteria pour out in rich food, acts as a signal between species that shapes biofilms. Biofilms are surface communities of bacteria, and indole was known to control several genes and drug pumps. Its effect on biofilm building had not been well studied.

Gene activity scans, microscopy, and mutant strains showed indole is a non-toxic signal that represses swimming, switches on the sensor protein SdiA, and boosts acid resistance. A mutant lacking SdiA formed 50 times more biofilm, tying the sensor directly to the effect. Indole flattened biofilm shape from scattered towers to even colonies. In mixed films, partner bacteria engineered to destroy indole let E. coli grow 12-fold more, confirming the signal crosses species lines.
europmc-pmc1968876:
Levine delivered the 1993 Walter Hubert Lecture, published in 1994, on p53, the gene most often broken in human cancer. The p53 gene is mutated in about 60 percent of human tumors. Its protein normally restrains cell division by switching on other genes.

Raising p53 levels either halts cells in the G1 resting phase or triggers apoptosis, their orderly death. DNA damage raises both the amount and the activity of p53, which likely protects the body from mutation buildup. After radiation, some cell types arrest while others, such as thymus cells, die. Cells lacking p53 lose that checkpoint and pile up damage-driven mutations on the road to cancer. Losing p53 also speeds tumor growth and alters responses to DNA-damaging treatment. Radiation therapy, Levine argues, should account for a tumor's tissue origin and p53 status.
europmc-pmc1974776:
Thibault, Gant and Landfield expanded in 2007 the calcium hypothesis, which blames faulty calcium control for brain aging and Alzheimer's disease. Two decades of work had tied faulty calcium control inside neurons to aging and dementia. In rodent and rabbit memory circuits, aging raises calcium-driven aftereffects, calcium currents, and L-type calcium channel activity, and several changes track memory loss.

One version of the hypothesis blames those surface channels for most other calcium changes. The authors shift focus to the cell's internal calcium store and its release channels, the ryanodine receptors. Those channels amplify incoming calcium by releasing stored calcium in response, and they work in series with the surface channels in heart and some brain cells. Evidence links altered store release to cell toxicity, aging, and Alzheimer's models. Minding the store, their title urges, is essential to the full picture.
europmc-pmc2073776:
THOMLINSON and GRAY studied the structure of human lung cancers in 1955 and its meaning for radiotherapy. These squamous tumours grow in solid cords of cells fed by surrounding tissue, not by vessels between cells. Large cords have dead centres ringed by living tumour cells. The authors reasoned that oxygen must fall from the cord edge toward its centre. Cells starved of oxygen resist radiation damage far more than well-oxygenated cells.

Simple calculations showed the oxygen drop could be large and significant. At the centre of a cord just 150 micrometres in radius, complete oxygen absence was expected, using average tumour oxygen use. The team then measured many tissue sections quantitatively. Most tumours studied were poorly differentiated squamous cancers, a pattern in about 40 percent of bronchial cancers examined.
europmc-pmc2125376: A medical paper on spontaneous and experimental leukemia of the fowl. The chicken leukemia. This article preserves that oncology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2126276: A medical paper on a pleomorphic bacillus from pneumonic calf lungs simulating actinomyces. The shape-shifting germ. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128576: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of pneumococcus, second paper. The germ's signature again. This article preserves that bacteriology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2131476: Putting pneumococcus beneath the rabbit's skin produced its own peculiar illness, and this paper pushed those intradermal experiments further. The team tested new variations of the skin infection. The under-the-skin disease, explored. The article preserves that bacteriology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2131776: Two bug germs looked just alike, so this paper drew the line between them. The team found the marks that set them apart. The twin germs, told apart. The article keeps that germ study. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut presented BEAST in 2007, a software package for Bayesian evolutionary analysis of DNA sequences. Evolutionary questions are statistical, and Bayesian methods combine prior knowledge with data through sampling. BEAST implements many stochastic models of sequence evolution, plus tree-based models for data within and between species. Its features include relaxed molecular clocks, population history analysis and handling of sequences sampled at different times.

Version 1.4.6 comprises 81,000 lines of Java code in 779 classes and 81 packages. The design is object-oriented and modular, making it a platform for developing new models. It offers a wide range of prior distribution options. The source is freely available under an open licence. The authors describe BEAST as a powerful, flexible framework for analysing molecular sequence variation and testing evolutionary hypotheses.
europmc-pmc2265676:
Fierro and co-workers evaluated methods in 2008 for reconstructing time profiles from complex two-colour microarray designs. Two-colour arrays compare two samples per slide, and alternative designs beat the standard reference design in theory. Their measurements, however, give ratios that must be mathematically converted into the true expression profile. The team compared how far different linear models agree in reconstructing ratios and time profiles from one complex design.

Estimated ratios correlated highly on average, and all methods predicted the same profile for most genes. Agreement was best for genes with large expression swings across time points. Methods sharing underlying principles gave the most similar results. Models including a dye effect proved more robust against array failure, compensating for dye-related inconsistencies. Normalisation choice mattered less, and its impact did not depend on the method.
europmc-pmc2360676:
Gray-Schopfer and co-authors examined how moles avoid becoming melanoma in 2006. Melanoma is a deadly skin cancer, and moles are its common starting point. Cells can enter senescence, a permanent stop to division, and the authors asked whether this stop acts as a barrier in real tissue.

In lab-grown human pigment cells, switching off a protein called p16 was required, alongside telomerase, for cells to divide forever. Staining of real moles showed wide p16 presence and signs of senescence, without rises in two other markers, p53 and p21. Early melanomas had less p16, while advanced melanomas lacked both p16 and p21 in most areas. A faulty growth gene, BRAF, found in about 80% of moles, switched p16 on. The authors concluded senescence blocks melanoma, which explains why p16 loss promotes it.
europmc-pmc2365976:
Forche and co-authors mapped a shortcut life cycle in a yeast-like fungus in 2008. Candida albicans is a fungus that lives on humans and can cause thrush and worse infections. It mates to form cells with double the usual DNA, but no true meiosis, the division that halves DNA in sex, had ever been seen in it.

Instead, doubled cells shed whole chromosomes at random until they return near the normal count. Using DNA arrays, the team showed the offspring carry shuffled mixes of the eight chromosomes. Many also swapped segments between matching chromosomes, including multiple small patch events. Removing a gene called SPO11, normally a meiosis gene in other fungi, stopped that swapping. Offspring colonies looked visibly different from parents, proving the cycle creates real variety without meiosis.
europmc-pmc2408576:
Riker and colleagues profiled gene activity in skin tumors and spread melanoma in 2008. Melanoma is a skin cancer that turns deadly when it spreads, or metastasises, to other organs. The team compared 42 primary skin tumors with 40 metastatic melanoma samples using gene chips that measure thousands of genes at once.

Primary tumors, including thin melanomas, ran high in skin-identity genes such as keratins and the gene LOR. Metastases instead ran high in a different set, including MAGE genes, the survival gene BCL2A1, and a matrix-cutting enzyme, MMP14. The switch between the two patterns happened as melanomas grew thicker, but each gene flipped at its own thickness. That makes the switch zone a window where spread begins. The authors listed candidate driver and brake genes that changed across it, checked by targeted tests.
europmc-pmc2430176:
Rehak and Rehak reviewed a blocked retinal vein condition in 2008. In branch retinal vein occlusion, a vein in the retina, the eye's light-sensing layer, is squeezed where an artery crosses it. Wall damage and abnormal blood factors complete the block, cutting blood drainage from part of the retina.

The outlook is often fair: 50% to 60% of eyes end with vision of 20/40 or better even without treatment. Vision at first presentation is the strongest clue to the final result. The main treatment problem is macular edema, swelling at the centre of vision. A grid pattern of laser burns is the established fix for a defined patient group. Injections of steroids or of new vessel-growth blockers showed promise, and surgery to free the vein helped some eyes that laser could not treat.
europmc-pmc2447176:
Driemeyer, Boyke, Gaser, Büchel, and May revisited how fast learning reshapes the adult brain in 2008. An earlier study from the same group found that three months of juggling practice grew gray matter in a motion-sensing brain area. Gray matter is the brain tissue packed with cell bodies. The open question was the time scale.

They rescanned 20 healthy adults learning the three-ball cascade, using a 3 Tesla scanner to track whole-brain structure. The growth in the occipito-temporal cortex, at the back underside of the brain, was already detectable after just seven days of training. Neither raw performance level nor sheer exercise amount explained the change. The authors concluded that the qualitative step of learning something new, not continued drill, is what drives structural change. The effect had earlier proved temporary once practice stops.
europmc-pmc2561076:
Caulfield and a large team of collaborators tested in 2008 whether a gene found in genome scans, SLC2A9, actually moves uric acid in the body. Uric acid levels track with gout, blood pressure, and diabetes, and scans had tied variants of this gene to higher levels. The gene makes a transporter protein in the kidney, where uric acid is handled, but its cargo was unproven.

Expressed in frog eggs, both forms of the protein carried uric acid fast, at rates 45 to 60 times faster than its known cargo, glucose. A gout drug blocked the transport, and human kidney cells given the gene took up at least twice as much uric acid. In men, gene variants matched reduced uric acid clearance in urine. However, meta-analyses found no link to blood pressure.
europmc-pmc2600276:
Zilberberg, Shorr, and Kollef documented in 2008 the rapid rise of Clostridium difficile disease in American hospitals. This gut infection, usually triggered when antibiotics clear normal gut bacteria, kills more Americans than all other intestinal infections combined. Using national hospital data from 2000 to 2005, the team asked whether more patients were being hospitalised and whether each case had grown deadlier.

Adult hospitalisations for the disease doubled over the period. The rate climbed from 5.5 cases per 10,000 people in 2000 to 11.2 cases five years later. The age-adjusted case-fatality rate climbed from 1.2 percent in 2000 to 2.2 percent in 2004, so the average case became more lethal as well as more common. The authors link the trend to hypervirulent strains and resistance to widely used antibiotics, and frame the infection as a growing public health hazard.
europmc-pmc2690576:
Bradley and colleagues argued in 2009 that health care improves fastest by studying its own stars, an approach called positive deviance. Decades of quality campaigns had left poor care stubbornly common, and under one percent of medical research money targeted delivery itself. The approach starts from a bet: somewhere, an organization already performs exceptionally with the same resources as everyone else.

The method runs in four steps. Find the consistently top performers. Study them closely, with interviews and observation, to form guesses about the practices behind their success. Test those guesses statistically across a broad sample. Then spread what survives, working with the very people expected to adopt it. The authors illustrate with hospital care for heart attacks, where speed of treatment varies hugely. The approach suits problems where the knowledge exists but sits trapped in a few bright spots.
europmc-pmc2729376:
Ji and co-authors showed in 2009 that restoring microRNA miR-34 shrinks the tumor-initiating cell pool in pancreatic cancer. MiR-34 is a small RNA switched on by the tumor guard p53. Pancreatic cancer cells that had lost p53 also lost miR-34, which normally lowers Bcl-2 and Notch proteins that help cells survive and self-renew. A small stem-like cell group drives new tumor growth in this cancer.

Restoring miR-34 in two human pancreatic cancer lines lowered Bcl-2 and Notch, slowed growth and invasion, and made cells more sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation. The stem-like cell group, rich in Notch and Bcl-2 and lacking miR-34, fell by nearly nine tenths. Sphere growth in dishes and tumor formation in animals also dropped sharply.
europmc-pmc2761376:
de Jager and co-authors set out in 2009 the prerequisites for measuring cytokines in clinical trials. Cytokines are immune signal proteins. Multiplex immunoassays read many cytokines from one sample. Such measures can track whether antibody drugs hit their immune targets in patients. Trivial handling steps, they warn, can badly distort the low natural levels.

Spiking known cytokine amounts into blood samples, they found recoveries mostly within eighty to one hundred twenty percent. Most cytokines stayed stable for up to two years frozen, but several fell sharply by four years. Only two of fifteen cytokines survived repeated freeze-thaw cycles well. They also demonstrate an internal control, and stress tube choice and storage rules for trials.
europmc-pmc2785876:
Kretschmer and co-authors traced in 2009 how fungicide use drives multidrug resistance in Botrytis cinerea. This grey mould fungus rots fruits, vegetables, and ornamentals worldwide. Yearly monitoring in French and German vineyards found three distinct resistance types rising fast. All resistant strains pumped fungicides out of their cells faster and overproduced the pump genes.

One type carried activating mutations in Mrr1, a switch gene for one pump. The second type owed its resistance to a rearranged control region before another pump gene, reshaped by inserted jumping-gene DNA. The same rearranged version appeared in both countries, suggesting migration from France to Germany. Crossing experiments showed that combining both changes yields a third, broader resistance. In field trials, fungicide sprays selected the combined strain over sensitive ones. Growers then lose spray tools they still need badly each year.
europmc-pmc2841576:
Carlsen and a large team built a worldwide antioxidant food table in 2010, measuring over thirty-one hundred foods, drinks, spices, herbs, and supplements. Antioxidants are plant chemicals that neutralize damaging free radicals, and plant-rich diets are tied to lower chronic disease. Samples were gathered from many countries and tested with one standard assay so the values could be compared fairly.

Scores ranged over several thousand-fold between foods. Spices, herbs, and supplements packed the most antioxidants, some exceptionally high, while berries, fruits, nuts, chocolate, and vegetables led the everyday foods. Plant foods delivered far more antioxidants than animal foods. The authors say such a full table is essential for diet studies to register foods correctly.
europmc-pmc2848976:
Halaban and colleagues reported a troubling paradox in 2010 for PLX4032, a drug built to block the mutant BRAF kinase that drives many melanomas. In tumor cells carrying the V600E or V600K mutation, the drug shut down the ERK growth pathway as designed. In cells with normal BRAF, however, it did the opposite.

Working through a partner kinase called RAF1, the drug switched ERK on persistently in normal-BRAF cells. Those cells changed gene activity widely, stuck less to surfaces, moved more, and in some cases multiplied faster. The authors warn the drug may hand an advantage to normal-BRAF tumor cells in patients, so treatment should target only mutation carriers, with monitoring for new growths.
europmc-pmc2871176:
Marre and the LEAD-1 SU study group tested in 2009 whether adding liraglutide, a once-daily copy of a gut hormone, beats other add-ons for type 2 diabetes. Over one thousand adults whose sugar stayed high on a standard pill, glimepiride, joined the twenty-six-week trial at sites in twenty-one countries. Extra arms added a rival drug, rosiglitazone, or a placebo for comparison.

The two higher liraglutide doses cut the long-term sugar marker far more than placebo or the rival drug did, with gains visible within two weeks. Patients on liraglutide also lost weight, while those on the rival drug gained, a double advantage for a disease tied to weight. Nausea was the main added side effect, and it faded with time on the drug.
europmc-pmc2887476:
Okagaki and colleagues showed in 2010 that the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans grows giant cells during infection, and that the size change reshapes the disease. Normal cells span a few micrometers, while the giants can reach ten times that width. Enlarged cells were found in infected tissue and studied for how they interact with host defenses.

Giant cells were swallowed far less by immune cells, tying size directly to survival in the host. They also resisted chemical attack by oxygen and nitrogen stress better than normal cells, though they crossed into the central nervous system less readily. Each giant carried many copies of the genome in a single nucleus and still budded off daughters. Living alongside the opposite mating type boosted enlargement, and mutant strains missing a pheromone sensor enlarged less.
europmc-pmc2924276:
Croset and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 that the smell and taste receptors of insects descend from an ancient family far older than insects themselves. The receptors, called ionotropic receptors, are variants of channels best known for carrying signals between brain cells. A cousin family, the odorant receptors, exists only in insects and was assumed to be the original animal smell system.

Surveying genomes and gene activity across the protostome branch of animals, arthropods, worms, and mollusks included, the team found ionotropic receptors switched on in smell organs throughout. A conserved core set, the antennal receptors, likely formed the first smell system of the protostome ancestor. Insects later bolted on their private odorant family, while the ancient system still handles acids, amines, and taste.
europmc-pmc2928176:
Kim and colleagues fed in 2010 silver nanoparticles to rats for thirteen weeks to set safe limits for a material now common in antibacterial consumer goods. The study followed international test guidelines, with groups receiving daily oral doses from low to high or a plain vehicle. The particles averaged fifty-six nanometers across, the size class used in sprays, fabrics, and medical products.

Males on the higher doses gained weight more slowly from the fourth week, though they ate and drank normally. Blood chemistry, tissue examination, and silver measurements in organs showed dose-dependent changes, with silver accumulating chiefly in liver and kidneys. The authors derive the dose levels that produce no observable harm, numbers regulators need as nano-silver spreads through homes and clinics.
europmc-pmc2944076:
Anenberg and co-authors estimated the worldwide death toll from human-made air pollution in a 2010 modelling study. Ground-level ozone and fine particles have risen since pre-industrial times and are tied to heart and lung deaths.

Using a global atmosphere model to contrast past and present air, they paired pollution levels with risk figures from health studies. Their estimates linked man-made ozone to hundreds of thousands of yearly respiratory deaths, and fine particles to several million heart, lung, and cancer deaths. Adding assumed safe thresholds cut the totals by roughly a third, showing how sensitive such counts are.
europmc-pmc3012676:
Du and co-authors compared two ways of summarising DNA methylation readings from a popular array platform in a 2010 study. The Beta value reads as a simple fraction methylated, while the M value stretches the same data on a log scale, and users lacked guidance on choosing.

They show the two are linked by a standard mathematical transform, but the Beta value's scatter balloons at the near-full and near-empty extremes. In a mixing experiment with known answers, the M value found truly differing sites far more reliably at both extremes. A minimum gap threshold helped the M value further. Intuition favours Beta; statistics favours M.
europmc-pmc3022776:
Buchon and coauthors studied in 2010 how the gut of the fruit fly rebuilds itself after a bacterial infection. Eating a mild pathogen had earlier been shown to trigger a sharp rise in stem cell division in the fly gut. The team measured gut cells and shapes in detail to see how new cells form, mature, and replace damaged ones.

One growth signal pathway, centered on the epidermal growth factor receptor, proved central at every step. It drove stem cells to divide, guided new gut cells to take proper shape, and helped push damaged cells out to die. A second pathway worked alongside it to boost division. Flies lacking the receptor could not keep the gut sealed and died easily from infection. The work shows gut repair is one coordinated program, not separate fixes.
europmc-pmc3053476:
Heeb and coauthors reviewed in 2011 the double life of quinolones, a family of ring shaped compounds found across nature. Relatives of quinine, the fever tree drug, these compounds show effects from allergy relief to killing cancer cells and microbes, and they inspired a major class of synthetic antibiotics. One notorious bacterium makes several quinolones of its own, not mainly as weapons but as signals.

In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these signals report how crowded the population is and switch on attack genes accordingly. The review covers the family's naming, chemistry, and making, plus side roles such as grabbing iron and blocking energy systems in rival cells. It also traces how the signals plug into the bacterium's wider control network. Understanding the signal system could suggest ways to disarm this hospital pathogen without classic antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3084176:
Russell and colleagues documented in 2011 how a decade of rising bed net use in rural Tanzania quietly rewired malaria mosquito behavior. Nets and indoor spraying work because local malaria mosquitoes bite people indoors late at night. The team compared hourly biting patterns from before nets arrived with two later milestones of community net coverage, during which malaria transmission had fallen dramatically.

By the final survey, one mosquito group bit less at night and had shifted toward a sibling species that bites earlier and more outdoors. The other group bit indoors only half as often as before. Overall, the share of human mosquito contact happening indoors fell sharply for both. The remaining transmission now happens where nets and sprays cannot reach. The authors call for new tools aimed at outdoor biting mosquitoes, as adults or as larvae, to finish the job.
europmc-pmc3176276:
Tiago dos Santos and colleagues probed how plastic nanoparticles enter human cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Particles sized like natural cell cargo are candidates for delivering drugs and genes, but their entry route decides where they end up inside. The team fed two particle sizes to three human cell lines while blocking known entry pathways one at a time.

Entry always needed cell energy, never passive drift. Beyond that, routes diverged sharply by cell type. Two lines leaned heavily on the cell skeleton's actin mesh, while lung cells suffered most from blocked microtubule tracks and from blocking one entry portal. A third blocker hit only the brain tumour line. The same particle, in short, sneaks in by different doors in different cells, a warning for delivery design.
europmc-pmc3180276:
Andrew Gaudet, Phillip Popovich, and Matt Ramer reviewed inflammation after peripheral nerve injury in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Unlike spinal cord axons, peripheral fibres can regrow, and that success depends on a well-run inflammatory cleanup in the severed stump. The review opens with history, then walks through the response stage by stage.

Damage signals open the blood-nerve barrier and wake support cells, which shed their insulation, multiply, eat debris, and call in blood-borne scavengers. Those cells finish the clearance within days and leave once re-insulation begins. The spinal cord runs the same programme badly, with lingering toxic inflammation and scarring. Comparing the two, the authors argue, points to ways of coaching the cord to behave more like the periphery.
europmc-pmc3261976:
Nicole Janssen and colleagues evaluated black carbon as an extra indicator for air quality policy in this 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Standards regulate particles by total mass, yet combustion particles are thought to be the most harmful fraction, and traffic measures barely move the total mass figure. The team systematically reviewed studies that measured both black carbon and particle mass.

Per unit of mass, black carbon showed larger health effects than the standard particle measures, and in studies modeling both at once, its effect held up more robustly. A worked example of traffic reduction suggested the gain in life expectancy looks four to nine times bigger when counted in black carbon than in fine particle mass. The authors recommend black carbon as a valuable additional indicator where combustion dominates.
europmc-pmc3297576:
Eizirik led a team that cataloged which genes are active in the human pancreatic islets, reporting in 2012. These cell clusters house the insulin making beta cells that the immune system destroys in type 1 diabetes. Using RNA sequencing, the team listed the genes switched on in healthy islets and in islets exposed to two inflammatory signals.

Nearly thirty thousand gene transcripts showed up in the islets, roughly doubling what was known before. Inflammatory signals changed about a fifth of them, including many alarm chemicals that call in immune cells. Many genes known to raise diabetes risk were active in the islets themselves. The signals also reshuffled how genes are spliced together, suggesting the islets talk back during immune attack.
europmc-pmc3335876:
Neal, Ahmad, Gordon-Weeks, and Ton showed that maize roots use a defense chemical to recruit helpful bacteria, in a 2012 study. Maize releases compounds called benzoxazinoids from its roots, known for fighting pests above ground and microbes below. The team asked what these chemicals do to Pseudomonas putida, a soil bacterium that colonizes maize roots and benefits the plant.

One compound, DIMBOA, proved to be the main form in root secretions. The bacterium tolerates it by breaking it down, and exposure switched on its genes for chemical sensing and movement. In swim tests the bacteria actively moved toward the compound. In soil, wild type maize roots, which make the chemical, drew far more of the bacteria than roots of a mutant that cannot. The authors cast the chemical as a recruitment signal protecting young, vulnerable maize.
europmc-pmc3338676:
Delhaes and colleagues mapped the full community of microbes living in the airways of cystic fibrosis patients, in a 2012 study. Cystic fibrosis thickens airway mucus, trapping bacteria and fungi that drive lung decline. Standard cultures catch only part of that community, so the team used high throughput gene reading on sputum from four adult patients, alongside normal cultures.

Sequencing revealed complex fungal communities, with most kinds missed entirely by culture, alongside the expected bacterial diversity. Patients with worse lung function and poorer clinical scores harbored noticeably poorer communities, with fewer kinds of both fungi and bacteria. Certain pairings recurred, such as a yeast appearing alongside the notorious Pseudomonas bacterium. The authors argue the whole community should be treated as one disease entity, and that fungi deserve a real place in care decisions.
europmc-pmc3445676:
Elwyn and a large team offered a practical model in 2012 for shared decision making between doctors and patients. The approach, where patients help choose their care, was well described in principle but rarely translated into routine steps a clinician can remember. Their answer is a three-step conversation built on relationship first.

Step one is choice talk, signaling that options exist. Step two is option talk, laying out the alternatives, often with patient decision aids. Step three is decision talk, drawing out what matters most to this patient and settling the choice together. The model treats decisions as the fruit of informed preferences, carefully explored, and doubles as a guide for training the skill.
europmc-pmc3447976:
Friedman and Alm exposed a statistical trap in 2012 lurking in microbial survey data, then built a tool to escape it. Surveys report each species as a share of the whole, not a headcount, and correlation on shares is notoriously unreliable, a warning going back to Pearson. Using simulated data and Human Microbiome Project samples, they showed how badly the standard approach misbehaves.

Many apparent links between species were artifacts, and some true links appeared with the wrong sign. Diverse communities softened the distortion; sparse ones suffered most. Their method, SparCC, estimates true correlations from share data anyway. Judged against its network, the standard approach invented roughly three false links per true one in gut data and missed most real ones.

europmc-pmc8749476: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at blood-based biomarkers (body signals that can be measured) for Alzheimer's disease. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc8910576: This research paper takes on plant secondary metabolites as defense tools against herbivores for sustainable crop protection. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. A tested new tool like this gives doctors a steadier way to measure what they see in patients.
europmc-pmc9388376: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on intratumoral oncolytic herpes virus G47∆ for residual or recurrent glioblastoma (an aggressive brain cancer): a phase 2 trial. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9684076: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on the effect of the intratumoral microbiota (the microbes living in the body) on spatial and of cells heterogeneity (mixed results) in cancer. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9812776: Doctors and scientists took on the WHO counts of excess deaths linked in this 2023 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9825576: Alcock and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on CARD 2023: expanded curation, support for machine learning (computers learning patterns), and resistome forecasting at the thorough antibiotic (bacteria-killing drug). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc9931576: Cao and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on imprinted SARS-CoV-2 humoral immunity (immune defense) triggers convergent omicron RBD evolution (gradual change). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9960276: Sun and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on treatment of phenolic compounds in medicinal plants-natural health products for human health. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
frus-1861-d176:
Writing on 15 August 1861, William H. Seward kept Carl Schurz inside his single linked plan. The letter is document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid August found Seward writing to Madrid in the same steady round as London and Paris. Each court got its own page, cut to its own needs. The letter to Schurz shows Spain held firmly inside the Secretary's single, linked plan. The single linked plan kept small courts from being played off against great ones. Small courts, held in one plan, could not be bought one by one by the South.
frus-1861-d276:
30 May 1861 is the date on a dispatch from Mr. Angel to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 276 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d76:
Writing to London on 7 September 1861, William H. Seward kept Charles Francis Adams to the autumn plan. The letter is document 76 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward kept up a near weekly rhythm of orders to London that autumn. Each letter bound Adams tighter to the cabinet's shared plan. For readers, the steady dates themselves tell a story: a government holding its nerve by routine. Routine was itself a message to London: the Union meant to outlast the crisis. The Union meant to outlast the crisis, and its mail said so in its steady dates.
frus-1862-d176:
The second Adams report of 24 October 1862 is printed as Document 176 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late October 1862 was a turning point in the war's foreign side: the French truce plan was taking shape, and Britain had to choose. Adams's twice-weekly reports were Washington's best window on that choice. This dispatch, read in sequence, shows the care with which he tracked each shift in British thinking. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d276:
On 8 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 276 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Early May brought word of the French defeat at Puebla and the Union hold on New Orleans, both useful to Washington's case in Paris. Seward's letters that month pressed a simple theme: the rebellion was failing, and friendship with it would cost France more than it could gain. This dispatch is one of the spring's many statements of that theme. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d376:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 August 1862, in a letter printed as Document 376 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. He wrote on the second day of the Bull Run battle.

Few dates in the file carry such a charge: while Treilhard wrote, the Union army was being beaten thirty miles away. The defeat would embolden those in Europe who wanted to act on the war. This letter, and the exchange around it, belongs to the record of how Washington's foreign dealings absorbed the shock in real time. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d476:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 476 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

By October 1862 the Confederate cruiser Alabama was loose on the Atlantic. Neutral ports from the Azores outward had become part of the war at sea. Seward's autumn orders to Lisbon kept the pressure on Portugal to hold raiders to the letter of neutrality law. Harvey's post, quiet in most histories, sat on a real front of the war. The dispatch closes the year's printed instructions to Portugal, a small file that shows how global the blockade's paper war had become.
frus-1862-d576:
On 21 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Watson Webb in Brazil. The instruction is Document 576 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's July orders everywhere carried the government's account of a hard summer, and the Brazilian instruction was no exception. Webb also needed the Department's current line on the cruiser war, since Confederate raiders would soon be working the South Atlantic and seeking Brazilian ports. By the time the letter reached Rio, the season it described had passed, which is why distant ministers held such wide discretion. The document shows the system working at its longest range.
frus-1862-d676:
Anson Burlingame sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 May 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and his mail formed the China section of the year's file. The letter is document 676 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Spring reports from China dealt with the state of the ports and the mood of the Qing court. Burlingame also had to weigh the moves of Britain and France, whose fleets and envoys loomed large there. His letter is a working part of that watch. It helped Washington hold a steady course in East Asia with few ships and fewer men to spare.
frus-1862-d76:
Writing from Washington on 2 June 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 76 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d176:
On 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Britain had declared itself neutral in 1861, yet many in its government and press leaned toward the South. Adams watched Parliament, the cabinet, and the newspapers for any sign of a shift. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d276:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 2 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 276 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d376:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 29 January 1863. The note is document 376 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d476:
On 23 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d576:
Under the date 22 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d676:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent this dispatch to London on 24 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The text is document 676 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that covers foreign affairs for 1863, part one.

Britain was the foreign power Washington watched most closely during the Civil War. Its ships, ports, and trade could help or hurt the Union cause. Adams had to press the American view in person, using notes like this one as his guide. The letter shows high-level orders moving from a desk in Washington to an envoy abroad, in plain official words.
frus-1863p1-d76:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 76 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-February mail from London took stock after the opening of Parliament. Adams wrote on the tone of the houses, the press, and the South's men in the city. His reports let Seward judge whether the calm of the Queen's speech would hold. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, in the legation's usual split of topics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d176: A third Roosevelt letter to Hull dated October 30, 1943 in the Moscow section stands as Document 176 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Repetition at this scale marks a day when much had to be settled at a distance: results weighed, thanks sent, and next steps set. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d276:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting at half past eleven that morning. American and British information and public relations officers settled how conference photographs and films would be handled. Army colonels sit alongside staff of the British and American information services.

The agreed rules are practical. Each side processes its own still photographs in Cairo under security conditions and exchanges material. American film goes unprocessed to Washington, while British film is processed in Cairo. No picture of any kind may be released before the final release date, given the secrecy of the Tehran leg. All conference pictures, still and moving, are pooled for every party and carry one credit line: United Nations Photographic Pool.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d376:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at one in the afternoon, dominated by the planned meeting with Turkey's president. The text of a telegram inviting President Inönü to Cairo for 3, 4, or 5 December was discussed and agreed.

Hopkins insists the allies must first settle exactly what military help Turkey would get if she entered the war. Churchill's offer stands at twenty squadrons, mostly fighters, and three anti-aircraft regiments, with no land forces and no promises beyond that. His prize would be Turkish air bases for steady bombing of the Ploesti oil fields, and he wants landing craft only for a temporary Rhodes assault in March. Roosevelt, caught between the Italian, French, and Overlord demands on the same craft, asks for military advice before anything is sandwiched in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d476:
On December 4, 1943, the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, the Combined Chiefs of Staff sent a message to General Dwight D. Eisenhower at Allied Force Headquarters. Eisenhower then commanded Allied forces in the Mediterranean, based in North Africa. The State Department printed the chiefs' message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Traffic from the Combined Chiefs to a theater commander carried the alliance's decisions out of the conference room and into the field. Eisenhower stood at the receiving end of Cairo's choices about where Allied strength would go next. For readers, the message marks the point where summit strategy began turning into orders for the armies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d576:
J. Leighton Stuart, the American ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State George C. Marshall on September 24, 1948. Stuart, a missionary educator born in China, was the last American ambassador to serve the Nationalist government on the mainland. His report is the final document in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By September 1948 the Chinese Communists were winning the civil war, and the China that the Cairo Declaration had promised so much was disappearing. An editor's choice to end the volume here is pointed: the story that began with Chiang at Cairo closes with his government's collapse. For readers, Stuart's report is a somber bookend to the whole record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d76: On October 30, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, the day the Moscow Conference formally ended. His message is Document 76 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London had its own reading of the Moscow results, and the prime minister kept his channel to Washington warm as ever. The record gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the day's other traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d176:
No official account survives of the dinner meeting on September 12, 1944, at the Governor General's residence. The editors reconstruct it from General Arnold's memoir. Messages from the Russians and from Harriman about the Polish patriots in Warsaw had arrived, and aid to Poland came up at the table. Marshall and Arnold talked the problem over at length.

Arnold records that helping Warsaw was a large problem never completely solved. Churchill also produced new ideas about winning the war: getting more British planes, ships, and soldiers into the final battle against Japan. Arnold answered that the Pacific lacked land masses for Europe's heavy bomber fleets. Even 1,500 of 3,500 bombers would be lucky to be usable, and B-29s were preferred anyway.
frus-1944-quebec-d276:
Somervell and Leathers, the American and British transport chiefs, reported on September 15, 1944, on the personnel movement problem after Germany's defeat. Their appendices size the task for the first year, assuming Germany fell on October 1. American operational movements alone totaled about 3.6 million men, including replacements, build-up, and redeployment for the war against Japan, plus 1.7 million for demobilization and repatriation.

British operational movements came to about 2.1 million, with nearly a million more to demobilize or repatriate. A precise analysis, the authors warn, was impossible until combined agencies studied the problem against the chiefs' strategy decisions. They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee take it up with the planners, the transportation committee, and the shipping authorities.
frus-1944-quebec-d76:
James W. Riddleberger wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944. Riddleberger headed the Division of Central European Affairs. Hopkins served as President Roosevelt's special assistant and closest aide. The State Department printed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Central European questions sat near the heart of the Quebec agenda. Germany's defeat raised hard choices about occupation and borders. A division chief writing to Hopkins put expert views near the President. For readers, the letter shows how regional knowledge reached the summit's inner circle. It arrived eleven days before the conference opened.
frus-1945-50-intel-d176:
The meeting named in the title took place on 7 November 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. Readers meet it as document 176 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d276:
A memorandum dated 19 May 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 276 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d376:
On 22 March 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 36th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 376 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. The writer's own views may color a line or two, which is part of what makes the form honest to read. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d76:
The Department of State sent a circular telegram to certain diplomatic missions on 22 October 1945. Circular telegrams carry one message to many posts at once. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A circular on intelligence business told embassies around the world how to handle the new order of things after the OSS. Posts had to know which secret duties were ending, which were passing to State, and what to tell host governments. Readers can see the change reaching the field here. It is not a plan in a Washington office. It is an instruction landing on desks from London to Chungking. The volume's State thread widens from an office to a worldwide service in papers like this.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d176:
King Peter gave his guarded yes to the Tito–Subasic draft, and Ambassador Patterson cabled the royal statement to Washington on 11 January 1945. The communiqué of the Royal Yugoslav Court is quoted in full. Patterson's cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The King has studied the draft closely, the statement says. He approves its basic proposals, under which Yugoslavia's future constitution and form of government rest solely on the free decision of her peoples. He will accept that decision. But as a constitutional monarch, he calls it his sacred duty to see the people truly consulted and their will fully respected. He also welcomes the widest grouping of democratic parties, from left to right, as the only sure ground of free expression.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d276:
Moscow's draft of a prisoners-and-civilians agreement is printed here in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet text answers a British note of 11 December 1944. It proposes the principles that should govern Soviet citizens and British subjects freed from the Germans by each other's armies.

The Soviet government is ready to conclude such an agreement, the note says, but its reach should be extended. It should cover not only prisoners of war but citizens interned or deported by force into Germany. Some paragraphs of the British draft should also be widened and defined. The first principle follows. All freed Soviet citizens held by the western allies are to be parted from enemy prisoners without delay. The same holds for freed British subjects in Red Army hands. Each group is kept apart in camps or gathering points until it is sent home.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d376:
Before sending his famous letter on Poland, Roosevelt's staff drafted it, and the draft survives here dated February 7, 1945. The President tells Stalin he has given much thought to their meeting that afternoon. He wants to say frankly what is on his mind. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed.

The three great powers, he writes, have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup. Moscow backs one government while Washington and London back another in London. That split puts all of them in a bad light before the world. People might think a breach had opened between the allies. The draft lets readers compare the plea planned with the plea sent.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d476:
Stettinius asked questions home in this cable of February 4, 1945. He wanted a summary of the Mikolajczyk memorandum shown to Bohlen. He also asked Grew to keep the delegation promptly informed on the Associated Nations. What was the present status of each of the five Latin American countries, other than Ecuador, and when might each act?

He further asked for at least a summary of the Department's cable to Moscow cited in an earlier message. The code words "Allstate Horseshoe" closed the wire. Read beside Grew's digests, the cable shows the two ends of the State Department working one set of files from Washington and Yalta at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d76:
Geneva, Prague, or somewhere new? This 15 November 1944 paper to the President weighs where the United Nations should make its home. Acting Secretary Stettinius reports that the question was never formally debated at Dumbarton Oaks. The memo is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Soviet delegates objected to Geneva, and one informally suggested Prague. Britain and China raised no objection to Geneva. An American study group reviewed six options, from Vienna to a district near Lake Como. Its pick was a neutral district joining the Swiss strip that held the League buildings with the French Pays de Gex next door. The memo urges the President to back that plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d176:
Ambassador Lord Halifax proposed adding war criminals to the summit agenda in a letter dated June 29, 1945. The letter is document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows up the British agenda list delivered a month earlier.

Four-power talks on war criminals had begun in London on June 26, Halifax notes, among American, British, Soviet, and French representatives. Even so, London expects some war crimes matters to remain unresolved by the time the heads of government meet. A brief review of the position by the leaders would be valuable in any case. The suggestion helped push the prosecution of the top Nazi leaders, then being negotiated in London, onto the Potsdam program.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d276:
Winant set down the U.S. caveat on Austrian reparations in a cable from London on July 4, 1945. The cable is document 276 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the words he used that day on signing the pact on control machinery for Austria.

In the talks on a reparations desk in the pact, he told his colleagues, the group had not weighed the real question of what Austria should pay. His government accepts in principle that Austria owes reparations, he said, but holds that the four powers should fix the form and sum in light of Austria's economy and its prospects. The British and French said much the same. The Soviet member, Winant notes, had long fought any such U.S. caveat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d376:
A progress report by the American delegation to the Reparations Commission, dated July 14, 1945, sums up what Moscow had settled and what it had not. Pauley had asked on July 3 for clarification of the open problems before the heads of government met. The supplement answers him point by point, with appendices for each topic.

On July 13 the delegations agreed the relative shares of the participating governments, and agreed rules for smaller nations' claims. No agreement came on defining reparation, restitution, and war booty, since the Soviets were not ready to discuss booty. General principles were settled except one: whether needed exports rank as a prior charge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d476:
British hopes for a lasting combined command fill Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 1, 1945. From talks with the chief of staff and other high British officers at Allied Force Headquarters, Kirk gathers what Field Marshal Alexander will do in England. Alexander will urge Churchill to persuade Truman, and senior American officials, at the Big Three meeting.

The aim is to maintain a combined command in this theater as long as possible. The British will hold out for maximum retention of a supreme commander, though they know America probably will not go along. They have therefore prepared fallback plans for an inter-allied service committee, to carry on functions of an allied character until a peace settlement is made.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d576:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent a memo to Secretary of State Byrnes on July 12, 1945. It is document 576 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Grew passes on a message for the President from China's leader, Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang thanks Truman for his June 15 wire, which sketched a proposed deal between China and the Soviet Union. He says he has sent T. V. Soong to Moscow to negotiate with the Soviet government. He will keep Truman informed through Ambassador Hurley in China. Chiang calls the matter grave for world peace as well as for China and Russia. He asks Truman to keep close watch on the talks and to share his views over time. The memo went by pouch, not wire, to keep the line to Potsdam free for urgent traffic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d676:
An extract from Villard's Paris wire of July 13, 1945, reports Britain's private plan on Tangier. It is document 676 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The extract is drawn from a longer report sent over Ambassador Caffery's signature.

Villard cites Peake, the British team head, on London's intent. Britain will not raise at Berlin any question of how far Russian participation should run. That participation is accepted in principle, Peake says. Any British-Russian talk on Tangier would be limited to a bargain. London would seek something in exchange for Russian admission to the conversations. Peake also held that France would accept putting the talks off until the first week of August. The extract lays bare the bargaining beneath the formal notes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d76:
President Truman denied a press story in a top secret telegram to Churchill on June 18, 1945. The message is document 76 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had asked about reports that Truman planned to stop in Paris and meet General de Gaulle before the Berlin conference.

Truman says the press reports Churchill mentioned are not authentic. He will keep the promise Roosevelt made to Churchill, he adds, if conditions at the time make it workable, a careful hedge. He ends by hoping the contents of the message will not get into the papers. The brief exchange shows both leaders managing the press, and French feelings, while the Berlin trip was being planned in secret.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1076:
Prime Minister Churchill circulated this extract of his Greece memorandum at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. The full text appears just earlier in the volume. Annexed to it is a report by Field Marshal Alexander, dated July 21. Alexander answers Soviet charges about Greece point by point, from the mood of the Greek people to the balance of forces on her borders.

Most Greeks, he writes, feel relief from terror thanks to British troops, and UNRRA relief now works where it could not under ELAS-EAM rule. Any Greek threat to Albania and Bulgaria is unfounded. Greece has one division, still training, against 52 Yugoslav, 18 Bulgarian, and 7 Albanian divisions nearby. A loud propaganda campaign from those three neighbors, he adds, poisons the air.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1176:
Winant cabled from London yet again on 18 July 1945. During the summit he filed almost daily. His reports built Washington's picture of British thinking piece by piece: politics, press, and the official mood in a capital awaiting an election count.

No single cable carried the whole story. The value lay in the stream, each report testing and adding to the last. This dispatch is one more layer in that piling up of detail. It shows the London embassy's steady work while the leaders bargained abroad. Readers who follow the sequence watch an ally's mind being read in real time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1276:
The United States Chiefs of Staff proposed this text on 21 July 1945. A proposed text from the chiefs put draft words on the table for the talks to accept or amend. Wording from the military staff could end up in the summit's own papers.

Drafting was power at Potsdam. The side that wrote the first text set the terms of the argument that followed. This entry preserves the chiefs' draft at its date, midway through the talks. Primary papers like this one let readers see the settlement being built from the staff level up, one clause at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1376:
Ambassador Edwin Wilson cabled the acting secretary of state from Turkey again on 27 July 1945. His earlier cable in the volume is dated 19 July. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Two cables, eight days apart, let readers watch an ambassador build a case over time. Turkey's spot between the Soviet Union and the Mediterranean kept Ankara in the summit's shadow talks as well as in its own file. Wilson's second report shows what had changed, or failed to change, while the leaders met in Germany. Posts like his supplied the facts on which the men at Potsdam judged the straits and the lands beyond them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-76:
Swedish requisitioning of shipping was the principal subject of a conversation that left no official record. An editorial note in volume two names that subject and marks the gap. It is the seventy-sixth unnumbered item following document 710, in the conference sequence of July 1945.

That question was expected to come up at a forthcoming meeting of the United Maritime Authority. The authority was the Allied body that allocated merchant shipping in the war's last phase. No official record of this conversation has been found, and the note gives no names or date beyond its place in the file. Entries like this one mark how much conference business ran through unminuted side talks. The editors preserve the topic and the gap together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d776:
Byrnes wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on July 20, 1945, in document 776. The Secretary kept the London embassy close through the conference. Winant's post made him a key partner in all Anglo-American work. This letter entered the second Potsdam volume, among several Byrnes-Winant exchanges.

The London channel carried more than news. Winant had to act on the conference's drift with his own hosts. Readers see a secretary managing an alliance by letter. The document shows Potsdam's work spreading outward in real time. Each such letter turned talk in Germany into action in a capital that had to live with it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d876: American drafters prepared this undated working paper on Article 19 during the Potsdam talks, filed with papers dated July 23, 1945. Reparations must leave Germans enough to live on without outside help. Paying for imports approved by the Control Council would be a first charge on export proceeds. If the council failed to agree, each zone commander could import supplies his government deemed vital, claiming first charge on his zone's exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d976: Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Molotov on August 1, 1945, now that a tripartite reparations plan stands agreed at Potsdam. The remaining work, he says, is carrying the deal out. The key task is deciding what will be removed from the western zones, and arranging Soviet deliveries of needed products in return. Byrnes therefore urges that the Allied Commission on Reparations assemble in Berlin at once, to work with the Control Council. He asks Molotov to instruct the Soviet representative accordingly.
frus-1958-60v09-d176: Another 1958-1960 FRUS document from the Berlin Crisis volume. The standoff continued. This document holds that record. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
gao-gaoreports-b-297176: Raloid Corporation took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298276: King Construction Company took its July 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Builders get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-298576: Singleton Enterprises took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299076: Fantastic Data came back for more in February 2007 — a second protest and a second ruling in the same month. The firm challenged another award, and the call tests these claims too. Repeat filers get repeat fairness, case by case. The second bite got the same fair look.
gao-gaoreports-b-299576: Meeks Disposal Corporation doubled its June 2007 protest — two case numbers, one trash-hauling fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim. Garbage contracts, the ruling shows, get first-class bid law.
gao-gaoreports-b-308476: The trucking safety agency's restitution money got a fiscal ruling in this December 2006 GAO call, which decides whether court-ordered funds could be kept. The decision reads the money law. The ruling settles the ledger on the ill-gotten gains. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310976: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Para Scientific Company. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-176: Head Start's financial risks needed a system in 2005, and GAO's report says a comprehensive approach could prevent grantee money troubles. The review prescribes the early warning. The little learners' funds deserved the guard. The approach had to be comprehensive. The little learners' funds deserved the guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-276: The budget office's tech reviews could bite harder in 2005, and GAO's report says OMB had room to make its investment checks more effective. The review pushes for tougher questions. The billions deserved the scrutiny. The reviews had to improve. The billions deserved the scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-376: Ecological indicator data programs got a GAO status check in 2005, and the report examines federal efforts. The findings take the measure. The report shows the nature numbers were being watched. The status had to be reported. The nature numbers were being watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-876: Iraq reconstruction funding got a GAO status check in 2005, and the report examines the money and efforts. The findings do the math. The report warns that the rebuilding dollars deserved honest tracking. The status had to be reported. The rebuilding dollars deserved honest tracking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1076: The federal buildings' guards needed measuring in 2006, and GAO's report says the protective service could better measure its control centers' performance. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the guardians needed grading too. The watch had to be watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-176: Veterans' job training needed labor action in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve accountability and help states. The findings demand the results. The report warns that the veterans deserved programs that worked. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-276: Mandatory spending needed budget triggers in 2006, and GAO's report says using triggers could constrain the autopilot growth. The findings prescribe the mechanism. The report warns that the unstoppable spending needed brakes. The triggers had to be used. The autopilot spending needed brakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-376: Shell company ownership stayed murky in 2006, and GAO's report says minimal ownership information was collected and available. The findings expose the fog. The report warns that the anonymous firms could hide mischief. The information had to be collected. The anonymous firms needed naming.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-476: The telecom transition needed better planning in 2006, and GAO's report says full adoption of sound practices could improve the GSA-led shift. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the government's phone lines should not go dark mid-move. The planning had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-676: Seniors' medical data was being outsourced in 2006, and GAO's report examines domestic and offshore handling of personal information in the health programs.
