The findings probe the privacy. The report warns that the patients' secrets deserved locks. The outsourcing had to be safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-76: Air cargo security needed federal action in 2005, and GAO's report says domestic cargo protection had to be strengthened. The findings demand the measures. The report warns that the freight holds deserved guarding. The action had to be taken. The freight holds deserved guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-276: Lejeune's poisoned water got a second GAO look in 2007 — the report details the follow-up on the Marine base's contamination legacy. The findings keep the official record straight. The report stands as the paper trail for families still seeking answers decades later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-376: The Army's future war machines faced their moment of truth in 2007, and GAO's report says the key decisions on the Future Combat System could not wait. The findings frame the fork in the road. The report's warning: decide with data, or pay in sunk billions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-76: The terror war's 2006 spending stayed within bounds, and GAO's report says the obligation rates fit the funding levels, with multiyear procurement noted. The findings do the accounting. The report shows the long war's ledger for the year. The books were kept, if heavily.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-276: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at VA Health Care: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury Screening and Evaluation Implemented for OEF/OIF Veterans, but Challenges Remain. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-76: GAO's 2007 report takes apart the FAA's math for billing airlines for air-traffic control. Much of the method passed muster, GAO found, but some key guesses and steps did not. The findings feed a never-ending air-policy brawl: who foots the bill for the skies, and whether the split is fair to the flyers paying it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-976: The Government Accountability Office dug into veterans Health Administration: Improvements Needed in Design of Controls over Miscellaneous Obligations in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-1-1776:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 1 of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776. Gibbon tells the story of Rome from its height under the Antonines to the age of Constantine. Armies, emperors, frontiers, and the rise of Christianity fill the narrative. His irony and learning made the book an instant classic.

Famous chapters on early Christianity blamed the new faith in part for Rome's decay. Churchmen attacked him, and Gibbon replied with relish. The prose is stately, balanced, and often quietly mocking. Many call the History the greatest work of history in English. Volume 1 alone would secure Gibbon's fame.
gill-myths-and-songs-from-the-south-paci:
William Wyatt Gill collected Myths and Songs from the South Pacific in 1876 from his years as a missionary in the Cook Islands. Mangaian traditions fill the volume: creation, the gods, and Avaiki, the underworld beneath the sea. Songs in native verse, Englished by Gill, carry the tales as the islanders themselves sang them.

Gill wrote down what elders told him before the old religion faded from living memory. Heroes, cannibal gods, and voyages of the soul pass in strange, splendid procession. The book remains a first source on Polynesian myth, gathered at the last moment it could be.
gray-darwiniana-1876:
Asa Gray was America's leading botanist and Darwin's chief ally across the Atlantic. His Darwiniana, from 1876, collects the essays and reviews he wrote as evolution fought for a hearing. Gray knew Darwin's work before most Americans did.

Gray explains natural selection in clear terms and answers its critics one by one. He also argues that faith and evolution need not clash, a view Darwin himself welcomed. The reviews trace the debate from the first shock of the Origin to wider acceptance. They show science being argued out in public, in real time. Gray wrote as both a working scientist and a man of faith.
hansard-suez-canal-shares-1876:
The House of Commons took up the Suez Canal share deal in its supply debate of February 14, 1876. Hansard holds the whole talk, word for word, in its record of that day. The deal had been struck in haste in the fall of 1875, with Rothschild cash.

The Prime Minister's men tell the House that the Rothschilds paid the Khedive near four million pounds at once. The price on the record is 3,976,582 pounds, with a fee of two and a half per cent. The debate is the chief first hand record of a deal that gave Britain a stake in Suez.
io-chrysippi-faniani-de-arte-metallicae-: Io. Chrysippi Faniani De arte metallicae metamorphoseos, 1576. The metallic metamorphosis. This book preserves that work. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucerne-10176:
Lucerne, a Swiss city in the canton of the same name, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. Jews lived there by the middle of the thirteenth century. The town’s earliest records already regulate how meat slaughtered by Jews had to be sold.

Those rules also promised protection: no one was to injure the Jews, on pain of a fine or banishment from the city. As elsewhere in Switzerland, Jews alone could charge interest on loans, and money-lending was their trade. Even so, they were expelled in 1401. No Jew settled again until about 1864, and the community counted forty-two members in 1904. The entry gives a compact history of early protection, expulsion, and a very late return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-markus-1:
Markus Magnus, an elder of Berlin's Jewish congregation, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as court Jew to the crown prince, later King Frederick William I. That royal backing set him against his rival, Jost Liebmann. King Frederick I favored Liebmann, and the community split into two hostile camps.

The article follows the feud to its end. After Liebmann's death his widow and sons kept the quarrel alive. Magnus won in the end. He persuaded the congregation to replace the private synagogues of the old families with one public synagogue. In 1722 the government issued new rules for the congregation's management. Magnus and Moses Levi Gumpertz were named permanent chief elders, each with a salary of three hundred thalers. The entry shows how court favor and rivalry shaped Berlin's Jewish self-government.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manresa-10376:
Manresa, a town in Spain's province of Barcelona, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In the twelfth century it is said to have held five hundred Jewish families. Most lived in a narrow lane by the town hall, the Grau dels Jueus. Their cemetery outside the city is still called Fossana dels Jueus.

The article describes livelihoods and mounting hostility. Manresa's Jews worked in manufacturing, trade, money-lending at twenty percent, and their own vineyards. In 1325 townspeople tried to stop them baking Passover bread, and the Jews appealed to the king. The persecution of 1391 struck Manresa too, and many Jews professed Christianity. After 1414 few remained. In 1492 the last of them sold their property for what it would fetch and left. The entry also notes the Zabarra family members who lived in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-joseph:
Meir ben Joseph ben Merwan ha-Levi was a French scholar of twelfth-century Narbonne. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn give him an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the brother of the nasi, the head of the community, R. Moses ben Joseph ben Merwan. He was a pupil of Isaac ben Merwan, who headed the Narbonne academy in the early twelfth century. He was held in great respect and moved in the circle of Abraham ben Isaac, president of the rabbinical college of Narbonne about 1165.

No book of his is named. His survival in the record rests on a conjecture by Gross. Gross held that this Meir is identical with Meir ben Jacob. That man appears, among five other scholars, at the end of a rabbinical responsum dated at Narbonne in the mid-twelfth century. The bibliography sends readers to chronicles and legal collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendlin-jacob-w:
Jacob Wolf Mendlin, a Russian Hebrew economist, is profiled by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the first Hebrew writer to take up economics for the Jewish masses of Russia. He was born at Moghilef-on-the-Dnieper in 1842. About 1862 he went to Germany. Studying the labor movement under Lassalle turned his ambition to economics and cooperation. From his first article in "Ha-Meliz" in 1879, he wrote steadily on the condition of Russian Jewry, in Hebrew, Russian, and Yiddish papers.

His books argue one remedy: "Ba-Meh Niwwashea'," By What Shall We Be Saved (1883), and "Mekore ha-Osher," Sources of Wealth (1898). With a Yiddish work on self-help, they point to mutual aid and cooperative organization. That, they argue, is the surest cure for the wretched state of the Jewish poor. He also founded charitable institutions at Odessa, where he was living in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metatron-hebr-g:
Meṭaṭron is an angel found only in Jewish literature, powerful enough that Elisha ben Abuyah, seeing him in heaven, believed there were two divine powers. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him in 1906. The entry gathers his roles from Talmud, Midrash, and later mystical books.

Meṭaṭron bears God's name, consoles God after the Temple's destruction, and yet may not be worshiped, the article stresses. Later sources call him prince of the presence, heavenly scribe, and lord of secrets, and identify him with Enoch. Closing sections weigh rival accounts of his origin, from Latin metator, meaning guide, to links with Mithra, Philo's Logos, and Horus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micah-10776:
Micah the prophet, author of the sixth book among the Twelve Minor Prophets, heads a Jewish Encyclopedia article written by Isidore Singer, M. Seligsohn, Solomon Schechter, and Emil G. Hirsch in 1906. His name is a short form of Micaiah, meaning Who is like Yhwh. Almost everything known of him comes from his book's opening line.

He was a Morasthite, from Moresheth-gath, and prophesied under the Judahite kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, a span the article dates to 756-697 B.C. at the outside. Later tradition confused him with Micaiah son of Imlah and told of his death under Ahab, claims the entry reports with doubt. After the prophet, the article takes up the other biblical Micahs, including the Ephraimite whose stolen silver funded a household shrine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moos-solomon-10:
Solomon Moos, born at Randegg near Constance on July 15, 1831, was the German ear specialist who built otology at Heidelberg, in an entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his medical degree there in 1856 and joined its faculty three years later. From 1875 he practised otology alone.

He founded Heidelberg's otological clinic and dispensary and directed it until his death — on his sixty-fourth birthday, in 1895. With Knapp he had founded the Archiv für Augen- und Ohrenheilkunde in 1868, and he translated Toynbee's Diseases of the Ear into German. His monographs run from the Eustachian tube to fungal invasion of the labyrinth after diphtheria and measles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-eliakim-b:
Moses Eliakim Beri'ah ben Israel was a Polish preacher born at Cozienice, where he died in 1825. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. Like his father, Israel of Cozienice, he was a disciple of Elimelech of Lysensk. Elimelech was one of the active leaders of Hasidism.

His printed book, Be'er Mosheh, gathers homilies arranged by the weekly portions of the Pentateuch. Two more works stayed in manuscript: Da'at Mosheh, a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch, and Matteh Mosheh, on the Passover Haggadah. The entry keeps a Hasidic preacher's name and books on record for later readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mossiri-hayyim-: Hayyim Nissim Raphael Mossiri was a Turkish rabbinical writer who died at Jerusalem about 1800. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had come to Jerusalem from Salonica. His one work is Be'er Mayim Hayyim, a book of responsa in two volumes, printed at Salonica in 1764 and 1814.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahash-serpent-:
Nahash, a name meaning serpent, belongs first to a king of the Ammonites in the days of Saul. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, tells his attack on Jabesh-gilead. He offered the town a choice: every right eye put out, or the sword. The town won seven days, and Saul came and routed him.

The article notes that fear of Nahash was itself a reason Israel demanded a king. David later sent condolences to Nahash's son, for Nahash had shown him kindness in flight. Two more Nahashes follow: the father of Shobi, who fed David in exile, and a name in Amasa's family line. The rabbis identified that Nahash with Jesse himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-bernh:
Bernhard Nathanson was a Russian Hebrew journalist and author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Satanow, Podolia, on April 15, 1832. His father guided his early Hebrew studies. When his father died in 1853, he moved to Odessa.

At Odessa he studied both sacred and secular subjects. He spent three years copying and fixing Levinsohn's manuscripts. In 1875 he went to Warsaw to publish Levinsohn's works. His own first article appeared in Ha-Maggid in 1864. He wrote a Bible name book in 1871. He also wrote Levinsohn's life and a Talmud word book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumark-mirels-:
Meshullam Zalman Neumark, called Mirels, was a German Talmudist. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and A. Peiginsky for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the father of Zebi Ashkenazi. He died at Hamburg on Nov. 28, 1706. Vienna's ghetto had counted him among its most respected men.

When Vienna expelled its Jews, he moved to Berlin. There too he rose to prominence among Jews. He joined Talmud study to business and to charity. In 1678 he returned briefly to Vienna on permit. He negotiated a loan there for the elector. Soon after, he gave up trade entirely. Hamburg and Altona took him as their rabbi. The sister communities shared his rabbinate from then on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nobah-11576:
Nobah names both a warrior and his captured town. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The man was a Manassite of the conquest age. He seized Kenath, east of the Jordan, with its villages. He then gave the place his own name.

Gideon passed Nobah chasing the Midianite kings eastward. Later ages called the town Canatha in their records. Coins suggest Gabinius restored it in Roman times. Herod met a crushing defeat there against Arabs. Inscriptions show councilors and a market clerk governed it. It also belonged, for a time, to Agrippa II. Today it is Ḳanawat, held by a few Druse families. It sits on the old Roman road to Damascus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohole-shem-asso:
The Ohole Shem Association was a group based in New York. Herman Rosenthal and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded on October 8, 1895. Its aim was to spur the study of Hebrew. It also backed study of kindred tongues and Jewish past.

Herman Rosenthal founded the group, with help from friends. Dr. A. Radin and Dr. S. Brainin stood with him. The group set up talks in three tongues at once. Those tongues were Hebrew, German, and English. It put out a Hebrew monthly in its first years. It marked the birth days of great Jewish men. In 1901 it marked one hundred years since Zacharias Frankel was born.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-zebi-h:
Zebi Hirsch Ornstein was an Austrian rabbi of Lemberg. The board and M. W. Rapoport wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lemberg and died there in 1888. His father was Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein of that city. His grandfather was Jacob Meshullam Ornstein, its rabbi.

Zebi was taught by his father and grandfather in youth. He showed rare talent while still a young man. Some of his replies were placed in his grandfather's book. That book was Yeshuot Yaakob, a famed work of replies. His name soon spread far past his own land. In 1855 he took his first post at Brest-Litovsk. There his great memory drew awe from all who heard him. The state forced him out of that town in 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palti-or-phalti: Palti, or Phalti, is a name borne by two men in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name is most likely a short form of Paltiel. The first Palti was a son of Raphu, of Benjamin. He was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. The second was the new husband of Michal, Saul's daughter. Michal had been the wife of David before that match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedat-b-eleazar:
Pedat ben Eleazar was a Palestinian teacher of the Talmud. He lived in the first half of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned the Law first from his own father.

Pedat served as the spokesman for Rabbi Assi in lecture. He passed on sayings from his father and from Rabbi Hoshaiah. He was a close friend of Zera and of Jeremiah ben Eleazar. A few of his readings of Scripture survive. One clears Moses of pride in a hard verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petronius-publi:
Publius Petronius governed Syria from 39 to 42. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His term forced him into close dealings with the Jews. He used that contact to shield them once.

Caligula ordered his statue set inside the Jerusalem Temple. Petronius had the statue made slowly at Sidon. He stalled at Ptolemais through the winter, talking with Jewish leaders. Crowds begged to die rather than yield the sanctuary. Moved, he marched his troops back to Antioch. He wrote the emperor asking him to cancel the order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-simhah-:
Simhah Pinsker was a Polish scholar of Hebrew antiquities. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tarnopol in 1801. He died at Odessa in 1864, pensioned and honored. His book later traced the rise of Karaism.

Pinsker failed in trade, then served Odessa's rabbi as secretary. His fine handwriting had won him the post. He helped found a public school for Jewish children. Then Firkovich brought strange old manuscripts from Crimea. Pinsker cracked their odd system of vowel points. Gold medals and a pension rewarded the feat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-josef-12:
Josef Popper was an Austrian engineer and author born at Kolin in Bohemia in 1838. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote essays on machines for learned journals. His books range far beyond his trade, though. They treat social questions, flight, and Jewish life.

Popper wrote on the right to live and the duty to die in 1878. He wrote against anti-Semitism in a book on Bismarck in 1886. His flight book came out in 1889. Best known is his early idea for sending electric power over wires. He set out that idea in 1862. A Vienna academy printed it twenty years later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-procurators-123:
Procurators were the Roman governors set over Judea. Gotthard Deutsch and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They took charge after Archelaus was banished in the year 6. From the year 44 they ruled the whole of Palestine. The land was joined to Syria in name. In fact it kept a governor of its own.

Josephus gives that governor more than one Greek title. His set title was procurator, or epitropos in Greek. At times Josephus calls him eparch or hegemon instead. The article lists the men who held the post in turn. It tells what each did in a tense land. Pontius Pilate stands among them in the full account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-hana-r:
Rabbah bar Hana was a Babylonian teacher of the first set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a nephew of Hiyya the Great. He was a cousin of Abba Arika, known as Rab. Like Rab, he went up to Palestine for his learning.

In Palestine Rabbah sat among the chief pupils of Judah the Prince. As he left, Judah gave him a broad right. He might rule on all points of Jewish law. He might sit as a judge in cases as well. Hiyya had asked that this honor be granted him. Back in Babylonia, his name stands with the great of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapoport-12576:
Rapoport is a family name shared by many Jewish branches. Isidore Singer, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Emil Jelinek, A. S. Waldstein, Peter Wiernik, M. Seligsohn, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. All branches claim a common Kohenitic origin. The name Rapa appears about 1450 on the Rhine.

The article traces the family from Mayence toward Italy. Jews were expelled from Mayence in 1462. Soon a wealthy Hayyim Rappe appears near Venice. A Polish branch told a legend to explain the name. The writers argue it comes from a word for raven. The family arms bear two ravens, they note. The entry opens a long family history in several lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remenyi-eduard-:
Eduard Remenyi was a Hungarian violinist born at Eged in 1830. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at New York on May 15, 1898. He studied under Böhm at the Vienna Conservatorium.

The article says Austria banished him for joining the 1848 revolution. He spent five years in America as a traveling player. Back in Europe, Liszt taught him at Weimar. In 1854 he became solo violinist to Queen Victoria. An amnesty let him return to Hungary in 1860. He toured France, Germany, Belgium, and Holland in 1865. A world tour in 1886 reached Japan and China. His best original work is a violin concerto. He also transcribed many piano pieces for violin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-morit:
Moritz Rosenthal was an Austrian pianist born at Lemberg in 1862. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied under several teachers before the family moved to Vienna in 1875.

At fourteen Rosenthal gave a first public concert that won wide praise. Its program ranged from Beethoven and Chopin to Mendelssohn and Liszt. A tour led to his naming as Rumanian court pianist at Bucharest. From 1876 to 1878 he studied under Liszt himself. He later toured America twice and published advanced technical studies for pianists. With L. Schytte he published technical studies for pianists of the highest development.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-johann-ja:
Johann Jacob Sachs was a German physician born at Märkisch Friedland on July 26, 1803. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Königsberg in 1827 and practised in Berlin.

In 1832 Sachs founded the Berliner Medizinische Zeitung, a medical weekly paper. Renamed over time, it was still being published when this entry appeared. He also issued a medical almanac and a yearly repertory of medical progress. His own books cover mineral waters, cholera on German soil, and influenza. Attacked by critics in 1842, he defended his literary work in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-jose:
Samson ben Joseph of Falaise was a tosafist of the twelfth century in France. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was grandfather of two famed tosafists, Isaac of Dampierre and Samson of Sens.

Jacob Tam, who corresponded with Samson on learned questions, esteemed him highly. Samson wrote tosafot to Shabbat, Erubin, Yebamot, and Hullin in the Talmud. His ritual decisions were cited by Joel ha-Levi under the title Pesakim. One ruling let a nursing woman remarry soon after her divorce. Jacob Tam attacked that decision severely in his Sefer ha-Yashar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandor-paul-131:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Paul Sándor. He was a Hungarian merchant and deputy. Sándor was born in 1860 at Hodmezövásárhely. He studied at the academies of commerce in Budapest and Dresden. That training prepared him for business and for public life in the capital.

In Budapest, Sándor sat on the municipal council. He also belonged to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In 1901 the Lipótváros district of Budapest sent him to the Hungarian Parliament. The entry is brief, and it rests on Sturm's parliamentary almanac for 1901 to 1906. It records a merchant who carried his standing in trade into national politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-her:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Herman Schlesinger. He was a German physician. Schlesinger was born at Adelebsen, in Hanover, on April 1, 1856. He took his medical degree at Göttingen in 1879. The same university gave him a prize for a treatise. It studied what long, small doses of mercury do to animals.

After further study in Berlin, Schlesinger settled at Frankfort-on-the-Main. In 1899 he became editor of Die Aerztliche Praxis, published at Würzburg. His handbook covers hygienic and dietetic rules, water cures, and other treatments. It reached a sixth edition in 1896. Raffaelo Supino translated it into Italian at Florence in 1897. The entry rests on Pagel's biographical lexicon of physicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seder-13376:
Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Seder. Seder is the Ashkenazic name for the Passover home service. It falls on the first night of the feast. Those who keep a second festival day repeat it then. Sephardic Jews call the service the Haggadah, the story. The book read aloud bears that same name.

Exodus pictures the first Passover as a household meal. Parents and children ate together at home. In Second Temple days only men were summoned to Jerusalem. Only city dwellers could keep the night as a family feast. The Temple's fall restored the home table. The father could again obey the command to tell his son. Four cups of wine mark the evening's joy. Roast lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs anchor the meal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Moses ha-Kohen was rabbi of a town near Tikoczin, Russia, in the early eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His lasting work was as an editor rather than an author. He prepared a Talmud commentary collection for print at Fürth in 1741.

That collection, Minhat Kohen, gathers fresh readings of the Talmud. Its authors were Abraham Broda, Zebi Ashkenazi, and Jacob Kohen Poppers of Frankfurt. Shabbethai added some readings of his own to theirs. The entry is short, yet it credits the quiet labor that carried other rabbis' learning into print for wider use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiggayon-13576:
Shiggayon is a puzzling term set at the head of Psalm seven. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. A plural form heads the third chapter of Habakkuk. Ancient versions read the word in differing ways.

Some old translators linked it to a word for trespass. Rashi and the Midrash took a similar view of it. The entry judges that reading incorrect, though. Shiggayon likely belongs with labels like mizmor and maskil. Those labels mark types of songs in the Psalms. Some scholars derive it from a root meaning to reel. They call it a wild, passionate lyric form. Yet Psalm seven is not unique in feeling. The term stays unexplained, and the entry says so plainly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-13676:
Simeon was the second son of Jacob, by his wife Leah. Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Padan-aram, far from Canaan. Genesis explains his name as God hath heard.

Leah felt herself hated, and the name marked that sorrow. Scholars offer other roots for the name as well. Simeon stands out in two famous incidents of Genesis. With Levi he massacred Shechem's men for wronging Dinah. Jacob rebuked both brothers sharply for that revenge. Later Joseph held Simeon hostage in an Egyptian prison. He stayed bound until the brothers returned with Benjamin. The entry weighs name lore against a violent, vivid story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-paul-137:
Paul Singer was a German Social Democrat and deputy born in Berlin in 1844. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He went into trade after real-school. In 1869 he set up a cloak factory with his brother. The business prospered and made him a fortune.

Singer turned to politics and the study of labor. He joined the Social-Democratic party and rose beside Bebel and Liebknecht. In 1884 Berlin voters sent him to the Reichstag. He gave 5,000 marks to aid families of exiled Socialists. An expulsion order against him in 1886 was soon withdrawn. He also helped found the Refuge for the Homeless in Berlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mei:
Solomon ben Meir was a French grammarian and Bible commentator. Crawford Howell Toy and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the twelfth century in France. He was a grandson of Rashi through his mother. His brothers were the famed tosafists Isaac, Samuel, and Jacob Tam.

Some authorities denied that Meir had a fourth son at all. Berliner found proof in Vatican fragments in 1874. Those fragments quote a commentary by Solomon ben Meir often. They call him brother of Jacob Tam in plain words. He was called father of grammarians for his skill. He served as prayer leader at Ramerupt and signed Tam's ordinances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-friedri:
Friedrich Samuel Spitzer was a French art collector and dealer of fame. Isidore Singer and Richard Gottheil wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Presburg in 1814, son of a grave-digger. He went penniless to Vienna to seek his fortune. A picture bought for five gulden proved to be a Dürer.

That find laid the foundation of his great wealth. He learned that old weapons drew high prices in England. He bought up old arms in Austria and sold them in London. Settled in Paris at Rothschild's urging, his business prospered greatly. Gambetta offered him six million francs for his collection. After his death in 1890 it sold for ten million francs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-gustave:
Gustave Louis Maurice Strauss was a British author born in Canada in 1807. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Trois-Rivières and educated in Hanover and Berlin. He also studied medicine at Montpellier. He died at Teddington on September 2, 1887.

Strauss served as assistant surgeon with the French army in Algiers. France banished him in 1839 over a suspected plot. He then settled in London as author and tutor. He also worked as linguist, dramatist, and surgeon there. His books include Men Who Have Made the German Empire. His Old Bohemian tales retell his own roaming life. He wrote grammars and translated many books into English. Gladstone later secured him a small government annuity. The entry recalls a restless, many-sided writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szenes-philip-1:
Philip Szenes was a Hungarian painter born at Török Szent Miklos in 1864. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied first at Budapest's technical school. Then he gave himself wholly to art. He lived years in Munich, Italy, and Paris.

In 1895 the Paris Academy of Art gave Szenes first prize. He returned to Budapest with that honor fresh. At once he ranked with Hungary's foremost painters. His chief works retell Bible scenes in paint. Samson and Delilah, Esther, and Judith lead the list. He also painted quiet scenes like After Dinner. His canvases hang in Budapest's National Museum. Emperor Francis Joseph kept some in his private gallery. The entry marks a painter crowned early by Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taylor-charles-:
Charles Taylor was an English Christian Hebraist born in London in 1840. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at King's College, London, and at Cambridge. He later became master of St. John's College there. His work centered on rabbinic texts in English.

In 1877 Taylor published Sayings of the Jewish Fathers. It is an elaborate edition of the Pirke Abot. A second edition followed in 1897. An 1899 appendix lists its manuscripts in full. Jacobs calls it the finest such work by a living Christian. Taylor found the Jewish source behind the Didache. With Schechter he edited the Wisdom of Ben Sira. Cambridge's Genizah gifts bear the Taylor-Schechter name. The entry honors a Christian master of rabbinic learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thorn-14376:
Thorn, a West Prussian town founded in 1233, long barred Jews from living there. Isidore Singer and I. Rosenberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Teutonic Knights founded Thorn and excluded Jews. Polish rule after 1453 admitted them only now and then.

Expulsions came in 1766, 1774, 1779, and 1797. Still, families kept returning over the years. By 1823 the community counted 52 families, or 248 people. Its first rabbi served without pay until 1847. A synagogue rose that same year. Scholars such as Zvi Hirsch Kalischer lived in Thorn. A home for the aged opened in 1892. The community also kept a loan society and a literary society. By 1903 the town held 1,200 Jews among 30,000 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verdun-hebrew-1:
Verdun is a French city, capital of the department of Meuse. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived at Verdun from the twelfth century. Its scholars included the tosafist Samuel ben Hayyim. Samuel ben Joseph and Jacob ben Joseph also taught there.

For long stretches, Jews could not live in Verdun at all. In 1433 the city asked Basel's council to let expelled Jews return. The request failed, and residence stayed banned until 1559. Later French kings let Metz Jews visit briefly for business. A Jew who stayed three days in 1774 was expelled. The entry traces this tight, shifting welcome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wanefrieden-eli:
Eliakim Getschlik Wanefrieden was a judge and preacher at Amsterdam. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at the end of the eighteenth century. In 1790 he published a pamphlet called Megillat Sefer. It holds sermons and a eulogy. The eulogy honors Saul Löwenstamm, Amsterdam's chief rabbi.

His surname points to Wannfried in Hesse as his birthplace. The entry separates him from a namesake in Moravia. That other Eliakim served as rabbi in Kanitz about 1760. He was likely father to Jeremiah Wanefrieden. Jeremiah defended Jonathan Eybeschütz against heresy charges. The brief note untangles two men of one name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-west-14876:
West is one of the four quarters of heaven and earth. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hebrew calls the east kedem, meaning front. The west is ahor, meaning rear. Since the Mediterranean Sea lay west of Palestine, the word sea itself came to mean west.

Another term, ma'arab, names the sunset point. In later Hebrew it became the common word for west. Rabbis debated where God's presence, the Shekinah, resides. R. Abbahu placed the Shekinah in the west. That view opposed Babylonian belief about death's gate. Palestine itself was called Ma'araba, the West, from Babylon. Its people were the sons of the West.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-gerson-149:
Gerson Wolf (1823-1892) was an Austrian historian and teacher of Jewish life. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Moravia, he learned Hebrew as a small boy. He later studied Talmud at Nikolsburg and went to Vienna in 1839.

At Vienna he took up teaching, thought, and new tongues. His first piece ran in print in 1845. It set Greek plays beside the plays of his own day. He took part in the street fights of 1848 and 1849. Bold pieces in two papers forced him to leave Vienna for a time. The long entry follows his books and his school work. It shows a writer caught up in the hopes of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yelisavetgrad-e:
Yelisavetgrad is a town in the state of Kherson in Russia. Herman Rosenthal, Isaac Broyde, and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded in the year 1754. It grew into a chief town of the south of Russia.

Its name stirs sad thoughts for the Jews of Russia. From that town came the spark for the riots of 1881. When a new czar took the throne, tales of a rise spread. The heads of the Jews asked the governor for guards. No heed was paid to their plea at that hour. On April 27, 1881, the mob broke out at last. A row in an inn on blood use served as the spark. The mob then fell on the shops of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarko-judah-ben:
Judah ben Abraham Zarko was a Hebrew poet famed for fine style. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at Rhodes in the sixteenth century of this era. On a stay at Constantinople he wrote his chief book.

That book bears the name Lehem Yehudah in Hebrew tongue. It holds a tale on the soul in figure form. It holds verse and prose poems side by side in it. It holds sharp short verse at the great men of his day. Some of that verse is aimed at Maimonides himself. A note of his stands at the head of a style book. More of his short poems came out in a London book. That book was made by Edelmann in the year 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zoan-15276:
Zoan was an ancient Egyptian city, nearly as old as Hebron in the Bible's telling. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Muller wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaiah ranks its princes beside those of Memphis, and Ezekiel names it with Thebes. Israelite embassies went to Zoan, which hints it was once a royal residence.

The Greeks called the city Tanis. It stood in the Nile Delta, on the Tanitic branch, near Lake Menzalah and Egypt's northeast frontier. Kings of the twenty-first dynasty, called Tanitic, ruled from there. Digging by Mariette in 1860 and Petrie in 1883 uncovered monuments from the sixth dynasty to Roman times. By then the great city had shrunk toward a fishing village.
legge-the-shih-king-or-book-of-poetry-sh:
James Legge Englished China's oldest songbook in The Shih King, issued in 1876 with the Chinese text beside his version. Its 305 songs date from about the eleventh to the seventh century before Christ. Love songs, war songs, and harvest hymns all stand in its pages.

Legge, a Scottish scholar and missionary, gave Victorian readers a window on ancient China. Court odes praise kings, while folk ballads sing of longing and toil. The book formed part of the Sacred Books of the East series. Few anthologies anywhere are older or more loved, and this version pairs sound learning with the original words.
life-of-johnson-volume-2-1765-1776:
Boswell's second volume covers Johnson's life from 1765 to 1776. Hill's edition places the years November 1765 to March 1776 inside. Appendices preserve Johnson's autograph records in the Bodleian Library. Another appendix gives his sentiments toward his American fellow-subjects.

The text opens with Johnson busy on his Shakespeare edition. For over two years he sent Boswell not a single letter. Yet he constantly helped friends revise works and dedications. In that courtly composition, Boswell says, no man excelled him. His sentiments toward American fellow-subjects fill another appendix section. Johnson apologised handsomely for the long epistolary silence later.
lissagaray-history-of-commune-1876:
Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray wrote this history of the Paris Commune. He composed the French original in 1876, close to events. Eleanor Marx Aveling translated it for English readers. New York's International Publishing Company issued her version in 1898.

She explains the translation follows Lissagaray's revised second edition. France's government had refused to allow that edition's publication. Lissagaray himself added nearly a hundred pages for English readers. Her father corrected the translation, and she left it as he knew it. Prisoners in New Caledonia dated some passages by 1898, she admits. Patchwork updating would spoil the work, she argues in her preface.
maskelyne-modern-spiritualism-1876:
John Nevil Maskelyne shows the tricks of the dark room in Modern Spiritualism, his bust book of 1876. Maskelyne was the top stage mage of London. He and his mate built a famed hall of feats. Seers, he says, use the same craft: hid ropes, false hands, and dark to fake the shapes and sounds that guests take for the dead at work.

He prints how each feat is done, step by step. His aim is to save the crowd from fraud. The book is the stage's best word on the theme. Its scorn still stings.
maxwell-matter-and-motion-1876:
Matter and Motion, published in 1876, is James Clerk Maxwell's short primer on the laws of moving bodies. Maxwell wrote it for beginners, not experts. In a few brief chapters he lays out the ground rules of Newtonian mechanics.

He covers space, time, velocity, force, and work, each defined with care. Worked examples show how the same laws govern a falling stone and a circling planet. Because Maxwell writes so clearly, the book became a model science primer, and students of physics still use it to meet the subject. Each short chapter builds on the last, so the logic stays easy to follow.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol4-1876:
Tartuffe, the most famous of all Molière's plays, leads volume four of van Laun's set, published in 1876. Tartuffe is a religious fraud who worms into a rich man's house and nearly steals all he owns. The play was banned for years in France for its daring.

Sharing the volume are Mélicerte, a pastoral piece left unfinished, and The Sicilian, a short musical comedy. Amphitryon retells the Greek myth of Jupiter wooing a mortal wife. George Dandin mocks a rich peasant who marries above his station and regrets it. Van Laun's notes trace how each play fared on the Paris stage.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol5-1876:
Volume five of van Laun's Molière, published in 1876, opens with The Miser. Harpagon, its grasping hero, loves his money box more than his own children. His greed drives the plot through loans, thefts, and crossed love affairs until the box itself is stolen.

The volume also gives Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, a farce about a country lawyer tormented in Paris. The Magnificent Lovers is a court spectacle in mythic dress. The Citizen Who Apes the Nobleman laughs at a rich tradesman hiring tutors to seem grand. Psyche, a grand verse tragedy with ballet, closes the volume in a very different key.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol6-1876:
Van Laun's sixth and last volume of Molière appeared in 1876 and holds the plays of his final years. The Rogueries of Scapin brings back the sly servant who beats his masters at their own game. The Learned Ladies satirizes women who prize book learning above sense, and men who flatter them.

The Imaginary Invalid, Molière's last play, mocks doctors and a hypochondriac who fears every ill. Tradition says Molière himself collapsed while playing that part and died soon after. The Countess of Escarbagnas and the early farces fill out the volume. With it, English readers gained the whole of Molière in one faithful set.
north-and-south-pg4276:
Mrs Gaskell's North and South appears in this copy from Walter Scott, Limited, of Paternoster Square in London. A picture up front shows Edith curled upon the sofa in the back drawing room. That image comes from page one, and chapter one starts at once. Its head is Haste to the Wedding.

Margaret calls gently to Edith, who has fallen asleep mid talk. The cousins had spoken of wedding dresses and wedding customs. Captain Lennox had told Edith of her future life at Corfu, where his regiment was stationed. Even the trouble of keeping a piano in tune there came up. Margaret, soon to lose her companion, sees her beauty afresh.
openalex-w1994930576:
Elodie Descloux, Morgan Mangeas, Christophe Menkes and colleagues studied dengue in Noumea, New Caledonia. Their paper asks how weather shapes dengue outbreaks there. Dengue spreads through Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The team wanted a climate-based early warning system for the city.

They studied health and weather records from 1971 to 2010. They also used mosquito survey data from 2000 to 2009. Outbreaks were strongly seasonal. Case peaks came one to two months after the hottest weather. Hot summers, rain and high humidity were linked with outbreak risk. The team built models that estimated yearly outbreak risk. The best signs were very hot days and very humid days in summer.
openalex-w2109701276:
Erika Tamm, Toomas Kivisild, Maere Reidla and colleagues traced how the first Americans arrived from Asia. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2007. Native Americans descend from few Asian founders. They crossed into the Americas through Beringia. The timing and pauses of that journey were unclear.

The team analysed mitochondrial DNA from many populations. Maternal lineages were compared across Siberia and the Americas. A single founding lineage group expanded widely. Their reading suggests a pause in Beringia. During that standstill, the founding population grew distinct. People then spread rapidly through the Americas. The pattern fits a swift coastal expansion. Genetic dates support the standstill model.
openalex-w2153692276:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in Physical Review Letters in 2015. They looked for signs that particles from proton-lead collisions move together as a group, not just in pairs. Pair patterns alone can be faked by jet fragments, so the team demanded links among six or more particles.

CMS data from the 2013 proton-lead run at the Large Hadron Collider were used. The second flow wave was measured across a wide span of angles and compared with lead-lead results. The many-particle links held up, which supports a collective origin for the pattern. The findings help judge whether a tiny, dense, fluid-like medium forms even in these small collision systems.
openalex-w2762931876:
Bruce Campbell, Doug Beare, and Elena M. Bennett lead a team examining farming's planetary footprint in Ecology and Society in 2017. They use the planetary boundaries framework, which sets safe limits for nine Earth system processes. Agriculture touches nearly all of them, from land use to freshwater and climate. The paper asks how much of today's boundary-breaking farming actually drives.

Two boundaries are already fully crossed: biosphere integrity and nutrient flows, with agriculture the main driver. Land-system change and freshwater use sit in the risk zone, again driven mainly by farming. Agriculture also contributes significantly to climate change, the third risky boundary. Even boundaries still in the safe zone feel farming's pressure. The authors conclude that many interventions across whole food systems are needed. Feeding humanity without destabilizing the planet is the central challenge they frame.
openalex-w2786291776:
Heileen Hsu-Kim, Chris S. Eckley, and Darío Achá, with colleagues, synthesized aquatic mercury management in Ambio in 2018. Land use changes can stir stored mercury into waterways and boost its conversion to methylmercury. That form accumulates in fish and endangers people and wildlife. Reservoirs, deforestation, rice farming, mining, and city growth all disturb mercury's cycle.

The paper walks through each landscape alteration, its challenges, and the management openings it offers. Knowing response times could help policy steer risky activities away from vulnerable systems. Cleanup of old mining pollution is shifting toward gentler in-place technologies, they note. Artisanal gold mining remains the hardest case, for social and political reasons more than technical ones. The synthesis helps managers pick battles where mercury exposure can really be cut.
openalex-w2910719176:
Ravin R. Kumar, Colin Carroll, and Ari Hartikainen introduced the ArviZ library in the Journal of Open Source Software in 2019. Bayesian modeling is elegant in idea but hard in practice. Probabilistic programming tools now automate the heavy inference. What users still need are tools to inspect, criticize, and compare the fitted models. ArviZ, a Python library, unifies exactly those tasks.

The workflow it supports starts with checking whether inference ran well. Model criticism checks assumptions and predictions against data. Model comparison then supports selection or averaging across candidates. Finally, results must be prepared for particular audiences, with honest visual summaries. ArviZ gives these steps one consistent interface across modeling libraries. Good tooling keeps Bayesian analysis iterative and self-critical, the authors argue. The paper documents the library for the open-source statistics world.
openalex-w3092778876:
Mitra Nadim, Lui Forni, Ravindra Mehta, and colleagues issued this consensus report in Nature Reviews Nephrology in 2020. It comes from the twenty-fifth Acute Disease Quality Initiative workgroup. Its subject is acute kidney injury linked to COVID-19, a sudden loss of kidney function in infected patients.

Kidney involvement in COVID-19 is common, ranging from protein or blood in the urine to failure needing dialysis. Such injury tracks with high death rates and stands as an independent risk factor for dying in hospital. Its causes are not fully worked out and seem to be many-sided. With surges straining dialysis supplies, the group gives advice on diagnosis, prevention, and management for strained hospitals.
openalex-w3144073776:
Leonardo Pepino, Pablo Riera, and Luciana Ferrer presented this paper at Interspeech in 2021. It tackles emotion recognition from speech, teaching computers to hear anger, joy, or sadness in a voice. Labeled emotion recordings are scarce, which starves the deep learning models that work best.

Their fix is transfer learning. A large speech model, wav2vec 2.0, first learns the sound of speech from unlabeled audio. Its internal features then feed a small network trained for emotion, blending several layers with learned weights. On two standard test sets the method beat earlier published results. The study shows borrowed knowledge can stand in for missing data in speech technology.
openalex-w4211233376:
Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, Nicolas Bériot, Fabio Corradini, and colleagues review how microplastics move from farm fields into the wider environment. Their review appeared in Chemical and Biological Technologies in Agriculture in 2022. Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments now found throughout soils. Farms both receive them, through mulches and composts, and export them onward. Very little is known about that journey compared with plastic in oceans.

The review covers direct and indirect sources, then transport by living things and by wind and water. It also examines models of soil plastic and the chemicals and pathogens that hitchhike on particles. The authors stress how thin the evidence remains. Their map of the problem runs from single soil organisms up to whole landscapes.
openalex-w4221023376:
Clement Goubert, Rory Craig, Agustin Bilat, and colleagues wrote a beginner's guide to curating transposable elements by hand, in Mobile DNA in 2022. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that can move around a genome. Studying them starts with building a trustworthy set of reference sequences for each family in a genome. Software can find candidate families automatically, yet polishing them into full-length references still takes manual work.

That know-how usually passes from mentor to student inside research groups, shutting out newcomers. The guide fills the gap with step-by-step computer protocols, software advice, and video tutorials. Its authors aim to make careful manual curation achievable for any researcher. Better reference libraries mean cleaner genome studies across the whole field.
openalex-w4411165576:
Tatsuya Yanagisawa, Ruo Hibino, Hiroyuki Hidaka, and colleagues report elastic softening in synthetic diamonds. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. Lab-grown diamonds serve quantum technologies through defect centres. Even the purest crystals contain a few single-atom vacancies.

Vacancies form unavoidably during crystal growth, at extremely low levels. They shape the crystal's elastic and quantum behaviour. The team measures the elastic response of synthetic diamonds with precision. Softening in that response reveals how defects and electrons interact. Controlling such defects is essential for diamond-based quantum sensors and devices. The work helps growers judge crystal quality beyond what optical checks can show.
openalex-w4416229476:
Motoki Kei, Shiori Sato, Ryosuke Yamaga, and colleagues study how body mass index relates to side effects of enfortumab vedotin. Their paper appeared in the Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin in 2026. The drug treats advanced bladder cancer. Skin problems are its troublesome side effect.

The team mined Japan's national side-effect database and checked hospital records. Heavier patients showed more skin disorders, itching, high blood sugar, and one severe skin reaction. Lighter patients showed more kidney infections instead. The hospital records linked skin toxicity to higher body weight and to larger doses per ideal weight. The authors urge dosing and risk checks fitted to each patient's build.
openalex-w7166542376:
Shiho Tsuge, of Juntendo University Hospital in Tokyo, found a 2026 case of suspected cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome in a traveler visiting Japan. The syndrome brings repeated nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain in long-term cannabis users. The patient was a 37-year-old Canadian man who came to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and persistent vomiting after years of using cannabis several times a week.

His urine test was positive for the main active compound in cannabis, and his symptoms matched the syndrome's vomiting phase. A firm diagnosis was impossible from a single visit with a partial history. The authors stress that emergency doctors in countries where cannabis is banned, Japan among them, should think of the syndrome early in travelers, despite language, cultural, and legal barriers.
openalex-w7204179076:
Silvania Maria Cardoso de Miranda and Wágner Bruno Silva Coelho released a Portuguese-language field study in Brazil in 2026 on school leadership in a municipal school in Trindade, Pernambuco. A principal must join office running with teaching practice, balancing leadership, self-rule, participation, and quality. The authors surveyed thirty-seven staff, including teachers, counselors, and coordinators, with an electronic questionnaire in April and May 2026.

About seven in ten respondents judged the administration adequate and the principal's choice self-rule high, with the rest rating it moderate. Student disinterest stood out as the main daily problem, also named by seven in ten. Teaching follow-up, communication, and team relations scored well. Community participation, office demands, and ongoing training still need work, the authors report.
openalex-w7204229376:
Bruna Mabilly Dias led a Portuguese-language literature review, published in Brazil in 2026, on osteosarcoma of the jaw bones and the molecular markers that might catch it earlier. This rare bone cancer produces bone-like matrix from tumor cells and is hard to diagnose, since its early signs are vague. When it strikes the maxilla or mandible it behaves differently from the same cancer in long bones, and delays are common.

Markers under study include gene changes tied to cell cycle control and DNA repair, proteins linked to cell growth, vessel-forming factors, and non-coding RNAs, especially microRNAs. Circulating markers may also help judge prognosis and follow patients. Clinical use is still limited, the authors note, by tumor diversity, few jaw-specific studies, and the need for validation in larger groups.
openalex-w7205001176:
Suellen Nascismento dos Santos and Guilherme Milagres Viana released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on school indiscipline and how families manage the transgressions of boys and girls. Indiscipline is a repeated problem involving students, educators, and families, and through a gender lens it exposes socially built expectations about boys' and girls' behavior. The study pairs earlier studies with direct watching of daily life at a state public school in Ouro Preto, Minas Gerais, mainly when families were called in over behavior judged undisciplined.

Families tended to defend and justify boys' behavior more, the fieldwork showed, while scolding and blaming girls more. Gender norms, the authors suggest, run through how families administer indiscipline, shaping blame differently by sex from an early age.
openalex-w7207777076:
Francine Kormann, Camila Gomes da Silva, and Valeria Becher Trentin read Brazil's rules on assessment in early childhood education with a critical eye. Their documentary study covers the national education law, the national curriculum guidelines for early childhood, and the common curricular base. Reading them through Michel Foucault's ideas on power and norms, the authors ask what kind of looking these rules train teachers to do.

On paper, assessment at this level means following and recording each child's development, never selecting, promoting, or holding a child back. Yet the authors show that records can still compare, sort, and position children against an implied normal child. Truly inclusive assessment, they conclude, must go past obeying the rules: it should welcome many kinds of childhood and question the standards behind the teacher's gaze.
openalex-w7214242876:
Maria Edwirges Vital Silva Diniz, Edjane Vieira Pires, and Fábio Campos Coutinho carried out a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence used to personalize teaching. Following a standard review protocol, they screened studies from 2015 to 2025 across five databases. Of more than three hundred studies found, thirty-seven met their inclusion rules.

Adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutors, and recommendation systems raised student motivation and performance in much of that research, and let teachers tailor help to each learner. Risks appeared too: unclear algorithms, less human contact, and teachers who lack training for the tools. The authors conclude that artificial intelligence can widen fairness in education only when used ethically, with teachers still guiding and choosing for their students.
openalex-w7220908676:
Luiza Farias Murta Dutra and two co-authors reviewed research from 2020 to 2026 on environmental risks to women's fertility. They asked whether secondhand smoke and air pollution harm the ovarian reserve, the supply of eggs a woman carries. Their 2026 article gathers observational and experimental studies found in major medical databases.

The studies link fine air particles and nitrogen dioxide to changes in reserve markers such as anti-Müllerian hormone and follicle counts. For secondhand smoke the clinical evidence stays mixed, though lab work shows tobacco compounds can reach the ovary and damage follicle cells. Proposed pathways include oxidative stress, inflammation, and DNA damage. The authors stress that firm causal proof is still missing and call for long-term studies with measured exposure.
ovid-fasti-tristia-ponto-riley-1876:
The later, sadder Ovid speaks in this volume of Henry T. Riley's Bohn prose translations. It gathers the Fasti, the Tristia, the Pontic Epistles, the Ibis, and the Halieuticon. Augustus exiled Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE, and most of these poems plead from that cold shore.

The Fasti walks through the Roman year feast by feast, a poem of the calendar left half done. The Tristia and the letters from Pontus beg friends and the emperor for recall that never came. The Ibis curses an enemy, and the Halieuticon sings of fish. Riley's plain prose makes the exile books easy to follow.
perez-galdos-dona-perfecta-1876:
Benito Pérez Galdós published Doña Perfecta in 1876, here in Mary J. Serrano's English translation of 1895. Serrano's version, with a Howells introduction, gives Galdós's novel of provincial bigotry to English readers. Galdós, Spain's great realist, set old Spain against new in one benighted provincial town.

Pepe Rey, a young engineer, visits Orbajosa to wed his cousin Rosario and inspect his aunt's estate there. Doña Perfecta, his devout aunt, turns priest, town, and guerrilla band against the liberal intruder by degrees in secret. Rosario loves Pepe, but her mother's piety and the town's fanaticism close around the pair like walls. The close is murder, madness, and a lie agreed by all, in Galdós's coldest verdict on intolerance in Spain. Serrano and Howells presented the novel as Spain's answer to the great realists of Europe.
plos-pbio-0020176:
Scott Makeig, Arnaud Delorme, Marissa Westerfield, and their team analyzed brain waves in PLOS Biology in 2004. They recorded scalp signals, called EEG, while people responded by hand to visual targets. The team broke the smooth EEG waves into sharper events tied to each response.

That finer view shows the brain's response as a set of brief bursts from distinct areas, not one slow wave. It changes how EEG data can be read and compared across studies. Brain-wave records are cheap and fast but blurry. Methods that sharpen them help labs link scalp signals to real events inside the brain. The timing is sharp, down to fractions of a second.
plos-pone-0000076:
Charles C. Carey, Kristen F. Gorman, and Suzannah Rutherford followed up on the Hsp90 buffer system in PLOS ONE in 2006. Hsp90 hides genetic variation by keeping flawed proteins working. The authors ask how that buffering is organized: whether it rests on one hub or spreads across connected parts, a property called modularity.

How the buffer is built decides how it fails. A modular buffer might release variation in one trait while holding the rest steady. That would make Hsp90 a finer tool for evolution than a simple on-off switch. The study refines the picture of a protein that many see as a capacitor for evolutionary change across species.
plos-pone-0000176:
Rebecca S. Levine, A. Townsend Peterson, Krista L. Yorita, and colleagues published this disease ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Monkeypox is a smallpox-like virus long present in forested parts of western and Central Africa. The authors map its ecological niche, the conditions where it occurs, to chart its geographic distribution across Africa.

Knowing where a zoonotic virus can live is the first step in predicting where it will strike. The authors model suitable habitat from known human cases. Their map guides surveillance toward the forests and climates where monkeypox is most likely to emerge.
plos-pone-0000276:
Reto Huber, Steve K. Esser, Fabio Ferrarelli, and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2007. They used TMS, magnetic pulses through the skull, to boost activity in a patch of cortex while subjects were awake. The title reports the result: that local boost later increased slow wave activity, the deep-sleep brain rhythm, in the same area during sleep.

Slow waves are thought to reflect how much sleep pressure a brain region has built up. Showing that waking stimulation raises them locally supports the idea that sleep need is tracked region by region. The finding links daytime brain use to the depth of the following night's sleep.
plos-pone-0000376:
Spyridon Drosopoulos and colleagues tested what sleep does for memory, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Remembering events in the right order is a basic part of memory: it matters whether the phone rang before or after the knock. The team asked whether sleep helps lock in that time order.

The study's title states its claim plainly: sleep enforces the temporal order in memory. Work like this supports a clear view of sleep. Sleep is not just rest but an active stage of memory building. During it, the brain sorts and firms up what was learned while awake. It speaks to students, shift workers, and anyone whose sleep is cut short.
plos-pone-0000476:
Nickolai A. Tchurikov and Olga V. Kretova used targeted gene silencing on a mobile DNA element in the fruit fly, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The element, called F, is a transposon-like sequence in Drosophila melanogaster that can move within the genome. Their method was suffix-specific RNAi, silencing aimed at a distinctive end region of the element's RNA.

Precise silencing matters because mobile elements share much of their sequence with each other and with normal genes. Hitting only the chosen target shows RNA interference can be aimed with fine resolution. Controlling mobile elements matters too, since their jumping can break genes and reshape genomes.
plos-pone-0000576:
Jean-Louis Boulay and colleagues reported a counterintuitive marker of brain tumor outcome, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. NOTCH2 is a gene in a signaling pathway that usually promotes growth. The team found that loss of NOTCH2 positively predicts survival in subgroups of human glial brain tumors: patients whose tumors lost it lived longer.

A marker that predicts survival helps doctors counsel patients and stratify trials, even before it suggests a treatment. The subgroup detail matters: gliomas are several diseases under one name, and a signal visible only in a subgroup would be missed in pooled data. The finding also hints that NOTCH2's growth role can cut the other way in these tumors.
plos-pone-0000676:
Henrik Bjørn Nielsen, John Mundy and Hanni Willenbrock offered a method for matching genes by how they respond, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Matching transcriptional responses across studies is a strong tool in functional genomics. A mutant, for example, can be described by matching its gene expression profile with profiles from other studies.

Their approach, FARO, stands for functional associations by response overlap. When two conditions move the same genes, they may share basic biology. Overlap in responses becomes a clue to function for genes whose role is still unknown. With expression data piling up in public archives, methods that mine overlaps turn old studies into new ideas.
plos-pone-0000776:
Zhen Xuan Yeo and colleagues modeled gene control as a sequence of logical steps, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cell signaling runs from a ligand binding a membrane receptor, through transcription factor activation, to induction of mRNA expression. The transcriptional-regulatory system plays a pivotal role in controlling gene expression, yet its dynamics over time are hard to follow from static data.

Their sequential logic model aims to decipher that dynamic control computationally. Step-by-step logic can simulate how a signal's timing shapes which genes turn on. Models of this kind let researchers test regulatory ideas cheaply before spending months on laboratory experiments.
plos-pone-0000876:
Rita Busuttil, Ana Maria Garcia, Robert Reddick and co-authors tracked how mutations build up with age inside mouse organs, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier work with a special test mouse had shown changes pile up far faster in the small intestine than in the brain. The open question was how uneven that pattern is within a single organ.

Using the same model, the team compared sites inside the small intestine. They report that point mutations, single letter changes in DNA, do not land evenly. Uneven damage may help explain why some tissues age faster and face higher cancer risk. The study treats aging as a local process, not a uniform one.
plos-pone-0001076:
Jeremy Parker, Brian Bradley, Arne Mooers and colleagues reconstructed the family tree of the Nek kinases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neks are kinases tied to cilia and the cell cycle. In the fungus Aspergillus a single Nek is essential for cycle control. The ciliate Tetrahymena, by contrast, carries more than thirty.

That spread raises an evolutionary question: when did this family diversify. Their phylogenetic analysis reveals early diversification of the ciliary and cell cycle kinases. Cilia are ancient cell parts, and their kinases splitting early fits that age. The tree gives cell biologists a map for comparing Nek jobs across species.
plos-pone-0001176:
When proteins unfold, they tend to clump, and clumping ruins lab work and drug making alike. Utpal Das and colleagues examined how arginine, a widely used additive, stops that clumping, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Aggregation happens mainly when exposed water-hating surfaces on unfolded proteins bond.

The authors argue that supramolecular assemblies of arginine hold the key to its protective effect. Arginine is used everywhere as an aggregation suppressor, yet how it works stayed unclear. Their account of how arginine shields those sticky surfaces gives protein chemists a firmer basis for a routine trick.
plos-pone-0001276:
How wild birds pick up viruses, and pass them on, is mostly undocumented. Jaime Potti and colleagues traced one virus, an avian polyomavirus, through a wild songbird population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Detailed patterns of primary virus acquisition and dispersal in wild vertebrates were virtually absent before such work.

The authors show that nestlings acquire polyomavirus infections from larval blowflies. These flies are common nest parasites of cavity-nesting birds. Breeding adults play a further role in spread. An insect parasite ferrying a bird virus is a transmission route few would have guessed. The study is a rare close-up of virus ecology in the wild.
plos-pone-0001376:
Eric Benner and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on Parkinson's disease, a brain ill that slowly kills nerve cells that make dopamine. Brains of patients show clumps of a changed protein inside nerve cells, plus signs of swelling in the tissue. The team asked how the immune response to that changed protein affects cell loss.

The authors report that immune action aimed at the changed protein speeds the death of dopamine nerve cells. That finding links the body's own defense to harm in this disease. It warns that shots or cures that stir this response must be used with care. The work adds a key piece to how Parkinson's grows worse.
plos-pone-0001476:
Margit Foss and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE caution on a cancer drug called Taxol. The drug binds and steadies the cell's inner rails, which blocks cell division. It had also been said to make the rails grow in new forms. The team asked whether some of those forms were in fact drug crystals.

They show that Taxol can form crystals that look much like steady rails under the scope. That likeness can fool even skilled eyes. Labs that study rail drugs must take care to split the two. The note saves others from building claims on a trick of the eye.
plos-pone-0001576:
Grit-Carsta Bulwin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a brake signal for immune cells. A cell marker best known for showing germ parts to T cells was their focus. The team show one part of that marker can also send a brake signal. It does so by binding a partner on lymphocytes, the white cells that drive immune replies.

That brake cut swelling and pushed some lymphocytes to die, in dish tests and in mice. A built in brake on the same marker that starts replies is a neat design. Copying it could yield drugs for ills where immune replies run too hot.
plos-pone-0001676:
Richard A. Holland, Joseph L. Kirschvink, Thomas G. Doak, and their co-authors tested how bats sense the Earth's magnetic field in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many animals use magnetic cues as a compass, but how any of them detects the field was unsettled. One proposed mechanism is light-based, as thought to work in birds. The other rests on magnetite, tiny magnetic mineral grains that could act as a built-in compass needle.

The authors' experiments support magnetite-based detection in bats, per the paper's title. The full text gives the behavioral tests, the magnetic pulses used to disturb magnetite, and how the bats' sense of direction changed. A magnetite compass in a mammal would show that nature evolved more than one way to read the planet's field.
plos-pone-0001776:
Tomokazu Fukuda, Yasuyuki Kondo, and Hitoshi Nakagama studied a tumor suppressor protein's parts in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is CHFR, built from a forkhead-associated domain and a RING finger domain. CHFR is frequently switched off in human colon and gastric cancers, in up to half of cases, because its gene's promoter becomes methylated. That pattern suggests it normally suppresses tumors.

The team separated CHFR's jobs. Its anti-proliferative effects depend on the forkhead-associated domain, not on the E3 ligase activity of the RING finger. The full text gives the cell growth tests for each domain mutant. Knowing which part does the work focuses drug ideas on restoring that function.
plos-pone-0001876:
Kristopher Clark and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two odd proteins, TRPM6 and TRPM7. Each one joins two jobs in a single chain. One part is a channel that lets charged atoms pass, and the other is a kinase that adds phosphate tags to proteins. How the kinase part is switched on and off was poorly known.

The team found that the kinase adds a great many tags to a rich stretch of its own chain, a process called autophosphorylation. They show that this self-tagging, on a scale they call massive, controls how active the kinase is. The result gives cell science a new lever for how these dual-role proteins are tuned.
plos-pone-0001976:
Jessica Jones-Carson and co-authors found how a host gas kills a dangerous bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Burkholderia mallei, causes glanders and resists many defenses. Much was unknown about how oxygen-based host defenses kill such a broad range of germs.

The team show that reactive nitrogen species, made by an enzyme that produces nitric oxide, account for the killing in their tests. As the title states, the attack works by inactivating the bacterium's iron-sulfur proteins, which are vital to its energy use. A clear kill step gives drug work a mechanism to mimic.
plos-pone-0002076:
Gisela Vaitaitis and David Wagner studied a rogue T cell group in autoimmune disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The pairing of CD40 on immune cells with its partner CD154 is critical in autoimmunity. A T cell group marked by CD40, called Th40 cells, harbors cells that attack the body's own tissue. In healthy people, that group is kept at contained levels.

The team found CD40 and a partner protein, TRAF2, packed at high levels in the raft domains of these cells' membranes. As the title states, that packing leads to preferential survival of this auto-aggressive group. A survival edge may be why such cells build up in illness.
plos-pone-0002176:
Ronald Miller, Nicolas Christoforou, Jonathan Pevsner, and co-authors searched for genes that build the heart, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Heart disease causes the largest share of adult death and illness in wealthy countries. Yet the gene programs that shape the early heart are still largely unknown. The team set out to find new cardiac genes in a systematic way.

They grew mouse embryonic stem cells and steered them toward heart cells, scanning gene activity with arrays as the cells changed. Genes that switched on along the way became candidates for roles in early heart formation. Each new gene on the list is a fresh lead for understanding birth defects of the heart.
plos-pone-0002276:
Amir Grosman and co-authors showed that a parasitic wasp turns its host into a bodyguard. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many parasites and parasitoids change their host's behavior, and the changes are usually assumed to serve the parasite. Field tests of that idea are scarce, and it is often unclear whether host or parasite profits.

The team tested a parasitoid whose pupae develop outside the host caterpillar. The infected host is induced to guard the pupae and fight off predators, raising the pupae's survival. The field evidence shows a parasite pulling a host's strings for its own young's safety.
plos-pone-0002376:
Müller and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Martina Müller, Kerstin Fink, Julia Geisel, and others. Its subject is intestinal Colonization of IL-2 Deficient Mice with Non-Colitogenic B. vulgatus Prevents DC Maturation and T-Cell Polarization. IL-2 deficient (IL-2 −/−) mice mono-colonized with E.

coli mpk develop colitis whereas IL-2 −/− -mice mono-colonized with B. vulgatus mpk do not and are even protected from E. coli mpk induced colitis. We studied if mono-colonization with E. coli mpk or B. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002476:
Led by Dalmasso, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Guillaume Dalmasso, Hang Thi Thu Nguyen, Yutao Yan, and others. Its subject is butyrate Transcriptionally Enhances Peptide Transporter PepT1 Expression and Activity. PepT1, an intestinal epithelial apical di/tripeptide transporter, is normally expressed in the small intestine and induced in colon during chronic inflammation.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002576:
Research by Dusek and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Jeffery A. Dusek, Hasan H. Otu, Ann L. Wohlhueter, and others. Its subject is genomic Counter-Stress Changes Induced by the Relaxation Response. Mind-body practices that elicit the relaxation response (RR) have been used worldwide for millennia to prevent and treat disease.

The RR is characterized by decreased oxygen consumption, increased exhaled nitric oxide, and reduced psychological distress.
