Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002676:
Work by Marion Coolen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was molecular characterization of the gastrula in the turtle emys orbicularis : an evolutionary perspective on gastrulation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Marion Coolen, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Due to the presence of a blastopore as in amphibians. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002776:
Work by Christian Gortázar and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was bovine tuberculosis in doñana biosphere reserve: the role of wild ungulates as disease reservoirs in the last iberian lynx strongholds. The catalog record names Christian Gortázar first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Doñana National Park (DNP) in southern Spain is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve where commercial hunting and wildlife artificial feeding do not take place and. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002876:
Simant Dube, Jian Qin and Ramesh Ramakrishnan presented a math method in PLOS ONE in 2008 for counting gene copies in a DNA sample. Copy number variation means stretches of the genome appear more or fewer times than usual, and such changes have been tied to disease. Their tool works with digital PCR run on a tiny fluid device.

The paper gives an algorithm the authors describe as sound in its math and fast to run. It turns raw device counts into an accurate copy number estimate. Labs that measure DNA dosage for research or diagnosis get a clearer way to handle the numbers these small devices produce.
plos-pone-0002976:
Joel Baumgart, Iuliia Vitko, Isabelle Bidaud and co-authors studied a loop inside low-voltage calcium channels in 2008. Calcium and sodium channels are built from four linked repeats, joined by inner loops with key regulatory roles. The loop joining repeats I and II matters greatly in high-voltage channels.

Here the focus is the same loop in low-voltage-activated channels, which govern rhythmic firing in brain and heart. The team identified structural parts of the loop that control gating and surface expression. Published in PLOS ONE, the detail aids design of drugs that target these channels. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003076:
Laura Reed, Brooke LaFlamme and Therese Markow studied hybrid male sterility in fruit flies in 2008. The genetic basis of postzygotic isolation is a central puzzle in evolutionary biology. Forces causing hybrid sterility act on the responsible genes while they are still varying within species, so the traits must be studied as they arise.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team analyzes intraspecies variation for interspecies isolation. That design catches sterility genes mid-process, before species fully split. The work helps explain how two populations become unable to breed, a core step in the origin of species.
plos-pone-0003176:
David M. Paterson, Rebecca J. Aspden, Pieter T. Visscher and colleagues study living sediment mats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. For the first time, they studied the power of stromatolite microbial groups to act as natural ecosystem engineers. Stromatolites are layered structures formed by microbial activity. They are thought to have ruled the shallows of the early oceans.

The team test light-dependent biostabilisation, the way these mats hold sediments together, and how it depends on light. Readers see ancient-style microbe groups doing work that can be measured in modern settings. The study links early Earth life to present coastal processes in a direct way, through tests.
plos-pone-0003276:
Shin-ichi Todoroki studies a destructive fibre phenomenon in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fiber fuse is a process of optical fiber destruction under the action of laser radiation, found twenty years earlier. Once initiated, optical discharge runs along the fiber core region toward the light source and leaves periodic voids whose shape looks like a bullet pointing in the direction of travel.

The author observes in situ the modulated light emission of fiber fuse synchronized with the void train over a hetero-core splice point. Readers get a close look at a failure mode that can destroy communication lines. Understanding the fuse may help design fibres or sensors that resist it.
plos-pone-0003376:
Nathan A. Baird and co-authors shared a cheaper way to map genes in this 2008 paper. Labs often track single-letter DNA changes, called SNPs, to build genetic maps. Good maps need many markers, and old ways to get them cost a lot. The team cut DNA at set points and read only the bits next to each cut.

Those short bits are called RAD markers, and each one can hold useful DNA changes. Reading them found many new markers and placed them on a map at once. The method is simple enough for species with few genetic tools. It opened genome mapping to far more kinds of plants and animals.
plos-pone-0003476:
Shuo Wang and co-authors traced a cancer control switch in this 2008 paper. A protein called p27 Kip1 restrains cell division. Losing that restraint is tied to many human cancers. The factor Stat1, key to immunity and tumor watch, acts in this pathway.

The team showed Stat1's phosphate state decides how Ras behaves. Ras is a growth signal that can turn cancerous. When Stat1 is set one way, it regulates p27 and checks Ras. The finding names a lever that helps decide tumor formation. Ras is among the most studied cancer genes in all of biology.
plos-pone-0003576:
Samir K. Saha and co-authors typed a meningitis germ without culture in this 2008 paper. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumococcal meningitis, often in children. Standard serotyping needs the germ grown in culture first. Many patient samples come back culture negative.

Their sequential multiplex PCR approach named serotypes directly. It had not been applied where Asian serotypes are diverse. Naming the strain guides surveillance of disease patterns. It also informs which vaccines a region needs most. Meningitis kills fast, so a name for the strain must come within hours, not days. Serotypes also shift over time as vaccines press on them.
plos-pone-0003676:
Dorit Ben-Shachar and Rachel Karry published this psychiatry study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Faults in mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, have been reported in three major mental illnesses. The authors asked whether those faults look the same in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression.

They measured parts of mitochondrial complex I, the first step in the energy chain, across brain regions. The abnormal patterns differed by disease, each with its own map of affected areas. That contrast suggests the three disorders disturb energy metabolism in their own ways, not through one shared break.
plos-pone-0003776:
Demetrios Kalaitzidis and Benjamin G. Neel published this blood methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hematopoietic stem cells are among the best-studied adult stem cells. Tools existed to read phosphoproteins in their offspring, but not in the rare stem cells themselves. The authors present a protocol to close that gap.

Using flow cytometry, they tracked protein phosphorylation in single stem and progenitor cells. Responses differed by the stimulus given and changed over time. The technique reveals how the blood system's root cells answer different calls, moment by moment. Rare cells like these are where blood diseases often begin.
plos-pone-0003876:
C. Jaco Klok and Jon F. Harrison tested how air oxygen shapes insect size in a 2009 PLOS ONE article. Fossil records link past swings in air oxygen with swings in insect body size. High oxygen seems to favor larger insects over long spans of time. The authors wanted a direct test of that link.

They bred the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster for large size under three oxygen levels. Low oxygen held back the gains that selection could make. The result supports the idea that thin air limits how big insects can grow. It helps explain why giant insects lived when air held more oxygen.
plos-pone-0003976:
Konrad U. Foerstner, Tobias Doerks, Jean Muller, and co-authors found an industrial enzyme in a eukaryote in 2008. Nitrile hydratases are bacterial enzymes used in industry and cleanup. They break down nitrile chemicals in wastewater. Computer screening searched many genomes for these enzymes.

Their PLOS ONE article reports one in Monosiga brevicollis, a single-celled eukaryote. Its two enzyme parts, usually separate, sit fused in one protein. A eukaryote copy widens the known spread of this enzyme family. It also hints at gene transfer between distant life forms. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004076:
Pablo Freire, Marco Vilela, Helena Deus, and co-authors explored DNA copy changes in a brain tumor in 2008. Glioblastoma multiforme is among the most lethal brain cancers. The Cancer Genome Atlas project began large-scale analysis of such tumors. It gathered genomic, expression, and clinical data together.

Their PLOS ONE article analyzes copy number alterations in glioblastoma samples. Gains and losses of DNA segments mark genes that drive growth. An exploratory pass shows patterns others can test in larger sets. The work demonstrates open analysis of shared cancer genome data. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004176:
Michael Tuvim and colleagues published this lung study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Influenza pneumonia kills many people every year, and pandemic flu has killed millions. Deaths have been blamed on a host response too weak to limit the virus. They have also been blamed on inflammation so strong that it damages the lung itself.

The team tested the second idea by boosting lung inflammation in advance. They report that augmented inflammation in the lung protects against influenza A pneumonia rather than worsening it. The result challenges the simple view that inflammation in flu is mostly harmful.
plos-pone-0004276:
Hirotaka Sakamoto and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many men suffering from stress, including post-traumatic stress disorder, report sexual dysfunction, usually treated with counselling. The team had earlier identified a gastrin-releasing peptide system in the lumbar spinal cord that acts as a primary mediator of male sexual function.

Here they show that stress affects this spinal peptide system. The peptide is called GRP for short. The finding gives psychogenic erectile dysfunction a physical address in the spinal cord. A defined neural target could support treatments beyond counselling alone.
plos-pone-0004376:
Yeast cells give scientists a simple way to study basic cell survival. Laurence Vernis, Céline Facca, Emmanuelle Delagoutte, and co-authors worked with a mutant form of a yeast gene called TAH18. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper names a protein pair that the gene helps form. The pair is called the Dre2-Tah18 complex.

The authors report that this complex guards the cell's mitochondria, its energy-making parts. It also shapes whether a cell dies after oxidative stress, damage caused by reactive oxygen. The gene had first turned up in a screen for partners of a DNA-copying enzyme. Connecting it to mitochondria widens the story. Cell death control is central to much disease research.
plos-pone-0004476:
Even blurry pictures of protein assemblies can reveal where their parts touch, show Rupali Gadkari, Deepthi Varughese, and N Srinivasan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Large assemblies of many proteins are still few in number, because they are hard to capture in detail. Yet they give deep insight into how cells organize and work.

Many such structures are known only at low resolution, where just the backbone anchor points, called Calpha atoms, are placed. The authors show those points alone can identify which building blocks sit at the interfaces between parts. That turns rough maps into useful guides. Knowing the contact points helps explain how assemblies form, and where a drug might wedge in to break a harmful complex apart.
plos-pone-0004576:
Changes across a growth signaling pathway decide which lung cancers answer a key drug class, report Jeet Gandhi, Jianling Zhang, Yang Xie, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pathway centers on EGFR, a receptor that drives cell growth. Its deregulation is common in non-small cell lung cancers. That led to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, drugs that are highly effective in a subset of patients.

The team studied lung cancer cell lines, cataloging mutations and copy number gains in EGFR and alterations in other genes of its pathway. They related those patterns to sensitivity to the inhibitors. Knowing which changes predict a response helps oncologists pick the patients a drug will help, instead of treating everyone and hoping.
plos-pone-0004676:
Irka Bargielowski and Jacob Koella tested a possible way that a tiny parasite blocks malaria spread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some microbes that infect mosquitoes can slow the growth of malaria parasites inside them. That effect could offer a fresh way to curb malaria, but the cause was not known.

The team looked at infection of young mosquitoes by one such microbe. They asked if early infection changes the mosquito in ways that later block the malaria parasite. A clear cause would help judge if these microbes can be used in the field. It would also guide safe use near people and farms.
plos-pone-0004776:
Yami Shapira and colleagues developed repeated laparoscopy in mice for continuous liver assessment across disease models, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Following liver disease in mice usually means killing animals at each time point for tissue. That blocks true tracking of progression in the same animal and uses many more animals for one study.

The team aimed to build a safe, repeatable scope method for the mouse liver. Their tool lets researchers watch change over time in living mice. Fewer animals are needed and each serves as its own baseline. The method suits drug and disease course studies.
plos-pone-0004876:
Isabel Gordo and colleagues modeled genetic diversity in the SIR model of pathogen evolution, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team introduces a model assessing levels and patterns of genetic diversity in pathogen groups whose epidemiology follows susceptible infected recovered dynamics. Pathogen groups are modeled as metapopulations composed of subpopulations within infected hosts connected by transmission events and bottlenecks.

Epidemic structure shapes viral diversity predictably. Bottlenecks purge variation at each transmission. Models connect within host and group scales. Forecasting evolution aids vaccine planning. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004976:
A master clock in the brain drives our daily rhythms. It sits in the suprachiasmatic nuclei, or SCN, at the base of the hypothalamus. Light reaches it directly from the eyes. Henk Tjebbe vanderLeest and colleagues studied its shifting power in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked what sets the clock's capacity to shift phase.

Light early in the night delays the rhythm. The size of that shift depends on the SCN's internal network. The authors traced shifting capacity to how the SCN neurons are organized. Wiring decides how far the clock can jump. The work links clock structure to jet-lag flexibility. It may help explain why some people adjust to new time zones faster.
plos-pone-0005076:
The Myc gene drives cell growth. It also brakes itself, repressing its own gene. Every tested tumor line has broken that self-brake. Their Myc levels run high as a result. Abid Khan and colleagues studied the brake in fruit flies. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

A protein called Su(z)2 antagonizes the auto-repression. It raises Myc levels and boosts Myc's activation of other genes. The tug-of-war reveals a new lever on a classic cancer gene. It may explain how tumors escape the brake. The fly system makes the mechanism easy to dissect. Lessons from flies often carry into human cancer biology. This lever is now a named target for deeper study.
plos-pone-0005176:
Reaching upward with an arm means the brain must plan for the pull of gravity. Many researchers think the cerebellum, at the back of the brain, works out those forces in advance. Gentili and colleagues tested that idea in PLOS ONE in 2009 using paths modeled on the cerebellum and a robot arm.

Their work shows how gravity torques can be folded into the inverse computation the brain needs for movement. In plain terms, the system works out which muscle forces will produce a planned motion. The robot tests help link brain theory to real control, with lessons for both neuroscience and robotics.
plos-pone-0005276:
Bacteria swap whole gene cassettes using platforms called integrons, speeding the spread of useful traits. Koenig and colleagues studied integrons at the Sydney Tar Ponds, a site polluted with industrial waste, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

At polluted sites, bacteria face compounds few organisms can break down. The study linked integron cassettes there to the degradation of industrial waste compounds. Gene swapping may help local microbes assemble the toolkit to live on pollution, a case of evolution answering human waste. Sites fouled by tar and oil are costly to clean by truck and fire. Germs that learn to eat the waste on site could do the job for far less, if the right gene sets are in place and can be kept at work.
plos-pone-0005376:
GAPDH is a workhorse enzyme of glycolysis, the sugar-burning pathway, with side roles as a kinase and stress switch. Ralser and colleagues disturbed glycolysis in yeast and reported an unexpected DNA effect in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Interfering with glycolysis caused hyper-recombination of plasmids, extra swapping of DNA pieces. The effect depended on Sir2, a protein tied to genome stability and aging. An energy pathway guarding the genome is a reminder that metabolism and DNA maintenance are deeply intertwined. When sugar use is blocked, a cell must burn other fuels, and the strain of that switch may be what shakes the genome loose. A link worth tests in yeast and in human cells alike.
plos-pone-0005476:
Lina Sun and colleagues made human antibodies against bird flu for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The H5N1 bird flu virus can kill people, and new treatments are badly needed. People who survive the illness carry antibodies that may point the way.

From survivors, the team built two human antibodies in the lab and mapped where they grab the virus. Both antibodies blocked the virus and protected animals in tests. Antibodies like these could become treatments for severe flu and could show vaccine makers which parts of the virus to target. Protective antibodies of this kind are rare, so each one found adds a useful lead for treatment design.
plos-pone-0005576:
Prateep Beed, Benedikt Salmen, and Dietmar Schmitz studied a receptor in a brain area for smell and memory, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. One receptor subunit, GluK2, is tied to how prone the brain is to seizures. Most work on it had focused on the hippocampus.

The team turned instead to the entorhinal cortex, the gateway between the hippocampus and the rest of the brain. They found that GluK2 shapes how excitable nerve cells are in its outer layers. That could matter for both memory and the start of epileptic seizures. This gateway area is also among the first harmed in Alzheimer's disease, which widens the interest in its receptors.
plos-pone-0005676:
Hui Peng and co-authors described a new compound in 2009 that blocks a pump cancer cells use to expel drugs. The pump, called ABCG2, sits in the cell wall and pushes out many chemo drugs. Tumors with high pump levels often shrug off treatment, a problem known as multidrug resistance.

The blocker works in two modes against the pump, the title reports. ABCG2 also shields cancer stem cells, the hard core that can regrow a tumor. Mice lacking the pump show no clear harm, which hints blocking it may be safe. A good blocker could make standard chemo work again in stubborn cancers.
plos-pone-0005776:
Annett Jacobi and co-authors mapped in 2009 how the body normally keeps DNA-reactive B cells in check, and where that control fails in lupus. Such B cells make antibodies against DNA, which precede lupus flares and drive kidney damage. Healthy people hold these cells at several checkpoints.

The team characterized the cells in lupus patients stage by stage. Comparing patients with the normal checkpoints shows which gates leak. Leaky gates are candidate targets for therapies that reset tolerance instead of suppressing all immunity. The work gives lupus research a detailed map of a central fault.
plos-pone-0005876:
Fang-Yu Chang and co-authors showed in 2009 that excess bilirubin can weaken the synaptic strengthening behind memory. Jaundice is common in newborns because their livers handle bilirubin poorly. Most cases are harmless, but severe build-up can injure the brain.

Exposing hippocampal tissue to unconjugated bilirubin impaired long-term potentiation, the lasting boost synapses use to store information. That impairment offers a mechanism for the learning problems seen after severe neonatal jaundice. It argues for prompt treatment thresholds that protect the brain. The study connects a familiar nursery problem to a precise cellular effect.
plos-pone-0005976:
Before a cell divides, it must build the poles that will pull its copies apart. Laurence Haren, Tim Stearns and Jens Lüders studied how those poles gather their key parts in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper centers on gamma-tubulin complexes, the starter kits from which the cell's inner tracks grow, and on the centrosomes where they collect.

A kinase called Plk1 drives that gathering, with help from several parts of the pole's core. Without this recruitment, the division machine cannot form on time. The work fills in a step every dividing cell must get right, and it matters for cancer research, since dividing cells are the ones most cancer drugs aim to stop.
plos-pone-0006076:
A transplanted heart can be taught to be accepted rather than attacked. Dahai Liu, Xiu-Da Shen, Yuan Zhai and colleagues explored how that lesson is written in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses rats made tolerant of a donor heart by hybrid MHC molecules, part donor and part recipient. It asks how the graft shapes the T cell repertoire inside it.

Class I MHC sequences in the graft select which T cell receptors survive there, the title reports. The graft thus sculpts its own defenders. Knowing that selection happens inside the organ gives transplant science a mechanism to aim at, as it works toward tolerance without lifelong immune-suppressing drugs.
plos-pone-0006176:
Most tools for studying protein change read only the long chain of letters in a protein. Matthias Haimel, Karin Proell, and Michael Rebhan argue that real function sits at a higher level. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper presents ProteinArchitect, a tool for studying how proteins evolve above the sequence level.

The tool focuses on domains, the parts of a protein that fold on their own, and on short motifs tucked inside them. Those features carry much of what a protein actually does in the cell. By tracking them, researchers can compare proteins that look unlike at letter level. The approach opens a wider view of how new protein jobs evolve.
plos-pone-0006276:
Trials of asthma drugs for children may be measuring too little, too briefly. Ian Sinha, Paula Williamson, and Rosalind Smyth reviewed trials of inhaled corticosteroids in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Regulators require short-term disease activity measures, but other outcome areas are not mandatory for licensing.

Trial outcomes proved narrowly focussed on that short-term activity, the authors conclude. Longer-term effects, daily life, and harm outcomes received far less attention. Parents and doctors need the wider picture when choosing treatments for years of use. The review argues for agreed core outcomes in children's asthma trials.
plos-pone-0006376:
Delivering a gene to the liver can teach the immune system to tolerate the protein it makes. Ashley Martino and colleagues used adeno-associated viral gene transfer to the liver in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their test antigen was beta-galactosidase, a bacterial enzyme placed inside cells. The approach had induced tolerance to several proteins in animal models of inherited deficiency.

The study examines what tolerance to a cytoplasmic antigen implies for antigen presentation and immune toxicity. Tolerance is the goal when replacing missing proteins in patients. But shutting down responses carries its own risks. The work maps both sides for gene therapy design.
plos-pone-0006476:
Dmitry Ivankov, Natalya Bogatyreva, and Michail Lobanov linked protein shape to folding speed in PLOS ONE in 2009. How fast a protein folds into its working shape is a basic puzzle in biology. Several open questions tie folding rate to simple properties of the final shape. The team studied a series of structural descriptors, numbers that summarize a protein's shape.

They tested how well those descriptors couple with measured folding rates. If shape alone predicts speed, folding follows rules we can compute. That would help design proteins and interpret mutations. The study adds to the search for a simple physics of protein folding.
plos-pone-0006576:
Julie Struble and Ryan Gill hunted hidden antibiotic resistance genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The ability of bacteria to rapidly evolve resistance to antibiotics is a critical public health problem. Resistance leads to increased disease severity and death rates. The team applied a genome-scale identification method to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hard-to-treat pathogen.

They searched for cryptic aminoglycoside resistance genes, genes present but silent until activated. Hidden resistance can wake under drug exposure and cause treatment failure. Finding such genes in advance warns clinicians which drugs may fail. The method can be reused for other pathogens and drug classes.
plos-pone-0006676:
Ben J. Hayes and co-authors applied genome-wide association methods to cattle breeding in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their concern was food production under climate change. Dairy regions of Australia face rising temperatures and water shortages. High-energy feeds are also expected to grow scarcer and costlier. Cattle will need to cope with heat and poorer feed.

The researchers validated a genome-wide association study aimed at finding useful genetic markers. Such markers can guide breeding toward animals suited to harsher conditions. Selection can then favor cattle that stay productive as environments shift. The work treats genetics as one practical tool for adapting farming. It offers a path for herds in regions hit hardest by warming.
plos-pone-0006776:
Raquel M. Raices and colleagues found a new job for an immune regulator protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is IκBζ, a member of the IκB family. Its relatives control the transcription factor NFκB. Unlike them, IκBζ works inside the nucleus itself. It is switched on by interleukin-1 and by several immune triggers.

The study shows IκBζ helps regulate production of interferon gamma. Interferon gamma is a key signal directing immune attack. A nuclear regulator shaping that output adds a control layer. It may explain how some immune responses are fine-tuned. The finding could matter for diseases where interferon gamma runs too high or too low.
plos-pone-0006876:
Ann E. McKellar and Andrew P. Hendry compared shape variation in humans with other animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Species vary in form, and so do individuals within them. Humans seem to show especially high morphological variation. That impression may only reflect our skill at telling faces apart. The authors set out to test the impression with data.

They measured levels of variation across species on common scales. Humans were compared against other animals fairly. Whether we are truly unusual shapes evolutionary thinking about our species. Exceptional variation might reflect relaxed selection or diverse environments. The comparison corrects a perception that face recognition inflates.
plos-pone-0006976:
Ellen Kenchington, Lorraine Hamilton, Andrew Cogswell, and colleagues studied mussel inheritance in PLOS ONE in 2009. Marine mussels of the genus Mytilus break a basic rule of biology. Most animals inherit mitochondria only from their mother. These mussels carry two mitochondrial genomes, one passed down through females and one through males.

The team tested whether the male-line genome also decides maleness itself. They found the two traits travel together but are not causally linked. That distinction matters for evolution research. This odd double system is a natural test of how mitochondrial inheritance can change.
plos-pone-0007076:
Maria Marchetto, Gene Yeo, Osamu Kainohana, and colleagues compared lab-grown stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scientists can reprogram body cells into induced pluripotent stem cells. These iPSCs promise disease models and future therapies. How closely they match true embryonic stem cells was still unclear.

The team compared the gene activity signatures of human iPSCs and embryonic cells. They also examined whether iPSCs retain a memory of their tissue of origin. Such memory could bias what the cells become later. Knowing the gaps between the two cell types is key to using iPSCs safely.
plos-pone-0007176:
Haley D. M. Wyatt, Allison R. Tsang, Deirdre A. Lobb, and colleagues examined a key part of the telomerase enzyme in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Telomerase keeps the ends of chromosomes, called telomeres, from shortening. Its core includes a protein subunit and an RNA subunit that work together.

The authors focus on one position in the human protein, labeled Q169. They test its role in lab cultures and in living systems. They report that this single site is essential for telomerase to work, which matters for studies of aging and cancer.
plos-pone-0007276:
Mari Järve, Lev A. Zhivotovsky, Siiri Rootsi, and colleagues studied mutation rates in Y chromosome markers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Short tandem repeats on the Y chromosome are widely used in population genetics. Most work uses short repeat units of two, three, or four DNA letters.

Repeats with longer units are rarer and less commonly used. The authors study the evolution of those larger-repeat loci. They report a decreased rate of evolution as repeat unit size increases. Their finding affects how geneticists date population events using Y chromosome markers.
plos-pone-0007376:
Zsuzsanna Sasvari, Stéphane Bach, Marc Blondel, and colleagues tested anti-prion compounds against an RNA virus in 2009. Small molecule inhibitors are potent antiviral tools. They also help dissect single steps in viral replication, showing exactly where a virus life cycle can be broken by drugs.

The authors test acridine derivatives with known anti-prion activities. Their target is Tomato bushy stunt virus, a model positive-strand RNA virus. They report inhibition of RNA recruitment and replication. Compounds that block both prions and viruses may reveal shared weaknesses in how pathogens copy themselves.
plos-pone-0007476:
Christian Beaulé and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on daily rhythms in astrocytes, the support cells of the brain. Circadian clocks drive daily cycles in sleep, hormones, and metabolism. They run on feedback loops that make gene activity rise and fall each day. Astrocytes carry such clocks of their own. The team asked which of their jobs follow the clock.

In mouse and rat astrocytes, gene expression clearly swung with the daily cycle. Yet the cells' uptake of glutamate, a key chemical messenger, stayed steady around the clock. So the clock controls some astrocyte tasks and leaves others alone. That split matters for understanding how the brain keeps its chemistry stable. It also cautions against assuming every cell function is rhythmic.
plos-pone-0007576:
Elena Lucchetta, Richard Carthew, and Rustem Ismagilov published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how fly embryos develop reliably in a changing world. Embryos must cope with natural swings in temperature. The mechanisms that compensate for temperature were largely unknown beyond daily clocks. The team focused on the endo-siRNA pathway, a system of small RNAs made inside the cell. They tested its role in the Drosophila embryo.

Disrupting that pathway made development fragile. Embryos lost their robustness against temperature fluctuation. So the small-RNA system acts as a hidden stabilizer of development. Stability, not just instruction, is something genes must supply. A buffer against environmental noise helps explain how development stays accurate outdoors. The finding adds a pathway to the short list of known robustness mechanisms.
plos-pone-0007676:
Isabelle Jeru and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns genes that soften or worsen inherited disease. One such gene, SAA1, changes the risk of kidney damage in people with familial Mediterranean fever. Few modifier genes have been proven in humans.

The team reports that SAA1 itself is under negative selection, a process where harmful versions are weeded out over time. That finding links two fields that rarely meet. It suggests that the same forces that shape disease genes also shape the genes that modify them.
plos-pone-0007776:
James Mark Simmerman and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures flu pneumonia in Thailand across four years, 2005 to 2008. Data on flu in subtropical, lower-income countries were scarce. Good numbers are needed to set vaccine policy and prepare for pandemics.

The team gathered prospective data from hospitals over several seasons. They calculated how often influenza caused pneumonia, when cases peaked, and how many patients died. Multi-year records like these give a true picture of flu's local burden. Thailand's health planners can use them to time vaccination campaigns.
plos-pone-0007876:
Alexander Ciota and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows St. Louis encephalitis virus as it passes through mosquitoes and chickens. The virus was once the main cause of epidemic viral brain inflammation in the United States. West Nile virus took that role after 1999.

The team passed the virus repeatedly in living hosts, a method called experimental passage. They watched which traits the virus kept or gained. Some characteristics that emerged carry evolutionary significance. Comparing the two viruses may explain why West Nile spread so much wider. The work informs how scientists judge outbreak risk.
plos-pone-0007976:
Andrew Serazin and colleagues mapped gene activity in a major malaria mosquito for PLOS ONE in 2009. Anopheles funestus spreads malaria across much of Africa and bites with great success. Yet its genes were far less studied than those of its better known cousin.

Using mosquitoes caught in Mali, the team read which genes were active and built a broad transcript map. That map lays groundwork for the full genome work still ahead. It also gives control teams fresh targets, since a germ spreader this important needs more than one way to fight it.
plos-pone-0008076:
Jorge Aguilar and colleagues studied how gut lining cells answer holes punched by bacterial toxins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many germs make pore-forming toxins that pierce cell walls. At low doses the cell survives and fights back, raising internal alarms led by MAPK signal chains.

Enzymes called phosphatases proved to tune that answer. They trim the alarm signals and keep the response in bounds. A measured response repairs the wall without wrecking the tissue. Knowing the tuning knobs may help doctors aid the gut during infections that use this attack.
plos-pone-0008176:
Dörte Becher and colleagues reported a proteomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Staphylococcus aureus, a major human pathogen. A genome gives the blueprint of life, yet proteins do the real work inside living cells. The team aimed to count and measure the full set of proteins this bacterium makes.

Bacteria are simple enough that a near complete protein list is within reach. The authors used that fact to push toward measuring the entire proteome of this germ. Their work shows how close science has come to listing every protein in one living cell type. Such a list can guide work on how the pathogen lives and causes disease.
plos-pone-0008276:
Brandon L. Guthrie and colleagues studied couples with differing HIV status in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. In Africa, many new HIV infections occur within stable discordant couples. In these couples, one partner has HIV and the other does not. Other sexually transmitted infections may raise the risk of transmission. They could account for a large share of new infections.

The team assessed sexually transmitted infections among such couples. Understanding which infections are common points to added prevention steps. Treating those infections might lower HIV spread within couples. The work supports combined care for partners in this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0008376:
Michael Forgber and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about skin lymphoma, a cancer of immune cells in the skin. Not much was known about how the blood of such patients reacts to their tumors. Blood holds defense proteins that latch onto parts of the tumor. Those parts are named tumor-associated antigens. The team used a screen based on the full set of cell proteins to find them.

They read the marks that each patient's own blood had picked out. A map of these marks shows how much of the tumor the body can see and fight. Such marks could serve as signs for tests or as aims for shots. The work grows what is known about blood responses to this cancer.
plos-pone-0008476:
Ana Villar and co-authors measure a growth factor in heart disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The factor is called TGF-beta1. It helps drive remodeling, the reshaping of heart muscle under strain. In aortic stenosis, a tight heart valve forces the left chamber to work against high pressure. That chamber thickens and changes shape over time.

The team check if blood levels of the factor reflect that reshaping. They study patients with aortic stenosis and mice under like pressure load. Blood levels line up with changes in the left chamber. Such a blood test could help track remodeling without repeated scans.
plos-pone-0008576:
Rafeeq Ahmed and co-authors test gene therapy for the heart in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They add a gene called Sonic Hedgehog to stem cells from marrow. That gene guides growth in embryos and in adult stem cells. The team put the altered cells into rodent hearts that lacked blood flow. They hoped the cells would survive better and grow new vessels.

The gene boosts vessel growth through a chain of signals. The chain runs through iNOS, Netrin-1, and PKC. Each step helps new vessels form in the damaged heart. The work offers a way to make stem cell therapy for heart disease stronger.
plos-pone-0008676:
An De Weer, Bruce Poppe, Sarah Vergult, and colleagues published a cancer genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was myeloid leukemia, a blood cancer tied to a gene called EVI1. When EVI1 works in the wrong way, patients tend to do poorly. Many such cases also lose part of chromosome 7.

Working with leukemia cell lines, the team mapped exactly which parts of segment 7q35-q36 were missing. They found two small zones that were deleted again and again. Pinpointing those zones helps other researchers hunt for the genes inside them. Those genes may explain why this form of leukemia behaves so badly.
plos-pone-0008776:
John Welch re-examined a famous size rule using deep-sea snails. His single-author paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The island rule says newcomers to islands tend toward medium size. Big species shrink while small species grow. The pattern was described in mammals and later claimed for other settings. Deep-sea gastropods offered a fresh testing ground.

Welch rechecked the evidence behind extending the rule to these snails. Weak methods can create patterns that are not really there. His audit questions whether the deep-sea case truly fits. Careful rechecks like this keep tidy rules honest in evolutionary biology.
plos-pone-0008876:
Klaus Becker, Gerhard Schneider, Matthias Eder, and colleagues tested a math method for tracking how deeply surgery patients sleep. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Too-light anesthesia risks a patient waking during an operation. Heart signs and movement tests can miss that awareness. Brain waves, recorded as EEG, offer a more direct window. Reading them by eye in real time is impractical, though.

Recurrence quantification analysis hunts repeating patterns in the brain signal. The method turned EEG streams into a depth score during anesthesia. A reliable score would warn teams before a patient stirs. Safer dosing of anesthetics is the practical prize.
plos-pone-0008976:
Christopher Spurney and co-authors tested a healing protein on mice with muscular dystrophy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lack dystrophin, the protein missing in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Their muscles weaken over time, and the heart muscle suffers too. The treatment was thymosin beta-4, a small protein that aids wound repair and calms inflammation.

The team gave the protein over a long period and then measured muscle performance. They checked both the limb muscles used for movement and the heart's pumping work. Long-term dosing let them judge benefit and safety together. Results like these shape whether the protein deserves trials in patients.
plos-pone-0009076:
Matthias Ringkamp and co-authors found a speed test that tells two kinds of monkey nerve fibres apart, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Peripheral nerves mix many fibre types in one cable. Some unmyelinated fibres carry signals away from the cord for the sympathetic system. Others carry pain and temperature signals toward the cord.

In anaesthetised monkeys, the team measured how nerve signals travel in each type. Their conduction properties differed enough to separate the classes. A reliable criterion helps researchers study one fibre type at a time. That separation matters for pain research, where the types play opposite roles.
plos-pone-0009176:
Kevin Morine and co-authors blocked a muscle brake across the whole body. Their method aimed gene therapy at the liver, and PLOS ONE published it in 2010. Myostatin is a protein that holds muscle mass down throughout life. Blocking it is a hopeful strategy against muscular dystrophy and muscle wasting. Earlier methods needed blockers injected straight into each single muscle.

The team used gene transfer aimed at the liver to make the blocker centrally. The liver then supplied the blocking effect to muscles all over the body. Both normal mice and dystrophic mice received the treatment in this study. One treated organ serving the whole body simplifies future therapy design.
plos-pone-0009276:
Sylvie Rato and co-authors published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV copies itself using the host cell's own machinery. Host proteins the virus depends on could become drug targets. Kinases and phosphatases, the cell's signal switches, are especially drug-friendly targets.

The team screened a library enriched for those switch proteins in Jurkat T cells. Using small hairpin RNAs, they knocked down one gene at a time. The long-term, repeated screen found new host factors HIV needs to thrive. Each new knockdown target is a candidate for a different kind of HIV therapy, one the virus cannot escape by mutating itself.
plos-pone-0009376:
Yong-Jun Shin and Mehrdad Nourani published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene networks behave like dynamic systems, switching states over time. State diagrams are a natural way to describe such behavior. For large networks, though, flat diagrams explode into too many states to manage.

The authors adapted statecharts, a layered kind of diagram from engineering, to gene network modeling. Layers let a modeler group states into higher-level states with shared transitions. That structure keeps big models readable and computable. The paper offers systems biologists a way to draw gene circuits that grow without becoming chaos.
plos-pone-0009476:
Stephen Collins and co-authors tested a new way to scan a gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fragile X syndrome is a leading inherited cause of learning disability. It comes from faults in the FMR1 gene. Most cases trace to a long repeat that shuts the gene off. Some patients with like symptoms lack that repeat, so other faults must be at work.

The team used an array based method to read FMR1 and to spot missing pieces. They applied it to patients whose picture fit the syndrome. A faster, fuller scan could find the rarer faults that standard tests miss. That would give more families a firm answer about the cause.
plos-pone-0009576:
Caroline Brorsson and colleagues combined genetics with protein maps for type 1 diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes in the HLA region carry much of the risk for this disease. Those genes sit close together and are inherited in blocks, which blurs blame. The team merged association data with maps of how proteins interact. Their aim was to find disease genes that act only with certain HLA types.

The combined view picked out candidates that genetics alone could not separate. Some risks appear only against a particular HLA background. That sharper picture helps explain why the disease strikes some people and not others. It may also guide the search for ways to prevent it.
plos-pone-0009676:
Daniele Conte, Harry MacWilliams, and Adriano Ceccarelli studied cell fate in a slime mold in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dictyostelium is a simple organism that lives as single cells and then gathers into a many celled body. Within that body, cells take on different fates. The team showed that a protein called BTG interacts with a retinoblastoma like protein. Together they help control which fate a cell takes.

Retinoblastoma is famous as a cancer guard in animals. Finding its partnership at work in a slime mold pushes the system's roots deep in time. Cell fate control may be older than animals themselves. Simple organisms like this one let scientists study that ancient machinery in clean form.
plos-pone-0009776:
Patricia Andressa de Almeida Buranello and co-authors published an immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study tests ArtinM, a sugar-binding protein, on mast cells in rats. ArtinM was known to draw in other immune cells and to empty mast cells of their stored signals.

ArtinM emptied mast cells from the belly lining and gut membrane in dishes, the team reports. Three days after a shot into the belly, mast cell counts there had fallen, and by seven days they were near normal. Bone marrow mast cells rose after the shot, even in rats whose belly mast cells had been wiped out first. The authors credit fresh recruitment from the marrow.
plos-pone-0009876:
Some journal issues are paid supplements, and readers may wonder if their articles get cited less. Leslie Citrome compared how often papers are cited across journals and their sponsored supplements. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Citability means how likely an article is to be cited by later work. Citrome weighed original research and reviews in regular issues against sponsored supplements. Supplements often carry a weaker reputation, deserved or not. Citations are the currency of academic reputation. Evidence on their citation record helps editors and readers judge fairly. Readers can weigh reputation against the actual record.
plos-pone-0009976:
Families with inherited breast cancer risk carry clues in regions of DNA flagged by linkage studies. Juan Manuel Rosa-Rosa and colleagues sequenced those regions in depth. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Deep sequencing reads a DNA stretch many times to catch rare variants. The regions came from a target linkage assay that narrowed the hunt first. Troubleshooting covers the snags that stall such projects. The authors lay out methods, an analysis pipeline, and troubleshooting. Sharing the full workflow helps other labs repeat the hunt in their own families.
plos-pone-0010076:
John Maniscalco, Alan Springer, and Pamela Parker reported sea lion counts in Alaska in 2010. Steller sea lions had crashed by more than eighty percent across their western range. That decline ran from the late 1970s through the 1990s. One leading idea blamed low birth rates among females in the Gulf of Alaska.

Working in Kenai Fjords, the team found high birth rates instead. Their PLOS ONE report argues that local evidence can clash with broad claims about population status. Getting that picture right matters, because fishing rules and protection plans rest on it.
plos-pone-0010176:
The authors were Mario Alvarez, Felipe López-Pacheco, José Aguilar-Yañez, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper built a simple flu test that needs no live virus. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic likely infected millions of people in its first months. Knowing the true count requires testing blood for antibodies across whole populations, at large scale.

Their method, a form of ELISA test, spots antibodies specific to the 2009 strain in human serum. A virus-free test is safer and easier to run in ordinary labs. Such surveys reveal how far a pandemic really spread, beyond cases seen by doctors.
plos-pone-0010276:
The authors were Anne Guézou, Mandy Trueman, Christopher Buddenhagen, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study inventoried alien plants on the Galapagos Islands. Introduced plants are degrading habitats across the archipelago. Problems concentrate on the four inhabited islands. Farms in humid highlands and towns on the dry coast act as starting points for invasions.

From those footholds, alien plants spread into the surrounding national park. The team compiled an extensive inventory for the inhabited areas. A full list of what has arrived, and where, is the baseline for control work in a famous protected ecosystem.
plos-pone-0010376:
John Kauh and colleagues found a way to make pancreatic cancer cells easier to kill, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A signal called TRAIL can order cancer cells to self-destruct while sparing most normal cells. Many tumors resist it, though, including pancreatic ones. A protein named c-FLIP acts as a shield against that order. The team tested a drug that blocks histone deacetylases, enzymes that manage gene activity.

The drug, LBH589, caused the shield protein to break down. With the shield gone, TRAIL could kill the cancer cells. Pairing the two treatments thus worked better than TRAIL alone. Pancreatic cancer badly needs such openings, since it resists most therapy. This study names a shield and a way to strip it.
plos-pone-0010476:
Philippe Cinquin and colleagues implanted a glucose-powered fuel cell in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Future implants, like pacemakers or sensors, need power without bulky batteries or wires through the skin. Harvesting energy from the body itself would be ideal. No working solution existed when this study began. The team built a cell that makes electricity from glucose, the sugar in body fluids.

Implanted in rats, the device generated power from the animals' own glucose. Even modest power could run low-demand medical sensors. The result is a proof that body chemistry can feed electronics. Challenges of lifetime and safety remain large. Still, the study moved an idea from speculation to a working implant.
plos-pone-0010576:
Véronique Ménoni and colleagues examined medical consent forms in France for PLOS ONE in 2010. People who join a clinical study sign forms that should explain risks and procedures in plain language. The team measured how easy those forms actually are to read.

Using standard readability scores, the forms scored poorly. Most were written well above the reading level of typical patients. Long sentences and technical words made key facts hard to follow. The authors argue that simpler forms are needed if consent is to mean real understanding rather than just a signature.
plos-pone-0010676:
Jeffrey Williams and colleagues counted the fishes of Saba Bank in the Caribbean, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saba Bank is a huge flat-topped seamount under clear, shallow water. Its fish life had never been fully surveyed, though the bank faces anchoring damage from large ships.

Divers recorded species across many habitats on the bank. The tally was rich compared with other Caribbean sites that had been surveyed the same way. The list also gave a first estimate of the bank's full fish count. Baselines like this let future surveys tell real decline from natural change, and they support calls to protect the bank.
plos-pone-0010776:
Nicolas Mouchet and colleagues mapped genes that switch on in sun-exposed skin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sunlight is the most common threat the skin faces. Exposure triggers a protective response inside skin cells, but the full gene program behind that response was only partly known. Whole-genome chips can read the whole program at once.

Volunteer skin was exposed to simulated sunlight, then sampled for gene activity. A network of responsive genes emerged, with the stress kinase p38 at a key control point. Blocking that kinase changed much of the program. The map suggests new ways to protect skin and to understand sun-linked aging and cancer.
plos-pone-0010876:
Zeineb Es-Salah-Lamoureux, Robert Fougere, Ping Yu Xiong and co-authors published this heart channel study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hERG channel helps reset the heart's electric signal after each beat, but it opens unusually slowly and shuts very fast. Why activation is so slow was unclear, so the team watched the channel's moving parts directly.

They attached a fluorescent dye that reports movement of the channel's voltage sensor, the S4 segment, and compared that signal with the pore actually opening. The sensor moved quickly, while the pore opened slowly afterward, uncoupling the two steps in time. Es-Salah-Lamoureux and colleagues thus locate the delay after the sensor moves. That detail matters because many drugs block hERG and can disturb heart rhythm, a major safety concern in medicine.
plos-pone-0010976:
Victoria Demetriou, David van de Vijver, Ioanna Kousiappa and co-authors published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transmitted drug resistance affects about one in eleven newly diagnosed patients in Europe and threatens treatment success. Separately, the amount of viral DNA stored in blood cells predicts how fast disease progresses, and the authors asked whether resistant strains store more or less.

Using a sensitive molecular beacon test on samples from newly diagnosed patients across Europe, they measured a specific form of viral DNA in both resistant and sensitive infections. Stored DNA levels came out essentially the same in the two groups. Demetriou and colleagues report the first direct comparison of this kind. The result suggests resistance mutations, at diagnosis, do not change the size of the viral reservoir that doctors watch for prognosis.
plos-pone-0011076:
Restall and Lorimer published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their work deals with small cell lung cancer, a fast growing form of the disease. The team asked what happens when a heat shock protein called Hsp90 is blocked in these tumor cells.

Blocking Hsp90 pushed the cancer cells into early senescence, a state where cells stop dividing for good. That result turns a normal aging process against the tumor itself. The authors present this forced growth arrest as a possible new way to treat the disease. It also hints at care that may be gentler than standard harsh drugs.
plos-pone-0011176:
Markel, Bar-Haim, Zahavy and colleagues studied inhaled tularemia in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Tularemia germs breathed into the lungs can cause severe disease. At a dose below the lethal level, the team examined one immune signal, IL-17A, for its part in the mouse response.

The signal played a protective role in helping mice survive the inhaled infection. Knowing which signals protect the lungs can guide vaccine design against this germ. Tularemia is also a concern for defense planning, since it can spread through air. A defined protective signal gives vaccine tests a clear marker to measure.
plos-pone-0011276:
Badaut, Bertin, Rustico and colleagues designed a malaria vaccine concept in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria in pregnancy harms both mother and unborn child, and the parasite uses a special protein to stick in the placenta. A vaccine should target parts of that protein that stay the same across parasite strains.

The team identified conserved sequences in one key domain of the protein. Conserved parts make the best vaccine targets because the parasite cannot easily change them. Their blueprint moves a maternal vaccine closer to testing. Protecting pregnant women would save mothers and babies in malaria regions.
plos-pone-0011376:
Zachary Knight and colleagues reported in 2010 that high levels of the hormone leptin are needed before the body stops responding to it. Leptin normally signals fullness and keeps weight steady, but in obesity the brain ignores it, a state called leptin resistance. Whether resistance is caused by high leptin itself, or merely travels with it, was unsettled.

Their experiments showed that sustained high leptin drives the resistant state, while keeping leptin low preserved sensitivity. That finding reframes obesity treatment: lowering leptin may restore the signal rather than adding still more of it. It also warns that leptin-based drugs can defeat themselves if they push levels higher. The work points researchers toward ways of resetting the system instead of shouting louder at a brain that has stopped listening.
plos-pone-0011476:
Jordi Planas and Josep Serrat found in 2010 that evolution rewires gene switches most at the center of the human protein network. Proteins interact in a vast web, and the busiest hubs at its center touch many processes at once. Changing a hub protein itself is risky, but changing its promoter, the switch that sets when it is made, is a gentler way for evolution to experiment.

Comparing promoters across the network, the authors found that genes at the center show the strongest signs of promoter evolution. Tweaking regulation at central hubs thus appears to have been evolution's favorite lever for building complexity. That insight redirects attention from protein changes to switch changes in human evolution. It also suggests disease studies should weigh promoter variants in hub genes heavily, since small timing changes there can echo widely.
plos-pone-0011576:
Nadine Werth and co-authors reported in 2010 that switching on the low-oxygen alarm is a general feature of infections. Hypoxia inducible factor 1, or HIF-1, normally answers when oxygen runs short, rewiring cells to cope. Infections also disturb oxygen and metabolism, and the team tested whether diverse human pathogens, not just one or two, activate this factor in the cells they infect.

Activation proved to be a general phenomenon across infections with human pathogens. Diverse germs thus trip the same oxygen alarm, which then shapes inflammation and defense for better or worse. A shared host response is an attractive drug target, since one treatment might aid many infections at once, the logic behind host-directed therapy. The finding also warns that the alarm can be part of the disease, not only the defense, so timing any intervention will matter.
plos-pone-0011676:
Chun-hong Xia, Zipora Yablonka-Reuveni and Xiaohua Gong studied blood vessel growth in the mouse retina, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A protein called LRP5 plays an important role in building the retina's vessel network. People and mice with faulty LRP5 develop an incomplete network, leaving parts of the eye under-supplied.

The team pinpointed where the failure bites hardest. Without working LRP5, vessels in the deeper layers of the retina fail to develop properly. The finding connects one protein to the plumbing of sight and clarifies why LRP5 faults cause particular patterns of human eye disease.
plos-pone-0011776:
Rowan Higgs and co-authors studied how cells brake their own antiviral alarms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein Ro52 tags other proteins for destruction and is itself a target of autoantibodies in lupus and Sjögren's syndrome. The team had earlier shown Ro52 promotes destruction of IRF3, one transcription factor in the virus-sensing system.

Here they showed Ro52 also promotes degradation of IRF7 downstream of the viral toll-like receptors. Eating its own alarm switches protects the body from prolonged antiviral responses. Understanding this self-protection may explain what goes wrong when autoimmunity targets Ro52.
plos-pone-0011876:
Francesco Lescai and Claudio Franceschi examined in 2010 a quiet problem that weakens the hunt for genes behind complex traits. Genome-wide association studies scan whole genomes for variants linked to disease. A phenocopy is a trait that looks genetic but was produced by other causes, and such look-alikes dilute the real signal.

The authors work through how the level of phenocopies cuts the power of these studies to find low-impact variants. Their analysis helps explain why some genuine gene effects stay hidden even in very large samples. For study designers, the message is practical: cleaner definitions of the trait can be worth as much as enrolling more people.
plos-pone-0011976:
Andrea Lancichinetti and co-workers tackled in 2010 a basic question about networks: what counts as a community inside one. Networks of friendships, proteins, or web pages tend to form clusters, and finding those clusters is a major research industry. Far less work had gone into characterizing the clusters once found.

The team examined the structure of communities in complex networks, their sizes, overlaps, and how sharply they separate from the rest. That characterization tells users of detection software what their results actually mean. For fields from epidemiology to sociology, the difference between a real community and a statistical smudge decides what action the map justifies.
plos-pone-0012076:
Douglas Smith and co-workers set in 2010 the coat proteins of one HIV type next to each other, hunting for the best base for a shot. The type, called clade C, drives most HIV cases in the south of Africa, so shots for that part of the world must be built from its coat. Plain coat shots had failed in past trials, while a Thai trial with a first shot and a later boost shot gave the first true hint of a guard.

The team weighed how strong an immune reply each coat protein could raise, with an eye to that first-shot, boost-shot plan. Coat proteins from one clade are not all alike, and the best mix is not plain to guess. Head-to-head checks like this pick which few builds earn the scarce room in human trials.
plos-pone-0012176:
Dan-Dan Li, Jing-Feng Guo, Jia-Jia Huang, and co-authors tested a marine compound against human cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells normally recycle worn parts through a self-eating process, and faults in that recycling can help tumors start. Compounds that switch the recycling on may therefore prevent or treat cancer, a logic that has drawn wide interest.

Their compound, drawn from a sea sponge family of chemicals, set cancer cells into a death tied to that self-eating process. It worked by blocking a growth pathway the cells rely on. Natural products remain a rich source of cancer drug leads, and a clear account of how one kills tumor cells guides the chemists who would improve it.
plos-pone-0012276:
Sanguthevar Rajasekaran, Tian Mi, Jerlin Camilus Merlin, and co-authors improved computer prediction of tiny functional protein snippets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Minimotifs are short stretches in a protein that carry a known job, like a docking site, and the same snippet often does the same job in other proteins. Predicting them by computer is easy; the problem is false alarms, which flood the results and limit their use.

Grouping minimotifs by their function first sharpened the predictions considerably. Cleaner predictions let biologists pick which snippets are worth testing at the bench. In a field drowning in sequence data, better filters are worth as much as new data.
plos-pone-0012376:
Christopher Mutch, Jessica Schulte, Eric Olson and co-authors studied how the growing brain cortex makes its nerve cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The cortex builds neurons in two waves: stem cells first divide directly, then make a second pool of progenitor cells that multiply the output. Too few or too many cells in that second pool can change brain size and wiring.

The team found that beta-catenin signaling, a major growth pathway, acts as a brake on the second progenitor pool rather than a simple gas pedal. Keeping the signal on too long shrank the pool's numbers. The result refines how scientists think growth signals balance brain building, with lessons for disorders of brain size.
plos-pone-0012476:
Marco Rincon, Bareket Dassa, Harry Flint and colleagues cataloged the grip proteins of a fiber-eating gut bacterium, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ruminococcus flavefaciens lives in the rumen of cattle and helps break down tough plant walls using a multi-enzyme machine called the cellulosome. Parts named dockerins act as plugs that snap enzymes into the machine.

The team counted and sorted the dockerin-bearing proteins of strain FD-1 and found a surprisingly large and varied set. Variety lets the bacterium attack many plant fibers. The catalog interests biofuel researchers, who hope to copy such machines to turn plant waste into fuel efficiently.
plos-pone-0012576:
Melissa Miller, Raphael Kudela, Abdu Mekebri and colleagues traced a freshwater toxin into sea otters, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Certain cyanobacteria in lakes and rivers bloom into super-blooms that release microcystin, a durable toxin. Monitoring had focused on fresh water, but runoff carries toxins to the coast, and sea otters were turning up exposed.

The team documented microcystin moving from land to sea and into otters, a newly recognized marine harmful algal bloom pathway. Sick otters are sentinels for coastal contamination that can also reach shellfish and people. The study argues for watershed-level monitoring that ignores the artificial line between fresh and salt water.
plos-pone-0012676:
Liu, Li, Yin and co-authors checked how often Chinese clinical trials ever publish their results. Publishing results is the step that makes a trial count for doctors and patients. Their 2010 study searched the World Health Organization's primary trial registries for Chinese trials and followed up their fate.

They measured what share reached publication and how long it took. Low or slow rates mean much patient effort never informs care. The audit gives Chinese research leaders a baseline for pushing fuller, faster reporting. Registries only help science when their trials report back in full, and this audit shows how far there is to go.
plos-pone-0322076:
Titilola Gbaja-Biamila led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of designing HIV prevention services with Nigerian youth. An open call in early 2024 invited fourteen to twenty-four year olds to propose ways community organizations could sustain self-testing and youth-friendly prevention. Ten finalist teams built out ideas in a three-day designathon.

Judges scored entries for relevance, novelty, and fairness. Young people produced workable service strategies rooted in their own communities. Gbaja-Biamila argues the format is practical, while noting only real implementation over time can prove the ideas last.
plos-pone-0331276:
Niroshica Mohanathas and colleagues report a randomized trial, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, on whether training the brain's control skills can help people listen and balance at the same time. Sixty-five adults took part. The groups were middle-aged and older adults whose hearing was normal, plus older adults with hearing loss who wore hearing aids.

Half of each group did twelve weeks of executive function training while the rest served as controls. Thinking skills generally improved, and some gains carried into balance and listening tasks. Balance gains came only among older adults whose hearing was better. The listening task, in contrast, helped most those with the poorest hearing and thinking scores. The team argues for stepping in early, before hearing loss grows severe.
plos-pone-0332676:
Mark Stoeckle and Jesse Ausubel spent a year scooping water from New York City's East River to see what DNA could reveal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The rocky channel is hard to survey with nets and receives treated wastewater, so the team sampled weekly and counted genetic traces left by vertebrates.

Fish DNA rose tenfold in summer and shifted with the seasons as expected, and two fish species appeared that a 2016 survey had missed. Wastewater carried DNA from pets, city mammals, and land birds, and the mix of food-animal DNA closely matched national eating statistics. The cheap shoreline routine offers cities a way to track wildlife and even diet.
plos-pone-0337676:
Sayyed Mohammad Pourya Momtaz Esfahani and co-authors built FairCareNLP, a system that reads written patient reviews and sorts them by sentiment and theme while actively fighting bias. Hospitals mine such comments to improve care, but standard language models can treat patients unfairly depending on gender, ethnicity, or income. Their 2026 system pairs language models with three different debiasing techniques.

One popular method, adversarial training, actually hurt accuracy across the board. Two others, which scrub bias from word representations, improved fairness scores while keeping performance intact. The best configuration reached solid accuracy and fairer treatment of gender in particular. The authors note that ethnicity and income bias remain harder to remove.
plos-pone-0338576:
Bohye Jeong and Peter Stoilov tested how much of a gene pair the light-sensing cells of the eye really need. The two Musashi genes make near-identical proteins that help photoreceptors include special segments in their messages, a job they seem to do only in these cells, where they are unusually abundant. The team bred mice with fewer and fewer working copies, down to a single allele from either gene.

One allele was enough. Photoreceptors kept working, and the special segments in four key vision genes were still included at high levels. The result overturns the guess that sheer abundance explains the proteins' eye-specific role, since even a quarter dose sustains it. The authors leave open what truly confines this splicing job to photoreceptors, while ruling out the simplest answer.
plos-pone-0342576:
Health before pregnancy shapes the health of mothers and babies, yet countries measure it in incompatible ways. Danielle Schoenaker and colleagues present a plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for experts worldwide to agree on a shared set of measures for tracking health before conception.

An international alliance of specialists from rich and poor countries held workshops to sort candidate measures. The protocol explains how the group will rank measures by importance, fairness, and whether data can actually be collected in low-income settings. No final list is published yet. The agreed measures should let governments compare progress and copy policies that work.
plos-pone-0345476:
Tan Zhang and colleagues improved how automated guided vehicles, the driverless carts that haul goods in warehouses, follow their planned paths. Their controller predicts the vehicle's motion and corrects it continuously, but its settings need constant retuning as loads and routes change. They coupled it with an upgraded sparrow-inspired search algorithm that retunes the settings online.

Chaotic starting points, a disturbance trick, and a mutation step keep the search from settling too early on mediocre settings. The score being minimized blends sideways drift and heading error. Simulations in a robotics environment and tests on a real vehicle checked the method. Factories run fleets of these carts, so even small gains in tracking accuracy and adaptability add up.
plos-pone-0345976:
Jinfeng Tang, Ping Li, and Rong Luo compare two ways of giving feedback on student writing. Their 2026 study ran for eight weeks at a Chinese university. Sixty-one students learning English produced two hundred forty-four texts. One route used traditional teacher feedback. The other used peer feedback assisted by artificial intelligence. The design rests on Vygotsky's idea of scaffolding, support pitched just beyond a learner's current reach.

The two scaffolds behaved differently. Teacher feedback covered more ground and adjusted dynamically to each writer. It produced strong short-term gains, but its momentum faded afterwards. AI-assisted peer feedback kept a steadier focus. Its benefits built gradually, like a learning curve. Word variety improved only in the first task under the peer route. The authors argue the modes complement each other, so blended feedback may beat either one alone.
plos-pone-0346076:
Zhixiang Liu, Wentao Hu, and Chunxue Xie tackle path planning for robots that install pipelines along mine roadways. The robot's six-axis arm must swing pipes into place without collisions in a cramped, changing space, and naive routes waste time or end in crashes. Their method improves a common sampling algorithm that grows two search trees toward each other.

A virtual force field nudges new branches toward the goal, and an adaptive step size keeps the search from getting trapped in dead ends. The combination should produce shorter, safer arm paths than the standard method. Mines are exactly the kind of rough workplace where better robot motion planning pays off in speed and safety.
plos-pone-0347176:
Aryan Kumar, Punit Gupta, and Rohit Verma blend two nature-inspired search methods to balance work across fog computing nodes. Fog nodes process data near its source to cut delay, but poor task placement leaves some nodes swamped and others idle. Their 2026 study mixes a bacteria-inspired search, good at roaming widely, with a swarm method that settles fast.

In simulated workloads running from one hundred to ten thousand tasks, the hybrid finished batches sooner and used machines better than either method alone. Its edge grew under heavy loads, cutting total time by roughly a third against a tuned rival. Faster settling also helped. The hybrid offers fog operators a practical way to keep service smooth as demand swings.
plos-pone-0347476:
Zaid A. Qureshi and co-workers study a strange fossil sponge that built early reefs in Cambrian seas hundreds of millions of years ago. Its skeleton stacks round, porous chambers, each ringed at the base by a thorny, bowl-like collar. Their 2026 study runs water-flow and stress computer models to learn what those odd parts did for the living animal.

Flow models showed the thorny collar steered water away from outer pores on the chambers. Stress models showed odd ridges on the spines bore extra load rather than stiffening the skeleton, so they likely served some other purpose. Testing body parts this way helps scientists read how the first animal reef builders fed and lived.
plos-pone-0347776:
The soil clinging to crop roots hosts microbes that feed plants and keep soil healthy. Mamonokane Olga Diale-Makhongela and colleagues profiled those microbes under sorghum and pearl millet on farms in two South African provinces, in this 2026 PLOS One study using gene-based identification.

Thirty-four pooled samples were tested for microbe identity, soil chemistry, and what carbon foods the community could use. One location, Jane Furse, stood out for richer microbe communities and stronger carbon use. Heavy chemical farming can thin this diversity, the authors note, so their census offers a baseline for judging whether gentler practices restore soil life.
plos-pone-0347876:
Mohammad Rasouli, Elham Rahimi, and Arshia Ilaty wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on monitoring thyroid cancer treatment. Care runs in several stages, and the authors build a control chart, a statistical alarm tool, tuned by a genetic algorithm. The chart type is EWMA, which weighs recent results more heavily.

Integrated with the chart is risk prediction, based on machine learning, for each stage of treatment. The aim is earlier warning when a patient's course drifts off track during multistage therapy. Hospital quality teams and thyroid specialists are the audience for monitoring that blends classic statistics with learned risk scores.
plos-pone-0348076:
Kibir Temesgen Assefa and colleagues map where Ethiopian teenage girls are missing the cervical-cancer vaccine, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The HPV vaccine prevents most cervical cancer, yet uptake in Ethiopia is low and uneven. Drawing on the national immunization survey's weighted sample of more than five thousand girls, the team analyzed the geography of non-vaccination.

About forty-six percent of girls had not received the vaccine, and the maps showed clustering rather than random scatter, with hotspots identifiable down to local level. Geographically weighted analysis linked the gaps to place-specific factors. National averages hide these pockets; the study argues vaccination drives should be aimed by map, not by blanket campaign.
plos-pone-0348276:
Changfu Liu and Jinju Li reviewed ninety-three intensive care patients treated for bleeding in the digestive tract, focusing on the forty-two whose bleeding tipped into shock. Such cases turn deadly fast, and spotting who will crash matters. Their 2026 study compared the shock and non-shock groups across routine clinical measures and followed both groups' outcomes.

Two blood measures stood out as warning signs: urea nitrogen, a waste product, and fibrinogen, a clotting protein. Urea nitrogen was the most specific predictor, fibrinogen the most sensitive. Overall illness severity, breathing failure, and fibrinogen also predicted who would die, and the shock group died at higher rates. The authors advise watching these markers closely.
plos-pone-0348376:
Shengtian Zhang and co-workers design a learning algorithm that decides where ships should run their computing tasks. Connected ships can send work to nearby edge servers instead of far-off clouds, saving time and power. Their 2026 study tackles the hard mix of choices involved, which shifts as sea channels change minute by minute.

The method splits big decisions into smaller factors and reads the situation through a transformer-style encoder. In tests it beat rival approaches on a combined score of delay and energy.
