It also never produced an invalid choice, so every plan it made could actually run. Smarter offloading could help fleets digitize without draining batteries or clogging links.
plos-pone-0348476:
Keeping spare parts ready keeps big machines running, but replacing parts on a fixed calendar wastes money and still misses failures. Yongjia Gao and colleagues propose timing part supply by how far a machine's performance has worn down, in this 2026 PLOS One engineering paper.

Their method scores machine health from several signs, draws a band describing how health declines, and fits a standard wear curve to that band. From expected health, they compute how many parts will be needed and when to order, allowing for shipping time. The aim is shorter stoppages and fewer parts bought too early or too late.
plos-pone-0348576:
Seo-Yun Choi and Yuri Jang ask whether poor sleep carries part of the harm that a frightening neighborhood does to older adults' mood. Feeling unsafe close to home is a known strain in later life. Their 2026 study analyzes survey data from more than two thousand Americans aged sixty-five and over, testing insomnia as the middle step between danger felt and depressive symptoms.

Both felt danger and insomnia symptoms linked with more depressive symptoms on their own. The step-through-sleep path proved real, carrying about a quarter of danger's total effect. In plain terms, unsafe-feeling streets keep older people awake, and lost sleep feeds low mood. Safer blocks and sleep help could protect mental health together.
plos-pone-0348676:
Jiyang Liao and colleagues used machine learning on a large intensive care database in 2026 to test a simple inflammation ratio as a death predictor in sepsis. The ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes had given mixed answers in smaller studies.

More than four thousand sepsis patients were grouped by the ratio, and models adjusted step by step for clinical factors. Twenty-eight day death ran near one in five overall. The learned model beat standard severity scores at prediction, and the ratio kept independent value. A free number from a routine blood count may help intensive care teams rank risk sooner.
plos-pone-0348776:
Rongjing Ni and Ying Yu build a measurement scale for physical literacy among Chinese college students, covering skill, habits, knowledge, and feelings about movement. No fitting local tool existed for this group. Their 2026 study drafts dozens of candidate questions, screens them with expert rounds and surveys, then gives the final scale to more than three thousand students.

The settled scale holds thirty-two items across four parts, each part scoring consistently. Scores differed by gender, year of study, home registration, and type and district of university. Group gaps appeared in every part of the scale, not just one. Universities now have a checked yardstick for spotting which students need a nudge toward active life.
plos-pone-0348876:
Yangyang Chen and colleagues evaluated a scoring system that decides which early stomach cancer patients need follow-up surgery after a non-curative endoscopic removal. The endoscopic procedure spares the stomach when it fully clears the cancer, but pathology sometimes shows leftovers, and the standard score guiding the surgery decision can misjudge risk. Their weighted version was tested on two hundred ninety patients treated at a Fujian hospital over thirteen years.

Both scores were used to stratify patients, and survival methods tracked who actually had residual cancer or recurrence. The weighted system aimed to sort patients more accurately, sparing low-risk patients an operation and catching high-risk ones reliably. Refining this single decision matters enormously, since salvage stomach surgery is major, while a missed residual tumor can be fatal.
plos-pone-0348976:
Zhixuan Wei and co-workers teach a computer to find key landmarks inside the inner ear on medical scans. The marks sit on the curved canals that help with balance, deep in the bone behind the ear. Their 2026 paper builds a deep learning system that could give surgeons and researchers one shared map for comparing scans across patients.

Expert marks on scans from twenty patients served as the guide for training and checking. The system's errors were about as small as the gaps between human experts themselves. On scans from fourteen more patients, accuracy stayed within limits doctors find acceptable. Automating this fiddly step could speed up ear research and planning for care.
plos-pone-0349376:
Guoqiang Bian and co-authors ran a fully computer-based hunt for ways that Pinellia ternata, a plant long used in Chinese medicine for chest complaints, might act against lung cancer. Using a neural network that weighs links between plant compounds, body targets, and disease genes. They ranked which of the plant's chemicals and which human proteins matter most. Then they simulated how the chemicals dock into those proteins.

One compound, baicalein, gripped several cancer-linked proteins in the same snug way, and long simulations suggested the grip holds steady. Seven proteins emerged as likely hubs of the plant's action. The study offers a map for later bench work rather than proof of benefit, showing how traditional multi-ingredient remedies can be picked apart target by target in silico.
plos-pone-0349576:
Rita Abramov and colleagues describe a planned trial of Just Play, an arts-based program where mothers and their young children with intellectual disability play together with a therapist's guidance. Play builds thinking, social, and emotional skills, yet children with intellectual disability often struggle to play, and their parents face stress that drains playfulness. Most existing programs train parents to manage behavior instead.

Sixty mother-child pairs, with children aged three to seven, will be assigned to the play program or to parent counseling. The team will measure the quality of mother-child interaction and related outcomes with mixed methods. Testing a joyful, relationship-first approach fills a gap left by behavior-focused programs that rarely target play itself.
plos-pone-0349676:
Abdul Rehman Chishti and co-authors designed a tiny multi-band antenna for medical uses in 2026. One small device that works across low and high frequency bands can serve body sensors without crowding the patient or the gadget.

Their folded design, printed on a common board material, shrinks the antenna greatly while keeping three working bands. Tests also used a substance that mimics cancer tissue, which shifted the signal in a detectable way at one band. A single cheap antenna that both communicates and senses could simplify future wearable and implant linked health devices.
plos-pone-0349876:
Haian Liang and co-authors built a better way to predict how a special foundation pile carries weight in soft ground. The pile pairs a stiff precast concrete core with an outer shell of soil mixed with cement. Older design models assumed the layers stayed perfectly glued, but real interfaces weaken gradually under load. Their 2026 model tracks damage at both the inner and outer surfaces of the shell.

Field readings from a full-size trial pile in Jiangxi matched the model's output closely. It showed the concrete core carries more than nine tenths of the load at the pile top, with a distinctive pattern of force along the shell. Engineers can use the model to design these foundations with a clearer picture of how load is shared as damage grows.
plos-pone-0350376:
Jaime Yan presents a validation system for catching logical contradictions inside the data packages that drug companies submit to regulators, in this 2026 paper. The industry's standard checker verifies each data domain separately, so a cancer response rating that conflicts with the underlying lesion measurements sails through. Yan's engine rebuilds the submission as a knowledge graph. It applies a layer of declarative rules, including cross-domain ones modeled on oncology response criteria. An AI agent layer handles the trickiest verification table.

On clean data the new layer flagged almost wholly different material than the checker, showing the two are complementary. On data seeded with twenty contradiction types, it caught every one, while two industry validators caught only the structural cases and none of the cross-domain response contradictions. Three experts endorsed the archetypes. Yan is careful to call this a demonstration of expressiveness, not a real-world detection rate.
plos-pone-0350676:
Javeed and colleagues built a two-stream AI system for sorting network alerts by business importance in a 2026 study. Control centers drown in alerts, and raw oddity scores ignore how much a failure would hurt services. One stream learns time patterns in performance data, while the other reads context about risk and service value.

Merged scores decide which alerts to escalate first, weighted by business impact rather than oddity alone. Tests on public network data plus a factory data set for severity context showed earlier, sharper escalation of serious events and lower running costs. The design speaks to a daily pain in operations: too many alarms, too little guidance on which matter.
plos-pone-0351176:
Oleksandr Bolshov and Dmytro Chumachenko reviewed how reinforcement learning, where software learns by trial and reward, has been used to design epidemic controls. Fast moving outbreaks outpace fixed rules. Thirteen studies from 2014 to 2025 passed their screen across four databases plus reference lists. Models split between simple compartment maths and agent simulations of single people.

Most studies set rewards as a trade off between disease harm and social or economic cost. Actions were usually stepped restriction levels, like school closures by tier. Methods and reporting varied widely, which blocks fair comparison. Standard reporting and shared test outbreaks, the authors urge, are needed before learning based policy can be trusted in a real crisis.
plos-pone-0351576:
Alessandro Suter and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One trial of a simpler two-drug maintenance treatment for people living with HIV. Participants had already kept the virus suppressed for at least two years on standard combined therapy. The study switched them to just nevirapine and lamivudine for forty-eight weeks and compared their results against a simulated control group assumed to have no treatment failures.

About two hundred patients at five centers in Switzerland and Germany took part, and nearly all finished the study. Only two had confirmed viral rebound, both tied to missed doses, and none failed during a further year of follow-up. The authors say the two-drug regimen held up as well as the ideal control, while noting the result applies only to patients who meet the study's strict entry rules.
plos-pone-0351676:
Ahadul Hassan Bhuiyan Konok, Md Shahadoth Hossain, and Md Hafizul Islam used a national health survey to count poor birth outcomes across Bangladesh. Their 2026 PLOS One paper reviewed more than ten thousand pregnancies and grouped stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight, and newborn death together.

About one birth in seven involved at least one of these outcomes, with low birth weight the most common. Twins carried much higher risk across the board. Poorer households, births outside proper facilities, and mothers with little say in decisions also lined up with worse outcomes. The authors call for fairer maternal care and stronger decision power for women.
plos-pone-0351776:
Yinfeng Lin and five colleagues compare two treatments for a stubborn inflammatory breast disease. Their 2026 two-centre study reviews women treated between 2020 and 2025. Granulomatous lobular mastitis brings pain, disfigurement, and real psychological distress. One option is conventional open surgery. The other is ultrasound-guided microwave ablation, which destroys diseased tissue with targeted heat. Two hundred thirty-three patients were split between them by ordinary clinical decisions, not randomisation.

Cure rates were nearly identical, around ninety-seven percent in both groups. Recurrence was low in both, a few percent over a median eighteen months of follow-up. The ablation route spared more blood and finished procedures faster. Patient-reported breast outcomes were surveyed as well. For women weighing a scar against a needle-based procedure, near-equal cure with a gentler operation is meaningful. The authors are careful, though: non-random allocation means fitter patients may have been steered toward ablation.
plos-pone-0351876:
Abu Islam and three colleagues chart sixty years of livestock change in Bangladesh. Their 2026 study assembles records from 1961 to 2020. Cattle, poultry, and other stock supply protein, fertiliser, jobs, and income, especially for women. The team measured growth in animal numbers and products like milk and meat. An instability index captured how wildly the series swung year to year. Forecasting models then projected the sector forward to 2041.

The approach assumes yesterday's patterns broadly persist. It also assumes no massive shocks rewrite the system mid-forecast. Model choice rested on fit statistics and checks that leftover errors behaved randomly. Such projections feed directly into food security planning. Governments deciding on imports, feed supply, and self-sufficiency targets need defensible numbers, not hunches. A careful instability record also warns planners which livestock lines are steady foundations and which swing too hard to build policy on.
plos-pone-0352176:
Florie Monier and seven colleagues ask whether Parkinson's disease changes how time itself seems to pass, in this 2026 PLOS ONE psychology study. Patients and healthy people of similar age judged how fast time had flowed over recent days and over distant stretches of life. They also rated their health, emotions, and self-transcendence — how much they look beyond their own needs toward wider meaning.

Parkinson's, it turned out, did not distort either kind of time judgement. Judging the distant past drew on self-awareness and one's life story, while judging recent days tracked bodily state and mood. Time's felt speed, the authors conclude, says more about how a person feels than about this disease.
plos-pone-0352276:
Aleksi Reito and a team of orthopedic researchers ask a practical question about recovery after a broken shoulder in older adults. In 2026 they re-examined data from two earlier randomized trials involving patients aged sixty and over. One hundred participants wore motion sensors on both arms for four days, a full year after their fracture.

The team compared those real-world movement records with what patients said about their own function on standard questionnaires covering arm disability and quality of life. The two kinds of measure barely matched: self-reports showed only a weak, uncertain link to actual arm activity. That mismatch matters because trials often rely on questionnaires alone, and these results suggest reported recovery and daily movement can tell quite different stories.
plos-pone-0352576:
Chapman and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, examine a defined hypochlorite solution, a bleach-like antiseptic used for over a century. Work with badly burned patients found better survival after tough infections than germ killing alone seemed to explain. The team asked whether the solution also changes inflammation signals.

In dishes, one set strength of the solution killed both major classes of bacteria. The same strength also broke down two immune signal proteins at unequal rates: the one that drives inflammation lost its function about three times faster than the one that calms it. That lopsided effect held across a range of strengths and exposure times. Tests on skin cells checked harm to the body's own cells. The authors propose a double action: the antiseptic clears germs while trimming a pro-inflammation signal more than its calming counterpart, which could ease scarring and help wounds close.
plos-pone-0352676:
Isak Karlsson and four colleagues ask whether memory test scores can forecast motor learning in mice. Their 2026 study used female mice put through several behaviour tasks. Exploration was watched in an open field. Memory was tested with new objects and a Y-shaped maze. Fine motor skill was measured by climbing a pole and reaching for food pellets.

Mice that explored the Y-maze more also succeeded more at pellet reaching. The link was strong enough to predict reaching scores for individual animals. Other task pairings did not show the same connection. For researchers, a quick maze test could flag which mice will handle hard motor tasks well. That saves time and animals in studies where training is long and demanding.
plos-pone-0352776:
Andreas Oelker led a team including the FOR2974 Consortium on this 2026 study of problematic internet use in daily life. Nine hundred people whose gaming, social media, shopping, or pornography use ranged from harmless to pathological kept end-of-day diaries for two weeks after a diagnostic interview. The team modeled how mood and stress led to use.

Temptation stood out as the central driver between bad feelings and actual use, while pleasure and relief reinforced the loop. Oelker's everyday-life evidence backs the theory behind internet addiction models and points treatment at temptation itself.
plos-pone-0352876:
Keira Dyck and three co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One perception study of the Colavita effect. In that effect, people miss a sound when it arrives with a picture. The effect had seemed immune to whether sound and picture meant the same thing. The sounds used before may have been too brief to recognize. This team used words and meaningful sounds. They paired them with pictures that matched or clashed in meaning.

They first reproduced the effect using words. Then they showed that clashing meanings shrank it. When a cat picture came with a dog's bark, people missed the sound less often. The word 'dog' had the same effect. Stimuli from wholly different classes shrank it further. The authors argue that shared meaning helps bind sight and sound into one event. When the binding fails, vision dominates less.
plos-pone-0352976:
Doris Haydee Rosero Salazar, Edward M Weaver, and Zi-Jun Liu published this 2026 animal study of how tongue base size affects eating and breathing. Using young minipigs, they compared siblings made obese on rich feed, whose tongues enlarged, with normal-weight siblings whose tongue base was surgically reduced. Muscle signals, airflow, and X-ray video were recorded during feeding.

The surgically reduced group faced swallowing risks, while the enlarged group showed weakened airflow and smaller breaths. Both groups adapted to keep feeding and breathing in sync. The results matter for treating sleep apnea and swallowing problems in people.
plos-pone-0353176:
Rebecca Roberts and seven co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a scoping review. The review will map how hospitals safely get patients with obesity moving again during a stay. Lying still in hospital weakens patients fast. Moving larger bodies raises safety questions for patients and staff alike. No full summary of the strategies exists yet. The review will search six major databases, using standard scoping methods.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan, not results. Two reviewers will screen studies on their own. They will chart the strategies reported in wards and rehab units. They will also log what helps and what blocks safe practice. The authors aim to give clinicians and planners a map of current practice and its gaps. The summary will be shared in journals and at rehab meetings.
plos-pone-0353276:
Vu Quang Huy led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of automatic weld inspection in precision manufacturing. Orbital TIG welds must be checked for flaws, but human review of weld images is slow and defects vary in shape and size. The team trained a system on more than three thousand weld photos sorted into normal welds and three fault types.

A deep network first extracted visual features, then a random forest classifier made the final call, reaching high accuracy across repeated testing. The pairing beat plain neural networks and older machine learning. Huy offers it for factory quality lines.
plos-pone-0353376:
Shuai Nie and four colleagues investigate why some breast cancers stop responding to a standard chemotherapy drug, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. They focused on a gene-switching protein called TBX20, which public cancer data showed running high in breast tumours. In two breast cancer cell lines, raising TBX20 made cells grow, move, and invade more aggressively, and shrug off the drug doxorubicin.

The protein was found to switch on a pump gene that ejects the drug from cells. It also suppressed the cell's recycling of worn-out power stations, another survival trick. Blocking the pump or restoring recycling reversed the resistance in dishes — two candidate routes for making chemotherapy bite again.
plos-pone-0353476:
Kang studied how family income shapes school results in Korean teenagers in a 2026 paper. Using three waves of a national youth survey covering more than two thousand students, the study tested two paths: money spent on private tutoring, and warmth of parent-child talk.

Higher income predicted more spending on private education, but not better communication. School results rose through the spending path, while the talk path showed no clear effect. The two paths did not differ significantly from each other, though. The findings highlight how paid tutoring converts income into grades in Korea's competitive system, raising fairness questions for poorer families.
plos-pone-0353676:
Sushan Gautam and seven colleagues compare two tape-measure numbers — waist size and body mass index — for predicting heart and metabolic risk in Nepal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Six hundred and seventy-eight adults were measured and checked for six problems, from high blood pressure and diabetes to fatty liver and abnormal cholesterol. South Asians tend to carry risky fat around the middle even at modest weights, so the imported cut-offs may mislead.

Waist size tracked blood fats more strongly and was the only measure tied to high blood pressure; both measures predicted fatty liver. The authors recommend using the two together, with age and sex, and calibrating thresholds to Nepalese bodies rather than borrowing them.
plos-pone-0353776:
Roberto Bonanni leads a 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review of whole-body vibration and bone health in mice. Vibration platforms mechanically stimulate bone and may reshape its turnover and fine structure. Mouse studies used many different settings, so a careful gathering of the evidence was needed.

Searching three databases under standard review rules, the authors included twenty-nine studies across healthy, bone-loss, and fracture healing models. Vibration generally improved bone formation, density, and inner and outer bone structure, but results varied with frequency, strength, session length, and rest times. Combined with hormone or estrogen treatment it sometimes helped more. Optimizing protocols and testing clinical impact, the authors say, are the next steps.
plos-pone-0353876:
Birhanu and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study, gather early reactions to a new sliding-scale health insurance scheme in Ethiopia. The national community insurance program, running since 2011, charges every household the same premium, which strains the poor and the scheme's own finances. The pilot charges premiums by household wealth instead, across thirteen districts in two regions.

Group talks and interviews with community members, local leaders, and officials found a generally warm reception. People judged the scheme on whether it felt affordable, fair, and relevant to their lives, and many welcomed paying according to means. Concerns remained about how wealth would be judged and whether the scheme could pay its way. The authors present these early voices as the first evidence on how communities receive fairness-based premiums, a design other countries watch with interest.
plos-pone-0354176:
Kyowon Gu and six colleagues published this 2026 study of forty-seven patients with intermediate or advanced liver cancer starting a combined modern immunotherapy and blood-vessel-blocking treatment. Using records and pre-treatment MRI scans from a Korean center, they searched for traits predicting how long the cancer stayed controlled.

Tumors spanning ten centimeters or more, and a bright rim pattern on scans, predicted earlier progression. Younger age and added radiotherapy also entered the picture in linked ways. Gu's findings may help clinicians doctors judge who needs closer watching or different first treatment.
plos-pone-0354276:
Aira and colleagues, in a 2026 study, watch the microbes of vermicompost, the rich material worms make from waste, change over time. A puzzle drives the work: communities can swap member species yet keep doing the same jobs, a property called functional redundancy. The team tracked both who was there and what the bacteria could do, across several starting materials.

Early on, function mirrored membership closely: different wastes hosted different bacteria doing different work. By the final stage the samples had converged on similar functional profiles while staying taxonomically distinct. Species turned over about twelve times faster than functions, and redundancy climbed steadily. The whole system churned far faster than ordinary soil. The authors note honestly that without a worm-free control, the speed cannot be credited to worms alone; worms and microbes together drive it. The study sharpens how composters think about a stable product from shifting life.
plos-pone-0354376:
Kazemi and colleagues present a 2026 protocol: a mixed-methods study of happiness among nurses in Iran. Nurses work under heavy stress, and burnout is common, yet what nurses themselves think would make them happier is rarely asked directly. The study will measure happiness levels and then listen for strategies in nurses' own words.

Hospitals in one province will be sampled in two stages for a survey phase, using a standard happiness questionnaire plus questions on background and job features. A second, interview phase will follow referrals from one nurse to the next until no new themes appear. The two strands will be combined into practical recommendations for hospital managers. As a protocol, the paper fixes the plan in advance; its contribution so far is a clear, two-lens design for a workforce question that numbers alone have not answered.
plos-pone-0354476:
Flaviane Gecler Parreira led a team of eight authors on this 2026 cost study of pneumonia treatment in four private Brazilian hospitals. One hundred and eighty-five patients followed a sequential protocol: antibiotics started by vein, then switched to pills once stable, with pharmacists prompting the change. Costs were tallied in fine detail, from drugs to staff time.

Three quarters of patients switched to oral treatment, most recovered well, and hospital stays shortened meaningfully compared with staying intravenous. Treatment costs ran well over half lower. Parreira presents the protocol as safer stewardship and real savings together.
plos-pone-0354676:
François Gernier and colleagues lay out a trial comparing two ways to cool the scalp and save hair during chemotherapy. Hair loss is among the most feared side effects for women treated for early breast cancer. Their 2026 protocol, run in three French cancer centres, randomly assigns patients to a machine cooling system or a standard cold cap.

Close to two hundred women receiving common drug combinations will take part. The main test is whether at least half the hair survives treatment, judged from standardised photos by blinded reviewers. The trial also tracks patient experience and costs. Because no results exist yet, the paper's value is its careful head-to-head design.
plos-pone-0354876:
Ingrid Dupraz led a team of eight authors on this 2026 computer study of a new knee replacement part, the oneKNEE tibial design. A good fit between implant and shinbone helps the artificial knee last. The team built statistical shape models from CT scans of Caucasian and Asian patients with worn knees, then fitted four implant systems virtually.

The new design covered more bone than long-established rivals, beating one named competitor clearly on coverage, though not on support against the hard outer bone. Dupraz stresses these are design-level gains on a computer, still awaiting hands-on and clinical testing.
plos-pone-0354976:
Abolfazl Danayi and Hamid Soltanian-Zadeh present a new architecture for brain-computer interfaces in this 2026 paper. Such systems let people control devices by imagining movements, but many designs are tied to one task, need heavy retraining for each user. They also raise privacy worries when raw brain signals leave the device. Their framework, called BELT, splits the work between a small device at the user and a cloud server.

A stripped-down version built only from simple signal-processing steps was tested on two standard datasets of imagined hand and foot movements. After light personal tuning it classified movements accurately and ran faster on modest hardware than a well-known neural network, at a small cost in accuracy. A compression step that shrank the data more than threefold, without being trained for the task, barely hurt accuracy, which helps keep raw brain data private.
plos-pone-0355276:
Ye Li leads a 2026 PLOS ONE validation study of surgical performance indicators, scores that measure surgeon movements and forces at key steps of an operation. Such scores are harvested automatically in robotic surgery and may grade skill. But step boundaries are matters of judgment, making scores wobble.

The team compared a new probabilistic method, which computes expected scores, against the standard method on over five thousand annotated steps from about a thousand cases. The new scores were biased less often, with smaller bias, and were steadier under annotator noise in many comparisons. Expected scores, the authors suggest, are more robust for analyzing surgical data.
plos-pone-0355376:
Laurits Taul-Madsen and seven colleagues publish the protocol for a pilot trial of artificial-intelligence-guided home rehabilitation for people with multiple sclerosis, in this 2026 paper. The disease commonly impairs balance and walking, and while exercise helps, fatigue and travel keep many patients from clinics. Their platform delivers exercises at home and uses AI to give patients and clinicians tailored feedback on performance and adherence, something earlier remote programs lacked.

Ninety-six participants across several countries will be randomized to ten weeks of the AI system or to a paper-based home exercise program. The main physical test is how many times a person can stand from a chair in thirty seconds, with balance, fatigue, quality of life, and costs also tracked. Because it is a pilot, the trial equally tests whether recruitment, retention, and adherence make a full-scale trial worthwhile.
plos-pone-0355476:
James Foley and colleagues set out in 2026 a review plan on artificial intelligence tools that read referral letters and help sort patients into urgent or specialist care. Sorting by hand is slow and uneven, adding to waiting lists. A check of a registry found no finished or ongoing review on the question, leaving a clear gap.

Searches across major databases will gather studies that test such tools on real referral text and report sorting results. Reviewers will judge bias with a tool made for prediction studies and map the field by model type and care route. Pooling results will happen only where studies truly match.
plos-pone-0355676:
Hongyi Chen and colleagues outline in 2026 a pilot trial for teenagers with major depression, testing brain stimulation guided by brain scans. Some teens respond poorly to standard medicines and talking therapy, so new options are needed. The plan compares usual target placement, placement chosen from each teen's own scan links, and fake stimulation, all over four weeks.

Main aims are practical: can the team recruit, keep teens attending, and keep them safe, with early signs of benefit also tracked. Mood, anxiety, sleep, and quality of life add detail. Findings will shape a larger trial rather than settle whether the method works.
plos-pone-0356376:
Qingshan Luo and four colleagues improve satellite orbit prediction with deep learning in this 2026 paper. Standard orbit models depend heavily on physics and starting conditions, and their errors grow over time, which matters for tracking space objects and warning about collisions. The team trained a memory-based neural network, enhanced with an attention mechanism, to learn the errors a standard model makes.

Working with a well-tracked geodetic satellite, the network used past position errors plus velocity and acceleration data to predict the next day's error, letting researchers correct the standard forecast. The attention-enhanced model beat several rival approaches, shrinking leftover errors to only a few percent of the original in each direction. It also held up on satellites at other altitudes, though longer forecasts grew harder. The authors see it as best suited to short-term corrections.
plos-pone-0356476:
Rasha El-Kotob and seven colleagues explore why patients hold back questions about their medicines, in this 2026 qualitative study from Ontario, Canada. Feeling safe to speak up matters: patients who stay silent about side effects or confusion can come to harm. The researchers interviewed and ran focus groups with twenty-one adults who had taken medication for at least three months, analyzing their accounts through a framework of belonging, learning, and participation.

Patients felt safe when clinicians listened properly, and dismissed when they were brushed off, which bred mistrust. Clear explanations in plain context eased anxiety, while feeling rushed or embarrassed shut learning down. Being invited into decisions left patients empowered; being excluded left them frustrated and disengaged. The title's quote, a patient not wanting to take up people's time, captures the barrier the authors say clinics must actively dismantle.
plos-pone-0356776:
Lolyne Gatwiri and colleagues surveyed 141 poultry vendors at Burma Market, Nairobi's largest live poultry market, on food safety knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice. Their 2026 cross-sectional study matters because wet markets are a known corridor where germs, including drug-resistant ones, pass from birds to people, and vendor behavior is the main gate.

The grades were poor: most vendors scored low on knowledge, a majority held negative attitudes, and half practiced badly. The youngest vendors and women fared worst on practice, income cut in complicated directions, and a positive attitude predicted good practice more reliably than knowledge did. The authors argue training alone will not fix market hygiene; attitudes and working conditions have to move too.
plos-pone-0356876:
Dessie Kassew and co-authors count helpful root fungi in teff and maize fields across northwest Ethiopia, testing how farming itself treats these underground partners. The fungi ferry hard-to-reach nutrients to crops, and fertilizer practice can feed or starve them. Soil from both crop types and from unmanaged control land was sieved for spores, which were sorted into species by shape.

Unfarmed control soil held denser fungal populations than cropland on average, and maize fields held far more spores than teff fields. Fourteen forms from three genera were found, with two genera dominating. Kassew and colleagues conclude that current fertility practice thins these allies, and they urge management that keeps fungal diversity alive as insurance for soil health under climate stress.
plos-pone-0357176:
Krisztián Havanecz, Tímea Téglás, and Leonidas Petridis published a 2026 sports science study in PLOS ONE on training load in elite under-17 soccer players. Coaches track outside work with GPS vests, such as distance run and explosive efforts, and inside strain with heart monitors. The authors asked how the two matched within the same player across nine weeks of training, using sessions from eleven academy players.

Total heart rate exertion tracked total distance and a combined load measure almost perfectly within each player, and it rose strongly with high-speed running and explosive efforts. Per-minute heart rate strain was better explained by intensity measures such as distance per minute. The authors conclude that total and per-minute heart rate numbers answer different questions. Staff who mix them up may misread how hard a player is working, so the two should be read separately.
plos-pone-0357276:
Laura Olivia Karika and colleagues pin down the job of a yeast protein that helps the cell's gene-editing machinery cut and rejoin messages. Before proteins are built, long gene messages must be spliced, and helper proteins guide the cutting machines. Working in a fission yeast used widely in labs, the team fished out what their target protein touches inside active splicing machines.

The protein sat mostly with a known partner group that switches the splicer on, and its strongest partner was a motor protein that pulls gene messages into place. Binding depended on one small region of the protein. Karika and colleagues suggest their protein tunes that motor during splicing, a control step shared in broad outline with human cells.
plos-pone-0357376:
Jhonatan D Quiñonez-Ensuncho and co-authors turn orange peel waste into soluble fiber, testing whether a burst of ultrasound before enzyme treatment improves the haul. Peel is rich in fiber and plant compounds but mostly discarded. The team compared plain enzyme extraction with the ultrasound version, plus an alkaline method, then measured yield, purity, water and oil handling, heat behavior, and whether the fiber feeds friendly gut bacteria.

The ultrasound version recovered the most fiber at high purity and left it less crystalline, more disrupted, and more heat stable. Alkaline fiber held the most water, while enzyme treatment trimmed fiber size and water affinity. Friendly gut species grew on the product. Quiñonez-Ensuncho and colleagues pitch the method for making tailored food ingredients from citrus waste.
plos-pone-0357476:
Brooklynn N. Joyner and colleagues published a 2026 survey study in PLOS ONE on how Americans relate to science, and whether taking part in citizen science changes that relationship. They questioned a demographically diverse sample of more than eighteen hundred adults in 2021, measuring beliefs about science's credibility and value alongside feelings of interest, confidence, belonging, and identity.

Most respondents were interested in science and saw its social value, but fewer than half found science credible, and even fewer felt they belonged in it. Women and people without graduate degrees reported less interest; Black Americans reported less perceived value. About one American in seven had done citizen science, and participants scored higher on interest, belonging, and value, though lower on perceived credibility. Women, Asian, and Hispanic Americans were underrepresented among participants. The authors call citizen science a promising bridge, provided it reaches the groups whose ties to science are weakest.
plos-pone-0357576:
Anja B Frank leads a team of eight tracing how much people moved around Bronze Age Greece, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Trade clearly linked distant towns, but whether traders also settled among strangers was unknown. The researchers read strontium isotopes in teeth and bone from nearly two hundred skeletons at six sites. Such isotopes form a chemical fingerprint of the landscape where a person grew up.

Seventeen individuals stood out as non locals, and all of them could plausibly have come from elsewhere within Greece rather than abroad. Across the whole Bronze Age, outsiders made up only about five to ten percent of each community, a steady trickle rather than waves. Both women and men appeared among the movers. The picture is of stable communities absorbing a modest flow of newcomers while exchange networks carried goods much farther than most people traveled.
plos-pone-0357776:
Haiyan Feng led a team of eight authors speeding up cancer gene sequencing prep, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Before DNA can be sequenced, labs must build libraries from samples, a slow and fiddly process. The team introduced a one-step method, called OS-MPCR, based on multiplex PCR, to prepare libraries for cancer sequencing.

Feng's method folds several steps into one, cutting time and cost in the pipeline. Faster prep means oncologists get results sooner, which can matter when treatment choices wait on gene findings. Lower cost also widens access for labs with small budgets. Methods papers like this rarely make headlines, but they are the kind of quiet advance that clinical sequencing depends on.
plos-pone-0357976:
Yen Hai Le and coauthors published a 2026 environmental health study in PLOS ONE tracking a mercury-resistance gene through people, food, and water in three countries. Bacteria carrying the merA gene can detoxify mercury, so its abundance fingerprints mercury pressure in an environment. The team built a precise gene test and screened human stool, retail chicken, and water samples from the environment in Japan, Vietnam, and Ghana.

The contrast was stark: the gene appeared in a small share of Japanese stool samples, most Vietnamese samples, and nearly every Ghanaian one; chicken showed the same ladder. Water carried the gene almost everywhere, more abundantly in Vietnam and Ghana, sometimes where chemical mercury readings were undetectably low, showing the gene test can be more sensitive. A resistant bacterium carried the gene on a transferable plasmid, ready to spread. Fecal gene screening is proposed as a practical gauge of population mercury exposure.
plos-pone-0358076: Balanta Martínez and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the ecological worth of palm wetlands in the Amazon foothills. The wetlands, called Cananguchales, center on the buriti palm, Mauritia flexuosa. The team used an emergy method, which counts the energy nature spent to build a system. Putting a number on nature's work can argue for protection in terms planners respect.
plos-pone-0358176:
Abbas Ahmad and coauthors published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune disease that inflames and destroys joints. Recent work implicates two metal-driven forms of cell death, one powered by iron and one by copper, but their shared controls were unclear. The team combined several gene-data techniques on blood immune cells from patients and healthy controls, seeking genes that differed and moved together in networks.

Three genes sat at the crossing point of both death pathways and were switched on more strongly in patients. One stores iron, one disarms damaging oxygen molecules, and one puts the brakes on cell division. These genes also lined up with a shift in immune cell mix, toward inflammatory types and away from calming regulatory cells. The trio is proposed as candidate regulators worth lab testing, possibly opening treatments aimed at metal-driven cell death.
plos-pone-0358476:
Jin-Hyang Park and three colleagues show how to measure muscle fibers on ordinary archived slides with a browser based tool, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fiber cross sectional area is the standard yardstick for muscle wasting and regrowth, but the usual workflow needs frozen tissue and fluorescent stains, so old paraffin blocks in hospital archives go unused. Their pipeline runs an artificial intelligence segmentation program through a public web interface, then tidies regions and measures fibers in free image software.

Validated in mouse muscle, the method's area distributions from routine pink stained paraffin sections matched those from a comparison stain and from frozen sections. In a nerve injury model it correctly registered the shrinkage of fibers cut off from their nerve. The payoff is access: decades of stored slides become measurable, and small laboratories without specialist kit can join neuromuscular research on equal terms.
plos-pone-0358576: Zuo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diet, sleep, and lung cancer in southwest China. They compared patients with lung cancer against people without it, in a case-control design. The focus was on polyunsaturated fats in food and on sleep patterns. Links found in such studies can shape diet and sleep advice, though they need care before being read as causes.
plos-pone-0358776: Shimagaki and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on outlook after liver cancer surgery. They tested a blood-based index, built from C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts, measured before surgery. The question was whether that index predicts how patients fare after part of the liver is removed. A cheap score from routine blood tests could help surgeons judge risk before operating.
plos-pone-0359776:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how medical students and residents around the world are taught telemedicine. Telemedicine, care delivered by video or phone, became a core skill during recent years, yet training in it varies wildly between schools.

A scoping review will map what is taught, where, and how it is evaluated, across countries. Medical schools building telemedicine teaching need that world map before writing their own courses. Educators and accreditation bodies are the audience for a review designed to show the gaps in training.
plos-pone-0359976:
Lei Zhu and colleagues built in 2026 a mosquito recognition system that runs on a mobile device. Identifying mosquito species matters because only some kinds spread diseases such as dengue and malaria, and control efforts differ by species. Their system uses a convolutional neural network, the image recognizing form of deep learning, trained to judge mosquitoes by two kinds of shape evidence at once, which the authors call dual morphology.

Putting the trained model on a phone moves identification out of the laboratory and into the field, where health workers and citizens actually encounter the insects. Fast, accurate identification can sharpen surveillance maps and help target spraying and breeding site removal. The study joins a growing set of phone based tools for tracking disease carrying insects.
plos-pone-0360076:
Andrew Tusubira and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how people living with HIV manage their own care when they also live with high blood pressure or diabetes. Their systematic review gathers studies from low and middle income countries, where clinics are stretched and patients carry much of the daily work of staying well. Self-care covers taking medicines faithfully, watching diet and symptoms, and knowing when to seek help.

Having three long term conditions at once multiplies that work, and health systems built around single diseases can leave such patients unsupported. By mapping what self-care looks like and what helps or hinders it, the review gives program designers a view from the patient's side of the clinic door.
plos-pone-0360376:
Jhon Zabaleta-Santisteban and a large team of collaborators mapped in 2026 where cacao could grow well in the Amazonas region of Peru. Their approach is an ensemble of predictive models, combined through a platform called BIOMOD2, that weighs many data sources at once. The maps fold in territorial management and plant health alongside climate and soil, so the result speaks to farming decisions rather than to climate alone.

Cacao is a valuable export crop and an alternative livelihood in regions pressed by deforestation. Knowing which land suits it, and which land should be left alone, helps planners steer planting toward success and away from forest clearing. The study gives regional authorities a planning tool grounded in the region's own conditions.
plos-pone-0360476:
Amine Ben Safta and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 on the pressure used during a common gallbladder operation. In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, surgeons inflate the abdomen with gas, a pneumoperitoneum, to see and work, and the operation is usually done at standard pressure. Some surgeons argued that a lower pressure, eight millimeters of mercury, would leave patients in less pain afterward.

Patients were assigned by chance to the low pressure or the standard approach, and their pain was scored on a visual analog scale after surgery. The trial's headline result is plainly stated: the lower pressure did not significantly reduce those pain scores. A clear negative answer is useful, since it tells surgical teams that this particular adjustment is not where pain relief will be found.
pmc-13155776:
Larissa Bianchini is first author on a 2026 review offering practical guidance for surveys in clinical research. Surveys capture what patients and other stakeholders know, believe, and do, and can measure how treatments are put into practice. They are versatile and cheap, but weak design ruins their value.

The review walks through each decision, from setting aims and choosing a sample to writing clear questions and picking how to deliver them. Knowledge, attitude, and practice frameworks can structure questionnaires. Online platforms widen reach and ease data handling. Low response rates and uneven engagement are named as key practical risks, with planning strategies offered to lift participation without harming data quality.
pmc-13196176:
Mustafa Al-jarshawi and colleagues offer a 2026 projection for oral semaglutide in the United States. Semaglutide is a drug for type 2 diabetes that also protects the heart. The team applied results from the SOUL trial to national survey data to estimate broad impact.

They estimate about six point one million adults would qualify for the drug. Over four and a half years, wide use could prevent about 118,664 major heart events. Those events include heart-related death, heart attack, and stroke. Gains held across sex and race groups. Even at half uptake, tens of thousands of events could be avoided. The authors argue that better access could bring large public gains.
pmc-13197376:
Albrecht Lindemann and colleagues report a 2026 case series on stopping leukemia therapy after remission. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia often get two drugs long term until the disease returns. Past work hints that stopping in deep remission may not hurt survival, so the team offered a fixed six-month course.

Seven patients reached full remission and chose to stop therapy. Five cleared their mutation traces to very low levels. Six of the seven stay in remission, from seven to fifty months so far. One patient relapsed after fourteen months and regained remission once therapy resumed. The authors suggest time-limited therapy may suit select patients, though the group is tiny.
pmc-13197476: Xiaoming Wang and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on forecasting the strength of permeable cement road base. The original source data file was an older, less complete version. The notice explains how one figure's results were built, adding nine outside strength values to three lab values for one mix design. It gives the full value list, the mean and spread used, and why a population formula was chosen for that larger set.
pmc-13202076:
Dementia care research rarely asks which questions matter most to affected families, and a 2026 plan by Elena Michel sets up a partnership to do exactly that. The plan presents GenderDem, a priority setting study on diversity-sensitive psychosocial programs for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia.

Following the James Lind Alliance approach, people with dementia, caregivers, and health professionals will serve together on a steering group as co-researchers. Two rounds of online surveys will gather and rank candidate research questions from wider participants, supported by a literature review. A final workshop will settle a top ten list meant to guide future dementia care research funding.
pmc-13202676:
One molecule hitting two cancer targets is the design goal of a 2026 study by Joydeep Chatterjee, which synthesizes eighteen new imidazoquinoxaline compounds. The research article uses a Pictet-Spengler route to build carboxamide-bearing molecules aimed at both the EGFR growth signal and the tubulin skeleton of cells.

Two compounds beat the approved drug erlotinib against breast cancer cells in culture and blocked EGFR enzyme activity at low concentrations. One of them also stabilized microtubules much like paclitaxel, raised reactive oxygen species, and arrested cells before division. Docking and dynamics simulations showed both compounds sitting stably in the two target pockets, supporting the dual-action design.
pmc-13209476:
Evidence favors cemented hip implants for broken femoral necks, yet surgeons rarely use them, and a 2026 study authored by Hamed Tayyebi quantifies the gap. The retrospective cohort covers 4,407 patients over fifty who received partial hip replacement for intracapsular fractures across a hospital system between 2009 and 2018.

Only about one patient in nine received a cemented implant, despite cemented cases showing significantly fewer fractures around the implant during and after surgery. Surgeon background predicted the choice: trauma specialists used cement far more often than arthroplasty specialists in the data. The authors call the mismatch a stubborn evidence-practice gap needing stronger guideline uptake.
pmc-13210176:
HIV infections among people who inject drugs in Kyrgyzstan have fallen sharply, and a 2026 modeling study authored by Ainura Moldokmatova asks what really drove the drop. The research article runs a deterministic compartmental model under three scenarios, switching needle programs, substitution therapy, prevention, and antiretroviral treatment on and off.

The simulations point to a shrinking population of people who inject drugs as the main engine of the decline. Prevention programs and treatment still reduced the overall burden meaningfully, the model suggests, even if they were not the primary trend drivers. Reported case patterns, meanwhile, likely mirror changing testing behavior more than true swings in new infections.
pmc-13237576:
Mehrabian and colleagues report a hard case of Hailey-Hailey disease eased by an unexpected drug. The patient, a man of sixty-five, had endured three years of burning, itching, and splitting skin in the groin area. Creams, steroids, antifungals, and repeated antibiotics had all given little relief before a biopsy confirmed the inherited blistering disease.

Treatment with naltrexone, a drug better known for blocking opioids, brought success where standard care failed. Why it helps this skin disease is still debated, but case reports build the record doctors consult when usual options run out. For a painful, embarrassing condition, one well-documented success can open a new path.
pmc-13237976:
Brusco and colleagues cost out a new infection-tracking programme for Australian aged care homes. The programme, NISPAC, gives homes a standard, streamlined way to log infections and antibiotic use. Outbreaks in aged care can turn deadly fast, yet until now nobody knew what rolling the system out would cost.

The team tracked implementation costs prospectively, as the work happened, from the aged care sector's own viewpoint. Three coordinating bodies share the running of the programme, and their costs count too. A clear price tag lets funders judge the programme fairly, and lets other regions copy it with eyes open about staff time and money.
pmc-13240876:
Wu's team at Jining exposed autism-model brain organoids to two gut fatty acids and read the gene readout. Short-chain fatty acids are thought to stir inflammation and metabolic trouble in autism. Organoids received sodium acetate, sodium butyrate, or no treatment for seven days. Three repeats per group went through RNA reads.

The two pushed gene activity opposite ways. Acetate mainly shifted genes tied to gene-switch control, enzyme work, and membrane leakiness. Butyrate instead switched on immune processes, with the TGF-beta pathway standing out in the scan. The split suggests each fatty acid nudges the growing autistic brain through its own route.
pmc-13241376:
Feng's team at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan reviewed how rewired metabolism drives fibrosis across the body's organs. Scar-forming cells switch their glucose, amino acid, and fat handling in Warburg-like fashion. The review walks through core pathways before turning organ by organ. Heart, lung, liver, kidney, skin, and peritoneum each get a section.

Tags on metabolic enzymes, including the newly recognized lactylation, recur as control knobs. Some enzymes push fibrosis through side jobs unrelated to their chemistry. The authors close with therapies already aiming at glycolysis and lipid pathways. Targeting metabolism, they argue, could sit beside current anti-scar care.
pmc-13243876:
Alberte Aspaas Lundquist and colleagues add two patients to the tiny known group with disease caused by faulty MRPS34, a mitochondrial protein. Their report appeared in JIMD Reports in 2026. The gene builds part of the mitochondria's own protein factory, and damaging variants on both copies cause a Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder. One new patient died in infancy carrying two severe variants. The other, with two copies of a gentler splice variant, survived into mid-childhood.

The team then reviewed all eleven reported individuals to hunt for patterns. Developmental delay appeared in every case, and lactic acid buildup and brainstem lesions in nearly all. Carrying two copies of the milder variant tracked with longer survival, the clearest genotype-phenotype link so far. The disorder strikes many systems beyond the brain. With so few cases worldwide, the authors argue each new report materially sharpens counseling for families.
pmc-13244076:
Zhicheng Lai and colleagues ran a randomized phase two trial of two liver-directed combinations for advanced liver cancer. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Seventy-two patients with advanced tumors received chemotherapy infused into the liver's artery, paired either with the immunotherapy toripalimab or with the targeted drug sorafenib. The main measure was how many patients remained progression-free at six months.

The two arms finished close on that measure, at just under two-thirds of patients each. Survival leaned toward the immunotherapy pairing, with a median of 20.9 months against 16.4 months for sorafenib, and time without progression also ran longer. Serious side effects were fewer with toripalimab: a third of its group had severe events against well over two-fifths on sorafenib. The trial was not designed to crown a winner between the arms. The authors call the immunotherapy combination favorable and ready for a phase three test.
pmc-13245076:
Harry Magunia and colleagues surveyed how the world performs right-heart ultrasound, and found a specialty speaking many dialects. Their RVNet survey appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Guidelines have tried to standardize right heart checks, yet practice anecdotes suggested wide variation. The anonymous sixty-eight-question survey drew 588 replies from many countries in late 2024 and early 2025.

Most were certified and experienced, yet their methods diverged at nearly every step. Views captured, timing of measures, image orientation, and what gets reported all varied, in both exam types. The authors organize the chaos with a six-part framework covering views, phase, orientation, interface, timing, and scaling. They propose it as a simple shared checklist, V-POINTS, to make measurements comparable between labs. The message: the right heart deserves the discipline the left received years ago.
pmc-13246876:
Norman, Conduit, and Laycock asked what mental abilities make some people better at spotting changes in a scene, in this 2026 Psychonomic Bulletin and Review study. Missing changes, called change blindness, matters for drivers and radiologists alike. Two hundred sixty participants took a naturalistic flicker task, where two versions of a scene alternate until the change is found, plus nine cognitive tests.

The strongest links to spotting accuracy were top-down visual search control, visuospatial ability and memory, and basic visual inspection speed. Factor analysis grouped the test battery into flexibility, visuospatial working memory, and attention-speed factors, and the visuospatial memory factor was the main predictor of change detection. The authors conclude that holding a scene in spatial memory is central to noticing what changed.
pmc-13246976:
Yang, Huang, and Wei systematically reviewed how football boot design affects injury risk, in this 2026 Sports Medicine - Open article. Boots are the player's interface with the ground, and their studs and soles shape the forces reaching knees and ankles. The team searched two decades of literature and kept thirty-two studies, checking each one's quality with a standard scale.

Several patterns stood out. Screw-in and bladed studs grip so hard in rotation that the foot can lock, raising the risk of ligament tears, ankle sprains, and stress fractures. Sole stiffness showed a U-shaped risk curve, with both very stiff and very soft plates creating problems. Mismatches between boot, foot shape, and surface added further risk. The authors call for standardized boot testing.
pmc-13248376:
Farlie and an international group of colleagues argue for a better way to dose balance training, in this 2026 comment. Falls threaten older adults, and balance exercise helps, yet prescriptions rarely state how hard the exercise should feel. The authors say that missing measure, balance intensity, holds back both research and clinical advice.

They call for one standard yardstick of balance intensity and practical ways to sample it during training. With a shared measure, studies could pin down the level that best prevents falls and protects independence. The piece is a position statement, meant to steer future trials and guidelines rather than report new data.
pmc-13248876:
Khatatbeh and colleagues surveyed adolescents in Jordan in 2026 about online gaming habits and how they view its health effects. They used the Health Belief Model, a frame that links behavior to felt risk and prompts to act. Four hundred three students aged 10 to 17 answered an online form covering daily play time, game types, and views on body and mind.

Students played about three hours a day on average. More than a quarter saw no harm to physical or mental health, a sign of low felt risk. Over a third had never been counseled on gaming harms, with parents the main source when guidance came. Older age and longer daily play tracked with poorer self-rated physical and mental health, and beliefs about mental harm also shaped ratings. The authors urge awareness efforts aimed at adolescents, parents, teachers, and school health staff.
pmc-13248976:
Liu and co-authors studied rehearsal training for heart attack teams, in a 2026 report from a Chinese chest pain center. For the deadliest heart attacks, minutes spent reopening the blocked artery shape survival. The center introduced simulation-based team training, then compared two hundred sixty patients treated before and after the program began.

After training, the median time from hospital door to balloon treatment fell from ninety-two to sixty-eight minutes. Arrival-to-treatment times improved as well, and the authors link the drills to smoother teamwork under pressure. Because the study looked backward at one center, they ask for prospective multicenter trials before declaring the training a proven cause.
pmc-13250176:
Prestedge, El-Murr, and Williamson interview Australian health workers about testing done right beside the patient. Their 2026 BMJ Open study concerns point-of-care testing, where results come during the visit instead of from a distant laboratory. Eighteen participants took part, drawn from hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, emergency care, and pathology services.

Three themes ran through the interviews: care centered on communities, connected records, and sound quality control. Workers praised programs that improved fairness of access, but they named weak funding and poor information systems as major barriers. Clearer training guidance for staff outside laboratories was seen as a practical fix. The authors call for funding that covers testing, quality checks, and staff training together.
pmc-13250876:
Wang and co-authors measure how well heart and vessel nurses lead teams in China and what drives it. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine survey covers four hundred eleven such nurses at three large hospitals, surveyed in early 2025. Nurses rated their own leading, their workplace, and their confidence in their own abilities.

Scores ran above average, strongest for urging others on and setting an example, weakest for questioning the status quo. Job title, department, training in leading, workplace quality, and self-belief each lifted the scores. Workplace and self-belief linked most strongly with the ratings. The authors advise focused training, healthier work settings, and self-belief building to grow nurse leaders in practice.
pmc-13251076:
Haiyan Pan and co-authors are the subject of this 2026 retraction notice from the journal Cancer Cell International. It withdraws their earlier paper, published in 2020, which claimed a long non-coding RNA drives stomach cancer cell growth and spread through a partner RNA chain.

After publication, concerns were raised about the Western blot and flow cytometry data in three of the paper's figures. The authors could not provide the raw data when asked to back it up. The editors state they have lost confidence in the results and conclusions. The notice adds that none of the authors replied to letters about the retraction.
pmc-13252976:
Meijun Jiang, Shaoyun Zhang, and Cong Xiao review electrical stimulation around flap surgery in this 2026 article. Skin flaps moved to cover wounds from cancer or injury can partly or wholly die, and no drug has reliably prevented that loss.

Drawing on more than 120 studies, the review sorts benefits by timing. Stimulation before surgery encourages new blood vessel growth into the flap. After surgery, it helps fight infection, drain swelling, and speed wound healing, while also guiding cells to move and multiply. Because one drug usually hits only one part of the failure process, the authors argue that a physical method touching many steps at once holds real promise.
pmc-13256176:
Jessica Appleton and colleagues report a 2026 study of SleepWellBaby, a phone app that gives parents a seven-day program on infant sleep. The program can be repeated and mixes facts with interactive features on helping babies sleep in a responsive way. Parents of infants under six months joined online and filled in surveys at the start, after seven days, and after thirty days.

Seven hundred parents started the study, with 339 still responding at seven days and 220 at thirty days. Most said the app was easy to use and that they trusted its content, though most had stopped using it by one month. Parents who used it more, or found it most helpful, showed the greatest drop in fatigue. Some also said it kept them on their phones too long.
pmc-13257876:
Xiaoqi Zhang and colleagues study a welding problem that arises when stainless steel meets ordinary carbon steel. Rail vehicle bodies join these metals with resistance spot welding, but mismatched properties shift the weld nugget off center. Their 2026 analysis inserts a thin nickel layer between the sheets.

Computer models tracked force and heat fields through the welding process with the nickel layer in place. Physical welds then confirmed what the models predicted. The nickel insert curbed nugget drift and evened out the metal's internal structure. Hardness varied more smoothly across the joint, and the finished spot welds came out stronger.
pmc-13257976:
Elizabeth A Cook leads a 2026 animal study of two drugs that block chemokine receptors, proteins that guide immune cells, during treatment for hemorrhagic shock. Hemorrhagic shock is a life-threatening state after heavy blood loss. In rats, the team compared the drugs BX471 and INCB3284, given alone or together, against a control fluid. They measured how much fluid was needed to restore blood pressure over six hours.

With control treatment, fluid needs rose sharply and averaged 108 units per kilogram of body weight. With BX471 the average was 31, with INCB3284 it was 51, and with both drugs it was 36.5. Death rates differed between groups but not significantly, and survival time in a second test did not change. Both drugs also shifted markers of body-wide inflammation, which the authors link to their fluid-saving effect.
pmc-13259576: CMAJ's June 2026 obituaries column records the deaths of Canadian physicians in short, uniform notices. Each entry names the doctor, home city, medical school and graduation year, and specialty, from family medicine and surgery to neurosurgery and radiology. Ages at death stretch from the thirties to past one hundred, and every notice links to a fuller published obituary. The column serves as the journal's running roll of the profession's losses.
pmc-13260976:
Neil Ming leads a 2026 case report of subcutaneous emphysema, air trapped under the skin, following postoperative nausea after dental extraction. An 18-year-old female had four wisdom teeth removed in a routine procedure without air-driven instruments, which are the usual source of such air. After multiple episodes of retching and vomiting she developed progressive facial swelling and was transferred to a tertiary care center for evaluation and treatment.

Imaging showed widespread air tracking through the chewing muscle and under-jaw spaces, with no abscess present. She was managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics, sinus precautions, and supportive care, and the swelling gradually resolved. The authors warn that this complication can spread toward the chest and threaten the airway. They argue that vomiting may force air into unhealed extraction sites, so early recognition matters even without an air source.
pmc-13261976:
Jarosław Kopko and colleagues report a hard-won birth in a woman with Swyer syndrome. In this rare condition, a person with XY chromosomes develops as female but without working ovaries. Donor egg IVF can still work when the uterus is intact, as this 2026 case shows.

The twenty-nine-year-old patient, whose ovaries had been removed earlier, conceived after a frozen embryo transfer. That first pregnancy lodged dangerously in the uterine wall and was dissolved with methotrexate. Six months later a second transfer grew normally, ending in a healthy boy delivered by cesarean at thirty-nine weeks. Early ultrasound for every IVF pregnancy is their firm lesson.
pmc-13262176:
Wenjie Sun and colleagues sew a medicated patch that cooks tumors with light while leaking chemotherapy on cue. Inoperable abdominal tumors need options gentler than surgery and systemic drugs. Their 2026 electrospun patch embeds copper sulfide and polydopamine, which heat under near-infrared light.

Acidic tumor surroundings and light-triggered warmth both unlock the drug stored inside. In animals, the combined patch killed far more tumor cells than heat-only or drug-only versions. Every treated mouse survived the ninety-day watch, with little body-wide toxicity. The authors pitch the implant as a surgical alternative for selected patients.
pmc-13262276:
Franziska Ulrich and colleagues take a famous diabetes drug duel out of the trial clinic and into British general practice. Once-weekly semaglutide beat dulaglutide in a controlled trial, but strict trial entry rules left real-world patients untested. Their 2026 cohort follows over six thousand new users in UK primary care records.

After one year, semaglutide users lost more weight and trimmed blood sugar further than dulaglutide users. The edge survived in the large majority who would never have qualified for the original trial. Trial-eligible patients, though, improved most on either drug. Safety events were tracked while treatment continued, completing the real-world picture.
pmc-13262676:
Tian-Tian Liu and colleagues find obese children need less sedative per kilogram than lean peers, a counterintuitive dosing result. Remimazolam, a new ultra-short benzodiazepine, is spreading into pediatric procedure rooms with thin data on obesity. Their 2026 trial enrolls sixty children, half obese, alongside a fixed pain-drug partner.

A staircase design adjusted each dose by the last child's response until the midpoint dose emerged. In obese children that midpoint sat roughly a quarter lower than in normal-weight children. Dosing strictly by the scale would therefore overshoot in heavier patients. The authors urge weight-band care when sedating obese children for procedures.
pmc-13263276:
Sota Ihara and Akihiro Okamoto propose a new bacterial species from an electricity-linked growth culture in a 2026 journal article. The rod-shaped bacterium was isolated from filtered liquid of an electrochemical enrichment culture, a setup that grows microbes able to move electrons to solid surfaces. They named it Cellulomonas electrica and compared it with its closest relatives by genes and chemistry.

Whole-genome similarity values fell well below the thresholds that define a species, while broader measures kept it inside the Cellulomonas genus. Its main cell fat and its chief quinone, a molecule used in energy handling, set it apart from relatives. It grew best at around 30 degrees and mildly acidic conditions. The strain is deposited in two public culture collections.
pmc-13263376:
Yichen Li and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on an electronic skin inspired by the pitcher plant Nepenthes, whose rim channels liquid in one direction. Their Janus e-skin moves sweat away from the body actively while staying breathable and waterproof. It aims to keep skin dry during long wear.

The material stretches to more than six times its length and senses in several modes, including touch-free signals and Morse code taps. It records brain, muscle, heart, and eye signals cleanly. Paired with machine learning, muscle signals from the skin steered a four-legged robot, and the system recognized letters with over ninety-five percent accuracy.
pmc-13264276:
Nidhal Ben Abdlekrim led a 2026 study of match demands in elite under-19 female basketball players from North Africa. Most past profiles came from men or adults, so youth data were thin. The team compared guards, forwards, and centers, and national against world-level play.

Thirty Tunisian players were tracked through eight playoff games with video, heart-rate bands, and blood tests. World-level players did more hard efforts and spent more time at near-max heart rate. Guards did the most hard side-to-side moves, while centers did more still, hard work and had higher blood lactate, a fatigue marker. Hard effort fell from the first to the last quarter in both groups, less so for world-level players.
pmc-13266276:
Ruth-Ann Yaa Frimpong and colleagues published a 2026 food study on plant-based mayonnaise made by swapping egg yolk for protein from sprouted moringa seeds. Egg yolk stabilizes the sauce's oil droplets, so a plant swap must match its texture. They extracted the seed protein three ways: with ultrasound, with enzymes, or with both together.

Swaps from five to fifty percent were tested. Texture improved over the all-egg control up to a twenty percent swap, then declined. At twenty percent, the combined-extraction version matched a commercial benchmark in firmness, consistency, and stickiness. Several mixes also gave finer oil droplets than the control. Yellowness faded as swap levels rose, and acidity stayed in the low-acid food range. The authors back sprouted moringa protein as a working partial egg replacer.
pmc-13267276:
Marie Oosterlynck and a large team report a 2026 study of tiny particles that may spread tau damage in the brain. In Alzheimer's disease, the tau protein clumps and seems to pass from cell to cell. Small sacs released by brain cells, called extracellular vesicles, carry tau seeds, but which tau forms drive the spread was unknown.

The team took these sacs from frozen brain tissue of patients with three tau diseases and from healthy controls. Protein profiling showed that each disease left a distinct tau pattern in the sacs. Alzheimer's sacs were rich in tau pieces from one key region. A short piece named PHF6 did most of the seeding work. The authors name PHF6 as a possible drug target.
pmc-13267976:
Cristina Kontogiannis, Sami Asif, and Amit Kharod present a 2026 case report on a rare artery squeeze after major weight loss. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome occurs when the gut's third section is pinched between two large vessels. Their patient was a 28-year-old woman with lasting nausea and vomiting after losing 110 pounds. She also had a heart-rhythm condition and slow stomach emptying, which muddied the picture.

Standard scope and ultrasound checks found nothing. A CT scan showed the tight vessel angle and short gap that mark the syndrome. Surgeons used a robot to join the pinched gut section to the next part of the small bowel, bypassing the squeeze. Her symptoms resolved. The authors present the robotic route as a workable fix for this rare problem.
pmc-13268076:
T D Barry and a large team report a 2026 evaluation of Wales' national TB cohort review program. Cohort review is a structured team audit of every TB case, checking care quality and public health data. Wales started its national program in 2012. The team analyzed all notified TB cases from 2012 to 2022 in this low-incidence country.

Of 1,175 cases, 985, about 83 percent, were presented at cohort review. Many care outcomes reached near their targets. Support to finish treatment was aimed more and more at patients with social complexity and higher spread risk. The completeness of surveillance data improved substantially. Weak spots persisted in finding and assessing contacts of cases. The authors offer the program as an efficient model for other low-incidence countries nearing TB elimination.
pmc-13268176:
The editors of PLOS One published a 2026 editorial note on a greenhouse tomato study. The original paper tested a micro-fog system that cools and humidifies greenhouse air, improving tomato growth in summer. After publication, concerns arose about where some of the data came from. The first author admitted that a figure's environmental data came from a different institution and was included by mistake.

The note prints a corrected figure and fixes several results sentences, including midday temperature and humidity readings for the fogged and control sections. The greenhouse's reported dimensions were also wrong and are corrected. Raw data behind the figures and tables, missing from the original submission, are now supplied. The editors state they cannot verify the data's origin because the institutions involved gave conflicting advice.
