pmc-13269876: An author correction from 2026, for a paper led by Zicong Huang on a protein that organizes sperm maturation, fixes swapped labels in one table and one sentence. In Table 2, the column headings for two patient groups, labeled NOA and OA, had been exchanged. The correction also reverses the group counts in the results text, which now reads 30 OA samples and 25 NOA samples. Both changes were made in the online and PDF versions.
pmc-13270876:
Yangyang Zhang is lead author of a 2026 review article on the HOXA gene cluster and bone disorders. Bone stays healthy through a balance of building and breakdown, and losing that balance drives diseases such as osteoporosis, where bones thin. HOXA genes help direct early body patterning and cell fate.

The review gathers recent work on how HOXA family members act in bone disease, finding wide, uneven roles across the family. It groups their effects into three shared patterns: setting regional pattern in the skeleton, adjusting signalling pathways, and joining gene-control networks with non-coding RNAs. The authors argue these roles offer possible targets for new bone treatments.
pmc-13271476:
Rui Sun and Zhihao Chen report a 2026 journal article designing a syllabus for Architectural Art English, an English for Academic Purposes course for undergraduate architecture students. The design draws on needs analysis, asking what students must do in English, and genre analysis, studying the text types architects actually read and write.

A university-wide questionnaire gathered 650 students and faculty. It found a sharp gap between students' aims, such as joining international projects, studying abroad, and following foreign lectures, and their current weak listening skills and subject vocabulary. The proposed syllabus teaches seven genres, from textbooks and research papers to design statements and presentation scripts, through themed units using real cases and task-based projects.
pmc-13272276:
Arve Opheim is lead author of a 2026 study protocol, a published plan, for PEER-HOMEcare, a feasibility study of enriched-environment rehab at home after stroke. Recovery happens mostly at home as hospital pressure rises. Animal research shows that stimulating surroundings prompt frequent exploratory use of a weakened arm. Such use drives learning and brain rewiring. But human home translation is limited.

The single-group study will enrol 45 stroke survivors within six months of their stroke across Norway, Sweden, and Latvia. Homes will be modified in meaningful, progressive ways to encourage arm use in daily tasks, and wearable sensors will track exploratory behaviour. Main outcomes are feasibility and acceptability, from surveys, logs, and interviews, with arm function and daily living as secondary measures.
pmc-13272576:
Wenqiao Chang leads a 2026 review of spatial multi-omics, a set of methods that map many kinds of molecules inside intact tumor tissue. Older methods lose where in the tissue each signal came from. The review covers methods that map gene activity, small chemicals, and proteins in place, and how to combine them.

Used together, these tools have shown niches at the edge where tumors invade, shifts in the immune setting over time, and signals cells pass as cancer spreads. The authors say the approach can help sort patients, plan treatment, and tackle drug resistance. They also set out current limits and next steps for the field.
pmc-13272676:
Ludwig Svensson leads a 2026 randomised trial asking whether extra iron for breastfed babies affects behavior at age three. Breastfed infants can run low on iron, which the brain needs, but benefits in healthy infants are unclear. The trial ran in Warsaw, Poland, and Umea, Sweden.

Healthy full-term babies got a low daily iron dose or a placebo from 4 to 9 months of age. Of 221 babies randomised, 133 were assessed at age three with a child behavior checklist. The iron group scored lower for outward behavior problems, 45.6 against 48.6, and for aggressive behavior. The authors urge caution until other studies repeat the finding.
pmc-13272776:
Seleem Ahmad leads a 2026 study of concrete that replaces some stone or sand with recycled plastic particles. The plastic came from polyethylene waste reshaped into pellets. Seven mixes were made at replacement levels of 2.5, 7.5, and 15 percent by weight, for coarse and fine material separately, and cured for 7 and 28 days.

A 2.5 percent replacement of fine material gave the highest compressive strength, about 26.22 megapascals, and the best splitting strength. At 15 percent, strength fell, but replacing coarse material cut density most, by 3.66 percent, aiding light concrete. The authors suggest non-structural uses such as paths and paving blocks, if workability is managed.
pmc-13276376:
Sayyed Ali Siyadati and co-authors report a 2026 engineering article on how fast cooling harms asphalt in freeze-thaw weather. Cracking in cold regions is a leading cause of road damage. Many factors are well studied, but the speed of temperature drop during each freeze cycle had been largely overlooked.

The team made half-disc samples, dry and water-soaked, and put them through seven freeze-thaw cycles. Cooling rates ranged from very slow to a shock freeze, at three low temperatures. Faster cooling cut fracture toughness, fracture energy, and a cracking resistance index. Slow cooling cost the samples about a sixth of their toughness; shock freezing cost nearly half their fracture energy. The authors blame stress that cannot relax in time, steep temperature gradients, and expanding trapped water. Peak load rose as temperature fell to a point, then dropped.
pmc-13276676:
Junru Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how climate change may rewrite the genetics of a Chinese flowering dogwood tree. Cornus kousa subspecies chinensis adapts well but spreads slowly, making it a good test case for woody plant responses to a warming world. Its rich internal variation is at stake.

The team gathered leaf samples from three hundred forty-eight trees across twenty-five populations in China. Today's populations hold abundant genetic diversity. Models of future climates for 2060 to 2080, under two emission paths, forecast a sharp squeeze. Over ninety percent of populations would collapse into one shared genetic cluster, homogenizing variation. Sixty-seven DNA markers tied to climate stood out, and almost all linked to average yearly temperature. The authors say temperature is the main selective force, and they offer guidance for conserving the tree's genetic resources.
pmc-13277276:
Anett Wolgast leads a 2026 systematic review of how organizations and communities prepare for natural crises linked to climate change. Such crises, from floods to heat events, are growing more frequent and severe. The preregistered review screened 2,356 records and kept 57 studies of preparedness and resilience programs in local or workplace settings.

Programs that worked best drew on local conditions, community input, and place-based learning. Education that empowered people, above all youth, lifted preparedness. Many programs, though, were short-term, reactive, and lacked lasting support or shared design. Resilience grows from local life and learning over time, the authors conclude, not from one-off projects dropped into a place.
pmc-13278476:
Bethany J Ridley leads a 2026 validation study of photorealistic body size scales for young adults, built from three-dimensional scans of White Europeans. Young adults face high weight-related health risk, and accurate visual tools can improve communication about body size. A total of 110 adults aged eighteen to twenty-five estimated relative sizes and ranked bodies by weight, then repeated both tasks three days later.

Participants estimated sizes accurately and ranked the images in line with the built-in body mass changes. Repeat scores showed good to excellent reliability for both tasks. The gender-specific scales are judged accurate and valid for body size estimation. They offer researchers and clinicians a robust resource for work with young adults, the authors conclude.
pmc-13279276:
Daniela Fidalgo and a large team report a 2026 multi country test of a fear of childbirth scale. The fear, called tokophobia, can harm mental health and shape birth choices. Sound tools are needed to spot women at risk. The scale under test is the Tokophobia Severity Scale, a short self report form.

Data came from one thousand five hundred eighty five women in four countries: Australia, Lithuania, Poland and Portugal. Groups held women who had not given birth, pregnant women and new mothers two months after birth. Women also filled forms on mood, birth trauma views and a second fear scale. Early results backed a three part structure for the scale. Full checks of trust and fit guide its use across lands and life stages.
pmc-13279576:
S. J. van Alfen and colleagues give a 2026 review of Von Hippel Lindau disease, a rare inherited tumour syndrome. A fault in the VHL gene, passed in families, raises risk of tumours in kidney, eye, brain, pancreas and adrenal glands. Loss of the gene lets low oxygen signal proteins, called HIF, build up. Those signals drive vessel growth and red cell making, which feed tumours.

A drug that blocks the HIF two alpha part, belzutifan, marks a major step in care. Health agencies in the United States and Europe have approved it for a range of tumours from this disease. New work shows the VHL protein also has jobs past HIF control. Loss of those jobs may add to tumour growth. The review maps both the classic path and the new leads.
pmc-13279776:
Benedikt Maier and colleagues report a 2026 study of granite blocks in the Kings Chamber of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The ScanPyramids project used ultrasound shear wave arrays, a sound echo tool, to probe block insides without harm. Campaigns in 2022 covered the lower two block rows of all four walls. First, fast scans with an eight channel tool flagged zones of interest.

High detail scans then ran at those zones, most on the north wall, with a paired tool set for sixteen channels. A math method called FT-SAFT turned echoes in two dimensional cross section images. Images reveal internal reflectors, which are echoes from cracks, joints or gaps in the stone. Block thickness and joint shape data can refine stress models of the chamber. Such maps aid long term preservation of the monument and teach how it was built.
pmc-13279876:
Meiling Liu and colleagues report a 2026 case of a rare finger tumour in a young child, with a review of past cases. A glomus tumour is a small, benign growth from vessel wall cells, most seen in adults of twenty to forty years. Under the nail, it can harm the nail plate itself. No clear past report held nail plate harm in a child. Their patient was a six year old boy.

The tumour sat under the nail of his left ring finger, with nail plate damage on view. Ultrasound scans proved the diagnosis before surgery. Full removal of the tumour led to good recovery. Glomus tumours make about two percent of soft tissue tumours and are rare in children. Early scans in painful finger lumps can spare long delays in care.
pmc-13280376:
Balew Arega and Asnake Agunie present a 2026 perspective on antibiotic stewardship in Ethiopia, called stewardship without walls. Ethiopia has an unregulated private antibiotic economy that spans hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, drug shops and informal vendors. Non prescribed dispensing is the norm there and selects resistant bacteria. Three forces drive it: family self medication habits passed down, a sales imperative that ties profit to customer satisfaction, and a corner shop calculus that favours fast access over slow public care.

The authors propose a six pillar framework to tame the market. Pillars hold tiered accreditation, point of service education and supply chain engagement. Mystery client support, technology enabled consultation and operational research complete the set. The frame works outside hospital walls, where most antibiotics change hands. They call it an urgent priority for Ethiopia and like settings, where resistance grows in the open market.
pmc-13280676:
Abdullah Hasan Safir and colleagues wrote a 2026 commentary on what AI image tools may take from art. A recent study ran image tools in a loop, where each output fed the next round. The images soon turned bland and alike, like stock photos. The authors say the loss is not just a tech flaw. It is a loss of knowledge and culture.

They argue that artists and users on the margins face the most harm from these tools. Their styles and stories are the first to be flattened or lost. The authors call for design talks that hear those voices, above all in poorer countries. They ask for AI tools that can hold many world views at once.
pmc-13281276:
Svetlana N Zykova and colleagues set normal ranges for stress hormones in newborn saliva in a 2026 study. Spit tests hurt less than blood tests, which matters for fragile babies. The team collected more than four hundred spit samples from one hundred seventy-four infants. Babies were up to four weeks old, born early or on time. Samples came from three newborn intensive units and one maternity ward. A precise lab method measured fourteen hormones.

Early birth changed many hormone levels, some by a great deal. Breathing support shifted all hormone paths in the study. The first two days of life brought their own pattern of highs. A steroid drug given around birth lowered one key stress hormone by about a third. The authors say doctors must weigh birth timing, breathing help, and drug exposure when reading a baby's spit test.
pmc-13281776:
Dong-Youl Kim and colleagues compared brain signals for craving control in a 2026 study. Some care uses live brain feedback to help people steer their own states. A screen shows a brain signal, and the person learns to move it. Better signals should split mental states more cleanly. The team reused data from thirty-one smokers in a scanner. Across three runs, the smokers tried to raise or lower their urge to smoke. A learning model turned brain patterns into the feedback line.

Four signal sources were put head to head. They were activity in single brain spots and links between spots. Two more were sorting scores built from each of those. The team tracked how well each split the crave and no-crave states across runs. Their aim was groundwork: pick the source that splits states best before building care on it.
pmc-13281876:
Kaiyuan Zhang and Yanche Ren reviewed bladder-sparing care for a hard bladder cancer in a 2026 paper. The cancer sits in the bladder lining and has stopped answering a standard immune rinse. Removing the whole bladder controls it best, but many patients cannot face or survive that surgery. The review sorts the sparing options now on offer. Some wake the bladder's own immune defenses. Others use devices to hold drugs in the bladder longer or push them deeper.

Whole-body immune drugs and plain chemo rinses round out the menu. Many options show real activity in studies. Yet most proof comes from one-arm trials with unlike patients and yardsticks. No ranking of the options can yet be called settled. The authors say choice must weigh lasting power, harms, burden, and access for each patient. Shared trial rules and tissue markers are the field's next needs.
pmc-13282476:
Ingeborg S Skre and co-authors present a 2026 imaging study using two hyperpolarized probes to separate liver injury from fuel-processing failure in rats. Magnetic resonance imaging normally shows structure, but hyperpolarized probes, whose signal is boosted, let scanners watch metabolism live. Rats were fed a diet lacking two nutrients to induce steatohepatitis, a fatty, inflamed liver disease. Each animal received both probes in turn.

The first probe converted strongly to a second chemical in diseased livers, signalling cell membrane breakdown from injury. The second probe tracked methyl-donor metabolism, a chemical donation system tied to liver health. Its downstream product fell in diseased livers even though delivery of the probe was unchanged, pointing to impaired processing rather than poor supply. The two readouts moved in opposite directions, cleanly separating injury from metabolic failure. The authors say pairing such probes extends live metabolic imaging over longer timescales.
pmc-13282676:
Lucas Ivan Sebastian Rundblad and co-authors describe a 2026 case of fatal air entering the brain's blood vessels after a dialysis catheter was mishandled. Air embolism, air bubbles in the bloodstream, is a rare but deadly risk of central venous catheters, tubes placed in large veins. Their patient was a man in his early sixties with diabetes and kidney disease who had a stroke and received a catheter for dialysis.

Seventeen days after the stroke he was found unconscious, with seizures and sudden brain decline. His catheter was discovered unplugged and unclamped, suggesting he may have tampered with it himself. Scans confirmed a massive air blockage in both arterial and venous brain circulation. Despite urgent treatment he never woke and died five days later. Autopsy confirmed the cause and ruled out heart or lung shunts. The authors stress meticulous catheter care, staff training, and warning patients about the risk.
pmc-13282876:
Ontario's lockdown period frames a 2026 mixed-methods inquiry into partner violence and health, directed by Dina Idriss-Wheeler. Women who faced abuse at home were locked in with stress and harm. The study compares their health paths with women who did not report such violence.

A survey covered 653 women, and 150 reported partner violence during lockdowns. Interviews added views from 14 survivors and 10 service providers. Survivors reported more alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, and drug use, plus worse sleep. They also used formal supports more, while informal support often fell. The work shows wide health strain during lockdown periods.
pmc-13282976:
Patient navigators who clear hurdles to eye surgery are evaluated in a 2026 program review by Pooja Sree Tallapaneni's group. Navigators help patients beat transport, cost, and social barriers to care. The study was set at a large academic eye institute.

Records covered 82 eyes from 64 patients referred in 2023 for surgical help. Surgery was completed for 64 of the 82 eyes in the cohort. Help worked best for transport needs and for finding a companion for surgery day. Cases that lacked insurance had lower success. Cataract surgery was the most common need. Median wait from referral to surgery was 39 days in this program.
pmc-13283176:
HIV hiding in brain tissue differs from HIV in spinal fluid, a distinction Thomas A Angelovich and fellow reviewers press in 2026. Even when drugs suppress HIV, virus can persist in the central nervous system. Such persistence may drive inflammation and thinking problems that last for years.

Recent work found intact and faulty HIV DNA in brain tissue and spinal fluid. Virus from both sites can still make proteins and restart spread without drugs. Brain tissue and spinal fluid differ in cell sources and reservoir behavior. Those gaps may shape distinct effects on brain health and cognition. The review urges cure research to treat each brain region on its own terms, not as one pool.
pmc-13284276:
Biologic drugs for stubborn eczema and hives are weighed by Aikaterini Salavoura in a 2026 review of trial and real-world proof. Severe cases are uncommon yet costly and burdensome for patients. Antibody drugs transformed other skin diseases, but these two conditions follow tangled cytokine networks.

Dupilumab leads eczema care, helping a large share of severe cases in trials. Three further approved options serve as alternatives for eczema patients. For chronic hives, omalizumab holds guideline backing as an add-on therapy. Debate over its true benefit in hives continues in the literature. Disease subtype knowledge should guide precise drug choice ahead.
pmc-13284476:
Yingying Cui and co-authors give a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on immune checkpoints as warning signs for mouth lesions turning cancerous. Oral potentially malignant disorders can progress to cancer, but markers of that risk stay unclear. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies linking checkpoint expression to later malignant change.

Only five studies met the criteria, covering 613 patients, of whom 129 had malignant change in the pooled set. Just two checkpoints had been tested. PD-L1 showed some promise as a predictor, but proof stays thin and clinical use is not yet set. The authors call for prospective studies and trials to test whether such markers can guide early action.
pmc-13284676:
Rafael Cañones-Zafra and co-authors report a 2026 randomized eye study on lubricant drops around LASIK surgery. Dry eye and discomfort often rise after laser vision correction. The trial split myopic patients into two groups of 22: one used lubricant for a week before surgery, the other only after surgery, with checks to one month.

Discomfort scores worsened for the whole group by one month after surgery, the authors report. At that point, the early-use and late-use groups did not differ on symptoms, tear salt levels, or tear break-up time. Baseline measures were also alike. The authors conclude a week of pre-treatment gave no added gain and call for longer trials.
pmc-13285276:
İbrahim Arslan and co-authors study secretoneurin as a possible marker of metabolic syndrome in sleep apnea patients in a 2026 article. Blocked breathing in sleep raises risk of weight gain, diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, and metabolic syndrome is far more common in these patients than in the wider public. Secretoneurin is a small protein released by nerve and hormone cells under low oxygen stress.

The authors frame secretoneurin as a candidate early signal, since it rises with hypoxia and links to inflammation and vessel action. Its level tracks with blood triglyceride levels in the work highlighted here. They argue a simple blood marker could help flag apnea patients who are moving toward metabolic syndrome.
pmc-13285676:
Deep seawater sprayed on apple trees rewires thousands of peel genes, Bimpe Suliyat Azeez, Se-Jin Oh, and Jong-Kuk Na report in a 2026 dataset. Deep seawater brims with dissolved minerals and is eyed as a natural farm input, yet its gene-level mark on apples was unmapped. Peel from treated and plain Fuji Hubrax trees went through paired RNA reads.

Treated peel yielded slightly fewer reads, both sets scored high on quality, and most reads mapped to the apple genome. Roughly twenty-three hundred genes rose and fifteen hundred fell with treatment. The full read sets now sit in a public archive, ready for teams hunting which paths drive growth or stress gains from mineral water.
pmc-13286076:
Dong-soo Shin and colleagues study mobile health services in rural South Korea in a 2026 mixed methods study. Older villagers with long-term illness face scarce doctors, long trips, and thin support, while phone-based care promises steady watch from afar. The team asked long-time users in one county what kept them engaged with the services month after month.

Talks and surveys covered 24 users of four public programs, most of them women in their early seventies with high blood pressure. Nearly all planned to keep using the tools, and every user said they would urge the services on others. Live feedback sharpened health awareness and nudged better eating and more walking day to day. Nurses from the public health center anchored the system, training users and cheering them on, while family and habits locked the routine in place.
pmc-13286876:
Yan Chen and Ronghua Chu report an immunotherapy pairing that shrank a stubborn sarcoma in a case report published in 2026. The high-grade leg sarcoma of a 73-year-old woman, removed in 2022 with positive margins, returned two years later, invaded the shin bone, and seeded a lung spot. Standard chemotherapy made her too ill to continue, and after a year without treatment the leg tumor ulcerated down to bone.

Following amputation for local control, she received sintilimab, an immune checkpoint antibody, together with the vessel-targeting drug anlotinib. Her lung metastases shrank dramatically, scoring a partial response with a 76.6% reduction in tumor burden. The authors present the combination as a candidate route for advanced patients of this sarcoma type who cannot tolerate chemotherapy, while calling for proper trials.
pmc-13287576:
Edgar Gonzalez-Kozlova and co-authors report in 2026 a newly defined group of very small particles in human brain and blood, named SECmeres, that differ from the better-known vesicles cells shed. The team compared RNA carried by each particle type as a possible blood test for Alzheimer disease.

RNA tied to SECmeres separated patients from controls more strongly than RNA from small vesicles. Large vesicles showed no gap at all. Tracing RNA back to cell types suggested SECmeres draw heavily from vessel-lining brain cells. The authors say the finding shifts attention away from vesicles alone, though larger blinded trials must confirm any test.
pmc-13288376:
Mary E Carrington, Michael S Ross, and Suresh C Subedi tested a shortcut used in forest science in 2026. The shortcut reads forest ageing from a row of sites of different ages. It avoids waiting decades for one site to age. Dry tropical forest plots in North Key Largo, Florida, were measured in 1993 and again in 2013 to check the shortcut.

Real change inside each site matched the pattern read across sites, for both species mix and leaf traits. Early fast-growing leaf-shedding species gave way to tougher evergreen kinds, as expected. One surprise stood out: leaf traits spread widest late in ageing, not narrowest. The authors blame crowding and scarce resources as unlike evergreens meet at high numbers.
pmc-13288676:
Shaista Rehman leads a 2026 study of colon cancer risks in Oman. The study ran at two Muscat hospitals. It compared 166 cancer patients with 166 controls. A survey tapped habits and body measures. Family history and other illness were also logged.

Smoking stood out in the results. It meant roughly four times the odds of cancer. Higher body weight also raised odds. Polyps, diabetes, and high blood pressure raised them too. Bowel inflammation raised odds as well. Family history more than doubled the odds. That held for close and distant kin. The authors press for risk-based screening. Quitting help and weight care should join it.
pmc-13288876:
Rutakayile Bizoza and colleagues follow long-acting schizophrenia shots in Rwanda in 2026. Five centers hosted the work. It held 93 adults aged eighteen to thirty-five. Usual oral drugs ran for twenty-four weeks. Monthly paliperidone shots came next. A three-monthly form followed later.

In all, 86 people finished the study. That is 92.5 percent of those enrolled. Severity scores barely moved on oral drugs. They improved clearly once shots began. Social performance scores rose alongside. Three-quarters reported at least one side effect. Most effects were mild or moderate. Weakness and nasal infections were common complaints.
pmc-13288976:
Mi Mi Ko and colleagues profile a Korean aging cohort in 2026. The KoMAC study tracks adults aged 50 to 65. It blends standard care with Korean medicine views. Recruitment began in August 2023. Sites span city and rural areas.

The goal is 1,000 adults in all. Early data show town and country gaps. Rural adults drank and smoked more. City adults had weaker lung scores. Hearing also ran worse in city adults. Aging cut body and social function for most. Women showed the steepest drops. Korean pattern checks shifted with age too. Yearly follow-ups will track risk over time.
pmc-13289076:
Taalke Maria Sitter and colleagues study drug links to force and relapse in Sweden. Their 2026 study deals with forensic mental care. It covers all new patients from 2009 to 2024. In all, 2,690 patients were tracked. Each patient was compared with themselves over time.

About one in four faced force at least once. About one in four also relapsed into crime. Newer antipsychotic drugs tied to less force. They also tied to less relapse. Drugs for addiction tied to less force too. Clozapine showed the largest drops of all. Shot, pill, and mixed plans did not differ. The authors urge care in reading cause and effect.
pmc-13289176:
Goodluck Willey Lyatuu and colleagues introduce a 2026 project plan in Tanzania. The ENGAGE project deals with young mothers with HIV. It aims to stop HIV passing to infants. Teen girls face high pregnancy and HIV rates. Their care dropout risks infant infection.

Phase one will study a cohort of 10,147 young women. They all use routine mother-to-child prevention care. Phase two will probe social drivers by talks. An evidence scan will hunt for fixes. Phase three will co-create a care package. Young women and staff will shape it in workshops. A test version will run at picked sites. Later work will pilot it in full.
pmc-13289376:
Owen Hibberd headed a 2026 survey on measuring and replacing calcium in children with major trauma. Low ionized calcium can worsen bleeding by hurting clot formation, vessel tone, and heart squeeze. Guidelines say to keep calcium normal, yet they do not say when to test or top up in injured children, leaving practice unclear.

Answers came from 67 emergency departments and 99 clinicians across 19 countries via research networks. Most departments had a major bleeding protocol, but nearly a quarter left calcium out entirely. Timing for replacement was missing or vague in most protocols that did mention calcium at all. Clinician views on a sample case, stable versus unstable, showed wide variation in when to act.
pmc-13289576:
Toshinao Kawai headed a 2026 randomized, blinded trial of thalidomide for bowel inflammation in chronic granulomatous disease. That rare immune defect, present in about 1 in 225,000 births, impairs germ killing and sparks excess inflammation. Nearly half of patients develop bowel disease with diarrhea, bleeding, pain, and fever, resembling classic inflammatory bowel disease in symptoms.

Patients aged one year or older received thalidomide or placebo under double-blind conditions for comparison. The abstract reports potential benefit with acceptable safety and no added infection risk signal in this first controlled trial of its kind. Standard options include steroids, immune suppressants, and biologics, all with trade-offs. A repurposed oral option would matter for families facing limited choices.
pmc-13289776:
Humphrey Deogratias Mazigo led a 2026 report on building an endoscopy unit for liver and spleen harm from schistosomiasis in northwestern Tanzania. That parasite disease is a common cause of severe illness and death in adults locally, yet treatment capacity was very low. A needs check at Nansio District Hospital confirmed demand, missing skills, and building needs before work began in earnest.

The unit opened in August 2023 and has seen 666 patients so far, about two thirds of them men. Belly swelling, vomiting blood, and black stools were common reasons for care. Ultrasound found scarring around liver vessels in 71.5 percent, and most scoped patients had severe esophageal varices needing banding. Follow-up showed strong early success.
pmc-13290876:
Dental implant surgery quietly lowers pain thresholds in the face for weeks, Kiyomi Uehashi and colleagues report in an exploratory study from 2026. Why some patients develop lasting nerve pain after implants is unresolved, and no objective test exists, so the team tracked heat pain thresholds around surgery in 76 outpatients in Osaka.

Thresholds were measured before and after surgery in the cheek, jaw, and neck regions the trigeminal and cervical nerves serve. On the operated side, the share of patients showing a threshold drop ranged from about 29 to 49% at one week, then shrank steadily to near zero by twelve weeks. The changes were subclinical: sensation shifted without patients reporting pain. Uehashi and colleagues read the pattern as a common, transient nerve response worth monitoring in implant care.
pmc-13290976:
Zhenzhen Dou heads a 2026 nationwide study of brain abscess in children in China, covering the years 2016 through 2023. Brain abscess is rare in children yet can threaten life, and large studies of its changing pattern have been scarce, so the team used discharge records from 33 tertiary children’s hospitals.

Altogether 799 children were identified, with yearly rates staying broadly flat across the study span. After 2020 the age mix shifted away from toddlers toward older children and teens. Infections spreading from a nearby site also became more common in the later years, while heart defects present at birth held steady as a risk factor. Surgery, complications, hospital stay length, and costs all ran higher after 2020 in adjusted comparisons.
pmc-13291076:
Which needle points work best in electroacupuncture for bowel inflammation is probed in a 2026 mouse study led by Jiayin Lu. Three points used in Chinese medicine, Dachangshu, Tianshu, and Shangjuxu, were compared in mice given a chemical that triggers inflammatory bowel disease, with body weight, colon shape, and inflammation signals all tracked.

Needle treatment at all three points eased tissue damage and slowed weight loss, and each point lowered one key inflammation signal, IL-6, with the strongest drop at Dachangshu. A second signal, IL-1β, barely moved under any point tested. Gut microbe mixes and body chemicals also shifted after treatment, mostly along lipid, amino acid, and energy pathways, which may explain why point choice changes the result.
pmc-13291476:
Patients and dentists in Saudi Arabia judge AI tools for teeth. Shimaa Rifaat leads a 2026 survey in the eastern province. Smart tools are entering dental care fast. Their success rests on trust from both sides of the chair.

A self-filled survey ran in English and Arabic. It held 38 questions in five parts. Topics spanned tech comfort, AI awareness, and worries. Both patients and dental staff took part. Views were compared across age and job traits. Few past studies set both groups side by side. Local culture shapes how new tools land. Results can guide a smoother rollout in clinics.
pmc-13291776:
Bao-Hua Wei and Hong-Ju Da report a 2026 case report and literature review on purulent pericarditis caused by mouth bacteria. Their patient was a 66-year-old man with no known gum disease or recent dental work. He arrived with pus around the heart plus an abscess below the diaphragm.

Gene sequencing of the pericardial fluid found three periodontal pathogens together: Tannerella forsythia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and Porphyromonas gingivalis. Doctors drained the fluid, gave targeted antibiotics, and supported his organs until he stabilized. The authors argue that oral bacteria can travel through the blood and seed distant sterile sites even without obvious mouth disease. They also praise broad molecular testing for naming hard-to-grow organisms in infections of unknown origin.
pmc-13292376:
Elsa-Rush Eyang-Assengone and a large team survey a 2026 rural Gabonese village, Dienga, for filarial worm infections using molecular tools. Control programs lack current local data, and Loa loa co-presence makes mass drug campaigns risky. PCR found infections in 23.33 percent of volunteers, well above the 13.33 percent microscopy caught, confirming its edge for hidden cases. Loa loa dominated, with Mansonella perstans at just 1.11 percent of those tested. Men were hit far harder than women, 40.5 against 11.32 percent in the survey, and rates peaked past age 61. Itching, Calabar swelling, and eyeworm together strongly predicted infection. Only 10 percent of villagers knew the vector.
pmc-13292576:
Youngsu Kim and co-authors explore a 2026 home-dialysis reality: peritoneal dialysis sells freedom from the clinic, but patients must turn their houses into safe treatment rooms. Patients described three kinds of space. Hospitals meant delegated safety, trusted to professionals. Homes meant internalized safety, where they rearranged routines and storage to keep sterile control. Everywhere else brought a paradox: travel is theoretically easy, yet unpredictable environments triggered such careful risk checks that many simply narrowed their world. Control over the surroundings, more than the place itself, decided whether a space felt safe. The authors urge educators to teach the spatial work honestly.
pmc-13292676:
Mihiprabha Rathnayake and co-authors spray a 2026 shortcut onto incubating chicken eggs: probiotics misted over the shell so chicks hatch with a head start on gut microbes. First they timed Enterococcus faecalis sprays across embryo days, checking colonization by culture and genome sequencing. Then five probiotic strains, alone and mixed, were sprayed and the chicks' jejunal communities tracked to thirty days after hatching.

Spraying on days 15 and 17 of incubation colonized embryos best. Ligilactobacillus salivarius, Lactobacillus plantarum, and the full mixture pushed gut communities toward the mature profile significantly faster than oral dosing did. Group differences peaked at day two after hatching, then communities converged, with the sprayed mixture staying distinct longest and richest early on. The authors call coarse spraying a practical, industry-ready delivery route.
pmc-13293476:
Mary Kamillah Grace Reyes and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how artificial intelligence tools help people manage stress on their own, outside clinics. Stress is widespread, yet therapist-led care is limited by capacity, cost, and stigma.

Following standard review steps, the team searched six databases for English studies from 2000 to 2025 and kept 35 of 3008 records found. Quality was checked with a mixed methods tool. Five core roles emerged: direct therapy support, behavior support, teaching, companionship with emotional support, and stress tracking with triage. Early proof looks promising, though the authors stress that evidence is still taking shape.
pmc-13293576:
Mingyue Fan and Binbin Gu build, in a 2026 study, a chart tool to predict when hands-on realignment of a broken wrist will fail. Wrist breaks are very common, and knowing failure risk early can steer patients to the right first treatment.

Records covered 822 patients whose breaks were classed by whether manual realignment worked or failed. Eight factors entered the final model, from break type and swelling to drinking history and time since injury. The tool sorted risk well in internal checks and matched observed outcomes closely. The authors suggest it can support personal treatment choices, though outside testing is still needed to confirm its worth.
pmc-13293776:
Masamitsu Eitoku and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, Japan's notebook health record system for retired workers once exposed to hazardous agents, including migrant workers. Japan's aging population draws more migrant labor, and past exposure can sicken workers long after jobs end.

The scheme, set in law, gives former workers a personal record book and free checkups for 15 named agents or jobs. New books issued for major agents have slowly fallen in recent years. Over two decades, three more agent types joined the scheme, and asbestos rules widened. Public hospitals may serve as checkup sites in workers' home countries, the authors suggest.
pmc-13293876:
Yuan-Hao Mao and coauthors describe a 2026 advance in ring laser gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation from tiny frequency shifts between two beams. At very slow rotation the beams lock together, a flaw that blocks precise sensing. Past fixes add moving parts or extra optics, which hinder small designs. The new approach needs no inserted elements.

Inside a helium-neon device, chiral symmetry breaking and nonlinear pulling bias the system on its own. Experiments showed beam direction switching that followed rotation direction, with a linear response near zero rate. Bias instability reached 2.2 × 10−2 degrees per hour at a 10 s integration time, pointing toward compact high-precision sensors.
pmc-13294276:
Zhenyue Qin and colleagues test a uterus-sparing plan for severe adenomyosis in a 2026 retrospective case series. Care choices hinge on fertility wishes and disease pattern, and the Kishi scan classes sort cases by where growth sits. Their patients wanted no future pregnancy but wished to keep the uterus. Partial removal of diseased tissue was paired with hormone device and drug steps afterward.

All 34 patients treated from December 2017 to October 2022 completed surgery. Pain scores, bleeding scores, hemoglobin, a blood marker, and uterine size all improved clearly after treatment in the reported comparisons. One hormone device slipped downward. Longer follow-up will judge lasting relief.
pmc-13294376:
Niousha Sadjadi and coauthors test how far a species' word-pattern fingerprint stretches across its genome in a 2026 study. Short DNA word frequencies form chaos game pictures that identify species without alignment. Complete chromosome sets from humans and three other eukaryotes from distinct kingdoms were scanned, hunting spots where the local fingerprint strays from the genome-wide one.

Most regions matched the home fingerprint closely. In humans, 80% of half-million-letter segments sat within 0.24 of the chosen reference on a zero-to-one scale in the reported metric. Stray segments clustered where short and long repeat runs pile up. One short reference stretch can thus stand in for most of a genome in sorting tasks.
pmc-13295376:
Laura Franziska Flach, Emilio Sabia, and Thomas Zanon study dairy goat farms in South Tyrol in a 2026 article. Mountain goat keeping supports rural income, old landscapes, and farm diversity under hard conditions. How profits and environmental costs interact on such farms was little documented.

Ten alpine farms shared interview answers and accounting records for the analysis. Full-cost accounts measured money performance, while life cycle methods scored impacts per litre of corrected milk and per hectare. Joining the two views exposes trade-offs that single scores would hide. The framework aims to guide support that lifts both earnings and environmental care in mountain systems.
pmc-13295776:
Katarina Ulfsdotter Gunnarsson, Martin Henriksson, and Marcus Bendtsen simulate lifelong gains from a digital alcohol programme in a 2026 study. Online help for risky drinking can shift behaviour, but whether shifts pay off in health and costs over decades was unclear. A person-level model followed two virtual groups through life.

One group received the digital programme and the other usual care, with ten alcohol-linked diseases tracked. Lasting effects gave the programme group fewer illnesses, slightly more quality-adjusted life years, and lower healthcare costs per person. Gains shrank as the assumed effect faded faster, and vanished when fading ran quickest, stressing proof of lasting change.
pmc-13297076:
Anamaria Violeta Țuțuianu and colleagues examine, in 2026, the home lives behind 333 Romanian children treated for dental neglect between 2020 and 2024. Records from a city hospital and a private practice profile caregivers' age, schooling, income, substance use and family stability.

Most caregivers were young adults, many with little schooling, and nearly half used alcohol. Low income, present in most families, tied closely to dropping out of the treatment plan. Children of drug-using caregivers arrived years later than others, and over half lived in disrupted homes. The authors stress neglect's many-sided roots.
pmc-13298776:
Bone density can be read from ordinary chest scans if the calibration holds up, and Yizhang Tong with colleagues validated an automated phantom-less system in a 2026 prospective study. Among 252 people having routine chest CT, the system measured spinal density at T11 to L1 without a physical reference phantom.

Against phantom-based measurement, results correlated strongly, with r = 0.867, and the system detected osteoporosis with an AUC of 0.962. Manually chosen visceral fat calibration beat the automatic subcutaneous fat choice for spotting early bone loss. Readings stayed consistent across five different scanners. The authors endorse the approach for opportunistic screening during scans done for other reasons.
pmc-13299476:
Cell-shed specks are the skin trade's new hope, and Candelaria Contreras and Amin Ariza-Donado grade that hope in a 2026 review. The specks, sold as exosomes, pass proteins and gene bits from cell to cell.

Trials hint at gains for skin youth, hair growth, wound mend, and dark spot care. Gains may flow through fresh skin frame, new blood paths, and calmer immune fire. The team also asked twelve skin doctors in Colombia how the tools feel in real work. Their word is care: goods swing wide in source and make, hard trials are few, harm has come from goods with no stamp of law, and rules are far from set.
pmc-13299576:
Women may break down one common mood drug through a liver path more fast than men. Janina Eiberger and her team hint at that in a 2026 blood-level study. They mined past blood checks from sick people on one of three mood drugs and set drug break pace by sex, grouped by gene type.

For two drugs worked by the CYP2D6 path, no sex gap showed in 117 and 73 blood sets. For the third drug, escitalopram, worked by CYP2C19, men with the plain gene type held more drug per dose in the blood than women. That hints women clear it more fast. With just 51 sets for that drug, the team call the find a first hint, not a fact, and ask for a big check.
pmc-13300276:
How stem cells guard their glutathione supply changes as they turn toward neurons, Nobuko Matsumura and colleagues show in a 2026 cell study. Removing GTRAP3-18 lowered glutathione in stem cells but raised both EAAC1 and glutathione in neuron-like cells. pmc-13300576:
Carbon dioxide calms bees for handling, yet its inner effects vary with age, Ying Wang and two colleagues show in a 2026 proteomics study. They exposed honey bee workers at three life stages, newly emerged, nurse, and forager, then compared protein patterns in hemolymph and brain tissue.

Newly emerged bees proved the hardiest, leaning on chemical defense pathways in both blood and brain. Nurse bees mounted weaker blood responses but guarded the brain first. Foragers instead favored blood detoxification paired with brain energy control. Across all ages, bees shifted energy use to ride out the stress, a finding with practical value for transport and colony care.
pmc-13300876:
In a 2026 retrospective study, Zeynel Mert Asfuroğlu and colleagues find that rebuilt web spaces between fused fingers generally serve patients well for decades. Appearance, hand function, and psychosocial state were scored with the Withey scale, QuickDASH, and a purpose-built survey.

Median follow-up reached ten years, and the typical scores, Withey 2, QuickDASH 14, and psychosocial 29, all sat in the favorable band. Surgery between ages one and five and repeat operations also tracked with poorer appearance, guiding family counseling.
pmc-13301176:
Should every aortic repair patient get a heart artery check first? Half the group received coronary angiography before surgery; survival was tracked for a median of 4.9 years.

The test uncovered new or worsening coronary disease in 44.7 percent of those tested, and 13.6 percent of all patients had their heart arteries treated before repair. Coronary disease itself looked deadlier before adjustment, a gap the authors trace to wider artery disease across the body.
pmc-13301376:
As grassland turns to desert, the fungi nursing plant roots swap identity, Xue Wang and colleagues show in a 2026 field study. Along a drying gradient, they sampled rhizosphere soil around Stipa breviflora and Artemisia frigida, sequencing fungi and scoring root colonization. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, the classic root partners, lost diversity and root foothold as dryness deepened. Dark septate endophytes moved the other way, gaining ground in roots and inferred abundance. Fungal networks broke into looser fragments, a shift the models tie to the guild swap itself. Soil usefulness fell too, marking wider decline beneath the visible plants.
pmc-13305176:
Mei An and co-authors review sulfur movement in coal chemical looping combustion in a 2026 synthesis. The clean coal method captures concentrated carbon dioxide with low nitrogen oxide output, but sulfur in coal poisons the oxygen carriers and dirties the gas stream.

Sulfur release during coal heating and gas steps is mapped for two looping styles, and paths that spread sulfur through the system are traced. Rather than merely tolerating sulfur, the authors urge carriers designed to grab it on site. Multi-job oxygen carriers could protect themselves while cleaning the stream, speeding real-world use.
pmc-13306576:
Faouzia Tayari reviewed greener sound-absorbing materials and shapes in a 2026 critical survey. Standard mineral wool and foams soak up sound well but cost heavy energy and rely on non-renewable inputs to produce.

Pore layout, airflow resistance, thickness and layered or resonant shapes all shape performance in the gathered work. Printed structures now allow precise geometry control alongside bio-based and recycled fillings. Weak low-frequency capture, durability and fire safety still limit wider use, so the authors favour hybrid designs that join material and shape gains. The team sees hybrid builds as the best path to green quiet rooms.
pmc-13306976:

Recovery meant pumping fraction climbing back above 35% after treatment in the study definition. Baseline and follow-up scans, heart tracings, clinical notes and lab values fed a prediction model built with a bias-aware regression method. Later heart death and heart failure readmission were also tracked, aiming to flag patients needing closer watch and device review.
pmc-13308676:
Xin Li and co-authors chart in 2026 the load carried by patients in China who start triple inhaler therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Records from Tianjin for 2019 to mid 2023 held 7871 starters, split between one inhaler and many inhaler forms of the triple mix.

Mean age was 65.8 years, and most patients were men who had first gone to a top tier hospital for care. High blood pressure and asthma led the list of side ills at the start date for this group. Use of clinics and hospitals stayed high, and drug cover days sat low at a mean share of 0.35 overall. Better adherence could cut the heavy cost and visit load.
pmc-13309376:
Sandra Furlan Nogueira and colleagues offer a 2026 analysis of nitrous oxide released from farm fertilizer in Brazil. The team reviewed 56 papers covering 325 field trials in sugarcane, grain, and pasture systems. They compared climate, biome, soil, and fertilizer type to build sharper emission factors for each system. Pasture and some warm-climate grain and cane fields showed higher factors. The authors argue that local factors give Brazil a fairer and more accurate emissions count.
pmc-13310676:
Hongzhan Cui and co-authors assess hole closure between the heart atria as migraine care in China in a 2026 study. Closing it with a catheter device is offered as treatment, yet large real-world Chinese data were scarce.

The responder rate, set at halving headache impact or migraine days, reached 83.98 percent at follow-up in the cohort, with 59.90 percent gaining complete or near-complete relief. Younger age predicted better response. Safety and operator learning effects were also tracked.
pmc-13310776:
Rula Odeh Alsawalqa and co-authors study feelings at work among social workers in Jordan in a 2026 survey. Women and master degree holders scored higher on skill use, while men reported more calming trouble. Training in these skills may support staff health and service quality.
pmc-13310876:
Xiaoyu Liao and co-authors study a tryptophan byproduct that eases liver swelling and insulin resistance in mice in a 2026 paper. Levels of the compound, called 5MT, fell in obese and diabetic mice and rose after a diabetes drug, which hinted at a guard role. The team tested direct dosing in two mouse models.

Dosed mice showed better insulin response and less liver fat. Blocking a cell sensor removed much of the gain. Gene tests showed the compound raised a signal protein in liver immune cells, and mice lacking that protein in those cells lost the benefit. The path may seed new metabolic drugs.
pmc-13310976:
Hui Li led a 2026 trial of a low dose lung artery scan for suspected lung clots. Standard scans use high radiation and iodine doses, which raise cancer and kidney concerns. A spectral scan with tiny iodine dose and blended injection was tested against standard care.

Patients totaled 160 in number, split evenly between the new and standard scans. Expert readers rated the new scans higher in quality, and key contrast scores stayed above the needed bar. Radiation fell by over two fifths and iodine by two thirds compared with standard care. Clot finding rates were alike. Iodine maps showed flow gaps clearly.
pmc-13311176:
Allison L. Harris and co-authors build whole brain imaging for spreading depolarization in fruit flies in a 2026 study. The wave of nerve shutdown links to migraine, stroke, and brain injury, yet its start and spread rules are hard to watch in large brains. Fly brains allow fast, whole organ views with rich gene tools.

Waves began at many shifting sites across and within flies and spread through the whole nervous system in adults and larvae alike. After one wave, tissue resisted a second wave for a time through a raised threshold that did not depend on shutdown itself. Home balance shifts may explain the pause.
pmc-13311676:
Takahito Miyake, Hideshi Okada, and Norihide Kanda review fat embolism syndrome in a 2026 article. Fat drops entering the blood after injury can harm lungs, brain, and skin, sometimes with fatal results.

Classic sign triads exist, but the illness varies widely and old scoring rules lack solid proof. Chest and brain scans plus new blood markers may sharpen diagnosis, though none is specific. Care stays supportive, early bone fixing within 24 hours prevents best, and steroid use remains in dispute.
pmc-13311976:
Elham Khoori and Tayebe Ziaei write a 2026 commentary on a qualitative study of maternal grief after stillbirth in China, faulting paternalistic medical culture for deepening that grief. A baby born sleeping brings losses across identity and family life.

The discussed study by Zheng and colleagues traced how culture and spirituality shape grief after stillbirth. The commentators urge providers to weigh cultural and spiritual beliefs when designing support for bereaved mothers. They call for studies comparing grief across diverse populations. Their title makes the charge plain: ignoring how staff power and habits affect grieving mothers compounds the harm.
pmc-13312176:
Han Xiao and colleagues report a 2026 study on the receptor RAGE in lung adenocarcinoma growing under low oxygen. Tumors of this common lung cancer type showed reduced RAGE levels, and lower amounts tracked with poorer patient survival, even as hypoxia markers rose inside the tumors.

Experiments gave a split picture. Blocking RAGE slowed cancer cell growth and migration in cell culture, yet inhibiting it sped tumor growth in living animals, where tumors switched on alternative routes to keep progressing. The authors trace the harm to damage-associated molecular pattern signaling, the alarm molecules stressed and dying cells release in oxygen-starved tissue. Their account warns that a target can look protective in a dish yet act differently in a whole tumor, which matters for drug design.
pmc-13313376:
Abida Sanjana Shemonti and a large team present CARGO, a new way to draw and study flow cytometry data, in work published in 2026. Standard plots and maps such as PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP often flatten the rich data from these tests and give weak grounds for firm number work.

The frame gives labs a clearer, more principled view of high-parameter cell data than the usual scatter maps.
pmc-13313476:
Peter Dimitrion and colleagues report in 2026 that the tunnels formed in hidradenitis suppurativa, a painful skin disease, carry a mucosal-like gene pattern. The team used STEREOseq, a spatial method that reads genes at single-cell detail, on sore and healthy skin from one patient with advanced disease. They compared tunnel lining with sore and non-sore outer skin. The tunnel cells showed a gene signature like mucosal surfaces rather than normal skin, a trait that may feed the ongoing inflammation. The finding reframes tunnels as active, mucosa-like tissue and points to new targets for calming this hard disease.
pmc-13314476:
Caitlin Fountain and co-workers test how self-chosen music lifts mood after stress in a 2026 study. Music is more and more used as a low-cost aid for well-being and calm, yet how song type shapes emotion repair after a blow was not well mapped.

The study began with a screen of 795 undergraduate students in the United States, counted in the report, who rated their music tastes. Those ratings built personal playlists of two kinds: upbeat and fast songs meant to empower, and upbeat but slow songs meant to calm. After a social rejection stress task, students heard their music while the team tracked gains in positive feelings and drops in negative ones. The design shows whether picking your own songs, and their tempo, changes how fast mood recovers.
pmc-13316076:
Mengjiao Wang and colleagues propose in 2026 an integrated sustainability hierarchy that crosses topic silos, to close the gap between global pledges and real action. Single-issue fixes stay fragmented and often treat damage downstream instead of preventing it upstream, the authors argue.

Reviewing existing hierarchies for waste, climate, biodiversity, and more, they build a cross-domain compass for policy agendas, finance portfolios, and judging interventions. The ongoing Global Plastics Treaty talks serve as a worked example. The frame offers a practical, theory-based tool for systemic action amid rising social and ecological risk and political backsliding.
pmc-13316276:
Sandro Tiziano Stoffel, Helene Seaward, and Aksha Balakrishnan held focus groups in 2026 with patients to understand why Swiss cancer trials struggle to recruit. Cancer ranks second among causes of death in Switzerland, and about a quarter of randomized trials there stop early, often for low enrollment, wasting resources.

Known barriers include fear of randomization, side effect worry, travel and time load, cost, low awareness, and distrust, while hope of benefit draws others in. Patient voices add lived detail on those trade-offs, pointing to changes in information, logistics, and trust building that could raise participation.
pmc-13316576:
Jin Zhang and Hao Feng report a 2026 case of blood clots found just after a kinked PICC line was straightened in a 78-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy. The line, placed for long-term drug delivery, first blocked, then ran freely after adjustment, then blocked again the next day.

Ultrasound imaging revealed several deep vein clots, a known cause of unplanned line removal that can grow silently. The authors review current guidance and suggest ultrasound checks within the first one to two weeks after placement, plus follow-up scans for high-risk patients. Relying on nurse checks at weekly care visits, they argue, misses early clots that imaging would catch while treatment can still help.
pmc-13316676:
Mitsuru Mizuno and co-authors surveyed, in a 2026 study, how cleanroom monitoring is actually done across regulated factories in Japan, with a focus on regenerative medicine plants. Cell therapy making leans heavily on hand work, so watching air and surfaces for germs is central, yet practice varies.

Fifty-five monitoring staff from six sectors answered a 55-item questionnaire. Statistical grouping showed wide gaps: how often surfaces are checked in mid-grade clean areas, how growth media are tested, and when air particles are counted. Regenerative sites mixed frequent media tests with uneven coverage. The authors say naming the high-impact gaps gives these plants a base for sharper, risk-based monitoring, cleaner records, and better training.
pmc-13317776:
Chungang Zhang, Deyu Fang, and Lin Zhang reframe, in a 2026 review, the blood-brain barrier in Alzheimer's disease around its sugar-rich skin. That layer, the endothelial glycocalyx, faces the blood and decides what passes. Leakiness alone, they argue, is too crude a lens for this interface.

They sort the evidence, strong in mice and thin in humans, and propose grading the interface on four axes: structure, sugar pattern, transport, and inflammation. Damage looks patchy, with early loss of one domain rather than wholesale shedding. A repair window may stay open in APOE4 carriers and early memory loss, then close when vessel amyloid joins. pmc-13318076:
Katlin T Wilson, Areeba H Rizvi, and Kevin O Turner describe a 2026 case of collagenous gastroduodenitis in a previously healthy 13-year-old girl who arrived with severe tiredness and breathlessness on effort. The rare stomach disorder lays down a thick collagen band under the gut lining alongside chronic inflammation.

The authors say such a triple meeting is highly uncommon in children. Because causes remain unknown and care is limited to watching and easing symptoms, each well-documented case sharpens ideas about how the disease starts and what targeted treatment might one day do.
pmc-13318576:
Ampuan Shazani bin Ampuan Haji Sadikin and Heru Susanto offer a 2026 security study. It is set in Brunei's instant payment system. They test a two-layer shield for payment data. It survived 87.5 percent of eight scenarios in the testing. Average processing time was 568.82 ms per task, with sound quality still acceptable. The method also worked inside a test payment flow. The authors argue inner protection can compensate where people remain the weak point.
pmc-13318676:

Uses span asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumonia, fibrosis, and lung cancer. Inhaled forms spread evenly and start working quickly. They also avoid the liver first-pass effect that weakens oral drugs. The authors see broad prospects for safer, stronger lung treatments built on nanotechnology and new materials.
pmc-13318876:
Antonella Mosca and colleagues present a 2026 case report with a narrative review on allergy arising after childhood liver transplant. New IgE-mediated food allergy and asthma are recognised problems in young recipients. Their patient was a 15-year-old boy transplanted at 28 days old for newborn liver failure. He later developed severe asthma and multiple food allergies.

His asthma came under excellent control, and background medicines were stopped. His diet became far less restricted. Liver graft function stayed stable throughout, with no graft problems over more than five years of follow-up. The authors present the drug as safe and effective in this setting.
pmc-13320376:
Kai Li and Grit Walther present a cleaned data set on fast fashion clothes in a 2026 data article for reuse research. After cleaning and checks, the set holds 47522 color level garment records, each with source links, shop and region, item name, color, and fabric shares split by garment part. Fabric names and garment classes were mapped to shared terms for fair counts. Photos, raw page grabs, and shopper reviews were left out of the public set. The files may aid sorting, recycling, and green audits.
pmc-13321376:

The category scale overstated strength at low doses, above all for intense sweeteners. pmc-13322076:
