A mass reporter test of 7760 duplicated and chimpanzee matching stretches found 14 to 24 percent with differing activity, mostly by small amounts. Predicted switch activity tracked gene output in nerve cells, and checks on three genes supported copy specific expression patterns.
pmc-13322876:
Jianting Wen and Jian Liu review Tripterygium wilfordii and Xinfeng capsule for rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2026 article weighing benefit against harm. The plant has a long history in traditional use for this joint disease, and its tablets and capsule forms are widely studied in China.

Lab work links its compounds to signals such as NF-kB and PI3K/AKT/mTOR, to inflammasome activity, joint lining growth, blood vessel growth and immune cell faults. Clinical reports suggest gains in disease activity, joint symptoms and inflammation markers, alone or with standard drugs. Wider multi-part action in the capsule may raise benefit and lower toxicity, yet safety worries, weak large trials and poor standard dosing still limit use.
pmc-13325376:
Anand U. Kyatanwar and Bala R. Prabhakar test whether blended polymers can match single-grade polymers in peptide microspheres in a 2026 study. Peptide drugs need carriers that shield them and release them slowly, but top-grade polymers are scarce and pricey.

Two shelf polymers, R202H and RG502H, were mixed in varied ratios to mimic custom grades. Microspheres loaded with the heart drug eptifibatide were made from blends and from plain shelf polymers. Both sets performed the same on structure and release in side-by-side checks. The match matters because blending stocked grades skips costly custom synthesis. Peptide delivery projects gain a cheaper formulation path without giving up quality.
pmc-13327876:
Wan Qin and co-authors probe why students grow bored in AI-assisted English learning in a 2026 survey study. Boredom can drain drive and results, and a growth mindset is thought to soften it, but the path in AI settings was untested. The team followed 536 first-year university students in eastern China across three waves, two months apart.

Mindset was measured first, then AI literacy and confidence in using AI, and finally boredom. A growth mindset predicted stronger AI literacy and confidence, and both of those predicted less boredom, while mindset alone showed no direct link to boredom. AI literacy also fed confidence, forming a chain that teachers can build on by training skills, not just attitudes.
pmc-13328176:
Yi Zhao and co-authors trace how a mother's low iron may slow a newborn's hearing development in a 2026 study. Data from 696 mother-infant pairs were joined with pregnant mouse models and cochlear tissue experiments. Iron shortage without anemia is common in pregnancy, and its hearing effects were unclear.

Higher maternal ferritin and hemoglobin went with faster auditory brain responses in newborns, and newborn ferritin carried part of that link, with mediation shares from 28.57 to 76.32 percent across the measures reported. Iron-short mouse pups showed weaker, slower responses, fewer ribbon synapses in inner ear hair cells, and damaged mitochondria, while added pyruvate partly restored synapse function. Energy failure in support cells is the proposed chain.
pmc-13329376:
Philipp Schenk and a large study group report in 2026 on bone drug care for inpatients with spine breaks from weak bones. Such drugs help prevent further breaks but are often missed. Data came from the prospective EOFTT study, with 518 patients in 17 clinics who had breaks in the chest or lower spine area.

Hospital stay raised treatment a lot: among women the share rose from 36 percent at entry to 83 percent in the reported results, with a smaller rise in men. Months later, shares fell sharply again for both sexes. Calcium and vitamin D use followed the same rise and fall. Proven bone drugs stayed rare. The authors flag long-term follow-up as the weak point in care.
pmc-13331176:
Ali Hammed and colleagues pool trials on surgery for bleeding inside the brain in a 2026 meta-analysis. Whether removing the clot beats drug care alone has long been debated. The pool held 29 randomised trials with 5,531 patients, comparing surgery with standard medical care on function and death.

Surgery linked to better function and lower death overall in the pooled odds given. Turned into plain terms, gains ran near 6 to 7 extra good outcomes per 100 patients in the authors' worked examples. Surgery inside 24 hours gave the largest gains, with a clear timing interaction for function but not for death. Site, size, and technique showed no firm modifying effect in their checks.
pmc-13332476:
AE Carolus and colleagues describe GripAgain, a 2026 mobile app project supporting hand training after nerve surgery. Recovery of grip and fine movement shapes quality of life after such operations, and the team's earlier work showed intense targeted training speeds recovery.

Built with FlutterFlow for the interface and Firebase behind it, with data security addressed throughout, the app packages 21 exercise videos with progress tracking meant to keep patients engaged between clinic visits. The team compared it with current therapy apps on friendliness and content and gathered feedback from varied users. Judged competitive on usability and function, it still needs better tailoring of plans and stronger long-term motivation features. The authors conclude the app can carry current treatment pathways into patients' homes.
pmc-13333376:
Ke Wang and colleagues packaged a protective drug into clay-like nanoparticles in 2026 to stop acute kidney injury from hardening into chronic kidney disease. Butylphthalide guards organs in principle, but the body clears it fast and absorbs it poorly, so little reaches injured kidneys.

Their layered double hydroxide carrier released the drug faster in mild acidity, matching the sour conditions inside damaged, scarring kidney tubules. In rats with one kidney injured by a blocked-then-restored blood supply, the loaded particles eased kidney dysfunction, curbed scar tissue, and restored mitochondrial health. Human kidney cells provoked with a scarring signal answered the same way. Blocking mitophagy, the cell's mitochondrial cleanup program, erased every benefit, proving that route central. Gene signals pointed to the PINK1-Parkin pathway as the switch the treatment turns on. The authors present the system as a translatable strategy against the injury-to-chronic slide.
pmc-13333476:
Yue Li and co-authors document a bladder cancer mistaken for a bowel one in a 2026 case report with a review of cases. Primary mucinous adenocarcinoma of the bladder is rare and aggressive. Because it looks glandular, proving it did not spread from the gut is the diagnostic battle.

Their patient, a 70-year-old woman, had difficulty urinating but no blood in the urine. A marker panel pointed away from a colorectal origin: CK7 negative, CK20 and CDX-2 positive, beta-catenin staining confined to the membrane, and SATB2 and GATA3 negative. Endoscopy found no gut tumor. She had a transurethral resection, then robot-assisted removal of the bladder, staged pT4aN0M0, and declined treatment. Six months on she remained free of recurrence or spread. The authors use the case to show how a marker panel secures the diagnosis, and how treatment choices get made without guidelines.
pmc-13333676:
Jianpeng Liu and co-authors translated an AI literacy questionnaire for China's pre-service teachers and validated the adapted scale in a 2026 study. The work tests whether the scale measures what it should and whether teacher profiles differ in useful ways.

The sample held 341 pre-service teachers from Guangdong Province, most of them women in their third year. Factor analyses supported a 24-item scale with five parts: AI ethics, behavioral commitment, self-efficacy, cognitive application, and intrinsic motivation. Reliability and validity checks were supportive, and three parts of the scale correlated with how much teachers integrated AI into teaching. A profile analysis sorted respondents into four groups, from overall high to overall low, giving teacher educators a basis for tailored support.
pmc-13333776:
Tim Ho and Mark Ryan propose a new model of chronic pain in a 2026 narrative review, treating it as a state-constrained disorder of brain networks. Imaging reliably shows altered salience, default mode, and central executive networks in persistent pain, yet older models explain its stubbornness poorly.

Their triple-network account adds body-level regulation to the picture. Sleep organization, autonomic balance, and interoceptive signals continually shape how the three networks interact. When regulation falters, salience processing tilts toward bodily threat and the networks settle into a stable pattern that keeps self-focused pain processing going. Viewed through dynamical systems, chronic pain becomes a locked-in attractor state. The framing suggests treatments, including brain stimulation, should aim to loosen that state rather than silence one region.
pmc-13335076:
Alexandra Lecours and co-authors studied telework used as a health accommodation in a 2026 qualitative study, centered on the relationship between employee and manager. Workers with chronic illness or caregiving duties often need changes to stay employed, and remote work became a common one after the pandemic.

Two focus groups brought 12 people together, eight workers with chronic illness and four caregivers, in an interpretive descriptive design. Four themes named friction points with managers: negotiating the accommodation itself, day-to-day running of telework, honoring boundaries, and keeping social ties alive. The findings argue that telework succeeds as an accommodation mainly when the manager relationship is strong, since flexibility and trust are worked out there.
pmc-13335676:
Qiannan Jia and co-authors characterized cutaneous mastocytosis in Chinese patients in a 2026 ten-year pathology study. The disease, driven by mast cell buildup in skin, varies widely in form, and its detailed features in Chinese patients were poorly mapped.

The cohort held 88 patients diagnosed by skin biopsy in a dermatology department between 2015 and 2024. Mast cell burden tracked with subtype: lowest in telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans, higher in urticaria pigmentosa, and highest in diffuse disease and mastocytoma. Heavy burden also went with raised lesions and earlier onset. Staining patterns for CD2, CD25, and CD30 differed by subtype and clustered with high-burden disease, offering diagnostic clues. The authors highlight easily neglected features that pathologists should watch for.
pmc-13336676:
Chen Wang and a large team investigate a receptor called GPR124 after traumatic brain injury in a 2026 study. Brain injury is a top cause of death among young adults, and damage to the blood-brain barrier worsens outcomes. The team mapped where GPR124 appears using single-cell data and a controlled impact model in mice.

Mice lacking GPR124 in vessel-lining cells recovered worse, and stretched cells without it worked poorly in lab tests. Tight seals between vessel cells broke down when the receptor was reduced. The receptor partners with a binding protein to switch on the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway. Supporting this receptor could help protect the barrier and improve recovery after head injury.
pmc-13336876:
Xiaolin Li and a large team pack six health sensors onto one tiny photonic chip in a 2026 study. Light-based sensors can track glucose, pressure, temperature, and heart signals, but separate devices are hard to combine. Their polymer chip, about 1 cm by 0.5 cm in footprint in the prototype, merges grating sensors with an on-chip unit that reads them all.

Tests showed stable ranges for blood glucose from 0 to 2.3 mg/mL, pressure from 0 to 12 kPa, and temperature from 35 to 41°C in bench checks. A sweat glucose sensor covered 0–0.2 mg/mL with strong linearity in tests. The heart-signal sensor matched commercial gear. All-in-one chips could anchor future wearable health monitors.
pmc-13336976:
Sihao Wu and a large team build artificial skin from display transistor technology in a 2026 study. Their active skin uses thin-film transistors, a mass-production process on large sheets, as its base. Each touch pixel mixes light and electric-field sensing to extract richer contact features than either mode alone.

A 10×10 sample fitted within 1 cm2 read Braille patterns in validation tests. It kept 81.7% accuracy on hard fingerprint tasks even with 45% of information lost in stress tests. A fully wrapped robot hand with varied pixel density recognized objects by texture and shape while moving 80% less data and cutting computing cost by 76.6% in the reported system. Transistor skin could cover whole robot bodies.
pmc-13338676:
David M Huebner leads a 2026 trial protocol for a web program helping parents support gay and bisexual teen sons. Most teen HIV infections in the United States follow male-to-male contact, yet few proven programs target this group. Talking with parents about sex can lower risk, but no parent program for these teens had been trialed.

The PATHS program teaches parents to discuss sexuality and HIV and to support their sons' health. A total of 350 parents recruited online will be assigned at random to PATHS or a control path. Teen health outcomes at 6 and 12 months are the test, with parent behavior changes checked as the pathway.
pmc-13339876:
Cheng-Ta Li and colleagues use brainwave patterns plus machine learning to sort depression features in a 2026 exploratory study. Depression varies in severity, treatment resistance, and suicide risk, usually judged by subjective scales. Frontal brain networks are implicated, so EEG offered an objective angle.

Resting and task-based EEG from 209 patients fed several classifiers after a frontal-engaging thinking task. Random forest models led, reaching about 83 percent accuracy for severity and 87 percent for treatment resistance in the reported results. Suicide risk classification used balanced training to handle rare cases. Brain signatures may one day support, not replace, clinical judgment.
pmc-13340676:
Dental implants placed decades after a childhood jaw disorder settled down are described by Mergime P. Loxha and colleagues in a 2026 case report with 23 years of follow-up. The patient had cherubism, a rare condition that expands both jaws in childhood and often eases after puberty.

Long monitoring confirmed the disease had stabilized before guided implant surgery was done without bone grafting. The implants integrated well, and the prosthetic result stayed stable, restoring chewing and facial appearance. The authors argue that waiting for skeletal maturity and disease quiet, then planning treatment case by case, can make implant rehabilitation work for chosen patients.
pmc-13340776:
Spotting drug-resistant tumor cells by imaging an enzyme inside them is the aim of a 2026 study by Xin-Yu Luo and colleagues. The enzyme, MGMT, repairs chemotherapy damage and helps explain why resistance drives roughly 90% of cancer deaths.

The team built a tetrahedral DNA framework carrying four identical probes. Each probe senses MGMT, switches on a DNAzyme, and releases a fluorescent signal once the enzyme removes a methyl lesion. The scaffold's tight spacing made signals in resistant cells over three times stronger than in sensitive ones. Such a platform could support earlier detection of resistance and closer study of how it develops.
pmc-13341476:
Sorting stroke from other causes of lasting vertigo is the aim of a 2026 prediction model by Yue Ba and colleagues. The retrospective study covered 689 patients whose vertigo lasted over 24 hours, of whom 165 (23.9%) had clinically diagnosed strokes.

Regularized regression picked predictors including older age, smoking, hypertension, high lipids, and diabetes, with hypertension carrying an odds ratio of 5.452. Internal validation used cross-validation and bootstrapping, and the model was benchmarked against the ABCD2, CNS, and Triage-Plus scores. A bedside tool like this could speed imaging decisions when vertigo might hide a stroke.
pmc-13342876:
I Andriot and a large team present a 2026 dataset on how aroma compounds escape from food-like systems over time. Flavor release shapes taste perception, and lab models let researchers vary heat or container size in ways real eating does not allow, so the team tracked release under controlled settings.

Across 84 experiments, two aroma compounds, isoamyl acetate and diacetyl, were measured in water or gelatin discs with a proton transfer reaction mass spectrometer. Conditions varied in temperature, starting amount, and settling time before measurement. Files pair raw time-series readings with full details on products, compounds, and instrument settings, giving modelers clean data for linking signal strength to real concentration.
pmc-13345376:
Steven L Zeng and co-authors compare wound dressings after breast reduction surgery in a 2026 review of 250 patients covering 439 breasts. Dressing choice varies with little shared evidence, so the team tallied skin reactions, wound splitting, reoperations, and scarring across six dressing types used at one institution.

Groups started uneven, largely because Prineo patients carried more risk, and removing that group cleared most baseline gaps. Sylke tape predicted lower skin reaction and wound splitting in adjusted models, with odds roughly halved or better. Prineo tracked with more reoperations and poor scarring, though patient selection clouds that signal. The authors call for prospective trials before dressings get ranked firmly.
pmc-13347076:
Chengcheng Yu and co-authors test whether adding a large language model helps peer teaching in orthopaedic training, in a cohort study from 2026. Two student groups at a Hangzhou teaching hospital were compared. One group held 96 students taught the usual way in 2024. The other held 94 students given access to DeepSeek-V3 as support in 2025.

Outcomes covered a 50-item knowledge test, a four-station skills exam, engagement and satisfaction ratings, and retention after three months, all scored with shared rubrics. Peer teaching is praised for closeness but faulted for uneven quality, so the study asks whether on-demand model help can steady knowledge support without replacing student teachers. Full comparative results follow the setup described here.
pmc-13347776:
Hussein N Yassine and a large team test high-dose fish oil in older adults at risk for dementia, in a randomised trial published in 2026. The 24-month study at the University of Southern California enrolled adults aged 55 to 80 years without dementia who ate little DHA, giving 2 g per day of DHA or placebo. A willing subgroup also gave spinal fluid checks.

Of 739 people screened, 365 were randomised, and DHA raised the spinal fluid DHA ratio by a clear margin at six months against placebo in the reported result. Brain size and thinking scores showed no treatment gap over two years, dropout reached 38 percent. Side effects looked alike across arms, so brain entry is proven while benefit stays open.
pmc-13348076:
Ting Lin and colleagues follow pulse pressure and the march of heart-metabolic disease in UK Biobank, in a cohort study from 2026. A total of 403,851 adults free of such disease at entry were tracked for first illness, spread to two or more of diabetes, heart disease. Stroke, and death, with pulse width scored per standard step and by quarters.

Each step up in pulse pressure raised the hazard of first illness and of spread in the reported models. The top quarter carried 36 percent higher risks than the bottom quarter for both steps. The spread link ran strongest after stroke and in younger, female, and leaner groups, arguing for early pulse checks.
pmc-13350476:
Soetkin D'Haens and co-authors reviewed real-world use of a strong chemotherapy combination before surgery for pancreatic cancer in a 2026 single-centre study. Eighty-one patients with borderline removable or locally advanced tumours received FOLFIRINOX or a softened version between 2020 and 2023.

The median number of cycles delivered was six, and most patients had good fitness scores at entry. The team recorded doses, serious side effects, and why treatment stopped; surgery was the commonest reason, accounting for 45 patients. Pre-surgery chemotherapy is spreading, but its toxicity and delays are real, and honest completion numbers help design fair trials of the strategy.
pmc-13350676:
Yao Peng and colleagues built a risk model in 2026 for predicting newborn breathing distress from mid-pregnancy placenta scans. They studied 362 women scanned at a Xiangyang hospital between 2021 and 2024. Fifty-eight of their babies developed the syndrome.

Three-dimensional Doppler measures of placental vessel density and flow were gathered. Standard artery readings and mothers' clinical details were added. Together they fed a scoring chart for personal risk. Current antenatal checks guess this risk only crudely, with little basis in body function. A better forecast lets delivery teams prepare breathing support in advance. It also helps choose where a baby should be born.
pmc-13351276:
Bonnie Alberry and colleagues studied how poor metabolic conditions before birth rewire insulin responses in the brain's reward centre in a 2026 rodent study. Growth-restricted fetuses are known to carry lifelong changes in body and brain insulin sensitivity, but effects on reward circuits were unclear.

In their model, food reward triggered a blunted dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, a deficit that insulin specifically reversed, and the animals also ate palatable food faster at first. Gene activity in the reward centre was profiled at birth, weaning, and adulthood, with and without insulin. Early metabolic stress appears to programme how the brain values food, with lasting taste for quick reward.
pmc-13351476:
Rogerson and colleagues speak with shift workers who make food in United Kingdom plants. The study asks what helps or blocks healthy eating at work. Eleven workers took part in online talks. Most were men with long shift records. Eight themes came out. Workers knew what healthy food was. What they ate still bent toward what was fast and close at hand. Breaks were short and not safe to use in full.

Plant rules on hygiene and safety shut off some food choices. Night shifts made fresh food hard to find. The team says plants must first fix access and breaks. Only then can coaching on food choices help staff.
pmc-13351876:
Hua Sun and co-authors compare two ways of clearing older patients for lung surgery in a 2026 cohort study. Many patients are turned down because breathing tests look poor. From 2022 to 2024, patients first had standard breathing tests, and those with weak results went on to exercise testing before a decision.

In total, 130 older patients had surgery, with 71 in the breathing-test group and 59 in the exercise-test group. Complication rates were close, at 23.94 percent versus 25.42 percent, with no clear difference. Hospital stay and chest tube time did differ between groups. Results suggest exercise testing can safely widen access to surgery for patients with weak breathing tests.
pmc-13352176:
Ding-Tian Yu, Si-Si Xie, and Cheng-Guo Duan study how chromatin changes steer immune gene switching in Arabidopsis in 2026. Plant defence depends on fast rewriting of gene activity, but the chromatin controls behind it stay unclear. The team combined RNA, chromatin, and access profiling after treatment with salicylic acid or the peptide flg22.

Each signal reshaped chromatin and gene activity in its own broad pattern. Salicylic acid raised two activating histone marks together at defence sites, while flg22 worked mainly through one mark. Open chromatin tracked closely with active defence genes. Network checks highlighted NPR1, ICS1, and PR1 as hubs. Results show two signals can reach defence through partly separate chromatin routes.
pmc-13352376:
Hongqiang Li and co-authors profile the chemistry of eggs from five poultry species in 2026. Eggs are a rich nutrient source, and knowing species differences can guide production and new products. Chicken, duck, goose, quail, and pigeon eggs were split into yolk and white and screened with untargeted metabolomics.

Analysis found 519 differing compounds in yolks and 312 in whites across species, spanning lipids, ring compounds, and benzenoids. Yolk networks showed tighter grouping than white networks. Transport and amino acid pathways stood out as enriched routes. Machine learning picked 9 candidate markers that may separate species, though the authors say outside validation with targeted tests is still required.
pmc-13352476:
Jingnan Xue and colleagues report a 2026 surgical case of thyroid tissue found beside the bile duct. Misplaced thyroid tissue is uncommon, and spots near the gallbladder are extremely rare, yet such lumps can mimic bile or gallbladder tumours. A 50-year-old woman had 2 years of on-and-off pain in the upper right belly.

Scans showed a dense lump of 22 by 14 mm at the liver hilum next to the gallbladder neck. She declined further imaging for cost reasons and asked for surgery. Keyhole removal took the gallbladder and lump together, and tissue study showed benign mature thyroid follicles. Her own thyroid gland was normal, and she stayed symptom-free after surgery.
pmc-13353876:
Ayako Ijuin and colleagues test a multi-constriction nanopore called Epx4 for single-molecule protein reading in 2026. Nanopores sense molecules label-free as they pass through, and extra narrow points can sharpen signals. Epx4 is a pore-forming toxin with two separate barrels and up to four constrictions along its path.

In single-molecule runs, Epx4 caught positively charged polypeptides more often than the standard alpha-hemolysin pore. Machine learning on its signals reached an area under the curve of 0.82 and an F1 score of 0.72, both above the standard pore. Geometry checks confirmed the multi-grip layout. The authors propose Epx4 as a strong base for accurate protein sensors.
pmc-13354576:
Nidal H Abu-Hamdeh and co-authors used computer models in 2026 to test ways to speed up cold storage freezing. Their design used a ring-shaped tank, metal foam, a fluid with tiny mixed particles, and heat rays to move cold through the space. A math model tracked the line between liquid and solid as freezing went on.

Metal foam gave the biggest gain, cutting freezing time by about 79 percent in the model. Heat rays cut the time by about 23 percent, and the special fluid added a smaller gain. The work points to foam as a strong tool for fridges, air cooling, and other cold storage uses.
pmc-13355276:
Avinav Bharati and co-authors tested three AI chatbots in 2026 on questions about medical physics in cancer care. Experts wrote 11 questions and put each to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, asking each one twice. Three experts then scored the answers for correctness, completeness, ease of reading, trust, and fit for local practice.

DeepSeek scored highest on correctness and gave the most complete answers, at ten of eleven questions. Still, no chatbot matched human skill on any measure, and scores for real-world use did not differ much. The authors argue that chatbots should support medical staff, not replace them, in a paired way of working.
pmc-13357076:
Ming Yan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how targeted drugs perform when bowel cancer spreads to the liver, a leading cause of death in these patients. Such targeted therapy is now common, but its exact gains in survival, shrinkage, and surgery chances were unclear. They pooled randomized trials and cohort studies found in four databases through July 2025.

Thirty-four studies with 12,084 patients showed targeted therapy lengthened overall and progression-free survival and raised response rates. It also increased the chance of surgery to remove liver tumors, most clearly in first-line and marker-selected patients. Severe side effects were more common but manageable. The authors support targeted drugs within team-based, precision care.
pmc-13358476:
Ya Wang and co-authors present a 2026 review of breathing support for acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure. Machines that breathe for patients can also harm the lungs if each breath is too big. Doctors already use small breaths; the team asked if even smaller breaths help more.

They combined six studies with 1,102 patients that compared ultra-low with low breath sizes. Most patients on the smallest breaths also used life-support machines that take over gas exchange for the lungs. The review weighs the gain in lower lung stress against the risks of extra machines, to guide care in intensive care units.
pmc-13358576:
Xuanyu Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 study on a warning sign in early lung cancer. Some tumors shed cells into nearby air spaces, a pattern called spread through air spaces. It raises the risk of the cancer coming back, yet doctors can only confirm it after surgery. The team built computer models to predict it before the operation.

They used records and CT scans from 445 patients with the earliest stage of non-small cell lung cancer. Machine learning models weighed scan traits and patient facts to sort likely cases. A good forecast matters because it can steer the choice between a small, lung-saving cut and a larger, safer one.
pmc-13362776:
Maryam Choulli and a large team report a 2026 study of throat cancer patients at three Barcelona hospitals, asking whether nutrition at diagnosis forecasts early response to curative treatment. The virus HPV splits this cancer into types with different outlooks. The team measured body size, muscle from scans, fitness tests, blood markers, and a standard nutrition score in 101 patients before therapy began.

Among virus-positive patients, the nutrition score split outcomes clearly: about three quarters with good scores cleared the cancer early, versus a third with poor scores. Among virus-negative patients, fitness level and age split outcomes instead. Muscle scans and blood markers added nothing once nutrition and fitness counted. Diet care at diagnosis may thus help, the authors suggest.
pmc-13363576:
Xiangjun Kong, Xia Wang, and Wulan Zeng present a 2026 review of nanostructured catalysts for clean energy conversion, covering both electric and light-driven reactions. These tiny engineered materials sit at the heart of water splitting, fuel cells, and carbon dioxide reuse. The review follows five catalyst families, from single metals to single-atom designs, and the recipes that shape them with care.

Five levers for better performance get close treatment: shape, doping, layered junctions, defects, and supports. For each key reaction, the authors name the measures that best predict success. Their verdict is pointed: raw activity is rarely the bottleneck now; holding performance under harsh, factory-grade loads is. Earth-abundant stand-ins for precious metals get special attention.
pmc-13365476:
Udomsak Saengow and co-workers set in 2026 how folks with long ills in south Thailand smoke, by zone: leaf grow zones and plain zones. They ask 879 patients face to face from care lists in both zone types. Hand rolled leaf rolls rule use, more so in grow zones.

Near one in five had smoked at some point, and all but a few past smokers were men. Smokers show high lung ill rates and more care stays per year. Grow zone life and more house cash lift smoke odds, while women smoke far less. Rules must face cheap leaf reach in farm towns.
pmc-13371876:
Amaya Daniels and co-authors tell of a huge gallstone that moved in an odd way in a 2026 case report. An 82-year-old woman had a drain tube path from her gallbladder to her skin. Such paths are used when surgery is too risky for a sick patient.

A stone about 65 mm long moved through the path and got stuck just under the skin. Scans can miss how much hard stone sits in such a lump, the team warns. They cut the path open and took the stone out, and her symptoms eased fast. The case is said to be the first of its kind with a stone this large.
pmc-13372376:
Eanna Johnston and co-authors built a fine eye scan to track burns in a 2026 study. Alkali burns are a harsh type of eye harm and can blind. Plain scans see shape well but miss tiny shifts in the clear front window of the eye.

The new scan reads light in a way that picks up shifts far below the plain scan's limit. The team used it on a burn model and on care with cell-based drops. Scan shifts tracked harm and heal steps as they changed. A tool that watches heal steps without touch could help eye teams time care and test new drops in trials.
pmc-13373676:
Shuroog Nabhan and co-authors summed up switch data for a gut drug and its copies in a 2026 review. The drug calms bowel swelling, and cheaper copies are now in wide use. Doubts stay on what switch steps do to health in daily care.

The search found seven studies with 5,721 adults in all. Three were planned ahead, three looked back, and one took a one-time snapshot. Watch time ran from six months to just over two years. The sum-up weighs if health held firm after a switch, and in which ways. Such proof helps clinics and patients trust a switch made to cut costs.
pmc-13374176:
Li Zhang and co-authors mapped a view-sort method in long ill work in a 2026 review. The method asks people to sort views into piles, which shows how groups truly see a point. It suits the mix of tales that long ills bring, where one fixed plan fits few.

The team used firm review steps and searched four data banks to late 2025. Each past use was logged for its ask, its craft twists, and its gains. Use has spread across many long ills, from pain to heart and mind care. The map shows where the method shines and where reports are thin, to guide new work.
pmc-13374276:
Caiping Liu and co-authors linked long calm-drug use to thought skill in a 2026 study in China. The drugs in view calm nerves and aid sleep, and are often used long in mind care. The group came from a large watch study of a grave mind ill.

Fifty-seven long users were matched to 57 non-users by age, sex, ill span, and main drugs. A set test scored thought, and scales scored signs, weight of ill, and daily life skill. Long users scored worse on thought tests in the match. The team says long use should be weighed with care, and thought should be checked in this group.
pmc-13379376:
Noel George, Usha Arcot, and Bruntha Devi Palanisamy published a 2026 mathematics paper on six common plastics, treated as chains of repeating units. They use a formula called the M-polynomial, which captures the structure of a molecular graph in algebraic form. From that single formula, many numerical measures of structure can be derived.

The plastics covered are polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon-6,6, and PET. For each chain the authors work out the formula as a function of chain length, then compute eleven standard measures, including the Zagreb and Randic indices. Graphs comparing the plastics show how the measures grow and differ, which can help predict material properties from structure alone.
pmc-13379976:
Yecheng Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study of blood sugar stress measures in critically ill patients with heart failure. Illness can push blood sugar up sharply, and that rise is linked with worse outcomes. One measure corrects the rise for a patient's usual sugar level, but people differ in how their blood sugar marks long-term control.

Records for 2,488 patients came from three intensive care databases. The team grouped patients by a glycation index, which captures that personal difference, and tracked how the stress measure changed over time against death rates. The link between the stress measure and death differed across the groups, so the same reading may not mean the same risk for every patient.
pmc-13382776:
Eric N. Enyong and co-authors examine caveolin-1 outside its usual membrane pockets in retinal support cells in 2026 work. Prescott explains Aztec government, religion, warfare, and daily life in detail drawn from Spanish and native sources. He writes history in the manner of a novel, with vivid scenes and strong characters. Readers get both a rich portrait of a lost civilization and the background they need for the clash that follows in later volumes.
tob-9052-15476:
Grief rules volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, as the war of Kurukshetra ends. The field lies covered with the dead of both houses. Widows and mothers search the corpses, and the victors find their crown brings no joy.

Funeral rites, laments, and hard reckonings take the place of battles. The epic turns, by design, from action to mourning and reflection on what violence costs. Yudhishthira rules a kingdom of ashes and doubts his own part in winning it. Ganguli carries the slow, somber books with patience. Readers feel the full weight the Sanskrit poem places on victory.
tob-9776: A. J. Maas wrote this Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Hexaemeron, the six days of creation described in the first chapter of Genesis. It sums up how early Church writers and later theologians read those six days, whether as plain days, ages, or figures of speech. Maas writes as a scholar for general readers who need a clear map of a long debate. Short and factual, the piece works as a starting point on how Christians have understood the creation story.
tumulus-hermetis-apertus-in-quo-ad-solem: Tumulus Hermetis apertus, 1676. The opened Hermes mound. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
twain-tom-sawyer-1876:
Mark Twain published The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876, complete in the first edition text. The beloved Mississippi boyhood novel drew on Twain's own youth in Hannibal, Missouri, on the river. Its sunny mischief made Twain famous on both sides of the Atlantic at once.

Tom, raised by Aunt Polly, dodges school and chores for swimming, pirates, and treasure hunts. He whitewashes a fence by making the chore look like rare sport to his friends. At night he sees Injun Joe murder Dr. Robinson in the town graveyard in secret. Lost in a cave with Becky Thatcher, Tom finds both terror and buried gold there. The book's glow of boyhood hides sharp satire of village piety and pride.
un-ga-res-376:
Korea's division hardened into war, and Resolution 376, adopted by the General Assembly on 7 October 1950, restates the UN aim. Past votes of 1947, 1948, and 1949 had set the goal: a free, united Korea. The UN Commission on Korea had now reported. The goals, the text admits, had not been met. Worse, an armed attack from North Korea had tried to wipe out the Republic of Korea by force.

The Assembly recalls its 1948 ruling on the south. A lawful state, the Government of the Republic of Korea, held real rule over the part of Korea the UN team could reach. That state rested on votes the team had watched. The text holds to the goal of one Korea, free of outside force.
un-ga-res-a-69-76:
The world's sole forum for arms talks gets a review in Resolution A/69/76, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Conference on Disarmament, based in Geneva, holds the prime role in hard talks on arms cuts. The Assembly had the conference's own report before it. Word from the Secretary-General, and speeches by foreign chiefs, had each voiced both support for the body and worry at its stall.

Real talks on firm points are needed, the text holds, and the state of the world should give them fresh push. Yet worry runs deep: for all the hard work of its member states, the conference had long failed to agree a plan of work. That deadlock, unbroken for years, hangs over the whole text.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 376 (V), adopted on 7 October 1950, addressed Korea in the first months of the Korean War. The Assembly noted that an armed attack from North Korea sought to wipe out the Government of the Republic of Korea by force. United Nations forces were fighting under Security Council calls. They were to repel the attack and restore peace.

The text urged steps for calm across Korea. It urged elections under United Nations watch. It urged one united, free, and democratic government. United Nations forces were to stay only as long as needed. It created the United Nations Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea, a seven-state body. It ordered plans for relief and rebuilding once the fighting ended.

Resolution 69/76 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, takes up the report of the Conference on Disarmament. It records that the Conference again failed in 2014 to begin substantive work or agree on a programme of work. That extended a deadlock of well over a decade. It notes the re-established informal working group. It notes consultations among its successive presidents meant to find a way forward.
un-sc-res-1376:
Congo's peace process gained its third MONUC phase on 9 November 2001. The Lusaka parties' political committee met the Council in joint session that day. The ceasefire generally held, though fighting went on in the east. Some foreign forces had left, including the whole Namibian contingent. The Secretary-General's report of 16 October set out the next deployment plan.

The Council welcomed the ceasefire's broad respect and called on the parties to stop backing armed groups in the east. It demanded again that Kisangani be demilitarized rapidly and without conditions, noting the RCD-Goma pledge on the city. The Council backed the inter-Congolese dialogue as a key part of the peace process. It approved phase III of MONUC's deployment, on the concept in the Secretary-General's report, with weight on the east and within the set ceiling. Grave concern was voiced at rights abuses and the country's humanitarian state.
un-sc-res-1476: Adopted in 2003, Resolution 1476 adds one more entry to the Security Council's long numbered run. The copy here is transcribed from the official record on English Wikisource. Like its neighbors in the sequence, it states the Council's grounds first and then records the decision in numbered operative paragraphs for governments to carry out and report on.
un-sc-res-1576:
Haiti's mission gained six months and a push on aid money in 2004. On 29 November 2004 the Security Council extended MINUSTAH until 1 June 2005. The transitional government was preparing free elections for 2005. The Council praised the Secretary-General's special representative and his support for dialogue. Political reconciliation and rebuilding were called essential and urgent. The mission's mandate stayed as set that April.

Transitional leaders had to widen the political process. Haitians who rejected violence should be brought into the transition. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's latest recommendations. It urged donors and banks to release pledged funds fast. That money had been promised at a Washington conference in July.
un-sc-res-1676: Resolution 1676 is a formal Security Council text held here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its shape is the standard one, and the standard is the story: the same architecture carries ceasefire orders, mission mandates, and court referrals alike. The entry lets readers see that architecture at work in one complete act.
un-sc-res-176:
Security Council Resolution 176, adopted on October 4, 1962, recommended Algeria for membership in the United Nations. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a war of eight years that shook both lands and killed vast numbers of people. A seat at the UN marked the new state's arrival on the world stage in formal terms.

The General Assembly admitted Algeria four days after the council acted. Few admissions carried such weight: France had long claimed Algeria was part of France itself, not a colony. The short resolution thus sealed a verdict that the war had already rendered, and Algeria soon became a leading voice for other peoples still under colonial rule.
un-sc-res-1776:
Afghanistan stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 1776 on Afghanistan on 19 September 2007. The vote passed with fourteen in favor and one abstention. Attacks by the Taliban and other armed groups had grown sharper. Roadside bombs, suicide blasts, and seizures of hostages struck civilians and soldiers alike.

The text extends the mandate of the International Security Assistance Force for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007. States in the force may take all needed steps to carry out that mandate. Members are urged to send more troops, gear, and funds. The Council also presses for faster training of Afghan soldiers and police, so Afghans can guard their own country in time.
un-sc-res-1876: Resolution 1876, from 2009, records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official form. The collection's copy follows the record held by English Wikisource. Inside the act, the preamble does the explaining and the operative clauses do the obliging. Both parts survive here, giving the decision its full context and its full force.
un-sc-res-2076:
M23's seizure of Goma drives Resolution 2076 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 20 November 2012. The rebel group had taken the city after fresh attacks in North Kivu. Reports said outside support kept flowing to the rebels. Crowds of displaced people were growing again across the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that M23 leave Goma at once. The group must halt all advances, disband, and lay down its arms for good. All outside support to M23 must stop now. The sanctions committee should review two named M23 commanders for listing at once. More targeted sanctions are under active consideration. The Secretary-General must report within days on the claims of foreign backing.
un-sc-res-276: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 276 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1970. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-476:
Jerusalem's status was defended by the Security Council on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, chairing the Organization of the Islamic Conference, had written on 28 May 1980. Israel kept changing the city's physical character, population makeup, institutions, and status. Steps in the Knesset toward a law on Jerusalem caused the Council grave concern.

The Council restated the overriding need to end the occupation of Arab lands held since 1967, Jerusalem included. It strongly deplored Israel's refusal to obey the Council and the General Assembly. All Israeli laws and acts meant to alter Jerusalem's character and status were declared without legal validity. They broke the Fourth Geneva Convention and blocked a full, just, and lasting peace. Such changes were named null and void. Israel was called urgently to drop them, and the Council vowed to examine practical steps if it did not.
un-sc-res-676: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 676 is catalogued here as dating from 1990. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-76: A wire from Batavia is passed on in Security Council Resolution 76, passed on 5 October 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had cabled the Council's president on 5 August. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the armed watchers in Indonesia, the men who kept eye on the truce between Dutch and Indonesian forces. The Council rules, in full, that the wire be sent to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-976:
Angola's new peace operation, UNAVEM III, was created on 8 February 1995. The Lusaka Protocol of 20 November 1994 promised peace after years of war. The ceasefire was generally holding, and the two armies' chiefs had met at Chipipa and Waco Kungo. Yet the protocol's timetable was slipping. Angola's offer of large in-kind support for the operation was welcomed.

The Council authorized UNAVEM III to help the parties restore peace and win national reconciliation. Military and police observers would deploy fast to watch the ceasefire. Infantry units would follow only on the Secretary-General's word that the conditions on the ground were met. A full mine clearance program for the country was named vital. The new force needed a strong public information voice, the Council agreed. The Secretary-General had to report each month on deployment and on the Lusaka Protocol's progress.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1376, adopted unanimously on 9 November 2001, reviews the Congo war's slow thaw. The Lusaka ceasefire was generally being respected, the Council found, though fighting continued in the east, where it told the parties to stop backing armed groups. Some foreign forces had withdrawn, including Namibia's whole contingent, which the Council counted as a real step.

Other states that had not yet begun pulling out were asked to start. The Council took note of the Secretary-General's October report and recommendations, and welcomed a joint meeting held that same day with the Lusaka agreement's political committee. Congo's sovereignty, including over its natural resources, was reaffirmed even as foreign armies still occupied much of its territory.

Emergency relief arrangements for Iraq are kept in force a little longer on 24 April 2003. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that paragraph 4 of its resolution 1472 of March 2003 would remain in force until 3 June 2003. Those provisions gave the oil-for-food machinery flexibility to deliver humanitarian relief after the outbreak of war, and the Council noted the measures could be renewed again.

Haiti's climb back from chaos took a new step in late 2004. A stand-in regime ran the land. Polls were set for 2005, with power to pass to elected hands. The UN force, MINUSTAH, kept the peace. The chief's report of 18 November 2004 drove the talks. Resolution 1576 passed on 29 November 2004.

The force's term ran to 1 June 2005. More terms were meant to come. Armed bands that played at police work drew blame. A swift arms hand-in drive was called urgent. Rights abuses were damned, as was jail with no charge for one's politics. Donors were told to pay pledges made in Washington that July at speed. Word on the work was due each three months.

Somalia's arms embargo monitoring team is set up once more on 10 May 2006. The country's transitional federal institutions were still struggling to build real national governance. The embargo, dating from 1992, continued to be broken, and the previous monitoring group's term had run out.

The Secretary-General is asked, in consultation with the sanctions committee, to set the Monitoring Group up again to track violations and gather evidence. Support for the transitional institutions and for the African Union and regional efforts behind them is repeated. Somali leaders are urged to keep up political dialogue, and all states are reminded of their duty to respect the arms embargo in full.

Algeria's admission to the United Nations is recommended in Resolution 176, adopted on 4 October 1962 by ten votes to none, with China abstaining. The Council had weighed the bid of Algeria, filed under the state's full formal name. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a brutal eight-year war that reshaped both countries.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit Algeria to membership. The recommendation capped a remarkable reversal: a state whose liberation movement the UN had debated for years now joined as a member. Algeria quickly became a leading voice for colonized peoples in the Assembly, and this short admission text is where that career formally begins.

Afghanistan's international force is renewed by Resolution 1776, adopted on 19 September 2007 by 14 votes to none with one abstention. The International Security Assistance Force, ISAF, had completed its expansion across the whole country under NATO leadership. Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other extremist attacks, including suicide bombings and abductions, were rising, and civilian casualties were a growing concern. Counter-narcotics and security-sector reform were tied to the fight.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends ISAF's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007 and authorizes its member states to take all necessary measures to fulfil the mandate. It calls on states to contribute personnel, equipment, and funds, and stresses training and mentoring the Afghan National Police and army so Afghan forces can take over in time. ISAF must work closely with the Afghan government and the UN mission, UNAMA, and report quarterly through the Secretary-General.

Guinea-Bissau's peacebuilding office is extended on 26 June 2009, and its upgrade is ordered. Political assassinations had rocked the country that year, showing again how fragile its institutions are. A presidential election was set for 28 June 2009, two days after adoption, and a free and fair vote is treated as the key step back to constitutional order.

The office's mandate is extended, and the Secretary-General is asked to establish a United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Guinea-Bissau in its place, with a strategic workplan. All sides are called on to respect the election result and keep the process peaceful. The armed forces, including their leaders, are urged to stay under civilian control, and security sector reform is restated as a national duty.

The fall of Goma draws condemnation and a withdrawal demand in Resolution 2076, adopted in November 2012. The 23 March Movement, M23, resumed attacks in North Kivu and entered Goma on 20 November 2012. It displaced people and committed abuses including summary executions, sexual violence, and child recruitment. Reports alleged external support to the rebels.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns the M23's attacks and demands its immediate withdrawal from Goma. It demands an end to advances, disbanding and disarmament of its members, and restoration of Congolese state authority in North Kivu. It demands all outside support cease. It asks the Secretary-General to report within days on the support allegations and on redeploying MONUSCO forces. It intends to consider sanctions against the M23 leadership and external backers under the Resolution 1857 (2008) criteria. The Great Lakes conference's joint verification mechanism is tasked with investigating the support reports.

South Africa's presence in Namibia is declared illegal by Resolution 276, adopted on 30 January 1970. The United Nations had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966. South Africa stayed anyway. It enforced its own laws there and put Namibians on trial in its courts.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's refusal to obey the United Nations decisions on Namibia. It declared that South Africa's continued presence was illegal. Every act South Africa had taken for Namibia since the mandate ended was illegal and invalid. The occupation was said to have grave effects on the rights of the Namibian people. All states were told to avoid dealings with South Africa that clashed with that ruling. A special sub-committee was set up to study how the decisions could be carried out.

The Comoros, an island chain between Madagascar and Mozambique, declared independence from France in July 1975. Its UN application moved quickly. Resolution 376 was adopted on 17 October 1975 by fourteen votes to none. The Council met for its 1848th session that day.

Members recommended the Comoros for membership. The General Assembly admitted the islands the next month. One island, Mayotte, voted to stay French, splitting the new state. That quarrel shadowed the Comoros for decades. Even so, admission confirmed the archipelago's statehood in law. This resolution preserves the moment. A tiny island nation took a seat equal in voting weight to the largest powers in the Assembly.

Jerusalem's fate is the theme of Resolution 476, passed on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, then chair of a bloc of Muslim states, had raised the matter in a May letter. The Council said land seized by force can never be owned by right. It stressed the city's rare place in three faiths. The holy sites, it said, need care and respect above all.

The Council deplored Israel's drive to change the city's shape, its people, its rules, and its status. It voiced grave fear at bills in Israel's Knesset that aimed to lock those changes in law. It told Israel to end its hold on Arab lands seized since 1967, Jerusalem among them. It deplored its refusal to obey past rulings.

Two more months for the Iran-Iraq observer group were granted on 28 November 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, watched a cease-fire that still held, although no full peace had followed it. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 23 November, had recommended the step. Resolution 676 records the renewal.

The Council extended UNIIMOG's mandate until 31 January 1991, as the Secretary-General had advised. He was asked to report during January 1991. His report would cover his further talks with Iran and Iraq about the observer group's future. Short renewals had become the pattern for the mission by then. Each one kept the observers on the ground for a few more weeks, while the Council waited to see whether the mission should continue at all.

A cable about the costs of military observers in Indonesia reached the Council in 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had written to the Council's president on 5 August that year. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the observers working in Indonesia. Resolution 76, adopted on 5 October 1949, does a single thing with that request. The Council transmitted the message to the Secretary-General. No sums were set, and the Council gave no answer on the request itself.

Angola's peace deal takes shape in Resolution 976, adopted on 8 February 1995. The government and UNITA had signed the Lusaka Protocol on 20 November 1994, and the ceasefire was broadly holding. Military chiefs from both sides had met to move the plan along. Still, carrying out the deal had fallen behind its timetable.

The Council sets up a new peacekeeping operation, UNAVEM III, to help restore peace and national unity. It allows up to 7,000 troops, plus 350 military observers and 260 police observers, with a first mandate until 8 August 1995. Infantry units deploy only once the Secretary-General confirms a real ceasefire, shared military data, and named quartering areas for UNITA forces. A mine clearance program and a UN radio station are backed. The mission is meant to end once the Lusaka goals are met, with completion expected by February 1997.
virginia-declaration-rights-1776: Virginia's 1776 Declaration of Rights, by George Mason, proclaimed natural liberties. It shaped the Bill of Rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It listed freedoms. Tyranny faced. Rights declared. America followed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
wallace-geographical-distribution-animal:
Alfred Russel Wallace, co-founder of the theory of evolution by natural selection, published the first volume of his Geographical Distribution of Animals in 1876. Wallace had spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay islands. He asked why each region holds the animals it does.

Volume One sets out the rules: how climate, seas, and land links shape where species can live. Wallace divides the world into six great regions, a scheme still in use. His maps and lists turned scattered facts into zoogeography, the study of animals across the map. Collectors and travelers supplied much of the raw data behind it.

Volume Two of Wallace's Geographical Distribution of Animals, also from 1876, puts his system to work region by region. Alfred Russel Wallace had catalogued thousands of species on his travels. Here he applies his rules to the lands of the Old World and beyond.

The volume works through Europe, Africa, Asia, and the islands of the Pacific in turn. For each region Wallace lists the families present and asks how they got there. Land bridges, past climates, and vanished seas all play a part. It completes the founding text of zoogeography. Readers meet the faunas of lands few had seen described before.
zola-his-excellency-1876:
Macmillan issued His Excellency in 1897 as the sole authorized English version, with Vizetelly's preface. Chapter heads run from The Corps Legislatif and Resignation to An Imperial Christening. Passion and Matrimony, In Retirement, and Recalled to Power follow in turn.

Eugene Rougon, the family's political genius, claws toward the top of the Second Empire. Minister and power broker, he masters the backroom deal and its price. Flatterers, mistresses, and favors traded like coin crowd around him. Zola dissects how power truly works with a razor edge. Few political novels match its grasp of influence, ambition, and the hunger that drives public men.
